To put this as bluntly as possible, so as to save people a bit of time, since there's a rant coming shortly:  I don't like this game.  It's not clever, it's not intuitive, it's just very, very marginally "artsy", so everyone will be drawn into what is otherwise a shallow and uninteresting experience.
I've had my eye on this game for a very long time, and I'd been intentionally avoiding the reviews to the best of my ability, because I felt as though this was the sort of game you wouldn't want to spoil by having any prior knowledge of any aspect of it.  The reviews looked positive, and that was the important part, in my eyes.  Naturally, once it finally went on sale I wasn't the least bit hesitant to snatch it up and install it as quickly as could be, because games like this (I thought.) always fascinate me and never fail to entertain.
I
the "off-kilter" genre, and I don't at all mind when a game wants to sit down and just walk me through a story.  Visceral Clean-up Detail, Dear Esther, Tiny & Big, Gone Home, these are games I've played more than once, or a dozen times over, just because I
it when a studio or an individual sits down and tries to defy a genre, because if no one ever did, we'd end up with a terribly stagnant market practically bereft of originality.
I've also never been one to shy away from a solidly-constructed puzzle game.  Portal needs no introduction, Braid--although overhyped--made you plan ahead so far that it occasionally became a little brain-bending. The Bridge, Antichamber, Myst, Kill the Bad Guy, FEZ, all of these came at the puzzle genre with something unique, and often very atmospheric.  They made you rack your brain to see a puzzle in a light it had never quite been presented in before, and you would walk away feeling accomplished when you'd finally figured out that one, little trick to cinching it all together.
Kairo does none of these things.  It attempts to paint a unique world full of mystery that begs to be explored, but in those rare instances where it rewards exploration, you get such a small, nonsensical snippet of the 'lore' that you're just left with more questions, or a flimsy little "piece" of the puzzle in the form of a slight JPG-artifacted "rune".  Often times Kairo will have entire rooms, entire cement-slathered, sprawling 'scapes to explore that serve
.
Kairo also does not approach the puzzle genre in any
way.  I know this is a matter of contention, because there are those that think the puzzles are just blatantly impossible, and then those that insist Kairo is brilliant because it
offer some semblances of clues in the form of pattern recognition, or subtle sound cues, but both of these trains of thought are ultimately flawed, because Kairo, to me, suffers from a cardinal sin when you examine its puzzles more closely:  Kairo's puzzles are
.
Once you've managed to work out exactly what it is that the game is expecting of you, you don't have one of those, "Oh God, really?!" moments that you'd have in Portal, you don't see all the little nuanced motions that you'll need to pull off to navigate through the level in The Bridge; in Kairo, once you've seen the puzzle for what it is, it is always something
.  Many of these puzzles--
too many of them--simply involve a trial-and-error style rote memorization of a keypad-like button press sequence.  One of them involves shuffling yourself into the right place until all the blocks line up with the other blocks.  I hope you enjoy this one, because you'll be doing it a
.
One of the "core" puzzles for the secret ending involves scouring this desolate, barren expanse of cement into every nook and cranny, until you find all 15 of the JPG artifacts, and the worst one of all?  Backtracking.  The last of the core puzzles involves a nearly-nonsensical amount of backtracking to accomplish.  Yes, you are given a very mild hint concerning what to do and where to go, but the fact of the matter is the game is shoving you ten to fifteen minutes out of your way, through uninteresting environments you've already seen, to do virtually nothing except headbutt a statue.
Clearly this is a game that's garnered an impressive following, and I've no doubt that there are plenty of people out there who enjoy this sort of game for what it is, but I came into this expecting a refreshingly-interesting story at best, a unique puzzle in the very least, and at the worst: An interesting world I could explore.  I found myself being offered none of these things.

Kairo is a beautifully eerie shapescape that combines original style with familiar puzzle questing.  It is a simple yet aw- filled atmospheric journey that takes place in this supernatural-like world you've stumbled upon.
Pros:
+ Increadible atmosphere.  Sometimes even daunting to look at with the great depth of field use by the dev.
+ Music is more like a drone in various keys and melodies.  It's unique and quite pleasing to listen to.
+ There is no linearity to it, well there is but you're free to tackle various areas at your leisure.
+ Puzzles are both easy and incredibly challenging.
+ Sandbox style freedom to explore the world.  It's not very large but the amount of rooms can make you forget where to go or where you've been.
Cons:
- There is very little if any backstory but some may say none is needed with just how odd and abstract the setting is.
- Some puzzles are a little too tough because they go completely unexplained or not elluded to.
Overall I would rate this game a solid 8/10.  If you're into puzzles and don't mind exploring abstract scenery with no AI interaction then this game is 100% worth it at it's price.  On sale even better.  I highly recommend it.

To people that say they can't run this game or they can't make it to run with Window 10,
don't be a total idiot and put a few minutes of thinking into it because it really isn't hard!
What you need to do is simple, so keep on reading if you don't already know what to do..
First install the game so it's been put into your Steam library.
Then within Windows 10 programs, go to Program Files (x86), Steam, SteamApps, Common,..
Disciples II (incl. the expansion if you have it) and check for the Discipl2.exe,..
Now change the compatibility mode to run it in Windows 7 and set it to run as administrator.
Make sure you have also set the advanced compatibility settings or it might not work!
Afterwards launch the configuration tools of the game and only select your optimal monitor
settings (1980x1080) while keeping the refresh rate at default (60Hrz) in my case.
Also set the game to Run in Direct3D mode. Additional options you should leave as is, because it might cause the game to run sluggish and the intro you can skip altogether whenever you experience issues while launching it.
For me it works like a charm now and i will gladly recommend this game to everyone i know,
just like i did many years ago..

Let's get this straight. This is an excellent game. I can understand why some don't like it but I personally do. I was a little skeptical before buying it, as I was a little worried about poor FPS that others were experiencing. But it turned out that I didn't have to worry at all, I get great FPS! Every aspect of the game is very authentic. It is most certainly one of the best games in the World of Subways series. It reminds me a bit of the first volume: The Path, as they was also set in New York, The outide graphics are excellent in detail. What more could you want from a subway simulator? The cab graphics and textures are also very good and I love the way that the controls in the cab have an 'old' look with the paint peeling off. A nice touch by the developers. Weather effects are also great. At least the game has a tutorial, unlike some of the other previous volumes. I love the way you can also see the Manhattan skyline in the distance, which I find a very nice touch to the game. Graphics on the track, inside the tunnels and stations are also extremely good, with dynamic passengers on the plaforms as well. Having the choice between local and express services is also a really cool feature, and really adds to the game. I don't understand why people don't like this game. What is there to complain about? I like the fact you can walk around the depot and talk to other colleagues and discuss shifts, etc. You can also be the conductor which I find a nice alternative to the normal driving mode. It's a shame there's not that many view mode choices. For example, I would have liked to have seen an interior (passenger view), as that would have been really cool. Another little bug is with the braking lever. The first three or four notches, seem to do hardly anything and the last three screech the train to a halt, which is a bit wierd, but it's not too much of an issue. One of my favourite aspects of this game is the incredible view distance. You can see for about a mile ahead of the train at once, and from station to station through the distant haze. And it doesn't make any impact on FPS! This is probably one of the best games I have ever played in terms of the view distance from where you are sitting. In most games, it significanly impacts FPS. World of Subways 1 and 2 had poor view distance, so bad that you could see the track loading ahead of you.
However, be aware that you will probably require a high end system to run this game, as the graphics are quite demanding on the CPU and graphics card. I had to alter a few settings to to get it to running absolutely perfect, and I'm sure that this will apply to most people as well.
I would say that this game is definitely overpriced in terms of the amount of content you get. For example, the line 7 is not that long, and only takes about 35 minutes to drive an all stopper service from end to end. So my advice is to wait for a sale, like I did.

I hate MOBAs and yet I love this game.
Yet calling this game a MOBA is unfair, since I think it has more in common with World of Warcraft's arenas, and surprisingly, fighting games. You control your character with WASD and aim every ability manually, no targeting here. Cooldowns are short and there's no resources to consider, like mana for example. Ultimates are handled differently too, they're more like "supers" in fighting games where you can only use them after buliding meter. Also like fighting games is the fact that instead of using your meter to ult, you can spend portions of it on "EX abilities" souped-up or altered forms of your standard ones.
The fat from MOBAs is completely cut out too: no item shops, no creeps, no objectives to defend, just pure combat in short, concise rounds. The game's brevity is important, since even the worst and most drawn out matches take around 12 minutes or less, so even losing becomes an easy pill to swallow.
This game has completely won me over and I look forward to playing more. If you're even vaguely interested, I heavily reccomend giving it a shot.

I really enjoyed this game. The gameplay, the objectives, and the contracts (sidemission things) were all very fun. I've always enjoyed exploring the Dishonored games and everything that they have to offer and I look foward to putting many hours into this installment of the series. The new mechanics were cool, the new environments too...
However, I do have a few complaints that I think everyone should know before they buy this game.
1. (this one is pretty obvious) The price - having played through the game fully once, I think that the price is a bit too steep for what you're getting. The average player would probably be able to finish the game within 5 hours and be left unsatisfied.
2. Lazy map design - As I've mentioned before, I really enjoy exploring the Dishonored games, and that includes the maps. Unfortunately, this game only has 4 maps for its 5 levels, and one of them is recycled from Dishonored 2. Although it's interesting to see how these places change overtime, it's also really disappointing when more than half of the game is ctrl+c, ctrl+v.
3. The Story - I'm not going to complain about Daud's intentions and reasoning for wanting to kill the Outsider, I think they're rational ENOUGH. The story was not bad, in my opinion, however, I would say that it was the worst out of all of the other games, including the DLC from the first game.
Overall, I had a good experience playing the game. The gameplay was exceptional, it was well-optimized this time around, and the new enemies and double bladed sword were f*cking awesome. I may have not liked the ending or the story in general very much, but I encourage you to form your own opinion. But what really matters is: Was it a fun game? Yes.

I usually don't buy games the day they drop, but I  took a chance here.
DOTO is a very entertaining and worthwhile Stand Alone DLC.  I would suggest playing D2 (awesome game) to get a little more background of the characters. The game picks up shortly after the events in Dishonored 2 but re-incorporates Doud from the first game. You play as Billy Lurk who was introduced as a disciple to Doud in the first game. She has similar powers of the original characeters but rechargeable mana  (no need for elixirs) and there is not penalty for killing or choosing not to.  You can try to make it steathily but that is a challenge. Her sword kills are pretty vicious but sometimes that's your only choice.
It is shorter but if you take your time and explore the world while doing a few side missions, it will stretch it out by a couple of hours.  The graphics remain solid and it runs without any glitches. I'm running on a Ryzen 5 1600 with 1060 6GB GTX. Very smooth and very little studder although I can see where 4GB cards will struggle: I turned settings up to Ultra and monitored the system and saw the most intensive levels used a wopping 5.7GB of video memory.  The game seems to have skipped the issues that plagues DisHo2 at launch.
So is it worth it? You could wait until a bundle or another Bethesda sale before you jump on it. I recommend the whole series.. If you have already played through Dishonored 2, then you might want this for a little fresh content. A bonus is the OG mode which allows you to play with powers from Dishonored 2.  So there is some replayability and plenty of areas to explore.

NEGATIVES:
This does not look like an AAA game that I paid $50 for. Firaxis apparently didn't learn a damn thing from their vanilla Civ V launch or listen to any complaints about the issues in G&K/BNW.
The AI feels barely functional just like Civ V vanilla's release.
Firaxis showed phenomenal ability to make their own idea as terrible a possible - if with CivV you had to deal with 5 or so TR now you have 3 per city, you have to manually reassign EACH an EVERY of them; why is there no 'automatically continue this trade route' option?!
Diplomacy somehow managed to become even worse than in CivV, which is achievement on its own.
The AI looks to be completely unchanged from Vanilla Civ V, despite the glaring deficiencies that AI had. Much of the text in the game is carried over verbatim from Civ V, such as diplomacy and alien alerts, with just words like "gold" substituted for their BE equivalent. Voice acting is extremely limited; take for example the AI condemning you. Now, I can understand that Civ V didn't have voice acting for that at release, since it wasn't in the game. But BE has no excuse. Or how about the tech quotes from the various leaders? SMAC had them voiced by the actual faction leaders, which helped flesh out their personality, but instead it's just the same base voice.  Virtues, like quests, seem mostly to be free bonuses you get to choose every few turns more to disguise the fact that you aren't doing anything else but click 'end turn' and movement orders than to actually progress the game.
Half of the wonders in the game are totally useless and they wouldn't even be good if you would double their yield.
And trade routes are so good that nothing else in the game really matters. if you would half their yield they would still be op. So i really have to asked: how can this be released in that state?
POSITIVES:
I really do like the new feel, and I can see the huge potential that this game could have, especially with the orbital layer.
Tech web is cool, great for having a more varied approach to the game.
OVERALL:
I'll play BE again, a bit here and there, mostly waiting to see what the mod community is able to do with it. But right now I have a tough time recommending it when BNW is still doing brisk business.

RaceRoom is mainly aimed at people who watch events like DTM, WTCC and GT Masters on TV. If you are not one of these people there's a risk you won't understand or appreciate the value of this content, since it's very much tied to real-life racing.
R3E is one of the best sim racing games around. The attention that Sector 3 applies to every single car and track impresses me all the time. Like all sims the game is best enjoyed with a wheel or perhaps a miniwheel racing controller, however I've tried the game with a regular gamepad and keyboard, and the game still plays really well.
Their business model gives you the basic stuff for free, you then pay for the extra content you want. The prices are reasonable considering how much depth each car offers. The game has three levels of technical difficulty: arcade, sim-arcade and simulation. So you don't have to be a racing game prodigee to enjoy this game.
The AI seems to adapt according to what racing event you are doing: it is quite aggressive in DTM and WTCC, which is consistent with the corresponding real-life events, while it is less aggressive in the custom championships.
RaceRoom aims for accessibility; anyone with an 'OK' PC should be able to play these games.
On the negative side: the game does not explain things like setting up pit stops, the adaptive AI system does not work particularily well, the game site can be clumsy to navigate through.
On the whole it's a great racing game that offers content that is different from Stock Car/Automobilista, Project Cars, Assetto Corsa and other sim games.

Beeftacular is the second game to enter Steam by developer Retrific. Their first game, Just Get Through, was released at the end of January this year. That game was received very positively (I personally enjoyed it) and therefore I entered this game with great hopes. Obviously with its name I was expecting it to have been partially inspired by Super Meat Boy. However, to my great surprise the game was most heavily inspired by 10 Seconds Ninja (it does state this in the game description).
The objective for each level is to complete it in ten seconds or less. However, the sense of reward in completing it faster makes it a worthy challenge. Each level of the game has a number of enemies and traps that have been implemented into the game to make each level a challenge.
The game comes jam packed with content. There are over 100 handcrafted levels that will test even the most skilful of platformer fanatics. In addition, there is a solid level editor that is simple and easy to use. I believe that even the most novice of aspiring level designers will be able to create something that is playable. That makes the sheer amount of content available to be played here a highlight of the game.
The thing that I most love about Beeftacular is the manner in which it has been developed with statistics and leaderboards in mind. Each level has an array of statistics including:
•	Your time, your best time, world record, best time between you and your friends
•	Global Rank
•	Ranged kills (you can shoot your enemies dead which can be faster so that you do not have to go to that piece of the map)
•	Ranged recovered
•	Ranged combos
•	Times level started and completed
•	Friends completed
•	Melee attack kills
•	Melee/Range kill share
•	Jumps, doublejumps and walljumps
•	Distance travelled (in pixels)
For a stathead like me this is a dream. Not only does it encourage me to get the most efficient and fastest time but it inspires me to see how I can improve in a number of different areas. This is exactly the type of statistics system that I’ve been wanting in a game like this. It is very intelligent game design that engages the player beyond the straight up level system.
Of course, arguably the single most important component of any platformer is whether or not it controls well. When a platformer plays poorly it will instantaneously deter the player from playing the game. This is because it means that the player will rarely be ever to complete the game the way in which it was intended to be. Their results will be slower and far less accurate than desired. This demotivates the player. However, thankfully in the case of both of Retrific’s games to date – including Beeftacular – the game controls so smoothly that it is easy to see where you are improving. It also means that there are no times where deaths and incompletions feel as though you have been cheated.
One of the cooler aspects of the game is that there have been game skins incorporated into the game. These can be unlocked as players’ progress. The first skin that I unlocked was ‘sponge.’ These skins, obviously, transforms the way the game looks. If you’re not into blood, then you can change the theme to something different.
The colour splatter left throughout each level makes the game worth playing again. Not only will you get an opportunity to get quicker times but the levels themselves can get particularly messy. Painting each level is a lot of fun in and of itself.
Beeftacular is almost Steamified to the max. The aforementioned level editor is founded on the Steam Workshop feature. There are 35 Steam achievements. The game utilizes the Steam Leaderboards system. The only thing lacking, as of writing, are Steam trading cards and Retrific has promised that they are incoming as well.
Retrific is fast becoming one of my go-to developers when I want great platformer action. Beeftacular is a well-developed game that is worthy of your time and effort. It is silky smooth and has had a lot of thought put into it beyond simple level design. With the significant amount of release content as well as the implemented level editor you’ll be set for hours of enjoyable content.

I’ve always been a fan of the Hitman series but it’s been a long time since I played any of them :S When I first heard that they had begun work on Hitman Absolution I was so excited to see Hitman on a next gen engine :D
The game is as good as I thought it would be and then some. Now a lot of die hard Hitman fans were actually upset with Absolution because they felt the gameplay and missions were too different when compared to the previous games. I think there are several levels that have a true Hitman vibe and others that have a new and different approach to the Hitman genre. The levels are so well designed that I feel overwhelmed at times. IO interactive have put a lot of effort into creating atmosphere using their new Glacier 2 engine. Everything looks fantastic.
There are so many options, so many choices, so many challenges to complete. Your character can unlock character upgrades and purchase “ upgrade-able attachments” for your 20+ weapons. The developers have made sure you always have choices and this is reflected in a real time points system that tracks your progress through each level. So basically you’ll know if you alert someone or ♥♥♥♥ up your Silent Assassin rating before you finish the level and discover you have to do it all over again. The points system also annoyed me a little though. I felt like I had to be perfect when I was playing, no alerts, no deductions in my points. This kinda made me feel handicapped towards playing the way I want to, but it’s not the end of the world.
The one problem I have noticed with Absolution is the disguise system. In previous games I could put on a disguise and access all sorts of areas with no problems at all. In Absolution (on higher difficulties) your disguise is pretty much useless. The enemies are perfectionists when it comes to sensing an odd disguise. It’s like a ♥♥♥♥ing sixth sense they have. You have to always keep your distance from them and continuously turn your back. If you get up close you’re screwed FOR SURE. This annoyed the hell out of me because I felt as though I wasn't even wearing a disguise. A lot of the time I would still hide behind cover and move through the environment as if I was but naked. Hopefully they’ll patch this broken disguise system because it’s one aspect of the Hitman games that I always enjoyed playing with. I don’t enjoy playing the same level over and over and over again because I keep getting discovered.  The AI could use a little work as well, they can see you from miles off :S
Apart from those issues, Absolution is a perfect game experience. I love the combat, feels like I’m in a movie! The graphics are incredible; the world really is living and breathing. And of course, I love having options. The level of replay ability and the new Contracts mode will give me a lot to play for a while. 12 hours in and I’m not even half way through my first playthrough. I highly recommend if you enjoy being stealthy and a serious challenge.

I bought this on sale for less than 1€, but I'd happily have paid the full price for it. it's an extremely minimalistic game, don't buy it if you absolutely need captivating plots, high-end graphics and complex gameplay or you'd be disappointed. the game is a fascinating journey through a beautifully designed surrealistic world. a really fitting ambient soundtrack adds a lot to the experience. if you've ever played Hiversaires and enjoyed it you'll really like this game as well (if you haven't go and play it). despite the 90s-like 3d graphics I was more than once amazed by the haunting and eerie scenarios and architecture of the game. along the journey you have to solve puzzles to proceed, which are decent, full of satisfying eureka-moments and quite never frustrating. it's a pretty short game tho, it took me less than 3 hours to get to the final credits, but still there were a couple of optional puzzles I didn't solve and some secrets I discovered that suggest there is something more if you find them all, so I might get back to it one day. one last note: most of the negative reviews complain about the lack of a plot and clear instructions. well I liked that instead, it's a plot device itself that adds to the unsettling feel of the game. you're thrown in without any explanation and are left with more questions than answers. picture it as a dream, no one is there to tell you where you are, what is happening and what you have to do, you just accept it and go on, and it's beautiful that way.
overall solid 7.5/10, would play again.

I bought Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag. I got Super Pirate Happy HIde and Go Seek Fun Time. Pretty much every single main story mission is "Tail the ......." or "Eavesdrop on the ......" aside from being frustrating and horribly uncreative, it's boring and takes away any desire to play the story, which otherwise was pretty good. This game got so much praise for being better than Assassin's Creed III, which outside of a few parts, I found rather enjoyable. If anything this game is worse. It took all of the good parts of III and all of the bad parts of III and made them all the mediocre parts of IV. It's not the worst game I've ever played, it's just... eh.
The Good:
You're a pirate and pirates are cool. You get to ride around in your very own ship plundering and listening to sea shanties sung by a half drunk crew, which is much more fun than the main missions.
The story inside and outside of the animus is as good as the other games.
That's pretty much it.
The Mediocre
It's pretty much the same as every other Assassin's Creed game there's a big expansive area with a butt ton of collectables that takes you hours to collect and adds nothing to the story and a couple of smaller cities with a slightly smaller butt ton of collectables that takes you slightly fewer hours to collect and adds nothing to the story.
Assassins Contracts and Naval Contracts are just, whatever. They add nothing but time to the game.
Diving Bell locations, eh, whatever.
The Bad and genuinely irritating
"Tail the ______" This is pretty much some part of every single main mission. Some of them are completely pointless because, more than once, you get spotted in a cutscene and have to chase the guy down anyway making yet another frustrating, idiotic "Tail the bad guy" mission completely pointless. This is the first Assassin's Creed game, including III that I had to take a week long break from because of the repeated awful tailing missions.

"Eavesdrop on .........." Remember that thing from III where you had to stay in a bubble to eavesdrop on someone while staying out of sight? There's a metric crap ton of them in this game, rather than a couple of optional objectives. If tailing missions had an inbred cousin, it would be eavesdropping missions.

"Assassin's Creed" not so much. You're not an assassin of any variety. Remember that thing you got to do in the other games where you went sneaking around or fighting your way into a palace and killed some evil dude to stop him from doing evil things? Not this time. In fact, at a little more than the halfway point, I think I've done an actual assassination on one guy in the main story. Everyone else who died was just killed in an epic game of Hide and Seek Deathmatch or because blow up that thar vessel because, pirates, yarrrr.

Shanties, remember those awful Almanac pages from III? They're back, and they didn't fix the thing where your character will just randomly stop moving or dive off a cliff into a pack of bad guys either. However, at least you get something for collecting them this time and if you just stand where they spawn for five minutes you can just instantly get it when it reappears.

Hunting, remember that thing that was really boring and pointless from III? It's back and it's still really boring and pointless. But you need the stuff to upgrade your gear you say? Nope, because you can just buy it at a store with the money you gained plundering. Making it more pointless than a new pencil.

If you really like following some guy really close, but not too close, without being seen, this game might be right for you. If all you want to do is plunder and sail around in you pirate ship, It's pretty fun. As far as being an Assassins Creed game, it's not even as good as III. It's a shame the developers put no thought into the actual story missions because the story itself is pretty good but endless tailing and eavesdropping ruins the experience. If you really must play it, get it on a really good sail.

If you're someone who's even slighty sensitive to frame pacing issues, and had issues with them from Dishonored 2, there's no changes here. Yes, the performance is much improved, but some people seem to have issues decerning between having a solid frame rate and a stable frame pace. I don't have any issues getting 100+ FPS at higher resolutions and settings, but that won't fix the microstutters associated with improper frame pacing.
From my testing with adaptive sync, if you lock the frame rate to 30, 60 or 120, and the frame rate can stay locked there without dipping, the frame pacing issues will vanish. But if you want a frame rate between 60 and 120 without frame pacing problems, you aren't going to get it. Even with my monitor's refresh rate locked to 75 or 90Hz, and the game frame capped to 75 or 90FPS, the issue persists. Triple buffering, as far as I can tell, has no effect on pacing. And no, as far as my tests have indicated, G-Sync and FreeSync don't help.
Unfortunately this seems to be a fundemental issue with the engine. I don't get the impression it was designed with variable frame rates in mind. The good news, at least, is if you're OK with 60FPS, or if you don't have a monitor that can do more than 60Hz anyway, you can maintain that frame rate with fairly light or moderate hardware. If you want to lock the game at 120Hz, however, expect to require a fairly beefy rig, or to make some serious sacrifices to either resolution or in-game settings.
If you're one of those lucky people that think this game is buttery smooth with an unlocked frame rate, and just can't percieve microstutters (or tearing for that matter), I do envy you.

My biggest problem with the game is with its presentation. It's so chaotic; so much stuff flying on the screen that you can't even see your own towers (aka "points"), let alone distuingish between different types of enemies or points or their levels, which points are shooting which enemies etc. It doesn't help that the path often intersects itself, making it difficult to see which enemies have moved furthest.
It also feels too fast paced, because enemies arrive so frequently and you have to be constantly manually shooting enemies with your cursor weapon and you don't get a single moment of peace to really think about what you're doing. To me, the best part of TD games is the planning. Planning where to place your towers and how to optimize their interactions. In this game you're in too much of a hurry to do everything.
The gameplay itself isn't even anything particularly in-depth. You place and upgrade points and help by manually shooting enemies. There's quite a few different types of points, so at least the game has that going for it.
There was an attempt at some kind of story but the writing was not very good and it wasn't enough to keep me interested.
The sound design in the game is also pretty bad (to the extent that I thought there was something wrong with my PC or headphones). It also lacks full screen support.

I've bought this game a number of times over the years, and the old executable has traveled with me from computer to computer. A surprise then, to see that the steam version has been improved from the old game drastically; looks better, plays better, achievements, and so on. I have long been inclined to call it the best tower defense ever made, now that's certain.
One could get really wanky with the "are games art" argument, because while tower defense games don't normally set high bars for craft and auteurism, this game certainly does. A story more compelling than it has any right to be, interesting worldcraft, engrossing (and sometimes distracting) visuals, this game oozes care in its construction.
And when it comes to the "is it fun" argument, simply a resounding yes. Excellent mechanics for a tower defense, with enough truly new and novel approaches that the same old tower defense techniques won't work just like you're used to. Add in a broad difficulty slider, new achievements, and some secrets, and there's enough game here to keep you interested for a long time.
I've really liked this game for a long time, and this version is truly excellent. Buy it!

This is my first review, ever. I haven't even made a joke review about bad rats. That's how much I love this game. With that in mind...
This game is definitely one of my alltime favorite games. It's a metroidvania with hints of darksouls style play on a 2D platformer type game. You play as a bug who descends into a world once called hallownest. Hallownest is a fallen society that is filled with mindless zombified bugs and critters everywhere. It used to be a bustling society of sophistication and cooperation. You are there to do two things: Save hallownest from its shallow grave and rid it of the infection that has been slowly consuming it.
Visuals: It is unbelievable that team cherry is only 3 people. The artwork is astonishing, atmospheric, and overwhelmingly well done. The theme stays the same throughout the game with awesome visual twists. Every section of the map has its own little unique theme, but everything ties in together with the overall theme of a bug filled society that has collapsed. The little subtle details tell a story thoughout the game. All of the visuals and artwork makes you really feel like you are experiencing the game rather than just playing it.
Story: This story is incredible without saying much at all. This is one of the first games that I actually wanted to read EVERY SINGLE piece of dialogue. It constantly keeps the player interested and makes you're feel really involved. The player has no mouth and thus cannot speak. {Spoiler:This is a small joke but also later becomes part of the story.} It made me want to look into every nook and cranny I could find to make sure I knew everything I could. I don't want to spoil too much of the game so I can't say too much about the story, other than that it is a cute, sad, heroic storyline that made me feel very good. Most things are optional, but extremely rewarding resource/gameplay wise, and even emotionally fulfilling.
Gameplay: Not the most groundbreaking combat or anything else, but flawlessly executed. The controls are smooth, responsive, and easy to pick up. It is interesting and fun gameplay that never gets old. As a metroidvania, you gather upgrades and gain power throughout the game, making combat easier. Yet of course the enemies also get tougher to keep things interesting and difficult. THIS IS A REALLY HARD GAME. If you don't like that, run. In the beginning, you are likely going to die. A lot. Once you get some practice, you'll still die in most first time boss fights. But after one playthrough I can beat most bosses first try. It's very similar to dark souls in that regard. Gameplay is immersive, and combines with the atmospheric visuals to be completely involved. Even after a 100% completion run and 9 Deathless steel soul speedrun attempts I am still not bored with it. It just gets more and more fun the better you get. My only reccomendation is that if you are a completionist like me, look up the full map of hallownest on the internet. It greatly helps in 100%ing the game. Otherwise if you want to do everything the hard way go ahead, I'm sure that would be fun too. After my first playthrough I don't use the full map anymore. I just used it to get my bearings but it isn't by any means required.
Conclusion: This is an extremely hard game that challenged me and gave me a great deal of satisfaction for completing any task. Including 100%ing the whole game and getting every achievement. The amount of content it has in it is gigantic. Its visuals are atmospheric and beautiful, the gameplay is intuitive and engaging, and the story is immersive and involving. This is so far my all time favorite game, and I will never regret buying and playing it. I wish the community was bigger so I could see more fanart and other things, because of how much I love this game. Team Cherry has knocked this kickstarter game out of the park and I am astonished by how well their team of 3 pulled it off.
[Edit] Forgot to mention the soundtrack is also amazing. I love it and it adds so much to the game. Even the basic sound system of getting hurt to defeating enemies makes me just happy. Its sad and immersive and brilliant.

If there's one strong positive that Immortal Defense nails in the tower defense genre, it's tower placement attack pattern/uniqueness. By that, I mean that most tower defense games have the fast-attacking tower, the slow-firing AoE tower, the speed-decreasing tower, etc., and the towers are very one-note and samey to all other tower defense games' towers.. In Immortal Defense, however, the towers attack in different literal patterns, sometimes apply different status effects, and all seem to have some use, depending on the map layout.
In my original review, I mentioned that there were a limited number of each type of tower you can place per level, and that you sometimes get more of the same tower, but there was no way to know if you would get them at all. The developer has been attentive and responded, informing me that most of the towers, upon getting a bunch of kills, will spawn new towers of the same type(s) getting bunches of kills, which you can then place. Also, this information is technically available in and in-game tutorial/information section, but that section was something like 15-19 pages long, somewhat buried and not pointed out as well as it should be.
I think it should have at least been mentioned in one of the early levels quite clearly, since this can be a
strategy for certain players, depending on play-style. I turned many losses and poor victories into very big successes.
Tower defense games often give the player something to do since the towers do much of the work. In Sanctum 2, your towers do their thing while you run about in first person, shooting at enemies inside and outside your maze. In Deathtrap, you're killing enemies Diablo-style (action RPG) while your towers do their thing. Unless you build the
maze and/or tower placement, or have incredibly good skills, you won't succeed with only towers or only attacking yourself, but each technique is very good and useful from the beginning of each level to the end.
To continue that line of thought into less "hybridized" tower defense games, you're kept busy in those by upgrading your towers and placing others, keeping the strategy element going strong, often with "waves" of enemies with a few seconds in between to give you a breather. There is no breather on each level of Immortal Defense, upgrades are so costly that earning enough cash to buy them was rare for me, and the player interaction after hitting start, for me, solely consists of moving my mouse around pointing at enemies, and firing charged shots on occasion.
This would be alright, except that enemies' health increases the longer you go in the level, which in my opinion, is a no-no in tower defense games. Why? Imagine you're playing a tower defense where there are very specific enemy types which, at the beginning, you know how much time/how many hits it takes to kill them. If one leaks through, you can quickly go "Oh, I need one archer tower," and place it, or whatever would kill it in time. In Immortal Defense, I'm pulling a number out of the air, but an enemy might have 100HP at the start of the level, but by the last minute, it has thousands of health. You lose the ability to easily gauge how easy/hard each enemy is to kill, which is the kiss of death for dealing with leaks, and this game
you to get as close to leaking as possible.
What do I mean by that? Well, in each level, you keep the best cash you had from the previous level, with a modifier based on how many enemies got through. That means that if you build a really good defense, you are losing out on your money for the next level, decreasing your odds of winning and getting better money. So the idea to play the game the "best" way is to build the bare minimum you need to succeed, and hope it's enough.
By the time an enemy leaks through, chances are it's too late to stop it, because it's late-game and you have no quick way of finding out how many hits of the shots from your cursor will kill it, or if you have time to place a new tower near the end and upgrade it, and then there's that hesitation of wondering how much money it's going to cost you to upgrade it enough to kill the baddie, and
wonder if you spent too much money doing that and if it will make this attempt at the level completely wasted because you spent more money than you did the time before.
This adds a level of hesitation for me that a game of this pacing simply does not accomodate, and removes that euphoric feeling of knowing you hit the sweet spot on the towers you need, watching for a little while as your towers lay waste to incoming baddies. Instead, I found myself sitting there initially nervous, wondering if my defense was enough, giving me less enjoyment.
However, I eventually stopped worrying and just felt bored, shift+tabbing to watch YouTube and talking with a family member in another room while the game played itself. I'd come back, see if I had success or failure, and if the latter, I would just do the same tower setup, pay for one more upgrade, hit start, and walk off again to come back in a few minutes and see how things went, because the cursor shots (player interaction) were so meaningless in my experience after the first couple of levels, even when charged.
Although I ended up with a more positive outlook on the game than I did when I initially reviewed it, and I played through to completion of the first of six campaigns this time around, my experience was not a fun one, because I was barely playing the game, with my level of player involvement genuinely being less than a clicker game upon hitting the start button each time.
Its ok. Nuff said.

Short version:
I enjoyed this game, but it wasn't worth £20. It's too short and the story has some issues. If you're a fan of the series, wait until it goes on sale. If you're just an action RPG fan, find another game.
Longer version:
If you take a long time to explore each level and really pull it to pieces, searching for every secret, you will squeeze about six hours of gameplay out of this game. The game has only five missions, of which one is fairly constrained and small, almost like a tutorial level, two take place in the same area of Karnacka (a new region aclled Upper Cyria District) meaning you spend about 60% of your time in the game there, one takes place in a rehashed map from Dishonred II, and the final mission takes place in an area that, although extremely large, is fairly linear. For a game that cost £20, I expected more than this - a couple of extra levels wouldn't be remiss.
The new powerset, while thematically interesting, introduces very little that we haven't seen in the series before. There's Displace, your mobility power, which acts like a limited-range Mark/Recall from Morrowind and can telefrag. There's Semblance, which acts like Corvo's Possess except you wear their face instead of their entire body. Foresight is equivalent to Dark Vision, except it can predict an enemy's footsteps, and while it's arguably the most innovative power, it's also the one I found the least use for. Void Strike is basically exactly like Windblast. It's also worth noting that you don't get any of your powers until the second mission, which, while consistent with the original two games, means you spend an appreciable chunk of the game powerless.
As for gadgets, the Hook Mine is basically a more hilarious stun mine. The Hyperbaric Grenade is interesting and useful but there's so goddamn few of them in the world that the only place you're likely to find them is at a black market shop. The Voltaic Gun combines the functions of both the pistol and the crossbow, replaces tranquiliser darts with shock darts, lets you shoot a really hard pearl at people for some reason and also features a chargeup function which I literally never found the need to use.
The story is weirdly paced and questionably written. Elements are brought into the game without very much explanation, and the way in which Billie Lurk gets her replacement arm and eye happens so abruptly and inexplicably I initially thought it must've been a glitch. The game's story - as with all Dishonored games, come to think of it - has a huge number of extremely interesting ideas and concepts that it has no idea what to do with, and which it has difficulty articulating. The story sure does a lot of telling, rather than showing, and there is an earthshatteringly significant revelation towards the end of the game that it is entirely possible for you to straight-up MISS if you skip past conversations or don't read the right books.
This game needed more love. At £10, it'd have been an absolute gem in terms of value for money. At £20 it's not that great.

A really original game amongst the rare hardcore RPG species. Age of Decadence gets rid of many problems plaguing the genre, like meaningless filler content and forced player character power fantasies. The game experience is condensed, but highly replayable and non-linear - you'll have to calculate your every step carefully and you never end up having to turn on that infamous "meaningless activities mop-up auto-pilot mode". Highly recommended for fellow "Ironmen", who have innate allergy to the "load game" button.
The game is really unforgiving, be prepared to invest some time learning the ropes. The combat uses a fairly robust turn-based system, which offers enough variety, like aimed attacks and a well designed weapons/armor system, to keep things interesting. Encounter design is mostly great. Most of the time combat is entirely avoidable, actually I think you can finish the whole game without getting into fight, if you play your cards right.
The pseudo-romanesque low-fantasy world is really well-though-out and original as is the story the game tells, and I can honestly say that I've never played a game with such a non-linear story design like in Age of Decadence. The amount of player agency is just staggering, and it proves how much dedication and love the developers have poured into this monster!
Download and try the demo and see for yourself. I doubt you'll be disappointed.

Then come the superb graphics and attention to details: the game is 'chock-full' of absent art banners and an occasional missing inventory item icon but beyond all that you still have to take a bow to the artist(s?!)' amazing rendering of armours & weapons; fluid combat animations, not to mention the surprisingly well done rendering of roman & eastern architecture you will often encounter...
Oh, have I mentioned the awesome TBS combat mechanics - if you don't know what that means then perhaps you aren't the target audience for this game... Red Spider 2: Exiled is a prequel to Red Spider: Vengeance (link:
, and the game would be much more enjoyable if you played that first since it builds on its predecessor. It's a visual novel, so the game lives and dies based on its story, so that’s what this review will focus on.
Red Spider 2 opens up with the protagonist, Lily, killing a corrupt police officer in order to protect an innocent bystander (an event with consequences that served as the driving force for the first game's story) and the game deals with what Lily does as she tries to escape a death squad out to capture and possibly kill her - and while there are a few subplots (which mostly change depending on which of the six routes you choose) that help reinforce the themes of the main story, that’s what Red Spider 2’s plot revolves around.
Instead of placing more importance on the plot and overall events, the game relies on its characters (who are impressively easy to get emotionally invested to, considering the short length of each route) to move the plot forward, which makes sense since this is Lily’s story and the player wouldn’t care about the story if they didn’t care about the characters first. Most of the cast consists of new characters not found in Red Spider, although there are a couple from the previous games that make appearances as well. The majority of the cast are based on existing archetypes, but are subverted in some way (such as how the strong sense of justice that Sam uses for his work contrasts with inadvertent injustice in his personal life).
It’s worth noting that, as a prequel, Red Spider 2’s plot does a good job at lending additional nuance to its predecessor and connects with it very well. Often, prequels often don’t build on the story they’re preceding very well and there’s an odd disconnect, or they might even ruin the previous stories retroactively (for example, Valkyrie Profile 2 and arguably Star Ocean 3 both trivialise the events of the games that came before them), but Red Spider 2 thankfully avoids this by showing how characters from the original Red Spider got to where they are (although this is sometimes indirect, as with Shawn and Luk, who are not referenced by their original names). Red Spider 2 does have a “canon” route by virtue of being a prequel, but some of the ties to the original game are only found on those non-canon routes, so the game doesn’t invalidate or waste your time if you don’t make the canon choice.
The game also has quite a few features that make it more convenient to replay once you’ve finished a route. On the load screen, there’s a route map that shows you which routes you’ve already completed and, if you click one of the branching points, you can load the game at that point and see the consequences of the choice you didn’t take before, which means you don’t have to replay the game from the beginning to view the consequences of the other choice (a feature that would be nice for WRPGs to take into account with the amount of decisions they have). There is also a trivia mode that explains the inspiration for certain aspects of the narrative and a sound test mode to listen to the music.
Speaking of the game’s music, most of the soundtrack consists of public domain tracks (which are fine and fit the tone of the story well), but there’s also quite a bit of original music, composed by Yasunori Shiono (the main composer of the Lufia series, and also a former co-worker of Motoi Sakuraba) and Yukio Nakajima (the composer for Energy Breaker and Puzzles & Dragons). These tracks are very good and fit the story as well, but a drawback of them fitting the tone of the story is that they’re a bit difficult to distinguish from each other (the high usage of the piano might have been a contributing factor for this).
As for complaints or things that the developer could have improved, the game has a significant amount of typos and grammatical errors, and these are all quite noticeable because of the large text size. The text always remains understandable despite these errors (you might expect a free game to have more errors because of the lack of budget, even), and the quality of the translation is good despite the game being free, so this doesn’t have a huge impact on the game.
To some people, the “romance” aspect of the game might also be a bit off-putting since Steam has a lot of visual novels that focus on that and players (presumably) would have hoped for something different in the Red Spider series, but this aspect doesn’t harm the game (and it could be seen as a good point since it helps humanise members of the underworld and make them easier to relate to), so this isn’t something that the game should be avoided for.
Red Spider 2: Exiled is free (as in, there’s no microtransactions) and it’s not a waste of your time (unless you dislike reading, but why would you still be reading my review, then?), so I'd recommend at least the first route if you've played the original Red Spider, and the other routes as well if you end up liking the first.

Quite refreshing RPG to scratch that old-school isometric itch.
The game writing is great, and really passes the feeling of those Glen Cook "Black Company" worlds, where life is short and brutal.
This game makes you think twice before going into the fight, and think triple before trusting someone, unlike easymode modern games where you play "Bill the Slayer of Rats and Destroyer of Worlds".
In AoD you can get betrayed and shanked by a successfull knife punch just like any other guy next door, thinking "why the hell did I have to play hero and went to save that damsel in distress", or "damn, it did seem like a too good deal to be true".
You get to choose your character gender, attributes and skills, as well as the very important initial employment or faction. The storyline is very branching for the path you will choose, very responsive to your decisions, sometimes with nice twists.
Do not expect a "kill 10 rats" kind of quests here, the tasks you face are much more complex and sometimes may be resolved in over 5 different ways, overall making up a very fun and immersive experience.
The game world itself is very detailed with very interesting lore and story behind and in front of it, and is very immersive.
Of course, if you are playing dumb and strong character, you will not be preoccupied with lore so much, being busy caving skulls of your employers' enemies in with a hammer.
On the other hand, for the intelligent and knowledgeable character the world is a whole different story with lore to uncover and people to manipulate.
That being said, some combat mechanics are very questionable, and since the developer team is quite small, does not seem they will be able to make any noticeable changes and improvements.
Overall, combat characters will have better quality of life, longer gameplay and overall enjoyment than social talkative characters.
I recommend this RPG, especially to those youngsters who had Skyrim as their first "RPG experience" to see how the actual RPG feels like.

This is an RPG Maker simpleton.
This game does not rank anywhere on a list of good games you just need to have. It is neither dissapointing nor is it exciting. All that aside, its not a bad game. Like I said, its a straight forward turn based RPG right out of the Maker; nothing more. Nothing about it breaks any molds and yet I still played it to its finish. If you do purchase this game, you will get a game that realistically takes about five hours for a playthrough. The map is small and simple, the monsters are fit for your level, the characters say things to one another. I would say this is a good game to get a brand new gamer accustomed to a turn based game. The problem is I don't know of any gamers that have never come across a turn based RPG; with the exception of perhaps my father who insists that Solitaire Suites is the only game that matters. I don't see myself ever selling him on this game.
It is...a game. In terms of the story, there really wasn't one. It seemed more like a quick jab a classic RPG tropes than anything else. On the plus side, it wasn't overbearing throughout gameplay and you only get quick blips of the humor here and there. In a strange way Breath of Death's subtle sarcasm is somewhat refreshing. Its almost as though the developers thought "hey, here are a couple of jokes. Oh and by the way you can play our game too." So...whats different about this game? Nodda. What does it have that other games dont? Not much. There is a glimmer of replayability to the game due to a modicum of choices in determining how the characters level up and a pick of their respective powers. Would I play it again? Maybe in a year or two when I am bored to tears. I am not planning on playing this game again anytime soon.  My initial reaction was to reccommend this game, but now that I am further into this review... I don't think I will. Not because its a bad game, rather because it is not a good game. This is one of those that I wish steam review would give me an option that was middle of the road. It seems tonight my glass is half empty. Hey, maybe Cthulu Saves the World will be better?

Not worth the money, the hype, or your time beyond perhaps one or two games (if you can stick it out that far).
A whole lot of flavor, and a whole lof of concepts and 'interesting' hooks.  Unfortunately, its all backed by what is actually a fairly tedious gameplay which is NOT a 4x in any traditional sense.  Most of the 'x's last a very short time, and then you're basically playing darts on the technology board and rushing wonders and stuff.  I found it really very boring after the first hundred turns.  In fact, pretty much nothing happened that was anything other than min/maxing repitition and micro management.  Which was not what I was hoping at all.
The expansion 'x' is totally anti-intuitive in that expansion is a massive negative against you for...no readily explored reason.  Your people get less healthy because you expanded and used more space.  Ahh, how on earth/centauri/whatever does that work?  So basically, play like India in Civ V and go just a couple of cities.  This is a major hudle that makes every group look and feel exactly the same with expansion plans.  What happened to small and concentrated vs spread thinly?  Nope, no such strategic choice any more.
Exploration is fairly dull and pointless.  You get some pods, you get some alien huts.  One gives random resources, the other one gold (oops, sorry, energy, must remember how totally different that makes it feel...not).
Extermination is...lifeless.  Ha ha.  Aliens are pretty much just like barbarians, and have about as much flavor. I had absolutely zero actual moments where aliens did anything other than sit around and annoy me.  No interaction.  No surprise.  No nothing.  They are just dull piecemeal opponents that you can wail on.  About the only cool thing is the first time you kill a worm.  Which rewards you with...a text window!  Hooray.  Naval stuff is pointless.  The aliens water-borne beasties are just enormously powerful and cannot be usefully sidelined.  Whereas land guys are easy to eliminate/remove/round-up.  It makes water basically like the black hole, except for coastline hugging trade routes which seem somehow almost immune.
Your units are pretty bland.  One melee troop, one ranged.  One melee tank, one ranged tank.  One plane.  One ship.  That's pretty much it.  Yes, they upgrade, but that's automatic when you get more tech and just raises numbers without providing any actual interest or adjustment.  Same movement, same shooting, same everything.  Experience for units is really, truly exciting - every level adds 10%.  That's it.  Nothing else.  Dull, lifeless, boring and could have had just as much impact if they were represented by rocks of various sizes.  There is absolutely nothing interesting or innovative about the units.  It would be like Civ where you only had archers, warriors, triremes and horsemen for the ENTIRE game, and with no promotions that allow you to create something different.  Oh yes, you can choose from one of two options when you do the upgrades, but that's the entire army - not unit by unit, which means that your selection just becomes 'normal' within a very short space of time.
Invention could really have used some clarity on the Science screen.  I mean come on lads, who wants to read a complex screen that uses a complete lack of iconography or colour information to help you understand what the hell everything is?  A real kludge that you'll have to learn by-heart in order to make any realistic use of.  How about the following improvements: 1. Your last researched tech is shown highlighted? 2. You've given us pretty colours for all the resources, how about colouring the building icons the same to help you hunt for that next science/food/whatever building rather than looking at every damn icon that means very little at all? 3. Once I've researched a full set of leaves, how about you hide them away?  Draw my eye to what is possible, not to what is already done.  Lastly, blue and purple are just not colours that leap out to help or provide any wizz-bang feel.  I got the feeling the layout was not done by anyone who had every considered how a layout could be useful - its just everything pushed together onto a single overweight chart.
So, am I impressed?  Initially, it was interesting and engrossing learning a little about the story.  But after that, it was no better than the Warlock version of the same game released a year or two back.  After the first fifty turns, there was no alien or world interaction that got me really interested.  The quests lack any real impetus, since they are off in a quest window (not the same window where you make quest choices, thats another window for no reason at all just to make you switch back and forth again).  After a bit, you stop reading the tedium, because they use the same tedium for every new building when you first build it and get the 'surprise' option of what the last bonus point should be placed into.  Every time.  Not even requiring some 'hurdle' or other use, just first of type every damn time.  A little variation would have killed us?
Diplomacy wasn't high on my list, and suffered the same as Civ V.  Its a little bit tedious, especially the 'can I extend that damn deal automatically rather than re-opening the same thing every 20 turns?  Its just make-work clicking.  How about permanent deals that you can break with a five turn notice once the first 20 turns run through?  Much less painful and interfering. Yes, I will, once again, renew my friendship with you, just like I did last time, and the time before, and....oh, sorry, fell asleep there for a bit.
So, overall rating is no more than 'meh'.  I'll be going back to Civ.  There's just something more tangible about how the inventions show progress in that game, and the visualisation of progress lends itself towards a feeling of achievement.  In this game, the achievement seemed to be all about sticking with it until you can't take it any more.

This game is fantastic, difficult and challenging with a fairly open ended way to go about everything. Long gone is the linear tech tree which has been replaced by the tech web, giving you choice in the direction you build and focus your empire. But with this comes the downside of spending too much time going with whatever looks neat, and having no progression towards your ultimate victory.
I can honestly see guides popping up on how to rush the right tech to the fastest victory.
Anyway, Gameplay is familiar to those who have played Civ5. The atmospheric layer adds wicked little temporay bonuses to your empire, from solar collects to orbital lasers. Making it neat to play with.
Diplomacy hasn't changed much, its solid with all the bells and whistles and a new Favor system. Ask for tech/trade whatever and offer favors that can be used and redeemed and it seems the AI has a harder time saying no too.
Spying is actually fun now, from defending your territory, stealing tech, money, research and units. Subversion and everything in between.
Speaking of units, the units in this game benefit from their own version of a tech tree. meshed with your affinity(which is chosen through tech and choices you make in the game) tech evolves into hyper futuristic stuff with wicked bonuses. gone is manually upgrading, just keep that research flowing.
Barbarians have evolved into aliens and this adds a whole new dynamic, attack and wipe them out, risks bigger badder alien Xenos coming after you. or tame them, study them, and gain their abilities or outright use them.
I could go on and on about this so ill focus on my own gripe at the moment.
Minus a few bugs(seems the ai likes to remind you constantly of things you did ONCE) because of how the tech web is designed, it feels like the game is much shorter then other Civs, then again, I started playing at 10pm release night all the way till 5am...so maybe not so much xD
I reccomend this game fully.
and to anyone who says its a reskinned Civ 5.

This is not Alpha Centauri 2. It feels more like a mod of Civilization 5. You've still got City States (Stations in BE) and you've still got the City's acting like big gun turrets. You get to pick an affinity, of which there are three... which is what your late game units will be but you aren't forced into just that one, if you tech fast enough you can get into all three of them.
Culture works exactly the same as Civ 5 too, and virtues don't really give much. Wonders are actually remarkably useless with the majority of them just giving a very small stat boost to that one city, and maybe giving a free structure, again to that one city. So there is no Human Genome Project in this.
On the 'This is not Alpha Centauri' news, there are no: Planet Busters. Planetary Council. Mind worms. Really game changing wonders. Probe teams. Overarching Planet Story. Fun different feeling factions with decent diplomacy.
So enough of the bad, onto the good:
Satellites are quite good, and you have a satellite layer - it's a bit finicky but some of these add some stats if you can be bothered with it. You can also get orbital lasers, but they generally get shot down the next turn so they are less good.
The early game is quite fun! Your explorers will die to any alien life, and you have to find ruins and things to help you along. The alien life at the start of the game is scary, and big. Fighting off the Thresher Maw with your first troops is a good challenge.
The mission system: Good, but doesn't really have a point in the end
Graphics: It looks beautiful.
But yeah, that's about it. I recommend it but it's only just a recommend. Not a must buy

I have changed my review to negative to reflect my thoughts better on things that I find troubling about this game.
As a game this game is excellent for the most part ,don't get me wrong. Very good tutorial and rewards for new players and excellent gameplay that uses mechanics that could only be used in a digital format game.  The unique gameplay leads to a lot of bluffing and second guessing and there's a lot of variety in deckbuilding.  Fine game for people who think Hearthstone may be a little simplistic and MTG is a little corporate.  This game is also gorgeous in every way, kudos to the art people and the UI designers.
However my problem with it makes me not want to play it.  It is a single problem and it's about the format of the game. It's a collectable card game and I am a veteran of those but this one feels like it steps over a line. I ran the MTG scene in my country, played pro tours and have played a variety of these games including L5R, Netrunner, Vampire, Hearthstone, Scrolls etc so I am coming from a background of knowing these kinds of games intimately.
The main problem is that this game has a really bad system regarding packs and rarity.  Firstly packs are very expensive.  Secondly legendary cards are very hard to get and are sadly essential to pull of a lot of good decks.  It is also very inconsistent which types of cards are legendary and which are not.  For instance Martyr Golem does not feel like a legendary card but still is so powerful that you need to have 3 to pull of a few decks.  The thing is though that I rarely see Martyr Golems around...because it is so hard to get legendary cards without putting down some serious money so no one has them.  Since I started I think I've opened about 70 packs (and note that each pack costs quite a bit).  Most of them were from rewards though but I did buy around 20 myself.  I've only opened 1 legendary and a handful of epics in those 70 packs which is an awful drop ratio for ultra rare cards.  When I purchased my 20 packs I did it one go and didn't open a single Epic or Legendary.  I should have uninstalled the game right then and there.
Summary. Great game but don't come near it unless you have a lot of money to spend on it.  I don't so I can't really keep on playing sadly.  That is why I am giving it a negative review.

If you want a tl;dr of my review, it's basically just "If you like atmospheric exploration games, buy it".
My ACTUAL review is:
Kairo is an interesting game to say the least, I feel like there was an actual vision behind the developer and for the most part I think his vision came through, however the limited resources he had are fatally apparent. The film grain effect is just a static overlay that feels more distracting than stylistic, and while early areas of the game are very visually engaging and seem like they have a plan and purpose behind their layout, later areas just feel slapped together, using almost random geometric shapes and often just feel like the design had little to no thought at all. A fair amount of rooms have a purposefully grand scale, which is usually unnessicary considering you have to run back and forth in them to solve a puzzle. Of course this might be a purposeful choice to evoke a specific emotion from that level, I just felt pulled out of the experience.
Now obviously I can't review a game without discussing how it plays and the mechanics, which also sadly fall flat. The game only gives you three commands, the ability to look, jump, and sprint. Nothing else. This is sometimes problematic to solving puzzles as you need to physically touch certain objects in order to "activate" them. While feeling awkward by itself, the player has a sort of floaty momentum to them that is accentuated by the fact you need to ram into objects to solve puzzles, which are also obtuse. There are different symbols used to differentiate switches, but the logic behind them often changes. Sometimes they're supposed to be literal, as in you have to activate the exact sime switch, but sometimes they're representations of numbers, which is confusing when the rest of the game had been using a literal interpretation. Luckily there is a hint system built in, which solves most of my gripes with the presentation not being very clear.
All in all, I feel like this game needs a lot of polish, but is still worth the price, especially if it's on sale.

This game has too many problems to recommend.
=> Uplay - be advised that the launcher which comes with the Steam version doesn't work at all, it won't connect. Ubisoft is too lazy or incompetent to patch this, so you have to download stand-alone Uplay from their website and run that to get the game registered to your account. After that you can play. This isn't clearly documented, so players could easily get stuck there.
=> Audio - in some cutscenes, the audio doesn't work and you completely lose track of the plot. Completely immersion shattering.
=> Controls - They are just terrible. Your character does the opposite of what you desire most of the time and chasing someone is an utter chore, rather than a free-running joy as it SHOULD be. So many other games get this right, it's ridiculous that Ubisoft still haven't cracked this one.
Never mind stealth-swimming. Keep Circle pressed and press X to assassinate at the same time. With what kind of alien hand would you accomplish this??
=> Stealth - What stealth? There are no real stealth mechanics, and sneaking involves finding bushes or haystacks. It's not very immersive and half the time it's utter frustration as the camera doesn't move in the angles you require.
=> Camera - Ocassionally infuriating, completely hiding the combat action and making it virtually impossible to dodge at times.
=> Combat - Boring and uninspiring when compared to the Warner Bross games. It feels clunky and dated, and the controls are often not very intuitive.
Long story short, I really wanted to like this game as the setting is awesome and exactly what I was in the mood for. But it's completely let down by Ubisoft's uninspired gameplay and out-of-animus sequences which completely shatter any immersion you may have had. I've spend 5 hours frustrated for 1 hour of fun. And that these days, just isn't good enough.

IW is fun and accessible to the flexible gamer, but be prepared for a rocky user experience and an odd juxtaposition of content.
Paying for advantage is an inseparable part of this genre.  However, IW does a very good job of giving new players and f2p'ers free decks and cards to play with.   If you get good, you can win cards and the in-game currency to buy card packs.
I didn't find the simultaneous turns clunky.  It's a relatively novel mechanic that is likely counter-intuitive to experienced card players.  As a dabbling TCG/CCG gamer, it wasn't any more challenging a mechanic than any other in the game.  This game is complex and a casual gamer should be prepared for tough play.
My concerns about the game are bugs in the client and the dev teams ability to ever iron out bugs and implement features.   The client has always been very, very buggy and prone to all sorts of weird behavior, including
between player clients!  I would caution potential spenders given the slow rate of development and the severity of some bugs.
I am extremely skeptical about the integrity of a team that would create crossovers with well-established franchises before their own game is even officially released.  I'm sure Star Trek decks appeal to some players, but, frankly, it smacks of pandering and, to my eyes, belies confidence in their original content and IP.  More to the point, Star Trek hardly shares common thematic elements, beyond very broad themes common to almost any sci-fi/science fantasy setting.  The very inclusion is jarring to me.
