The cursor acts as a tower as well, firing a steady stream of damage that gets larger as the round progresses, allowing you to prioritize the enemies at your door instead of feeling helpless.
The tower types are fantastic though, with firing patterns that match their personalities and they cause you to think about where they should be placed to maximize effectiveness which is one of the tennants of TD as a whole.
Overall, this game is well priced for the experience, has a ton of customization and creativity involved (Custom levels and diffficulty settings) and is chock full of enjoyable content.

I've given the software a fair whack over the time I've owned it, working on converting a story into ePub format for reading on a physical e-reader.
My time was not well spent, as it's been chasing down significantly harder to nail down formatting issues, coupled with the need to work with Markdown when editing.
Time would be better spent working directly in LibreOffice to handle the bulk of the formatting at a significantly faster pace, and then having access to far better export tools, along with being able to chain into the use of something like Pandoc once you have the formatting where you want it. It would net the benefit of having a better polished UI and additional formatting tools for when you're wanting to make a decently designed ePub out of a long story for a friend.
The overall UI, I'll freely admit, is designed to take your mind off the editing and cleanup aspect of creating, and put it squarely on letting your brain run free, but it's no good if all that free running doesn't have a place to run at the end of the world you've written. I find that it's a bit too simplistic for my needs, though..
I'm hoping for a bit more power in a future release, such as basic font choices - trying to represent text on a terminal as something separate from character text is nigh impossible, currently.

This is (so far) a simple application which accomplishes precisely what it set out to do: Keep writing neat and uncomplicated.
PROS:
- Some useful common features (such as spell checking, form templates)
- Workshop support for things such as themes, additional form templates, importing/exporting extentions, etc.
- A very active DEV who interacts with the user base and takes suggestions seriously
- Still in active development, so more features coming
CONS (as of the date of this posting):
- No grammer check
- No folder nesting for organizing reference material (promised in a future update)
- Few note templates provided with the application (can be remedied through the workshop)
- No in-app interface for creating forms, or help support for same. Form creation requires advanced  understanding of Steam folder structures and familiarity with basic scripting concepts and json files.
- Out-of-the-box not well suited for large projects requiring extensive organizational tools (but achievable through Steam Workshop)
This is a very good program for writing without needing to consider bloated software-required format layouts and other nonsense that gets in the way of being creative.
It is growing, with many planned features which hold onto the core spirit  of the software: Remaining unintrusive, so writers can write!
Strongly recommended for hobbyists, simple projects or people not needing an MS Word clone. If you need more features then the software provides at this time, then wait a bit - they're comming.

If you like old-school turn based RPGs or have played Call of Cthulu and enjoyed that you will enjoy this! A fun and light-hearted (despite what the opening cinematic wants you to believe) JRPG parody stuffed chock-a-block full of references to not just role-playing games but gaming classics in general (I particularly got a chuckle out of Motherbound). Gameplay is fairly simple, you move through the overworld to a variety of dungeons where you do random battles until you reach a boss. Random battles are turn-based and involve three novel mechanics: firstly is a combo system where each hit builds up a combo which increases the power of certain combo breaker moves (either attacking or healing), secondly each round the monsters power increases by 10% meaning that the longer a battle goes on the more difficult it gets and thirdly (to avoid you chugging potions willy nilly) all health is regenerated after battles. Another novelty is that there are a limited number of random battles in each area meaning if you get through them all you can explore without being interrupted (however you can still trigger some if you feel you need to grind). Note: The unique features I mentioned are also in Call of Cthulu.
My main comment is that I found this game great to play while watching something else. Its a simple story and a really simple gameplay loop which can be satisfying if you like finding the most efficient ways to win battles. However, there are moments when it can just be a case of mashing the "ENTER" key to get through battles. However, on sale and considering it is in a bundle with Call of Cthulu (which I preferred since the humour resonated better with me) I definitely can recommend purchasing it.

A modern masterpiece.
If you liked Axiom Verge or Ori and the Blind Forest you must play this game.  Epic music, combat, constant since of discovery with the map and level design, engaging NPCs, artistically distinct level and area design that gives a distinctive tone to each area and kept me completely enaged for the 33 hours that I played it to 98% completion.
One of the principle things that I find very worthwhile in games, and also very rare is a plot and dialogue that doesn't insult the players' intelligence.  The overly expository ("Go Here, Do This, Because This Reason, Or Else Evil Wins") kind of dialogue makes for boring and unimaginitive gameplay.  The triumph of this game is that the core plot of the game is only implied rather than expressly stated.  Rather than giving you a straight line of a plot, it gives you a trail of breadcrumbs, you must use your own mind and own imagination to connect to the dots of who/what your character is, what the Hollow Knight is, what the "infection" is, what the guardians' intentions and results were, and on down the line.  The plot is laden with symbolism, references to spiritual concepts, and compelling characters all without beating you over the head with anything or trying to wow you with it's own heady intellect.  This is game dialogue and plot development at it's finest.
And all of this in a game that is ostinsibly about a decaying Bug Kingdom, both meshing childhood story-book themes with a dark, entropic world makes for a perfect game tonality.  It's dark without being bleak, the variation of the areas and themes of the map and plot carry you in and out of that core theme so it doesn't overstate it's overall theme.  Also, the flicker of hope is ever present in this game as well.  As games that overdo the bleak side of things quickly lose contrast when not given a counterpoint, a factor that this game keeps in perfect harmony.

I was a massive fan of the original Assassin's creed games and quickly realized that the series was bound to lose quality over time (as it did).
So when I picked up Assassin's Creed Black Flag I didn't expect a great Assassin's Creed game.
And I didn't get one. Matter of fact, I think it would be a terrible game if it focused more on the Assassin aspect of the story, that didn't really seem to fit the main character or the situation he found himself in all that well.
But while Ubisoft may have given us a mediocre AC game with Black Flag it seems they accidentally created an amazing and beautiful pirate game.
The Pirate story is believable, the setting and maps are absolutely breathtaking, as is the experience out on sea, with the sound of waves crashing against your ship, cannons and seagulls in the distance and your crew singing shanties as you roam the map in search of adventure.
If this game is on sale and you can run it I see little reason to not pick it up, it's easy to lose yourself in the beautiful world and story and I can't think of a single pirate oriented game that can even reach the overall feel of this title.
TL;DR: Meh AC game, Amazing Pirate game. Do get.

Kairo is one of thise gems amongst the steam garbage I seem to keep running into. After playing antichamber, I absoultely had to play Kairo.
Kairo is a game in which you appear to be embarking into the depths of an ancient egypt-like machine that either uses magic or technology too far beyond you to understand. Either way, Kairo is one of those games that doesn't explain anything to you (though you have the option of hints, which don't help much) so it requires a lot of problem solving and logistics on your part.
Most of the puzzles are self-explanitory, and the ones that aren't normally are supplied with a stone or wall you have to look at. Once you find those, you then proceed to facepalm realizing how simple the complex-looking puzzle really is.  Even so, the puzzles really are challanging, to the point where I actually had to look up a walkthrough for one of them because it didn't seem to be based on any rhyme or reason (and that I couldn't find any stones or walls to explain it) I'm sure you'll identify the one I'm talking about if you play this game.
The story is widely open to interpretation though. There were points in the story that sent a legit chill down my spine. Other moments had me scratching my head wondering what just happened. In order to understand it, you're required to fill in a lot of blanks.
Overall, despite it's cheap graphics and oddly slippery controls, Kairo is a game that you'll enjoy figuring out for yourself, and then be proud to finish.

"Ehhh...." That's basically how I feel.
It really is just DLC for Dishonored 2 and it plays like it, with many reused assets. The game basically boils down to 4 maps over 5 missions, and that is being generous. The first map is a small tutorial map, while the second and third take place on the same map. The fouth mission is a small section of a map from Dishonored 2. The fifth mission is entirely unique, and there is an interior section on the third map that is quite large.
Some of the comments from the NPCs are incorrect for the setting, IE the former witches still talking about the coven in the present tense. The dialog from both Billie and Daud is not always appropriate given the context of the situation. Billie in particular sounds either bored or giddy instead of serious in the beginning. There are some very good examples, but I'll avoid spoilers.
The way Billie gets her "powers" is contrived. One artifact she obtains had a dedicated mission, while the other two are given to her with no context after the end of the first mission. There are only 3 powers, which wasn't a game breaker for me given the game's length, but it does limit your strategic options.
Overall, an Ehh rating, maybe 5/10. It has its good moments and its bad.
If they really wanted to, they could have easily done what they did with the Knife of Dunwall with this and put in more time to do so, and charged $30 ea for two parts. Would have been a better idea narratively, and probably from a buisness perspective. Hard to say on the latter.

The best entry in the Dishonored series to date. Take your pick, an awesome set of powers that supports any style of play, a story that is truly interesting with a protaganist that is far more interesting than her predecessors. Whereas previous entries have been standard revenge tales this time around you are presented with a morally grey objective with a conflicted character.
Michael Madsen is outstanding in his role as Daud, however I would have liked to hear more from him.
The campaign is very short if you are only interested in completing the objectives. They also take place on maps that were already used as assets in Dishonored 2 although since this is an expansion that is somewhat to be expected.
The best change in gameplay by far is the reworked void energy system, mana potions are no longer needed which is vastly superior to its predecessor. It never really made sense to me that characters with the Outsider's mark were forced to drink potions constantly. Now your mana recharges to full as long as you give it enough time.
Without delving into spoilers, I was disappointed in The Outsider because he was a great character. Saying any more would spoil the story.
The result of all these factors is a very focused experience that taken by itself or as a part of the Dishonored series is a joy to play through.
Overall the best game in the Dishonored franchise to date, the only drawbacks being that I wanted more of it bc this is the best set of powers, and also the lack of brand new levels with the notable exception of the final one.
Worth the price, buy it, play it, love it!

I picked up Death of the Outsider because Dishonored was one of my favourite games. While it plays similar to Dishonored, it's not one that I would include as a great game. What made Dishonored great was the varied ways in which you could complete a mission. While this game has different means of completing a mission, they're all various means to the same end. I enjoyed finding ways to slink through a level undetected, accomplishing everything there was to do, all while keeping my hands clean. Rather than killing an enemy, there was always a means of incapacitating them. If you didn't want to use the power of the void, you could still accomplish your goal, but it would be much more difficult. That's what it was all about.
Unfortunately, DotO doesn't allow this. In various missions, you are required to kill at least someone in certain contract missions unless you decide to skip it entirely. In the previous two titles, you could simply find a way to incapacitate them and still acquire the completion of a side objective. There are also various bottlenecks in which you will not be able to proceed without the use of the void, no matter how hard you try. That goes against the very heart of the game.
Now, despite the fact that any of my  other valid critisism is going to be ignored because of what I'm going to say next, I'm going to go ahead and say it anyway. Billie Lurk was easily the weakest part of the game. She had no depth. The character was deliberately written as a Mary Sue, drawing on real and modern socio-political dynamics to be the voice of reason in a world that the character obviously did not belong in. It's hard to understate the fact that she is literally the type of Mary Sue that everyone jokes about. To say it bluntly, she ruined the immersion. Most people play videogames to escape the real world. It's a disservice to fans to strip them of the immersion to make a political point on a platform that has openly rejected real world politics. That's just the base coat here. Her story was weak as well. Her betrayal didn't matter. Her attonement didn't matter. Daud certainly shouldn't have mattered. Her motivations make zero sense. Yet she was shoehorned into the story regardless.
Utterly disappointed. Mostly at the weak way in which missions are completed, and the weak protagonist as a secondary.

I purchased the original version of Immortal Defense quite a long time ago, and I'm glad that it has finally made its way to Steam. ID is one of the best Tower Defense style games I have ever played.
On a mechanical level, the towers are not the formulaic set you find in most other games. You know, the "weak but fast" tower, the "long range and slow" tower, the "splash damage" tower, etc. You won't find that here. Each of the towers has vastly different behaviors, making you think more carefully about placement. Behavior can change as you upgrade them, and they can also interact with your cursor as well (which is a weapon in its own right).
The game is also very challenging - experienced Tower Defense players will be tested here. But, the difficulty can be adjusted along the way, so if it's just too hard, you can dial the difficulty down a bit - for the one level you're having trouble with - and come back to it later if you want.
Visually, Immortal Defense is fun. This is an older game but it still looks great. It's somewhere between a dream, a laser light show, and an LSD experience all rolled up into one. The visuals can also be dialed up and down as needed, though, so if it is too much for you, you can get back to a more "sane" experience. I recommend keeping on the higher side.
The music is great too - it has a delicate, mystical quality that fits very well with the art style.
Generally, tower defense games have at most a token storyline, something that is easy to throw away and ignore. But Immortal Defense delivers here, too - taken as a whole, the story of Immortal Defense gets into some interesting philisophical questions about immortality, good and evil, what is really important, etc. The towers (called Points in the game) come out of the story, and their names and functionality are drawn out of it as well.
It might be a bit too cerebral for a lot of people, but it won't interfere with the gameplay.
For the Steam version of the game, there are new challenges that you can complete for additional bonuses during gameplay. There is also a leaderboard.
Overall, I rate this as a very strong buy for anyone who enjoys the Tower Defense genre and is looking for something a little different. Visuals aside, I put ID on the same level as other TD greats.
Disclosure: Studio Eres provided me with an advance copy of the Steam version for the purposes of play testing and review.

Playing Disciples II is the Turn-Based Strategy equivalent of sitting at home buzzsawing through a huge bag of greasy, salty potato chips. I know for a fact that there are way better things I could be doing.  I also know that what I'm eating has next to no meaningfull nutritional content. They don't even taste especially good, and I'm getting bored and frustrated and only eating out of habit.

Well, the game does look pretty, in that early-Rennaissance-variant Grimdark(TM) way. It also offers reasonably steady advancement in power, and a few head-scratching tactical challenges.
Mostly, though, it comes down to grinding, hoarding and (save) scumming. Grinding: learn to recognize the fights your troops can survive and still gain meaningful XP from, keep hitting as fast as you safely can till your dudes gain a few levels and a commensurate capacity to curb-stomp anything other than the final battle (troop upgrade levels determine any fight that hasn't been pre-determined by magic or thief spam: a difference of one level guarantees the higher-tier army will win, two or more guarantees a massacre.)  Hoarding: get mines and mana nodes. Money is necessary for Grinding, since the buildings needed to upgrade your troops get hella expensive at tiers 4 and 5, while mana powers the spells that tilt combats. Use as little mana and money as needed to keep your troops alive and upgrading, then when the map's big bad comes into view burn it to guarantee a win. Cast every spell you can, twice if you can, send mobs of Thieves to soften up fortified armies, send disposable heroes leading quick-firing ranged units, you get the idea. Scumming occurs when those first two don't work, or are derailed by unforseen circumstances, which becomes more common as you climb the difficulty levels. The couple of different auto-save functions make this slightly less irritating.
The end result is a game where fights can largely be predicted in advance (no tactical genius can offset spell bombardment or superior forces), and strategy between fights is largely a matter of trial and error. You can let it eat up a ton of time, or you could go play something more interesting.
(Yes, I know this review sounds like a three-hundred-pound couch potato telling his kids to exercise. Remember, folks: hypocrisy is the debt vice pays to virtue.)

Battlerite comes seemingly out of nowhere and nails everything just right.
From gameplay to balance to ease of play (fast games, fast queues and easy to understand whether you're doing well or not), to rewards.
Gameplay is extremely fast, mixing some MMO PvP elements like interrupting, focus shifting and LoSing. Rounds are 2 minutes long with a sudden death mechanic that isn't punishing to a certain type of heroes.
The balance is honestly very good, you can play every champion to a high level (I'm grade 14 and have played every champion in ranked to a level I'm happy with). There's obviously some slight balance issues (Jumong for example, is too strong right now), but there will always be. Stunlock is absolutely killing the early access, with often balance patches and new content coming out.

Strong points about Battlerite:
-Fast gameplay
-Most abilities are skillshots (save for shields, character-centered AoE)
-Every champion has a very high skill ceiling
-Wide range of champion types
-Fast games
-Champions feel extremely different from one another
-Extremely clear visuals, giving you a very readable approach to what's going on
-Decent customization
-Replay system built-in with share functions
-Option to pick which servers you will connect to
-Map is mirrored and symmetric, you always play from the left side
-Sandbox mode built-in
Weak points about Battlerite:
-Cosmetics are somewhat mediocre for now (majority being recolours)
-Rewards are purely based on gambling loot boxes (like Hearthstone and Overwatch)
-No emotes in game (you really want to BM sometimes)
-No pings in game
Things I wish Battlerite had:
-Build templates would feel cool (although not really needed)
-Pings in game
-Taunts / emotes
-Group chat window when in queue (you have to do extra clicks to bring it up)

Conflicted Review: Read on to see why.
Pros:
- Simple program and layout
- Able to add multiple pages along the side bar, to switch back and forth between notes/chapters
- Able to customize colors of entire appearance (and save it as a template for reuse later)
- Able to add a background
- Can upload photos
- Can use a side-by-side 'comparison' page view (advertised as typically used to show an 'inspiration' picture while writing)
- Can 'resize' the page (decide how much space each section in current view uses)
- Can toggle the list of pages to minimize
- Has a 'distraction free' mode (hides all the side bars and full screens the page and background in order to reduce all distractions and focus solely on the current page)
- Requires less processing power than other similar programs
- Easy learning curve (it takes about ten minutes of pushing random buttons to figure it all out)
Cons:
- Feels like a cheap version of Scrivener (but that's a personal opinion)
- Too simple for some people who like all the stylize/formatting options other word processors offer
- No ability to sort multiple pages under one folder; they simply form a long list down the side
For me, personally, I prefer investing the extra money into Scrivener (or waiting until it has a sale) because I like having the ability to sort all my files into different folders and not having one long list down the side (which was basically the deciding factor for me). That being said, I still recommend Nimble Writer because it's very useful when other programs are feeling too cluttered or chaotic.

When you first start playing you don't realize how many subtle mechanics there are that really allow a deep level of strategy and custom deck building.  Once you do; however, you quickly come to appreciate how intricate and sophisticated this game can be (and I mean that in a very good way!).  There are also a TON of cards and card combinations, so anyone who enjoys building a unique, custom deck is going to be in hog heaven.
When you do give this game a try don't be put off by the generic feeling tutorial and beginner campaign decks.  These are simple on purpose I believe to ease beginners into the game.  Once you have the basics under your belt try searching the web for some custom deck ideas.  You'll quickly see the amazing amount of different ways you can put together a devious combination of cards to wreck havoc on your opponent.
And did I mention the daily log in rewards, quests, tournaments, ranked play, leveling rewards, etc. etc.?  This game has a lot going for it to keep you engaged, and it's an indie title too boot.  You can't lose on that!
So, in summary:  This is a fantastic game, and if you should definitely give it a shot.  I'll bet you'll be hooked in no time.  :)
And feel free to hit me up for a game anytime.

I really draaaagged myself though this one, but I did play it through after it sat in my library for a while.
Design-wise, it's boring.
The game's pretty much entirely linear, unless you want to take a long route to a treasure chest you can see across the way, which is just drudgery after a good while.  The towns are practically all the same, with the same NPC's selling slightly better equipment... I guess they nailed that RPG trope.  Woo.  The dungeons are long halls with the occasional turn or dead-end.  Really thrilling stuff there.  Very few things in the game world are interactable with, which means the handful that are manage to be surprises when they shouldn't be.
The writing's a bore.
The references are just blah while the attempts at humor are worse.  The characters are just RPG archetypes wearing spooky monster costumes, teasing at crappy romance plots that hardly skirt amusing.  The plot is forgettable; the bookends of the intro fmv "Many years ago..." and the outro fmv "insert spoiler here* contain bewteen them effectively no plot content.  It's just, "Hey let's adventure.  Next town.  dungeon.  cavern. next town... yadda yadda."  Sprinkle in some boss battles that have virtually no weight in the plot, and that's it.  Some of this curiously plotless content mocks itself, while at the same time not really managing anything better.  It's kind of sad that way.
As far as retro RPG's go, this one presented only one surprising concept, the ability to customise your characters' abilities and stats on level up.  Granted, *every* modern RPG does that, so that's uh... nice, I guess.
Yes, I got this game for nearly free when it was on sale, and yes, I invested time to beat it.  But no, no, no, do not waste your quarter or your life on this.

I want to love The Swindle. I really do. The aesthetic is fun, the levels are generated well, and the main conceit of having 100 days to get ready for the big "job" is exciting and interesting.
All of these great things are marred by poor gameplay. Movement is imprecise and buggy, with the character sliding along sloped floors unable to jump. You have very little control over the height of your jump, making the precision jumps you sometimes need to avoid detection very hard to use. Your speed and control in mid-air is wildly inconsistent, sometimes launching you haphazardly into the sights of a patrolling robot and sometimes failing to jump from one wall to another leading you to land in a bed of spikes.
Like any other rogue-like/lite, you'll die. A lot. But it will often feel like it wasn't your fault. It often won't even feel like it was the level, or randomness's fault. Just the fault of bad controls.
Overall, a really fun concept with tons of potential has been kind of ruined for me because of extremely loose controls.

A shorter but fitting finale to the Dishonored series (or at the very least the current era,) this game is a must play for any Dishonored fan.
The game ties up a lot of loose ends concerning three pivotal characters from the series, as well as showing the aftereffects of a number of the events of the first two games. The callbacks are deftly handled, some series and some humourous, but never feeling forced - the game fits naturally into the Dishonored world.
Mechanically and thematically there's not a lot here that's particularly new, but for a series this good that doesn't really matter; it's just more of a good thing.The characters are generally strong and the story is compelling, even without many old favourites such as Corvo, Emily or Anton Sokolov, and it's good to see Daud and The Outsider doing their thing again.
The main criticism of this game for me is the loss of the Chaos system. While I understand the motivations behind this from the developers, the Chaos system is one of the most compelling elements of the series for me, providing greater replay value and differentiating the series from most other games on the market. Having said that, the game holds up well enough without it and there is still plenty of reason to play mercifully if you want to.
Coming into this game I felt quite sad that this was going to be the final Dishonored game, or at least the final in this specific series. I consider the Dishonored series to be among my all time favourite games and the idea that this is the end has been quite sad. Having finished Death of the Outsider however I have come to think that this is a good time to stop. We've heard the most compelling stories, seen many of the most compelling places and taken the mechanics of the series to their limit over the past three games. There is a time that every story should come to an end, lest to continue into irrelevance, and this is a satisfying time to end it.
I remain hopeful however that one day we'll return to this world, and maybe see some of those continents we've only heard about.

An excellent follow-up to Dishonored 2, building on its strengths and removing some of the fluff. The shorter length makes for a tighter and more focused experience, as each level is packed to the brim with alternate pathways and hidden items to discover. The available powers synergize very well, as they're all designed to be available alongside each other at all times. Some are iterations of previous abilities with added twists, while some bring entirely new flavors of their own. The new tools, while few, also add many ways to tackle, strangle, kill or otherwise maim your foes, and with the removal of the Chaos system, the series has never been closer to the immersive sim ethos of "play the way you want". As Billie, you're free to stealth or murder your way through the colorful steets of Karnaka once more, though she feels more grounded by the series' mythology than any character before her, and is probably the most credible and developed character we've been invited to incarnate as a Dishonored so far.
Recommended for: people who aren't afraid to get their hands dirty, people who value quality over quantity, people who like to experiment and replay within small dynamic sandboxes, people who always dreamed of befriending rats
Not recommended for: people who miss Corvo or Dunwall, people who beeline for objective markers, people who'd rather talk to monsters than dismember them in creative ways

There are many, many able reviews of this game so I'll just add some short remarks.
I find Kairo haunting and beautiful. Every time I reach the final goal, and the credits roll, and the music plays I think of creator Richard Perrin and his father — and the loss of my own — but it’s hopeful and optimistic. Still the entire experience exhibits a sense of loss and recapitulates same. For me the game is an expression that I enjoy somewhat plaintively in its context.
I play it often enough at my three-year-old's insistent request. He has none of this context! But he still wants to come back again and again. He finds it mesmerizing as he instructs me where to go and what to inspect next — the first time, his eyes wide in amazement. I think at his age he's captivated by the geometry and the color (children's entertainment is generally far from this). “Go see where the blocks are painted!”, “Go to the black moon!”, “Go in the elevator!”, “Show me the dinosaur!”, “Fly into the sky!” He’s still surprised when the environment springs to life. I’m surprised to see we’ve wandered around Kairo for over 150 hours in the last year or so.
In short, a moving experience for a parent, and a curious adventure for a child. Play it together. Appreciate the time you have together.
So really, this is a thank you note. Thank you, Richard Perrin and the rest that made Kairo possible.

One of the most excellent RPGs since the days of Fallout and Planescape: Torment. The days before dumbed down shooters became all the rage. A true must own for any hardcore RPG fan.
Plot:
The game is set in an alternate world, where a Roman-esque empire had mastered magic. The details have been lost to history, but apparently there was some sort of war that left the world in ruins. Now, hundreds of years later, modern leaders/robber barons have each set up their own little kingdoms and are vying for control over the remnants of the known world, like dogs over scraps.
The game is well written and filled with ancient secrets, plots, and intrigue - which the player may either ignore or participate in, but it will affect the game regardless. Choosing to help someone be named Emperor could cause someone else to panic and make drastic decisions. Choosing to do nothing might allow certain factions to gain more control than they would have had you intervened. Everything is connected and each choice you make or don't make will probably have some repercussions down the line. It feels really good to make choices that matter and aren't just window dressing.
Overall Gameplay:
Gameplay in this game is LARGELY based upon which skills you pick and which choices you make. A stealthy assassin working for the assassin's guild is going to meet different people and fight different battles than the cunning grifter who gets by on lies and deception. The streetwise thief is less likely to be taken in by the lies of others than a gullible mercenary.
Dialog itself might well be considered its own gameplay. Dialog is affected by your skills, but just because your skills give you an option doesn't mean that option is a generic "win button". In fact, different skills will open legitimately different paths and sometimes, a combination of skills are needed in order to achieve a certain outcome.
The game has multiple endings depending on your choices, so it really is almost as if there are several different games worth of content - and odds are that you won't be able to see all the content in one play-through, so multiple play-throughs are both recommended and enjoyable.
Combat:
For those of you waiting for a hardcore turn-based RPG that doesn't pull its punches, the past decade and a half has been full of mixed blessings and downright disappointments. Fans of the original Fallout's gameplay were told that Fallout's combat was "outdated" and Fallout 3 became a yet another shooter with RPG elements. Even the as early as 1999 Baldur's Gate and the infinity engine games gave us real-time with pause gameplay in lieu of actual turn-based gameplay - again with the excuse that turn-based games just wouldn't sell. Well, not Age of Decadence. From day one they've stuck to making a turn-based game for turn-based enthusiasts and they have succeeded brilliantly.
Combat is challenging, varied and - with the right skills and gameplay choices - completely optional. The game is single player, so it's similar to Fallout 1 & 2's turn-based gameplay - albeit with a variety of different moves and items you can use. For example, a fast attack will hit accurately, while a regular attack or a power attack will each do more damage, but be less likely to hit. You can attack multiple enemies at once with a whirlwind attack, or attack arms or legs to either trip your enemy or make them drop their weapon. Also, you can poison your weapons, use ranged weapons, throw nets, bombs or even acid. Different weapons have different options. A spear, for instance, can interrupt an enemy and hit him before he can approach you to attack. A dagger can strike faster and more often than a sword, but a big axe or a spear can strike diagonally. Because of these many options, combat can be just as much about good strategy as it is about stats.
There are no trash mobs, no rooms full of random enemies whose sole purpose is to slow you down and make the game longer. Each combat encounter is hand-designed and comes about due to the choices the player makes. Were you tricked into following the wrong sort of person into a dark alley? Well, enjoy the fight. Did you murder an Imperial guardsman? Well, his friends are going to want some payback. Did you tell the leader of an enemy army to stick his head between his legs and kiss his own rear end? You get the picture.
Overall I have to say I haven't played a game with this many choices and consequences in a long while. The fact that it has challenging combat is a welcome bonus, though many have said it's too hard.
So the question is: should you buy this game? Well, if you want your hand held, want to be guaranteed success and don't like reading, I suggest you wait until you are a bit older. To the rest of us who remember an era before player characters would magically resurrect at the end of every battle, before quest compasses let us play the game on auto-pilot, before "combat" meant mashing buttons: I say, welcome home.
If you want tactical like Ghost recon. Look elsewhere

LostWinds 2 starts exactly where LostWinds 1 left off.  Early in the game you find your long lost mother from the former game, but she can't be free until you save the kingdom from a curse. Eventually, the wind power receives upgrades to be able to have whirlwinds, the ability to blow fire, and much much more.  There is one new power that is offered in this game that was not offered in the previous game.  The addition of seasons also really drastically changes the gameplay as water that once could be swam through is no longer swimmable when it's a block of ice.
The story takes a backseat to the metroidvania like gameplay as you seek out treasures, new skills, and answers to the curse you are trying to solve.  There is a lot of back and forth, and this time the puzzles and monsters are a bit tougher.  I enjoyed it, it's very kid friendly as far as graphics, sound, and basic gameplay, but the wind function may leave them very frustrated as it's not always intuitive and simple.  Some areas may take a few trial and error moments rather than being automatically successful.
Overall, I highly recommend the series if you're all able to deal with the kid friendly atmosphere and the not too serious or difficult gameplay.

Sometimes failing in this game can be good for you, more often then not it will just lead you to another path in the story *unless you meet an untimely demise*.
Combat is extremely hard and while being extremely well balanced its balanced for veterans who played this game for ages, meaning this is like DoTA 3.0 - unless you know what you are doing you might not have as good of a time as you might desire. I might add that while it might seem that combat is unnecessarily hard at 1st in reality its done in a way to draw a line to what content your hero might see in the game.
Generally speaking there are 2 playstyles - social and combat. There are hybrid builds in the middle of them, but they are vastly harder to pull off then either of the main playstyles.
On the bright side - there is a lot of content and variability to the game * apart from neutral quests*. You will need at least 7 playthroughs to see 100% of the game. So there is that going for the game. There are a lot of choice and consequence decisions which GENUINELY MATTER. Yes im looking at you, ME3.
Its created by a really small but dedicated team and main developer is as down to customer as it can get pretty much. Basically - 'our guy'. So do support this awesome game, - yes it has its flaws, graphics are dated, there are errors and some imbalances, but the devs LISTEN to the community and change the game accoardingly, while maintaining the 'artistic integrity' making it for one hell of an experience.
TL DR:
Story 9/10 Original, Fun, Extremely realistic.
Gameplay 7/10 Somewhat flawed and unnecessarily hard at times.
Sound 6/10 Some of the tracks are not as good as others.
Graphics 3/10 ♥♥♥♥♥♥ customisation is included here aswell, but its engine limited.
Likeability 10/10 The game wins a lot of points by the overall spirit and charisma of it, - its a hand crafted and balanced world with a  lot of reworks based on community feedback.
Final Score: 8/10 The game loses points just because of how hard it is to get into it initially and the cummulative problems in it.
10/10 if you are a hard core RPG player and a MUST HAVE, otherwise its still a great purchase.
Absolutely recommended for purchase.

Civilization Beyond Earth is the latest Civ game from Firaxis, a company that feels like they can do no wrong - for years they've put out quality games and expansion packs that substantially improved those games and though some changes to the formula have upset some fans, most have found each new game to be better than the last. Have Firaxis built another wonder? Hit the link to find out!
The obvious comparison is the absolutely titanic Alpha Centauri, which also bears Sid Meier's name, and I can safely say that Beyond Earth is absolutely not a spiritual sequel, copy or otherwise related to Alpha Centauri. Beyond Earth is more like a space theme tacked on to the Civilization 5 framework. If you're looking for a brand new Alpha Centauri scale experience, look elsewhere.
Beyond Earth opens with a rather spectacular cinematic that shows off amazing pre-rendered footage of refugees and soldiers and rockets spewing smoke and dust everywhere as they take off to get you hyped for the game. It's one of the standout introduction videos from recent times and well worth seeking out on its own even if you don't intend on buying the game.
Sadly the graphical marvels end there; some assets from Civilization 5 have been shamelessly re-used, most notably the ice and shoreline effects but there's more hidden in there. It's kind of a Where's Wally, except instead of a bespectacled skinny git you've got all the things a lazy art department left laying about.
Some of the buildings look nice, though cities don't grow into the sprawling, wonder-dotted metropolises seen in Civilization 5. Wonders don't seem to show up at all, in the other Civilization games the wonders always appeared on the map (most notably the pyramids having a propensity for appearing in the sea) but Beyond Earth seems to forego the drawing of wonders at all beyond a little pop-up with a blueprint concept style drawing and blurb of text.
One graphical choice I can really commend is the level of detail afforded to the combat units; they're far more detailed than previous entries, with not just higher quality skins but also models that don't look like an amateur wood carving. There's also an impressive amount of difference between the visual styles of the units for the three different development paths, even if they don't have any significant functional or statistical differences.
That said, there's the small issue of units of the same type looking too similar, for example a marine squad and gunner squad side by side may as well be the same unit, only distinguishable by taking a close up look if it weren't for the floating symbols above their heads.
The units are tied to your research progress, now divided up beyond multi-tiered nodes in a kind of spider-web of technologies with various vaguely sci-fi sounding names like Xenobiology. You unlock units and unit upgrades via researching various nodes and sub-nodes on this web with the three affinity specific ones (Harmony, Purity, Supremacy) being marked with icons to make them stand out.
The problem with this web over the old tech tree style research is that it's confusing. Plain and simple works, the tech tree used to show how technologies progressed from developing paper to writing to the printing press it was all a logical and easily understandable progression. In Beyond Earth you just have a jumble of technologies loosely grouped by their overall role (things like "ballistics") that don't seem to have any kind of logical progression or clear organization to the way they're laid out.
The usability of this research web is also hampered by the descriptions and names disappearing in favour of pointless icons that display zero information if you scroll out only a little bit. Imagine if you were trying to read a family tree but you had to have your face so close to the paper that you could only read one or two names at once, and if you back up a little all the names and information disappear and turn into shapes that mean nothing - that's what the technology web is.
In addition to the research you also have the Virtues, Beyond Earth's equivalent of Civilization 5's Social Policies. They're even earned exactly the same way, by generating culture.
Thankfully these are arranged far more sensibly; there's four columns, each relating to a different aspect of play (might, prosperity, knowledge, industry) with a RPG-style tree of nodes that provide immediate buffs to different aspects. In addition to the individual nodes, you have synergies both in-virtue and cross-virtue which are unlocked by simply getting a certain amount of nodes either vertically in a single virtue or horizontally across multiple virtues.
Though fairly basic and not even remotely as in-depth as Civilization 5's social policies, and completely lacking and unlockable virtues, I did enjoy this aspect of the game. You get Virtues from culture at a fairly decent rate even if you're not focusing on deliberately earning them, which allows you to tailor the bonuses you earn to the current situation far more fluidly than the old social policies system and its method of linking you to a particular play style.
There's 7 Heavenly Virtues, but I think they ran out of different colours half way through.
Individual civilizations aren't fixed quantities either, upon starting a game the player is able to choose a sponsor, set of colonists, cargo and space-ship type which determines a set of four bonuses the player receives at the start of the game. These can be production or culture boosts, starting with extra energy (money, it's just Civ 5's gold rebranded) or more immediate benefits such as having coastlines mapped from the start, a larger landing zone to choose from or having the alien nests marked on the map at the start of the game.
Though the customization is welcome, the selections are sparse, there's only eight sponsors and the other categories only have four or five entries each and ultimately feel inconsequential - you'd be hard pressed to notice any significant difference if you just chose random when setting up a came as opposed to actually customizing your stuff.
The custom civilizations feature could have been an amazing addition if it had been more fleshed out, but as it is it's a step back from just choosing from a set of predefined civilizations.
Unfortunately this lack of choice bleeds into the actual gameplay, with only eight sponsors to choose from there can only be a maximum of eight players in a game so even the largest Beyond Earth games feel like the smallest Civilization 5 matches.
Also affected is the diplomacy aspect, without well defined civilizations the leaders are just blank slates with random personalities each time. Personality is a generous word though, they're about as complicated as a puppy, showing you heaps of love so long as you keep feeding them your excess resources.
Going to war in Civilization 5 could mean centuries of strife for all involved, with military production ramping up and civilian health taking a back-seat to siege weapon construction. In Beyond Earth it feels like kicking the aforementioned puppy.
I had one stand-out war in particular where I was playing Harmony and had zero military units, an aggressive civilization declared war and was promptly beaten by my neighbor, which prompted the warmonger to open negotiations for peace - offering a straight 10 turn peace treaty to which I demanded the addition of two of his largest cities, mostly to♥♥♥♥♥♥him off further. To my surprise the AI didn't say no or even make a counter-offer and instead rolled belly up and surrendered his two most powerful non-capital cities to me without so

This game is very similar to Civilization: V, but has a lot of new features added. I really like the sponsors and other options you have in the beginning. They really makes it varied every time I start a new game. The quests are very interesting as well. giving you goals to go for, while you are building up your empire. I enjoy playing this game overall, but this game does miss a lot of (in my opinion) obvious features (which Civ V did have):
Completed build:
When a city has finished a unit or building it doesn't get shown anywhere. This is annoying especially when you have a lot of cities.
The option to turn of Aliens:
While they are interesting with their semi-passive behavior, they are in some games a nuisance. Blocking paths and not moving at all for many, many turns.
Tech Tree:
I find myself most of the time lost in the tech tree. Wonders, buildings and so on are indicated with bland grey icons.
Tiles:
I often put my units on Miasma tiles on accident, since it's so hard to distinguish from especially the forest tiles. In some worlds it's also hard to distinguish a desert tile from a plains tile... especially for someone with bad eyesight this is going to be a nuisance.
Resource Tiles:
Something we did have in Civ V and I did (shouldn't have) take for granted was that when we hover over a resource tile we get to see if we have the correct tech unlocked for that. We don't have that in Civ BE and I often waste turns because of it.
The game overall is definitely enjoyable, with a few little nuisances, and I don't regret buying this.

It's been a while since I wrote a review, mainly bauce I only want to do proper ones, but don't expect any pro structure.
Ill just be noting down what I was thinking while playing this in one go.
Graphics - Basic Pixelart just like in the old times. At times hard to recognize which tiles you can pass through and whichones block you off, but you'll get used to it as they stay the same during game.
Soundtrack - Nothing bad, nothing special either. Fits the atmosphere and its purpose. Didnt get stuck in my ears tho.
Characters - Not much depth to them due to lack of dialogues. Still pretty unique tho and no stereotypes. Except for maybe Sara.
Legnth - I've been playing through easymode and it took me around 2h. Normal and Hard probably will take a fair amount longer and you also have an extra gamemode to check.
Combat - Classic turnbased RPG style as you should know from Earthbound and other series. Has it's own little detail tho as you can build up a combo and finish it off with 1 big attack dealing more dmg with higher numbers.
Leveling - Goes fairly fast and even at the end you will still receive enough xp to level up every 10-20 fights.
A lot of fun to grind while you can choose your own spells and levelups.
At times they will give you an option between HP or MP, or ask you if you want a stronger single-target spell or rather an AoE spell.
Humour - This is where the game really shines. You can't explain it unless you get stuck in the story yourself.
Dungeons - This is where I'm a little disappointed. The Dungeons start off really long, dont increase in complexity or length during your adventure and offer 0 puzzles. You basically have 1 labyrinth after an other and/or get forced to walk miles and miles just to get more randomencounters to make the game last longer. + They take so many turns that it is basically impossible to get any idea of their map in your head.
Don't get me wrong. They werent exactly difficult. Just really frustrating.
They left me with a "an other f*ing dungeon... yay... more walking...." thought.
Enemies - You have a lot of different troops to fight in each area. So it won't start to be boring.
I can't tell you if they were any different in combat tho. I didnt need any elemental weakness or special strategy for any enemy.
Not even for the bosses. Just a little bit grinding here, and a lot of AoE there.
Story - Can't really say much there... I kinda missed the depth as it's supposed to be an RPG but you can still summarize the entire mission in 2-3 sentences. But I guess I'm a bit spoiled from other RPGs.
All in All - For that price? Completly worth it. Like really. Its less than a coffee in germany.
So decide for yourself if you want to pay for a snack or have several hours of entertainment.

This game is a bit of a mixed bag for me. On one hand you have the great concept, music, and art style then in the other you have touchy controls, bad hit-detection, and poor registering of objects making dying something that will happen by no fault of your own sometimes. This game is one of my favorite action stealth heisters I've ever played, with awesome upgrades, fun parkour (if the wall clinging works the way you want it to), and a great steampunk aesthetic to boot; there's not much to go wrong with this game it may seem. Well... here's the part where I give this game some tough love; it gets extremely frustrating in the worst ways it could've done so. Sometimes when you jump to a wall, instead of clinging you'll fall down in the middle of a horde of robots, you can easily kill yourself by using the EMP on a roof and having it collapse like an explosion, the robot's vision can sometimes glitch through a door you're waiting behind and ruin the heist, etc. After dealing with enough of this BS myself, I have become quite good at being patient and just not killing myself due to this games bad controls, but still new players will find that their jump disappeared when going down stairs and they walk into the spikes on the ground. The game makes you buy the upgrade the hack terminals, but the first level can sometimes not have enough money to get a 100 pound upgrade which is stupid and frustrating. Nevertheless, I love this game even for all it's flaws and if it's on sale and you love fast-paced, action, stealth, steampunk, roguelike heists, then I believe you should give it a play.
If there's anything you believe you can add to this review or criticize, then please leave a comment though keep it civilized and constructive.

I don't usually write reviews but I feel like this is warranted.
It took me two runs to beat the game. I actived the final heist about 10 times across both runs. I'll focus on the 9 failed runs because they sum up my issues with the game. There are needed upgrades in order to beat the game. You MUST have the hacking upgrades to access security terminals, and max number of bombs / extended range of the explosives. The heist does not tell you this. I was wasting my time, during my first run, rolling the dice for a map of the $400,000 heist with each purchase hoping for a map that I would be able to complete. It didn't work.
The bombs and upgrades aren't my only issue though. There were several times where I got stuck in solid ground after I had nearly stole a quater million from one of the later areas. I died in several scenarios because my character was still seemingly in the air even though they were on the ground and I wasn't able to move out of the way to avoid detection.
The controls are also terrible. Your character feels like they are on ice 90% of the time and you keep slipping and sliding down stairs, roofs, and right into some type of trap.
The map generation just makes all of these issues even worse. As I mentioned before with the rng maps for the final heist, you run the risk of wasting not only money but your time with each mission you go on. Some of the earliest zones have terminals that were seemingly made by termites and need several bombs to get acces to, but can't because you don't have bombs or their upgrades, so you end up leaving early to roll the dice again and hope for a map with more accessible terminals.
This game becomes so much about the upgrades that the start makes you feel like a bull sneaking his way into a china shop that specializes in wind charms, fire alarms, and flood lights hooked up to miniguns. By the end, you are casually strolling in as you cause everything within a 30 yard radius to just explode and clear the way for you. The game is too focused on upgrades to enforce the skill based heists it's aiming to allow the player to feel. It's a mess.
Rouge-likes work when they can mix skill and the player's ability to adapt to changing variables. For The Swindle, it's focused on upgrades to the point that you can't even start the game without upgrades. You need the upgrade for hacking terminals to even play the game since that's your primary source of income and you have no hope of being the game without it. Establishing early how dependent you are on these upgrades in order to progress.
I like what The Swindle attempts to do. I can see what it's going for and I mostly enjoyed my time with the game, but these flaws are so glaring that following runs can just be replaced with going to a casino and playing slots.

A fitting end to the arc of Dishonored 1&2 but suffers from many of the same problems Dishonored 2 had.
+ Lurk and Daud are an interesting duo and a good choice for a final chapter
+ Simplified powers and mana regen focus the gameplay
+ Foresight is a much needed evolution of Darksight + interaction with Displace is great
+ Final mission has great atmosphere - reminds me of some of the later levels of Thief 2
+ Supplemental reading material is great as always - nice way to get epilogues on many of Dishonored's stories
+ Contract system nice way to add secondary objectives
+ Talk to rats!
- Reused maps - for the price it was a little disappointing to see mission 2 & 3 use the same hub and mission 4 is just a reskinned map from Dishonored 2
- Bonecharm system a little unpolished (so many useless ones) + bonecharm system comes out of nowhere (was blocked off for most of the game and then it was suddenly unlocked for the final mission?  Did I miss an earlier unlock?  Why was it locked to begin with?)
- Levels lacked the innovation we saw in Dishonored 2 (nothing close to the Jindosh mansion or "A Crack in the Slab")
- Performance is pretty much on par with Dishonored 2 which is not ideal - I hope Arkane works on a Void Engine v2 before they decide to use it again
- Original game+ purports the ability to play again with Dishonored 2 abilities but then limits its to THREE (Blink, Darksight, Domino)
- Rats never shut up
I do recommend the game if you love Dishonored as much as I do - even a mediocre Dishonored outing is a good game to me - but I hope they take some time away from this universe to refocus.  Death of the Outsider has some good ideas - experimenting with a regenerative mana system and gearing powers with an eye towards how they effect your gameplay (Foresight) are good steps.  But the narrative is just as disjointed as Dishonored 2 and didn't really solidify until the final mission.  Daud's, "Billie!  We have to cook...err...kill the Outsider!" feels unmotivated, Billie's transformation really amounts to "because it's cool", her relationship to Deidre really goes nowhere for as much as she mentions her...there's tremendous oppurtunity here to create strong narrative threads but they ultimately fall flat.  It feels like Arkane is interested in crafting strong atmosphere and supplemental stories but can't wait to "yada-yada-yada" over primary character motivations in effort to cut to the action.
But all that's subjective, of course.  I'm sure there are plenty of players who don't mind and this is a video game first.  The world of Dishonored will always have my interest.  A new story in the this universe free of Corvo/Daud/The Outsider might just be what they need.

Well, that was probably the most engrossed I've been in a game for a while.  It takes me right back to "Driller" or its sequel "Far Side" which, used "Freescape", an early 3D, to evoke alien and unusual environments.   Unlike those two early games, Kairo gives no backstory, and lets you attempt to figure it out for yourself. I love it...
The whole game is extremely minimalist in its level design, but extremely evocative of space and alienness.  The aesthetics are a mix of old and new:  blocky, simplistic but with texture mapping, reflections, fog, flames and more.  The overly simplistic design may deter some who would dismiss the game as dated, but anything more complex would start to get in the way of the narrative.
It may not have been the designer's "point", but the simplicity of the environment allows you to completely ignore it, and focus more on playing the game.  And playing may not be the best definition either:  experience, discover, enjoy are also great definitions for this.
The beginning makes it look like you'll be exploring ancient egyptian ruins (albeit in a dreamy world of whiteness), before  abruptly turning grey and industrial-feeling.  The game continues to take turns and each area feels and plays a lot different.
The only time that the simplicity works against the game is when an area is more complex than it looks. After traversing a dozen empty corridors, and passing stray cubes, you may not realise that another grey unmarked stray cube is, in fact, a trigger for some action, and be left puzzling for a while.  Such "difficulty through obscurity" is a hard one to balance right, to be honest, so I'll let it off, mostly.
I think the thing I enjoy most about Kairo is that it really plays with our preconceptions of what a 3d puzzle game is.  They jokingly call one of their achievements "Locked Door Puzzle" as a nod to other more mainstream games.
I really enjoyed playing Kairo, and then with the help of a cheat to find all the secrets.. A great minimal game.  If you do decide to play it, don't try and speed-run it.  although it looks shallow and simplistic, there are a lot of hidden (or just obscure) tidbits for the explorer.

Please try this:
1. In the Steam game library, right click the game
2. Select "Properties"
3. Select the "Local Files" tab
4. Click "Verify integrity of game cache"
This has been known to easily fix the "Failed to find steam" error. If the issue persists then it is recommended you try these steps:
1. Open the Start Menu, right click "Computer", and select "Properties".
2. From the column on the left of the new panel, select "Advanced System Settings".
3. From the new dialogue, press "Environment Variables..." (at the bottom of the "Advanced" panel, just above "OK", "Cancel", and "Apply").
4. In the top half of the newly opened dialogue (User variables) if there is:
a - no existing entry for PATH, use "New..." to add it (Variable Name: PATH, Variable Value: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam -- i.e. wherever you have Steam installed).
b - already an entry for PATH, use "Edit..." to add ;C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam (or wherever your Steam is installed) at the end of the existing value. (Note the semi-colon to separate the value that was already there from the new bit with the Steam path.)
5. Press "OK"
6. Log off and log on again. You should now be able to run the Steam titles without problems.
If you have further issues I suggest you contact Steam Support as there may be issues with your Steam Client.
After that the game will start, but it can be really slow ( about 1 FPS), try than setting at highest possible graphic settings and check box called 'User Direct3D'. It starts on fullscrean, but it is slightly smaller than your whole monitor, so it should allow you to run it and enjoy that great game!

Kairo is a game about exploration and puzzle-solving, but it is also much more than that. Kairo is something that demands your full attention. It is a game that you play in the dark, all alone. You won't be killing zombies or assassinating kings in Kairo, but you will be exploring a strange, impossible world filled with perplexing architecture.
The ambiance is unsettling, and even threatening at times. The music (written by Wounds) is alienating and absolutely beautiful. The graphics are simple, but this simplicity fits in perfectly in making you feel that you are truly in a foreign world; a place you do not understand. For those of us with low end computers, you'll find this to be a pleasantly smooth running game.
At its core Kairo is a puzzle game. Some puzzles are easy and won't strain you too badly, but others are so hard it's almost unrealistic to think any player could solve them on their own (looking at you, Clock Room). Each puzzle is intuitive though, and they always make sense after you solve them (even you, Clock Room).
Luckily if you get hopelessly stuck, each puzzle has three hints and the solution to help you along.
The story is what really ties the elements of Kairo together. From the start you'll have many questions: Where am I? Why am I here? WHO am I? Will these questions be answered? Well, that depends on you. There is little to no dialogue in Kairo. The story is expressed entirely through the environment and the things that you see. If you want to understand this place you're in, then you must actively think about the actions you take, and how they're affecting the world around you. There are answers to your questions, but Kairo leaves it entirely up to you to find them. If you take the time to uncover the mystery, you'll be glad that you did.
Kairo is a game that not everyone will love. But for those who do, it is a masterpiece. It is the kind of game that sticks with you long after you finish it. I wholeheartedly recommend Kairo.

This is actually really good.  I bought this looking for a way to format, and it works perfectly for me.  Although its chapter formatting isn't unique -- I can do the same on Google Docs -- I like being able to have notes on the side and a word count per chapter and per day in the corner.  You can fully flesh out characters.  And if you're like me and usually free - write rather than plan or storyboard, the sidenotes and character notes give your writing a little more strucutre, letting you add layers of detail and intricacies to your work.  It also feels really good writing.  As of this review, it says I only have 1.6 hours.  Maybe it's because I use it mostly in offline mode, but I've already gotten 6 chapters of 2 - 3k words down in a week while juggling other jobs.  Overall, it's a good alternative to Scrivener, and Microsoft Word is just an overpriced piece that doesn't offer the customization a writer needs in one program.
Pros:
- Chapter Management
- Side Notes
- Character Development Template
- Fullscreen
- Customizable
- Fairly User Friendly
Cons:
- Chapter Managment is clunky.  If you want to reorganize, you have to click on a tab, then click "Move Up" one at a time.
- Format feels like you're writing a blog rather than a book.
- Difficult to learn how to use at first, since there isn't any tutorial or guidance.
- Spell check is wonky.  I advise copypasta into a different program for spellcheck.

Having played the original Stronghold Cusader extensively, when I initially played this game I thought this was a dumbed down version of the original however there is more to this game than that.
I feel that this game is somewhat more balanced in the sense that stalemate seems to be less common, I attribute this to the fact that walls and towers are less powerful (and significatly more expensive) and archers on towers can be killed much more easily than in the original.
Another element which was improved in this second iteration of this game is the UI. The UI in the 1st game was already quite good, however this time around the UI tells you more information such as food generated vs food eaten and
In addition to this there are elements that make the game much more accessable and remove some of the quirks usually associated with older titles such as the clunky engineer system and confusing camera rotation.
There are some elements which I miss form the original game, such as the fear factor system, the moats and the somewhat more advanced walling and tower system.
In Conclusion I think that this game is better that it is made out to be, I understand this is not the ideal successor to Stronghold Crusader however it does improve on some key areas that make the game feel more polished.

Nimble Writer has the misfortune of sitting between free/cheap alternative that have most of the same features, while not having enough features on its own to satisfy the requirements of anyone who takes writing seriously. If you're a serious writer, Scrivener is a no-brainer despite being $40. If you're not, you'd probably do just as well with any number of free tools instead of spending $10 on this.
The deal breakers, for me, are the lack of real-time spellcheck and that the exporters are not perfectly reliable. If it actually supported spell checking in the way every Windows application more powerful than Notepad does, or it reliably exported documents without crashing or formatting corruption, I could give it a weak recommendation. But those two issues - which have existed for years - make it impossible to recommend this application

I honestly don't even know how or where to start with this game. It has no form of tutorial, guide, basic series of single player practice sessions to show you what you get with the game, what you have, game modes, anything. It is basically just a very very old school pick a series pick a car, hit race....that's pretty much it. I find it quite surprising that it has so many users with such a bad interface and menu structure. As a user you honestly don't know where to start.
After some trial and error I eventually discovered that most cars need to be bought, you only get....actually I don't know what you get because it doesn't list anywhere how many or which cars you do get. It's just such a bad user experience. Even ACR with all its problems and browser client mishmash was far supperior.
The first time I started it I basically just got the background cinematics and no menu. After googling around I found that you have to set a start parameter for the steam version. Why isn't this set as standard? Didn't I just install the game through steam?
So after you eventualy get it to work, you have to wonder if you actually have any sound, because there are no effects what so ever in the menu. No clicking efects, no music, no nothing. I played around with my volume until I entered a race and it was too loud.
And finaly we come to the actual driving experience....well...if you use a controller or keyboard you are basically hosed. The cars are mostly unconstrollable unless you have a wheel, and even then I'm not sure the default settings are ok. After much fiddling around with sensitivities, adaptive steering speeds and other settings, I managed to get a relatively ok setting. It worked fine for the car I was using at the time, but as soon as I changed cars, well I needed to see what I could do again.
The menu/interface thing is quite buggy and unintuitive. You have a back button to go back to the game and if you hit back inside the game, as in to go back to the main menu...it takes you back into the matchmaking menu...so basically and infinite loop of back buttons.
Now on to the plus points:
After trying out multiple cars, I do have to admit you could "feel" when one car was heavyer, or lighter, or had softer suspension and that is a very very good thing. It becomes pretty obvious that underneath the bad interface it is running a very good simulation engine.
On the polish oldtimer you can feel the heavy engine at the back trying to oversteer the car. On different DTM cars of the same era/class you can feel the different personlity of each car. I really like that. For example you can tell the Audi V8 is very heavy compared to the Merc 190 or the M3, you can feel that the Mustang has much softer suspension but is stil quite light. The FWD cars do understear in slow corners, and they do lift off oversteer just like they should. Dips in the road do make your car unstable and sometimes create wheelspin (this also sais a lot about the quality and detail of the tracks). This is especially noticeable on some longer high speed corners. The vibrators on the side of the track do unsettle your car and can make it jump up in the air.
So yes, the racing engine underheath is very very good.
The graphics do look good for a racing game. There's not much to say about them. Everything runs smoothly no stutters, high FPS. The amount of detail given to the sound during racing is quite high. It has suspension and pannel squeking.
I'm quite dissapointed to be honest, I really liked all their previous games and those did have much better interfaces and functionality. This is just slopy in so many ways.
From what I have played so far I am tempted to try it some more just because that surprisingly good engine underneath that crap interface. I haven't yet found out how exacly you enter a multiplayer race, there are some challenges and some servers, but instructions are scarce at best. I don't even think there is any form of experience or leveling, but if there is, I wasn't able to find it.

I don't often review games (or anything else), but with all the thumbs down this has gotten I decided it needed my input.  First let me say that I raced real cars for 9 years on both ovals and road courses. I've also sim raced on and off since about 1992.  I'm not an expert on sim racing, but I've tried most of the major players and R3E is among the very best -- I find the physics to be superb, at least when used with a good wheel and pedals.  I can't comment on how it plays on kb, controller or anything else and frankly I don't care.
One of the problems with sim racing is how to represent the loss of traction that one *feels* in the real world through balance, touch and seat of the pants. A common perception in the sim world is that a game is realistic when it is very difficult, but the real world isn't like that -- vehicles only get very difficult close to the limit.  I think R3E does an admirable job of balancing difficulty without crossing the line into "arcade".  Is it better than iRacing or Assetto Corsa? I don't know....that's really on a car-by-car basis for me, but some of them are better and none that I've driven are really bad (and even iRacing has had some stinkers).
I also don't think the "free to play" system is that bad.  You can have some great fun without ever buying anything!  Certain track and car combinations are always available (for free!) in the "competitions".  These are really just hot-lap contests, but they are fun and you get to try out the content.....and it is still free.  Raceroom is expensive if you buy all the DLC, but I just don't see a need for that -- just buy whatever series you want to race in, and if you are really cheap just by one car in each class.  Either way it is still a lot cheaper than iRacing.
The downsides of Raceroom:
-the severs are usually empty, but then I don't use this for online racing.
- the AI can be a bit aggressive, but are otherwise pretty good.
-can't save setups (really????).  I've heard this is coming in the next update

I've played every Civ game including Alpha Centauri.  I'm a pretty big fan of the games in general, but this one is a lame duck in my opinion.   The tech tree is messy and nonsensical, there are no faction specific units or buildings, and the unit progression is lame.  It is in every way significantly less good of a game than Alpha Centauri.  The fluff is boring, the end game is boring, the world interaction is boring.   Even though Alpha Centauri was an alien world,  it was easy to 'understand'.  The tech blurbs were sensible, the 'memoirs' phase of leadership added great fluff, units were awesomely customizable, the tech tree made sense.
Beyond Earth doesn't make much sense, doesn't really seek to appeal to the user.   Building a wonder feels boring.  Resources feel somehow both boring and disconnected.
It is literally like they took the worst parts of Civ 5 and the worst parts of Alpha Centauri and made a game from that.
There are some tiny UI improvements, I guess.

This is more of an "ehhh..." than a strict Thumbs Down- Kairo offers a sort of first person linked-chamber exploration game with simple puzzles unlocking further exploration. Lacking mechanical depth or logical difficulty (there's a lot of obvious "stand here, then touch there" stuff, though perhaps more lurking beneath the surface beyond my grasp), the puzzles generally feel like a bit of vestigial interactivty left there to regulate progression through the game's strengths of envrionment and atmosphere. Each area proffers a unique bit of architecture, either a room or  monument suspended in the void; In tandem with the monochromatic color scheme and sound design, the effect is rather evocative, but of nothing more particular than the tingly excitement of meandering through an abandoned alien kinetic sculpture garden.
Kairo exhausted my patience due to the tedium of its puzzling elements, but it could be worth exploring if you dont mind and find the screenshots compelling (if you do mind, I suggest Kairo's obverse, Antichamber- its world isn't exactly poetic, but does have a practical charm in service of the brain-bending environmental puzzling Kairo lacks.)

There are two ways to approach Kairo. The first is to view it as a meditative experience in an open world with many soothing  environments and lots of exploration. The second view is to see it as a string of puzzles that need to be solved to complete and beat the game.
You'll enjoy it either way you view it. If you decide to explore, you will see many different areas, and come to love the fact that you can hide away in the world of Kairo and relax after a long day. Walk around in the Park, look at the alien structures, and relax to the calm sounds of water rushing, or birds chirping.
And if you take it as a string of puzzles, you will be challenged with a system with no interaction button, with clues to guide you when you are lost. You will push things, pull things, and eventually get the machines that govern the world of Kairo running.
And be treated to a delightful and uplifting ending.

By the definition of MOBA (Multiplayer Online Battle Arena), Dungeon Defenders is one. Dungeon Defenders took this one step further, and added in Tower Defense to the mix. Makes for a nice variation of available playstyles, ranging from tactical tower placement, to full-on onslaught physical offense. Enjoyable little chibi-style characters give the game an entertaining environment. The audio tracks are very atmospheric for what's going on in-game, and most of the levels offer enough variety from one to the other to keep the game entertaining for playthrough one. However, after the initial playthrough, the game gets incredibly grindy. Having beaten most of the game on medium or hard difficulty on my first run, I ended at nearly level 50, but most of the post-game content (almost) requires levels into the seventies. Very entertaining game to grab a few friends and use for a LAN party or general multiplayer shenanigans, but can quickly become a grind-fest for any single-player fans out there.
