I'm seeing a lot of mixed reviews on this but I honestly say I love it. The setting is that you are a cat-burglar in a steampunk london tasked with hijacking an AI being developed in Scotland Yard to put yours (and fellow thieves) exploits to an end. You start off in the slum areas stealing small amounts of money, working your way up to areas with higher gain (as well as risk). The money you steal can be used to upgrade your skills and tools as well as slowing down the deployment of the AI. If you are caught or killed on a heist, you will assume the role of a new thief from there onwards.
PROs:
- Art design is gorgeous and unique
- Sound design is excellent (music and sound effects alike)
- Each level is procedurally generated so you will never have the same experience twice
- The variety of skills and tools give you more options for carrying out heists
- The variety of enemies keep heists interesting and keep you on your toes
- The gameplay is tense, thrilling and for the most part, very smooth
CONs:
- The procedural generation can cause you to become stuck or completely unable to collect any profit. It needs some refinement to take the players available tools and skill into account.
- Hitting enemies doesn't always connect. I found myself swinging at enemies whilst clearly in range and nothing happening only for them to turn around and run me down within a moment. This can be really frustrating if you have just worked for 15 minutes to clear a level of cash only to be killed because of a BS moment like that.
- The controls definitely need work. The fact they released this game a year and a half ago and still haven't resolved the occasional clunkiness of the controls really surpises me. There have been several moments where I have hit the jump or attack buttons only for nothing to happen until the second (sometimes third) hit of the button.
Overall, the game is very enjoyable and utilises a beautiful setting with some interesting mechanics. You feel compelled to continue on and complete your objective before your 100 days are up as well as a great deal of satisfaction for clearing a heist out. Although, it is apparent that the developers failed to fine-tune some mechanics. I am compelled to recommend this game though on the basis that I enjoyed it and got my moneys worth.

I've played quite a bit of this game, and without exaggerating*, I think I've come to a damn-near professional level with one character alone (Taya is super bae). Im a bit garbage at most other characters, but that in itself might be the biggest strength of the game. The skills are non-transferable. Just because I know how to trash face with one character doesn't mean Im a god a this game. It helps just as well that the game has no leveling or item system, making it 100% up to your character knowledge on how you want to approach a situation and win. If you like fast paced skill-based games, Battlerite is a must have.
All that said, the game isn't finished. Do no spend money if you value match making. Too many times I see people both above and below my own level being paired with or against me just for one side to steam roll the other. The close matches are intense, and will keep you playing, but these blow out matches are the more likely outcome and new players may find themselves frustrated. There are a few small balancing issues, namely with the more recent updates, though I feel those will be more or less weeded out as the game hits f2p.
Overall, I give this game a solid 8/10 for its fantastic visuals, unique cast of characters, and fast paced gameplay.

Possibly one of the most balanced skill-based MOBA-esque games of all time.  A few characters are top-tier and can't really be solo'd by lower-tiers and some match-ups are just outright unwinnable even with a good duo/trio (leading me to wonder exactly how the matching system works), but most times I feel like I had a chance and could have brought a potential win from what ended up as a loss.  Unlike some MOBAs in which the odds are stacked against you instantly and you have to spend the next half-hour wallowing in self-pity while you're getting creamed, some of the time when you lose in Battlerite is going to be partly your own fault but it will be MOSTLY the difference in skill.
Don't blame your teammates, blame your cooperation.  Don't flame your teammates, calm down and think rationally for a moment.  Chances are, there is something logical behind your loss because that's just the kind of game this is.

The options you have in this game is so immense, its replay value is outstanding, the amount of things I missed the first time really changed the game the second time through. From tricking an entire religion into believing you are the 'Chosen one', to saving a god trapped in eternal fog, killing anyone who enters it.
From an honest review I would rate this a 8/10, its not the best RPG, but its one of the top in my books.

This game is great! Very addictive swordplay and a great deal of challenge as you go on. If you're into FPS and hack and slash this game is perfect. It's not overly cinematic and focuses more on actual gameplay (which is what games should be) so that means more bloody and less talky but that's not to say the story isn't interesting.
However there are a few minor flaws I find a bit annoying in this game. The controls can get a little bit awkward at times. To perform certain special Katana/magic moves you have to double tap either of the WASD keys and hold the RMB or LMB at the same time and it works fine but sometimes when you're in a tight situation, it's hard to pull off certain special moves since you're constantly moving and trying to double tap the corresponding WASD buttons at the same time. I can't count how many times I've been killed trying to pull off the healing magic (double tap the 'D' key and hold RMB) while trying to get away from enemies.
It's also hard to figure out sometimes where you're supposed to go next. Although the game is linear and straighforward, it's still hard to find you're way around the next level except for a glowing door but sometimes it's almost impossible to locate the doors especially when you get into a larger and more vast level since there is no navigation or map system but I guess it's another way of making you explore the game more and find secrets which the game is full of.
Also the game can get a bit repetitive but the great gameplay more than makes up for it. If you have a few bucks to spare and a lust for blood and carnage then this game is worth every penny!

I cannot recommend this game enough. Great difficulty, immersive dystopian roman game world, good characters and storylines, lots of different ways to play. If you are looking for a challenging tactical rpg with great replay value this is it. If you want to feel godlike and wade through dead enemies, I'd head elsewhere.
1) High difficulty/you are not god. Not every fight/situation is win-able sometimes it's best to avoid an area/quest/person. I love this because it really enhances a feeling of realism/roleplay.
2) Immersive dystopian game world with tons of lore and a basis in roman history. I think that speaks for itself.
3) Characters and storylines. This definitely added to the immersion. Characters have their own personalities and motivations and on top of that, it always feels like everyone is trying to attain those goals (and stay alive, of course).
4) Lots of different ways to play. This should probably be at the top. While there are 8 "origins" you can choose to do pretty much anything you want with those origins. Want to be a thief with no sneak or lockpick and opt for disguise and persuasion? Go ahead. Want to completely screw with the system and play a hammer wielding, shield bearing thief with 0 social/subterfuge skills? Sure (though you may not last long if you keep thieving). But let's sum it up this way, I have 5 different Assassin files. Every single one is following a completely different path (some more succesfully than others).
To be fair there are a couple of issues I have with the game as it stands now (early Feb 2014). I'm sure others have mentioned many of these (although the game is still a work in progress so hopefully these will be fixed):
1) saves are sometimes problematic. You can't save during combat (good), but sometimes you don't get to save between combats or for prolonged periods of dialogue which can cause you to repeat certain game sections more than necessary. Also autosaves would've been helpful.
2) heavy armor and block are almost useless (although this is possibly my incompetence). I have only ever been successful with dagger and dodge in combat. Also, dagger is overpowered (which while I do enjoy sometimes should probably be fixed).
3) Not quite enough non-combat quests for certain classes in early game (this I definitely expect to be fixed by the end)
4) This might be intentional, but sometimes you get into a conversation with someone and get stuck at a dead end of the conversation where you only have one or two options, neither of which has a chance of success, and can't back out with a neutral or non-committal answer. These are at points I wouldn't expect (as opposed to the time I screwed up and put my poor character in a death-death situation). Again, it might be intentional and if you save frequently it's not too bad.

This game is pure, unadulterated awesome.  I cannot recommend this game enough.  If you like to think, if you like significant and meaningful choice and consequence, if you like character development, great TB combat, games where you can almost completely avoid combat through dialogue (if you want), a great story, and a very interesting setting, this game is a must buy.  I, personally, would like the game more if I could have a party (that I create myself).  This is a single character game like Fallout, Diablo, Lionheart, etc.
Also, as significant pros for me, this game has almost zero filler combat, and every battle is done for a reason.  There is no endless hordes of enemies, and there is no walking around smashing endless hordes of barrels filled with health potions and gold.  This game removed all the tripe from your garden variety RPG, and gave us a sensible game, in a realistic setting, and it all makes sense and is believable (for the most part – Mote in God’s Eye is a pretty far out there story but done believably).

I think people will enjoy this game more if they go into without pre-conceptions on how this game should be as it really turns some staples and conventions on their head.  I also think crpg fans who don’t need all the bells and whistles of the first/third person action games with rpg elements blockbusters from BioWare and Bethesda will find this game to be an instant classic with more replay value of any game I’ve ever played.

First off, everything in this review is my personal opinion and experience.  If your a casual gamer this game probably isn't for you.  Aside from having a rather non-interactive tutorial (except for the combat tutorial that is optional before you actually start the game) it also has a very steep learning curve.  Actually it's learning curve is nearly non-existent.
This is the only game that
am aware of that combat is completly optional.  This allows you to get more involved in the story and character interactions.
Combat isn't simple.  At the beginning of the game a one on one fight is about as much as you can handle.  If you end up against two people it's going to be a decent fight.  If you have to face three I hope you've saved recently because unless you have back-up (which you don't very often depending on your background) You're going to end up reloading.  This adds an element of difficulty that I feel is missing in many games.  You're never going to see a Dynasty Warrior's style hero slashing through 500 enemies in this game.
I've found that you pretty much need to play a combat character or a non-combat oriented character.  Trying to do a mix of the two is nearly impossible.  You'll find yourself in situations where you aren't skilled enough to talk your way out of a fight.  And then once you get into the fight you'll end up dying because you aren't strong enough to survive the fight that you weren't able to talk your way out of the game.  I list this as a con, but also find it to be one of the more entertaining aspects of the game.  Trying to strike a balance between a smooth talker and being able to keep yourself alive in a fight, or trying to figure out which non-combat skills your assassin needs to be able to get by without losing his edge and ability to take out his targets.
Biggest flaw I've found in the game is that combat is extremely dependent on item use.  When properly applied a few nets and bolas can make an unbeatable fight a flawless victory.
Overall an enjoyable game.  Hopefully it will get some tweaks as it progresses and will improve into an even better game.

Sid Meiers Civilization Beyond Earth is somewhat of a daunting shift from the familiar Civ 5 upon first glance.  The unfimiliar map, resources, and aliens are strange and annoying first, but easy to understand after a playthrough or so.  The tech web is an interesting and welcomed change to the franchise, but is hard to adapt to and learn the best ways of advancing.  The best addition to the game is the affinities, and the new upgrade system that comes with them.  The new covert ops system is a huge enhacement from espionage in Civ 5.  The game as a whole is great but not without its flaws.  After playing alot, the game starts to feel more and more like a Civ game with a Sci-fi skin - but this isn't an entirley bad thing especially if you love Civ games like myself. I found the most annoying or bland thing was the factions that you play as.  There are only eight, which is understandable considering there are many other ways to make your faction unique, but they all seem similar and theres no unique units or personalities to set them apart. While playing I found myself getting confused as to who I was talking to during diplomacy.  Overall the good things about this game outweigh the bad, and it is a great game that will consume many hours of time for the gamer.  Its definetly not the best in the franchise, but it still delivers.

Okay, you guys who read me might say: "This guys doesn't know the f*ck he's talking about, he only has 4.4 hrs on record!"...but hear me out real quick; I've played simulation games since my young age back in the days with Gran Turismo 1 on the 1st PS system, and I can tell you that on the "sim" side of things, this game nails it badly.
1) The sounds are majestic: all the cars that I've bought for DLC and that I've heard in real life sound exactly the same...I've been waiting for a long time for this to happen in a video game (Zonda R = music to my ears, you must try that car out).
2) The graphics aren't "Project Cars"-like, but they certainly do please my eyes...
3) Its free....so you have nothing to loose...try it out with the few cars/tracks that they offer and see for yourself if you want to get into the game deeper with the tons of add-ons that they offer at a fair price for their content :)
4) It doesn't take a deadly gaming setup to run it on a decent quality and decent FPS rate (im running a GTX 750Ti, probably the most mid-range GPU u could have, with a 4th gen i5 and 8 GB of RAM, and I run the game maxed out at around 100 FPS, sometimes going down to 40-50FPS when big crashes happen).
On the negative side of things, I would recommend that, if you really like this game, you should invest in a good quality wheel (a simple low-range logitec runs like a dream on mine), but most racing simulator fans already have one just like me...
All that said, I hope this was helpfull to you, and note that this game is used by some professional drivers to test their skills on some tracks, just to prove that the simulation is mostly flawless...

An extremely good Metroidvania type game, as everyone has been saying.
Hollow Knight is stellar from start to finish, with the really serious exception of one area called "The White Palace". While most of the level design is thoughtful and well-designed, the King of this particular palace decided to fill every single hallway with saws and spike traps. To realize how stupid this particular area is, just imagine yourself playing Symphony of the Night with its silky smooth gameplay and beautiful music when all of a sudden you are yanked straight out  and forced to play Super Meat Boy for an hour. That is what that area is like and it's like a turd in a bowl of ice cream. It should honestly just be patched out of the game.
With the exception of that, the game is really great. The Metroidvania mechanics are masterful and the game is quite challenging. The story is told gradually like Dark Souls, but isn't that hard to follow for the most part. The combat system is superb and the bosses are challenging, rewarding good decision making about when to attack, when to dodge and when to heal.
All in all, with the exception of the turd they left in the game, this is probably the best indie Metroidvania yet made.

This is a game I had been looking forward to for a long time now, I love Civilization 5 but sometimes I get bored of historical stuff, you can blame the American school system for that but regardless I loved the idea of a sci-fi Civ game and I was not dissapointed.
Now many accuse it of being a Civ 5 reskin, those people have either not played it or just not played it enough, playing this like would would Civ 5 isn't exactly a good idea, with the early game being more about survival and adapting rather than straight up expanding for intance. But the biggest difference between this and Civ 5 is the sheer amount of personalization one can put into their colony to truly make it their own, in the beginning rather than picking the civ with the nicest looking bonuses you pick your sponsor, your colonists, your cargo, a special feature for your ship and then finally choose a planet. From there the tech web and affinity system allow even more personalization, with the tech web being used to develop what you need at that moment to survive and the affinity you prefer influencing the look and abilities of your civ as you develop and the quest system sort of guiding you to some sort of end goal. The other civs that show up have all of those same options, and because of that games can proceed in wildly different ways which make for good story swapping sessions between friends.
It isn't perfect but it's pretty close in my opinion. The one more turn feeling is alive and well here

Allow me to preface this review by stating that I have used MANY writing programs over the years; Word, Writer, Scrivener, various other writing-specific programs and of course, Notepad++. Each of these programs offers features that are executed better within their environment than in the others, so when I bought Nimble Writer, I wasn't expecting much. In fact, I was actually expecting to have a difficult time getting into using it, since a wrting program being available on Steam, which as a writer and gamer, usually plays the role of the antagonist to my desire to write something worthwhile, seemed kind of strange.
I mean come on! A writing program on Steam? Seriously?
Well, I was wrong. Nimble Writer has a welcoming feel to it that many others lack, which is why when I opened it for the first time today with the intention of writing (I'd opened it once before just to peruse the features a bit), I was able to block out everything around me and put down over 2500 words in one sitting, which is great in my opinion.
Could I have written the same amount in Notepad++? Of course, but that's not the point, is it? This program was completely new to me, and in my first sitting, I was able to be extremely productive while working on my novella (hopefully a novel at some point, but that's neither here nor there). I even managed to utilize the character notes, and the wikipedia notes (which I found particularly helpful in keeping me focused on the task at-hand.
Nimble Writer has an inviting layout, distraction-free design and tools enough to get your work done.
In short: I highly recommend this program for anyone out there looking for a writing program that doesn't overwhelm you with its array of tools, but has enough of them to allow you to rarely (if ever) leave its environment for something you may need; because lets face it, once you step away from the word processor, that's where there be dragons lying in wait to torch any dream you ever had of completing a story in a timely fashion.

Nimble Writer is a general-purpose writing program that is comparable to other writing programs at a much lower cost.
I personal quite enjoy Nimble Writer for all my writing purposes. I use it to write essays for my English class. I use it to write scripts for possible videos. I also use it to write reviews for Steam (and yes, I am using Nimble Writer to write this review).
Nimble Writer is, at its base, a very simplistic and straight forward writing program. Nimble Writer markets itself as a distraction-free writing tool with full-screen capabilities in order to further distance yourself from distractions such as social media. With the Steam Workshop (more on that later), you can customize and change the backgrounds, fonts, colors, and more as you please. I personally use a space-themed background which I feel is very inspiring. Everyone has different preferences for what background they use IF they choose to use one.
There is no audio in Nimble Writer. I personally would love a built in music player that I could use without having to alt-tab out of Nimble Writer to something that can distract me from writing, but alas, some people would prefer to write in silence, alone with their thoughts. It's all up to your personal preference.
There is no gameplay in Nimble Writer. However, there are many features in Nimble Writer that I quite enjoy using. For example, you can use the "Notes" section built into Nimble Writer if you need the inspiration to write. You can have anything you want in the notes. Whether you want to have an image of something that you want to base a character on, or a quite jot list of features of a monster. The amount of tools built into Nimble Writer are very helpful, and the distraction-free overlay of the software itself is a great bonus over other writing tools.
One of Nimble Writer's greater advantages over other general writing tools (besides its low price) is it's Steam Workshop compatibility. You can add various different things in order to improve your writing experience and even the quality of your writing. Although I haven't been writing Fiction, I have added several extensions to the Notes feature in order to organize notes on different things such as Clans, Races, or Monsters. You can add exporters for different websites such as
.
Nimble Writer is one of the best writing tools I have ever used. Although there is a lot to be improved and new things to be added, Nimble Writer has the Steam Workshop to continue backing it up even if the Developer abandons it. If you like writing and want to be less distracted, Nimble Writer is the way to go.

As of Oct 24, 2014, this is very much a "wait and see" game. Things that Civ 5 had done well and refined, basic things, are missing from Beyond Earth (BE). There is currently an insultingly passive AI, missing end-of-game replay/continue feature, no diplomacy web, no demographic rankings, no ability to lock citizens to a hex. Lots of really basic stuff. Oh, and do you want to know what all the possible techs/improvements for a given hex are so you have an idea of the hex's potential? Forget it. All of the improvements made to the Civ 5 AI to make it challenging for the player are apparently gone. I was not challenged by the AI on my road to victory at any point. It was completely passive.
Even the new systems aren't all that compelling; the upgrade system is just about the only thing that stands out as an improvement. The orbital layer is nice enough but has limited usefulness unless you're clearing out miasma in the early game. The victory conditions are neat, but you aren't going to be making many hard choices as the AI just can't keep up with a determined intermediate-level player. The voiceovers and flavor text are poorly done and generally insipid. I was hoping for a real nod to Alpha Centauri, but the lore was just phoned in. I ended up shutting off the voices because it was painful to listen to. The music is a host of generic Wagnerian anthems and do not contribute anything to the mood or tone of the setting. it's completely out of place.
All in all this game, as of release, falls mostly flat and it's probably a good idea to save your money until there are patches and expansions to correct the numerous faults of the game. Though, even then, I don't think it can be rescued from its lackluster concept and samey gameplay. 5/10.

I watched a few hours of LPs on youtube for this game and was very excited. However, after playing for a few hours I could not contain my frustration with how unresponsive the controls are. They are not bugs, they are intentionally designed this way. For those who have not played it, allow me to explain.
Your character can hug on walls and climb up like many side scrolling platform games. However, you get stuck to the wall -very- easily and have little control of when you can detach from it. If you are expecting clean controls like a Megaman X series game, Mark of the Ninja, Castlevania, Metroid, or countless others: prepare to be disappointed. You will want to jump up one block to hit an enemy but sorry, you stood too close to the wall and you will hug the wall and face away instead. You will back up a little bit and try again, aiming to hit the enemy as they are within reach and facing away but sorry, the swing arc is not your attack arc and the window hole limits what you can hit.
Need to swiftly jump up and hit an enemy from behind? Hope there's no other wall above that space because you will stick to it and have to slide down and then go into the space in order to hit the enemy. This often makes it a very risky maneuver to perform. A maneuver you need to do -constantly-.
Sticking to every wall you come in contact with is extremely frustrating. You can hardly traverse the terrain without stopping to stick for a moment. Instead of other games where you fall and press left/right to hug the wall to slow down, you'll find yourself constantly pressing down to detach and then left/right to press into the wall again because the fall damage height is poorly indicated and feels extremely short, as well as missing your target height is all to easy.
The controls are frustrating and some mechanics in the game are not explained and I tried looking up a faq, wiki, or community but there's not much to find. The wikia is sparse (I went to view rewards, general tips, and skills. All pages were blank). I went to the subreddit and there are under 20 posts. I tried to find out what experience was for the characters and no results on google. I tried to find out what different skills did but there was no easy to find comprehensive (or even partial) list.
This is a game that you will be fighting the controls constantly while trying to enjoy the game. And I was too fed up with it and have asked for a refund.

This game has a few REALLY killer puzzles, and I am a snob about puzzles, so that is saying something.  I think the number one thing that made this game work is it's utter abstractness.  Many of the best puzzles were fairly simple tasks, but understanding how the mechanisms worked was a challending and engaging task, simply because of the lack of context.
One of the most interesting and unique things about this game is the cool control scheme in which the position where you are standing affects the state of the world.  This is used in a variety of ways, and it somehow manages to make very simple puzzles a lot more engaging.
On the down side, this game was definitely lacking in polish.  Movement was slightly glitchy - especially going up stairs and jumping off walls (which I'm not sure you were supposed to be able to do at all).  There were often cheap looking cracks between blocks that didn't quite touch.  Some icons looked like poorly clipped .pngs.  Just a little rough around the edges.
Also the "story" kept getting devastatingly interesting, and then leaving you hanging.  Ending was super weird (secret ending was even weirder.  But no, I didn't get it, I watched it on youtube :P)

Finally, after 6 years, 47 is back.
Hitman Absolution is classic Hitman. Gone are the clunky contols, weird AI, and♥♥♥♥♥♥story development. Hitman Absolution takes the classic Hitman formula, and streamlines it for the better. Gun play is smoother, and more balanced. Stealth mechanics are more complex, and the game overall is quite challenging.
While some have said that these mechanics have made the game "easier", they're wrong. You can no longer carry "health syringes", and you no longer have a map of the entire level. While you still have the mini-map, gone is the map of the whole map showing enemy positions. You now have the instinct mechanics, which shows near by enemy positions and where they'll be walking. Hitman Absolution also introduces Contracts mode. Which allows player to create their own hits, by playing out the hit ingame. You can also play other people's hits.
The story in Hitman Absolution is by far, the best in the series. All of the 20 missions in the game are connected by plot, and are all introduced with a cut scene forwarding the plot.
The presentation in this game is OUTSTANDING. The graphics are simply beautiful. Hi-res textures, well detailed models/levels, and excellent voice acting. The Glacier 2 engine renders the world almost as if it was a movie. With film grain and lens flair effects (similar to Kane and Lynch 2, but far more subtle).
All of this sounds great, but there is zero replayability. I enjoyed every minute of the game, then it was over. Contracts are boring, the missions lose their appeal after the first run, and the unlocks are pointless at best. Pick this game up on sale, its a fun weekend game. Hitman Blood money offers more replayibility, at the cost of dumber AI and poorer overall style. So pick your poisen.

I haven't been into the hitman series for a while. Since about hitman 2. I started to lose interest because I felt less like a hitman, and more like a puzzle-solver. I typically tried to sneak through a level looking for my target, silently removing obstacles in my way... and more often than not could not work out the "clever" way to kill the target in a single try. I usually resorted to shooting them with a silenced baller, and shaking pursuit. Even though I could *see* the electrical wires daggling into the pool, and I KNEW I was supposed to do something there... Clearly, the game was designed for you to play levels multiple times. Maybe go in guns blazing a few times so you can casually pull levers and search the level to see where everything was - but I didn't like that. I prefer stealth games that are challenging, but with enough preparation and care you really could get through it first try - like a "real" assassin would. This is one of the reasons I think Splintercell Conviction is the best stealth game made to date.
Hitman: Absolution gives it a great run for its money now, though. Although hitman's levels have been designed for you to be able to assassinate your way through the level, their embracing of the new (since the last Hitman) culture of challenges and acheivements has worked wonderfully. You can get through the crowd, grab a disguise, tail the target to a secluded area, and knife/gun/beat the target down easily enough. Despose of the body, and walk out of the zone. It's fun, and feels realistic - if a little easy. No problem, though, because there is so many *other* ways of killing your target that you are really encouraged to try again. And again. And again. Something that was a weakness of previous Hitman games, but giving us some forewarning and clues beforehand, has become its greatest strength.
Minor spoilers ahead - but I'm going to illustrate with one minor target to show you what I mean.
I typically start a level by looking at what challenges the level has for me. Many of these are mutually exclusive - for example different ways of killing the same guy. So you can't do them all in one play through. This makes it obvious from the outset they intend for you to play these levels multiple times. One of the challenges says "His disregard for public deceny is simply shocking!" Ok. Great. A clue on what to do, but without context it doesn't mean much. Still, I can keep an eye out as I scout the level. It comes with a screengrab (which frankly I have been getting most of my clues from) showing him peeing on one of those trike-cars. Ok. So putting what I have together so far, I guess it has something to do with getting him to pee on something electrical so he gets electricuted. Possibly near a trike.
So as I tail him through the crowd, he heads down an alley way that is, unfortunately, blocked by a policeman. I can't get down there directly. So I head round the side to find another route. As it happens, the route I had in mind has a trike parked in it, out of the way of prying eyes. Ah-ha! The clues are racking up now! I search around the trike and find that it has been rested against an electrical circuit box - I'm definitely on the right track. Searching around the box I find I can rig it to the trike, pull the lever, and the trap is set.
This is something I would never have been able to work out (certainly not first try) without the clues in the "challenges" tab. Perhaps some people won't like that, but I think it adds a lot to the game. It makes me feel able to pull off amazing assassinations first try and still feel clever for having deduced it.
Of course... I did see a katana lying around too, and I'm sure I saw a challenge called something like "sword play." Hmm. I guess I could just restart the level and go for a higher score...

A somewhat solid rogue-lite, wave-based shoot 'em up game.
There's an overall progression done by collecting gears in game, and once you reach a certain amount of gears collected, overall across all your games, the ship upgrades occur automatically, on-the-fly, while you are playing.
The game itself Is a bit tough in the beginning--I found myself dying many times at the first boss (wave 10), but the moment I beat that first boss I went on to beat the last boss, and continue on in an endless wave mode, which mixes up waves  (wave 46 one wave, wave 54 the next wave, wave 50 the wave after, and so on, on and on)--but after you get all upgrades, this game becomes an easy shmup that gets old fast.  After I beat the last boss, I played one more game, cleared all bosses, then played enough endless waves to get about 11,000 gears.  If felt like I'd never lose.  It tool about 3 hours to 100% this.
I don't think I'd return to this game, and the only way to do so would be to reset the progress, and go through the ship upgrade progression again.  Either way, it was fun.

Kairo is a game of exploration and mystery, putting a whole world of differently coloured rooms ahead of you, each with its own intrigues and puzzles; the design of those rooms is simplistic, each following a precise theme and colour, without adding too much detail on the ambient, but that's part of what makes Kairo's mystery so great, leaving you with questions about a certain object that you encountered and what useful information that object might have for you. While some of those questions will be answered by the end of the game, most of them won't, leaving you more confused than you were when you first started the game, and as great as that is from the mysterious perspective of the game, it somehow feels disappointing at the same time, as you probably were expecting at least some of the bigger mysteries to be answered in a way or another, but on the bright side that leaves a lot of room for interpretation, allowing each one of us to have our own verdict on what Kairo wanted to tell us. The greatest part about this game however, is the way it manages to shape its universe around you, constantly surprising you with what lies ahead in the next room and leaving you in doubt on how you should react to what you see before your eyes, but at the same time giving you complete freedom to move around and see what you can discover to help you solve that room's puzzle and move forward just to have the same thing happen to you all over again. In the end, judging by the amount of hours you've spent in Kairo it won't add up to more than a few hours, but really digging into the experience and enjoying the mysteries it has to tell, it will seem a lot longer while you're inside and exploring at will, even though for most times, the more you explore, the more unanswered questions you'll have at the end.
Every once in a while, you run into those type of games that offer a unique and thrilling experience without focusing too much on the gameplay, but rather on the experience you have by simply being a part of that game and uncovering its mysteries; Kairo is exactly that type of game, delivering a simplistic mechanic of navigating through its universe and clever ways to solve its puzzles by using nothing else besides the basic movements and the environment around you. This game is all about exploration and uncovering the numerous mysteries that lie ahead, using the things you've seen before and the things you see in that very moment to help you solve different puzzles that stand in the way of your progression, something that works wonderful in Kairo, following a logical way of seeing things and even though the solution might not be that obvious at first, exploring the environment around you will eventually give you the information you need. Most areas follow the same pattern, requiring you to enter all the side rooms, observe what you can do in there and get things moving again until each and every one of the required steps has been completed and the core of that area is up and running, allowing you to move forward on to the next one. By putting some of the information you need to unlock various secrets in the rooms ahead of you, Kairo requires you to return to previously visited areas without feeling repetitive or boring, as there will always be something new to uncover that you might have missed on your first visit, and with the information from the rooms ahead of you in mind, you will for most of the times, know what you're looking for already. Even with the usage of the movements keys only, some of the mechanics such as pushing objects around feel like they haven't reached their full potential, as such simple things could've expanded the way in which puzzles are treated in various ways, making the game longer and adding that extra gameplay portion that's missing.
It's hard not to appreciate the unique art style of Kairo and the wonderful and sometimes spooky environments it delivers, but even in all the simplicity of shapes and precise objects you can clearly see the outdated engine on which the game was built. There are an almost infinite number of ways in which this game could have been improved by using the latest game engines, especially in the lighting area, where the latest engines would've made a huge difference on how that room is viewed and the exact experience the game wanted to deliver.
There's always a great tune playing in the background to add to the feel of a certain room, sometimes adding to the feeling of joy and liberty, while other times cornering you in a small room with little light and a spooky theme to add to the mystery effect. The sound effects as low quality as they are do their job well enough, but there was room for a little more variety and a few more touches here and there to make you hear the world moving around you when it does visually happen on the screen.
It takes around four hours to complete Kairo, add an extra hour or two if you're looking to get the most out of it and collect all the glyphs, monoliths and solve all the secret puzzles, but also note that this is a game priced at 3.99€, so for that amount of money, it does more than enough to please. With the amount of mystery and out of place objects you can find in this game there was room for a lot more, as some of the areas are not used to their fullest and areas that seem to have some sort of puzzle attached to them at first, are just there to give the impression of having more to see.
Kairo isn't much of a game, but it's one great experience, especially if you're into the abstract puzzle genre, as its unique design and way of saying things make it a must play for any enthusiast of the genre. As in most cases, there was room for more in some areas and modern graphics would've made a huge difference in the way the game unveils to you, but considering the fact that this is an indie game, it did a great job delivering a worthy experience from a low budget production.

I am alone.
As with most places in this desolate world I find myself in, the room is almost entirely monochromatic. Green, but not a green like living plants, but a green like something sickly and dying. Rotten. Slimy. It is a long corridor, and unlike the other places I have visited, it is somewhat claustrophobic. Large caskets line the sides of the corridor, and as I walk slowly along, looking for something I am expected to do, I stop and investigate one.
There is a monitor on each casket. Some are broken, some flicker with static, but this one shows an image, though of what, I cannot see. I stand there for awhile, longer maybe than I should, waiting for something to appear on that monitor, but if the image changes, it is perhaps only my imagination. Or my reflection.
Kairo is a strange, ominous world. There are great monoliths to explore, machines that reach up to the heavens, and cramped corridors to wander through. Some rooms have puzzles, some are just desolate walkways, hanging out over an abyss.
I feel I am in purgatory. The very first action this game asks you to take is a leap of faith. This is what the game expects of you- perhaps not to understand, but to experience.
Visually, this game is a treat of abstract, bold art. Simple, yes, but the limited pallette serves to build the abandoned atmosphere of the game, and Kairo is more than capable of providing small details mixed in amongst the enormous structures. The appearance of the game almost looks somewhat grainy, like an old photograph.
The sound is just the howl of empty wind in enormous rooms. Rocks grind and scrape over surfaces as you move puzzles into place. There is some music, but it did not stand out to me in comparison to the rooms that whistle with loneliness.
Kairo is, for the most part, a puzzle game. You manipulate these great structures, these old, broken runes, to find your way through. Some of the puzzles are simple, some of them seem to make little sense, requiring simple trial and error. Kairo does provide 'hints' for each level, but they are otiose at best, perhaps deliberately. Still, there is a sense of accomplishment at defeating these particular puzzles, and a continual drive to see what might be next keeps you going.
Do I understand what is going on? I feel I do. But at the same time, I feel that there are many right answers.
So, come. Walk with me for awhile.

I had a winning streak, my xp multiplier was 2x. I had already hacked 2 of the 3 computers, only one left. Last thing on the agenda was to run down the stairs, double jump to avoid spike pit and kill the guard and I was going to finish up the level. So, I ran down the stairs and hit the jump button, only to realize it used up by mid-air jump, because apparently going down stairs counts as falling. So, I used up my only jump and then smashed into the spike pit, ending my winning streak and losing everything I had collected that round.
This game can be truly rage inducing at times. It's manageable, but you'll die several times after learning the quirks of the controls. For example, hitting jump immidiately before a pit can lead the character to move over the pit before actually jumping, canceling the jump and sending you into the abyss. I think this is the reason so many of the other reviews complain about the buttons not registering.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game. I had fun planning out how I'd tackle the rooms and strategizing which skills to get first, but heavy death penalties coupled with iffy controls became too much to handle. Even if the controls were tighter, the procedure generation needs some work. Sometimes the game would hide the computers (main source of exp) in rooms that aren't connected to any other room. This becomes less of a problem once you get bombs and gain the ability to tunnel through walls, but it would make sense to at least make the first level fully connected. New security measures come in regardless of what level you're on, so it's possible to waste an entire day because the computers are literately unreachable on the first stage.

The Swindle does many things very well, but with one severe flaw.
The style, artwork and music (although limited in quantity) make for a very competent game.
This game will see you hacking computers, diffusing bombs, dispatching guards, climbing and hanging from walls. The idea is to enter a level, try and collect as much money as possible without being detected or killed and to escape and spend the money you collect on upgrades and proceeding to new levels, which have higher difficulty and bigger rewards.
It is a very difficult game and one false move can and usually will result in death and this is where the main problem with the game lies, the controls.
Too often a double jump, a swipe at an enemy, a jump over a pit will not register. A game that is so difficult that requires such precision, to have such poor controls is extremely frustrating and as you progress in the game you will find yourself in more and more difficult situations where you will be at the mercy of whether the game decides to accept your controller inputs.
Sticking to walls is very irritating also as your character tends to want to stick to walls that are either above or below their range, so trying to leave an area quickly can result into a lot of hanging onto and sliding down walls.
It is very unfortunate as the overall game is very well executed and without this problem, would be easy to recommend,
I’m still going to rate the game positive but would not recommend to players that are easily frustrated or are expecting trouble free gameplay.

This game is great! Very addictive swordplay and a great deal of challenge as you go on. If you're into FPS and hack and slash this game is perfect. It's not overly cinematic and focuses more on actual gameplay (which is what games should be) so that means more bloody and less talky but that's not to say the story isn't interesting.
However there are a few minor flaws I find a bit annoying in this game. The controls can get a little bit awkward at times. To perform certain special Katana/magic moves you have to double tap either of the WASD keys and hold the RMB or LMB at the same time and it works fine but sometimes when you're in a tight situation, it's hard to pull off certain special moves since you're constantly moving and trying to double tap the corresponding WASD buttons at the same time. I can't count how many times I've been killed trying to pull off the healing magic (double tap the 'D' key and hold RMB) while trying to get away from enemies.
It's also hard to figure out sometimes where you're supposed to go next. Although the game is linear and straighforward, it's still hard to find you're way around the next level except for a glowing door but sometimes it's almost impossible to locate the doors especially when you get into a larger and more vast level since there is no navigation or map system but I guess it's another way of making you explore the game more and find secrets which the game is full of.
Also the game can get a bit repetitive but the great gameplay more than makes up for it. If you have a few bucks to spare and a lust for blood and carnage then this game is worth every penny!

I thought this would just be some FPS filler for me as I wait for Doom and Dishonored 2... but I was greatly mistaken. The game is awesome. The story isn't bad, it's actually pretty darn good aside from some mildly bad voice acting at times (not all times). The swordplay and gunplay are incredible. They really took time to add some very nice finishing touches. It's not just the cleaning of the sword, it's how you walk, how you run, how you walk up steps, etc. It all feels more realistic than any FPS I've played to date (besides ARMA). The graphics look incredible and the games a couples years old even. My dual r9 280s kill at this game. I get a consistent 120fps on ultra settings. The environment, level design, and artwork are top notch. I love the throwback secret areas that use the old textures. It's a nice touch. Hoenstly I could keep going on about this game for a while. I'm going to replay on Hard (because they let you keep all your stuffs and keep leveling up). I'm already finding new areas or new touches I hadn't caught the first time. This game is good for 15+ hours as that's what I've put and I'll probably log more. This game is probably on my top ten for best FPS (single player campaign) of all time now.

This is a very intriguing game that is not for everyone. It is very difficult but also very rewarding, and properly gives you the feeling of gaining in power, something done only in good RPGs. There are multiple ways of progressing through the game, although some skill choices are curently not very useful in the early release. $25 doesn't give you many hours of content, but you can replay with multiple characters and have a fairly different experience each time. Overall I support the development of games like this and can't wait to see how the finished game turns out.
Pros:
Immersive world, dialogue and characters.
Good music that fits the theme of the game.
Pretty deep skill system that rewards different styles of play.
Combat is challenging and is somewhat luck based but overall it's a good system.
The devs know what makes a good RPG and are excellent at having you "feel" the power of your character grow and feel like the decisions you make have an impact.
Multiple choices in quests, often with no clear answer. Some things will have negative or positive consequences much later in the game.
Cons:
Sometimes you can get stuck and be unable to progress due to putting points in the wrong skills. There is no way to "grind" more skill points, so in these situations you are sort of screwed (I'm sure this will be better addressed in the final version, and No I'm not saying they should add a way to grind skill points!)
Overall not much content yet, you can only go to about 5 locations out of the 20 total, and there aren't that many quests right now. Once again I'm sure the finished game will feel much larger and longer.
A little too linear - Yes there are multiple ways to go about things and the game is not too linear in this sense. But certain things bothered me, such as my sneaky assassin being unable to go to the temple in the slums without either paying 1000 gold or fighting like 7 guys by myself (100% impossible in this game). You would think I would be able to use my points in sneaking to wait until night and get to the temple, it is supposed to be a whole slums district and one band of thugs can completely seal the whole thing off from everyone?
Overall a very good game. I would give a 7/10 for the early alpha just because it is somewhat low on content but if the final game is as good as I think it will turn out to be this will be at least a 9/10 for sure.

Well well, after nearly sixty hours of use, it's time for me to make a review about this little software.
The sole purpose of Nimble Writer is to write novels. If you're looking for a word-like software, you've come to the wrong place, since you cannot really organize your document in pages with NW. It's really centered around writing novels, in which you focus more about the number of words and paragraphs rather than pages. Don't worry though, your whole document will not be in a single block; it's instead divided in chapters, allowing you to navigate through them easially within a single document.
For a novel writer, though, this thing is quite a gem. The idea of distraction-free interface is quite an advantage; you can customize what you want to appear on your screen and what you want to hide, that it be the options, the chapter selection or the statistics of your story (that one I would not hide, I find it really helpful to know how much numbers I wrote on a particular chapter). There is a correction tool, which is pretty helpful for people like me whose first language isn't english and yet who chose to write in English. Now I do not know if that also works for foreign language, since to be honest, I didn't try writing in french. If my memory is correct, there is also a thesaurus tool within the program, requiring Java to work. I didn't really test it, but I should try soon, since such tool should further help me.
Nimble has quite a few functions to overcome the serious issue that is writer's block. For instance, as mentionned before, the distraction-free interface, the stats and the achievements which motivates you to create. Yup, the ultimate challenge is to manage to write 2000 words each day for 21 days in a row. I'll probably work on that whenever my schedule allows me to. It also has a sidebar that you can either prompt or hide, in which you can manage your chapters and your notes. The note feature, that one is awesome. It allows to write multiple kind of "post-it" things, in which you can write notes related to your story, that it be places, characters or so. There's even a doodle note option, on which you can draw (thanks captain), but since my drawing skills are so low that I can't even draw stickmen correctly... yeah, you can guess I didn't really try. You can naturally search for words and replace them - or even replace a word by another in the whole text at once, if you want to completely change the name of a character or place, for instance. That option spared me a lot of time, so that's a big thumb up I give.
The software also allows you to save your work on steam cloud, if you wish. You can even encrypt your work with a unique key if you wish. That is pretty neat. Now, some people mentioned that they faced bugs and software-breaking bugs, that apparently caused quite some inconveniences to them. But if I'm correct, those issues seems to have been patched since last version, and myself have not yet been the victim of any bug of such - and hopefuly it will remain so. Checking through the forums, I discovered that the developer seems to be rather active with his community, trying to find solution to problems and always open to feedback.
So yeah, if you are into story writing, and that you're sick of Word, Wordpad or notepad (Why would you even use that for stories though?), Nimble Writer is in my opinion a very satisfactory software that allows you to manage your stories with ease. It really got me back into writing and I am thankful for that. So I definitely recommend it for you novelists.

As someone who has been writing stories for most of his life, I'm happy that I found Nimble Writer.
As has been spoken about in reviews below or above mine, Nimble Writer can not only be used to compose your stories, it can also allow you to keep all of your notes right there in the same file!
For example: I started working with RPG Maker VX Ace a while back. I wanted a way to keep EVERYTHING related to my game together, so that I wouldn't need to either search through a text document, or open up multiple documents, just to keep track of things.
With Nimble Writer, I can keep EVERYTHING on the same window. Dialouge scripts, shops lists, fixes, I can have a chapter tab for each one, allowing me to jump back and forth between them without having to sift through a ton of open tabs.
If you're like me, however, and you're easily distracted, Nimble Writer can go fullscreen, blocking off any other accessible thing on the desktop. Even your toolbar. Combine that with the ability to customize your writing space (backgrounds, color schemes, fonts), and some music, and you got yourself a great little distraction-free program to use for even the most casual of writing sessions.
Also: IT HAS ACHEIVEMENTS. Seriously, you can earn them just by writing (no cheating, scrub) so many words. It also comes with a built in Goal Counter. Want to write a certain number of words per day? Nimble Writer can keep an eye on your count and display it for you in the lower-right corner, along with the number of characters and words you've put into the document so far. It's excellent for keeping you on track, and even better and making you push yourself to best your record.
Yes, $10, to some, can be a bit much. But if you do a lot of writing, and you want to eliminate the chore of managing tons of windows trying to plot out and write your story, $10 is a very fair price to pay, considering how much you can do with this program. I highly reccommend Nimble Writer for anyone who spends a lot of time writing, but wants to better organize their work. It's a godsend.

This game is slightly disappointing to say the least.
The first game, while lacking in good graphics had a LOT more options for castle building, and management.
For Example, you could choose what kind of ruler to be. Feared, or Loved. Choosing Feared meant having torture instruments placed around your castle, and having higher taxes. This would reflect on your peasants' attitudes toward you, making them less happy but more hardworking.
Choosing to have a more peaceful castle meant lowering taxes and having the option to places statues or flower gardens in your castle to make your peasants happier, but work less hard. Regardless this added a lot more immersion and made you really feel like a Ruler, instead of just the castle's contractor placing walls and buildings.
While the graphics ARE indeed a large improvement, there seems to be a serious lack of unit types in this game.
Sure it has slaves, assassins, horses, archers and different types of swordsmen, but not much else other than the addition of the Sergeants, and conscripts (Crusaders) and the Whirling Dervishes (Arabic). I remember a time when we could make siege engineers at a Siege Guild building and have them man a variety of useful siege equipment, (Siege Towers, Ladders, Tower Defenses, etc)
It is easy to tell this game was rushed, and doesn't offer much except for shiny new graphics and the same old "Can't place that there m'lord" voice in the sky. Please please please devs, give us more to manage/produce next time you plan on releasing a game. What we have now is terribly bland, and basically the same as the last game. (With the exceptions I've listed above.
The other thing that really bugs me too is the lack of inventiveness on the devs part with the AI enemies. They have the same washed up foes we fought in the first game, and maybe a few more (that cost real money to have by the way). I think this is very unfair, and more should have been done before the initia release to introduce these new enemies beforehand so that we wouldn't have to cough up our precious cash to BUY them. I wish I hadn't. (P.S. Whoever animates your enemies when they talk to you makes me laugh every time at how bad they are)
The map editor is very simple to use and create wonderful maps, however. But like I said before, there is not a lot to work with, and sometimes even mods can't fix that. If anyone reads this, I would really like to say I do recommend this game, however it doesn't offer much in the way of troop management and castle building, other than placing a few buildings, collecting resources, and making weapons/ale/candles/etc.
I am sorry if you disagree with me, but it is how I feel on how this game turned out.
On the plus side, I once watched a tornado rip through an entire force of enemy troops which totally saved my life by the way. Had a rough start.

I'm not a creative professional or freelance writer. I'm a JavaScript developer. I have my tool set ready and one of the programs in this set is nimble writer. I don't use nimble writer for coding, hell no. I use it for productivity. To be honest with you, I still use paper notebooks with A5 sheets to take notes and I also have one around me all the time. However, I also like to make my notes digital. I don't want spend money for a fancy solution from 'Wacom' (i.e. smart notebook with cloud sync). So, I just needed a note taking app to backup my notes, lists, to do lists. I used to love 'Evernote' but their recent software became so slow. Literally, it takes a while to launch it and sync. Onenote - same thing, pretty heavy UI. So what should I use just for tacking notes? I decided to buy nimble writer and since then I use it. Do like the HTML export feature because its quite handy sometimes to export HTML-styled notes. I upload some of the notes on my FTP server to access/share them online. Sure, you could use notepad++ and HTML5 knowledge to make the exact same styling but let me tell you, nimble writer just saves a lot of time. And it's more human-friendly if you want to share your notes with non developers. Fullscreen feature does the job too! It helps to focus so much. There are also some other cool moments about using this software. For example, encryption, steam cloud, steam workshop. One other thing that I want to mention is that build-in spell checker is so poor. Not a deal breaker for me; thus I'm not crazy about it at all. But keep in mind for all the writers, creatives out there that you have to use other third party software for spell checking. Wish you had a Linux version and mobile for android, iphone, windows phone. Also if you add highlighting to the spell checker it would be awesome! Overall, nimble writer is a pretty good software. I can certainly recommend it.

Civilization Beyond Earth truly deserves the title of spiritual successor of Alpha Centauri. Although it requires a bit of unit diversity, even with the upgrades, you'd still miss the custom unit creation that was available in Alpha Centauri. Factions are diverse but not too distinct from each other, which makes them somewhat easier to get used to quickly. Gameplay and turn times are much smoother than in Civ 5, especially in later phases of the game in a very large map you'd feel the difference of ai completing their turns much quicker.
As i read the comments i see people who haven't played Alpha Centauri but fans of Civ series are a bit confused and calling this an expansion pack of sorts. It simply isn't. Just take it as exploring, or rather migrating to an alien planet because earth is no more habitable and imagine all that 'future tech' in Civ games are new set of techs in here. Sure it takes time to get used to but it doesn't prevent it being so much fun.
It will become a legendary successor when they add more factions, a little more unit diversity and some other dlc add ons but it's still a must buy right off the bat for any Civ or Alpha Centauri fan.
Update as of 23.11.2016 - It's still the closest thing to Alpha Centauri whether you like it or not.

TL;DR: it looks like a Civ5 reskin but feels like a mix between Civ5 and Alpha Centaury, but is neither a copy nor reskin of either one. This will be a gameplay/mechanics review.
Overview:
- Your unit types are upgraded together (for free) within their type (all melee, all archers, all ...)
- The tech web makes it more unlikely that all civs have the same techs (spies' "steal tech" is more useful)
- The spies can be used without cost, but you have a limited number of spies at any given time
- The ongoing quests are frequent and shape your bonuses considerably (and guides new players)
- The "barbarians" are more interesting than in previous games
- The "villages" consist of 4 types of sites which take 10 turns to "harvest", and I have seen at least one repop as part of a quest (fallen satellite)
- Cities start as "outposts" and mature into cities over approx 10 turns
- Trade is done using "caravans" which don't need to be replaced unless attacked (auto-move)
- Your ongoing choices shape your civ more than your starting selection
Note: Now that I think about it, it feels as if the game is more balanced for both single-player and multiplayer, where I'd say the past games were mostly single-player focused. I'm still going to sink several 100 hours into single-player.
Sure, the composition of the unit types is similar to Civ5 (melee, horseman, archer, artillery and fighter), and the city maintenance is similar (food, currency, production and health).
The combat mechanics are also similar to Civ 5.
When playing the game though, it definitely feels different to Civ 5.
You have "sponsors", which appear to be your civilization, but it's really just a small starting point. It doesn't really define who you are.
Beyond Earth feels as if it's mostly about shaping your civilization as you go, where Civ 5 was more "determine what you want to be up front, then optimize your game for that".
I say that, because you gain a lot of extra bonuses from the many small quests which pop up, and your unit types all upgrade together, within their type class, based on your "affinity" (from both research and quests).
The unit promotions (as far as I've played so far) don't seem as important as in Civ 5. You're not going to be able to make superman units by upgrading them with promotions and tech throughout the game. It's more focused on worker-built unit boosts, augmentation satellites (Which last 10 turns and affect ~ a 5-diameter area) and the overall affinity upgrades you choose for unit types.
The tech web seems confusing, but it plays well into the feeling I get from the game, that you need to adjust your choices continually. I feel the idea behind the game is "don't plan everything upfront", and more in the line of "shape it as you go".
The covert ops is more useful now because your spies don't spend money (energy) on tasks at all. The spies gain experience and they destaibilize the cities which enable higher level spy missions. They can be asked to take any job, and none of them cost anything, so you'll be using them a lot more than in previous games.
And of course, if you place counter-spies you can stabilize your cities and prevent the more destructive missions entirely. There are 5 stabilization levels (100pt scale), and only levels 4-5 are harmful to the owner.
Cultural upgrades feel somewhat similar to the ones from Civ5, except here there are 4 branches, and you get bonuses both from vertical and horizontal choices.
If you get a lot of "tier 1" upgrades from each of the brances, you'll get a couple of bonuses for that, and if you stick to one branch (offense, expansion, industry or reseach) you'll get other bonuses for that.
The aliens, which are essentially "barbarians" have more to them than in past games. If you don't mess with them, they'll for the most part leave you alone. There's also an equivalent to Alpha Centauri's fungi, which you can either use to your advantage or wipe out... but if you pick on the aliens, they'll pick on you. I haven't played as pro-alien yet, so I'm not sure how interesting it'll be to play thier side, but that's my next playthrough!
In conclusion, I'd say it feels like a mix between Civ5 and Alpha Centaury, but is neither a copy nor reskin of either one. It also feels as if it's trying to enable multiplayer without harming the singleplayer experience.

Utterly amazing, i have been a big fan of the civ games right back to when they began. Sid Meier is a genius. I have heard and read other reviews of this game, some think it should be an add on for Civ 5. I strongly disagree, this is an epic title in its own right, as a Civ veteran i love the time and dedication taken to build your empire to its fullest. This is something else. I expected something much along the same lines as Civ 5, but i was pleasently surprised, new planets, yes thats more than one, new techs, buildings, research etc. Everything is brand new. And let me tell you, i usually play in Diety mode for the challenge, i have this on Mecury (which is normal) still a massive challenge, i get my butt kicked from here to kingdom come by the indiginous population, amongst other things.
The new tech tree is a challenge at first, it all being straight there in your face, but after 2-3 games you will get the hang of it, mastering it is still on my list as that tech tree needs some serious time spent on it, just randomy selecting things doesn't cut it, you have to decide how you want to survive in such a hostile place and this tech tree once mastered could be epic. I am still learning, so i cannot judge.
As  for the buildings and units, they are as to be expected, with several changes plus other additional extras. The wonders change depending on what techs you choose, i like that, talking of techs you can bio-engineer your units and evolve them into something else entirely, upgrading them this time around is much much better, you upgrade one, they all get the same upgrade, so no constantly clicking each unit, finally.
The affinity tree, now seeing as we are no longer on earth, democracy, ideology, tradition etc, all this has gone, instead its replaced with four seperate trees, each have their own merits and if chosen in a certain order can prove very very helpful towards the survival of your colony, i am still mixing it up to see what works best.
To sum up, this game was well worth the wait, i have literally just bought it and already i'm hooked. I can see a lot of time and dedication was put into this game, i shall give it a lot of mine.
Visual - 9/10
Audio - 8/10
Tips/Advice - 8/10
Worth buying - 10/10

I won't be the first to say this, but the controls are the main problem in inhibiting this game from being GREAT.
I don't know if I'll be the first to say this, but I'll explain a few things that specifically control poorly.
Moving while in the air is inconsistent. I've died SO many times from detatching from a wall to fall faster, then dying because I can only sometimes reattach.
Double jumping, and what counts as 'landing' on an enemy isn't consistent on stairs. Stairs and diagonal surfaces will SOMETIMES count as a 'falling' state, which means if there's an enemy at the bottom of the stairs that you can walk past, but can't land on without dying, you'll sometimes just die by walking down the stairs. Also, if there's a simple spike pit (screw those spike pits btw) after a stairway, and you have the double jump maybe or maybe not required to clear it, you'll sometimes use that second jump just for jumping off the stairs.
[Quick note on those spike pits, the hit box is the exact same height as the floor, which can lead to some obvious problems. If only it was a LITTLE lower. Please.]
Jumping into a doorway that is one 'block' high (they're all that big), and one 'block' above where you jump from will sometimes auto-attach you to the block above the doorway
(e.g., you'll end up here    →  |____
instead of here→
_When jumping from here__-------)
which is really annoying, especially when trying to do quiet quick kills by jumping up to hit an enemy as they turn around, and accidentally end up ABOVE the doorway. Also:
Your jump height is dependant on where you're jumping FROM. For example, if there's a sheer wall with three panes of glass in the middle, you can clear it with a single air jump (or one 'double jump', or a 'second jump', whatever is least confusing) ONLY if you jump from the wall BELOW the lowest pane, not if you're standing on the same ledge as the lowest pane. That sounds confusing, but trust me, it gets annoying because of another issue I have with the game.
The levels are all randomly generated WHICH IS GREAT. There's a lot of replayability here, especially with the 100 day limit (that you can bypass in the late game, just FYI) but this means you can end up in a situation where you CAN'T clear a three pane high window, and the interior of the level doesn't lead to the side of the level you can exit on. (Yes, you can only leave the level from one side of the map, which is always a giant building). Times you are required to execute your character because there's literally no way out are really annoying.
If you can't tell, I've played more of this game than its quality may appear to warrant, but I've ranted about it because I actually do like it. The late game is REALLY fun, using the myriad of tools to pull off heists is very satisfying. It's frustrating to GET there though, and since I don't know you, you'll have to decide for yourself if you can look past the movement and programming problems I've listed here and more, to become familiar enough with the game to...not overcome the issues, but know how to avoid them. Once you're familiar with the game, and even more at a late-game point, it gets pretty fun.
TL;DR the game is fun once you know what really sucks about it, and avoid those parts as best you can.

The difficulty scaling is nonlinear and impacts previous areas. If you think a newly unlocked area is too difficult and want to go back to a lower security area you'll find that all of the new security measures are there too.
It's possible to have levels generate where you simply do not have the tools available to actually do the level. Rooms that are locked and you lack the skill, money buried where you don't have bombs, rooms overwhelmed with enemies and you don't have upgrades, etc.
For a procedural game the levels are disappointingly small. Given the above, sometimes it is possible to generate a level where you can't actually get any money... and with the 100 day limitation that is a big deal.
Enemies behave inconsistently. Sometimes they can spot you and be slow to react and miss you when shooting. Sometimes they spot you and act like a marksman shooter. The lack of consistency is frustrating because you can't come to rely on behavior.
I found myself more annoyed and frustrated than I did having fun trying to actually play.
