Admittedly at first, I was hesitant about this game. I loved Alpha Centauri, and was trying not to get my hopes up for this game, since I was expecting it to be a skin mod of Civ V. Let's just say, I am blown out of the water with this game. It is the perfect homage to Alpha Centauri, and the graphics are seamless and beautiful (what we have come to expect and love from Firaxis games).
With what there is new, there is also the old. The diplomacy system is relatively untweeked, though the introduction of "favors" - a diplomatic currency if you will that can be accumulated from the AI and used in future deals, is very promising and looks to solve the abysmal AI from Civ V.
The other critique is the UI and the tech web. very simple, yet complex at first, does take some getting used too. The colour palette is a very dull blue, which is hard on the eyes at first, compared to the stark colours from Civ V. But, once you get into the Civ Groove, you take off and lose all sense of time, like every other Civ game.
I highly suggest this game, it is a refreshing breath in the genre and the inventiveness that went into this game is evident from the opening video, all the way to end game.

This game is art. The music is incredible, the backrounds are stunning and the characters are all adorable. The exploration part of this game is a bit of an acquired taste, but I personally love it. The game gives you no objective, it doesn't tell you what you need to do. This lack of hand-holding is what made me love this game so much. The exploration is just so satisfying. There's always something new to find in hallownest, something you missed or could not access before.
The fighting element is also stellar. The controls are simple, but there's so much room for optimisation. Your spacing, timing and combination of attacks. These are all ways to expand and be rewarded with success. (The downstrike triple-jump for example might help you in the white palace if you're not afraid of the saws).
The story and lore in this game are also excellent. The mysterious narrative and the fact that the game never forces its lore on you is simply great. If you want to learn the history of Hallownest, best talk to NPCs and read journal entries and item descriptions
The bosses are also awesome, their moves are versatile and they're always a welcomed challenge. Their themes and visuals are appealing, and the many possible builds that work against them are all fun to play. Speaking of, the charm system is what makes this game shine over other games of this genre. You have to either buy, puzzle or fight for these, and most of them have cool abilities that you can find some way to use.
Overall I'd say this game's only negative is the occasional backtracking, but this is not really a problem as there's always something new to see.

A fun throwback to NES-era JRPGs of yore. The writing, story, and world-building are all intentionally cheeky and while not outright genius, had me laughing now and then. I can't speak much to the story, as it's very simple and silly, with no particularly amazing parts jumping out. Over all, it was the game mechanics that kept me invested til the end.
I really enjoyed how simple the character building was, with each level giving you two abilities (sometimes active, sometimes passive) to choose from, resulting in a few feasible builds for each character in your party. Another much appreciated feature was the Fight function, in which you can initiate a Fight automatically as long as you are in a dungeon or other area where there are enemies. This eliminates a lot of running in a circle for twenty minutes, waiting to for a Fight to start, that was so prevalent in the games that Breath of Death takes its inspiration from.
Additionally, HP is fully restored at the end of each fight, while MP is only slightly replenished. This makes HP a more immediate resource, with MP being something you want to ration. Potions are scarce, but will fully heal you, as well as cure any status effects, meaning that they're the only item you really need - which makes sense, as they're the only usable item in the game! This creates an interesting trade off of "Do I use MP to heal, or do I use a potion? Should I attack, or try to end the battle more quickly with offensive spells?" The latter might be a good choice, as the fewer turns you use to end a fight, the more MP you recover, gold you earn, and experience points you are awarded. All of Breath of Death's systems are thusly simple, with a tinge of complexity that makes it just right.
You can immediately see these definitive design choices evolve in Zeboyd's following games, and having started with PA, Episode 3, it has been fun for me to strip them all down to the bare minimum with Breath of Death VII.

Stronghold Crusader 2 is yet another attempt by Firefly Studios to capture the success of the old cult hits Stronghold and Stronghold Crusader. Yes, yet another - there have been three other installations that tried exactly that and failed hard. But as the old saying goes, third time's the charm... err, fourth time's the charm. Or, after the third time, a desert setting's the charm?
Not really.
The appeal of the original Stronghold and its standalone addon, Stronghold Crusader, was pretty clear. Unlike other RTS games at the time, it was very focused on style and believability, building a nice looking castle, seeing its populace bustle about as they produced goods. The block size for a wall was about 1x1m which was great for making highly individual castles.
Sadly the devs don't seem to understand that, and to my understanding, they've been trying to make the Stronghold games more like other RTS, at the expense of the small details that I loved the original games for.
Stronghold Crusader 2 is no exception for that. The block size for walls chunky, which doesn't exactly allow for sophisticated castle building. Towers don't seem to fit in very well. Many aspects were "gamified", defensive siege weapons for example work without a crew and are moving magically. Siege camps are built inside your castle instead of in front of the enemy, and immediately churn out catapults like in something like AoE. Also, many production chains were simplified.
Immersion took a second or third place to so-called "playability", perhaps to make it faster, more appealing to RTS fans.
Except those still won't touch this game with a 10 foot pole. The way units are produced, buildings are built, repairs are done instantly, the lack of fog of war and many of the other shortcomings just don't make for very good RTS gameplay.
For the rest of us, the whole immersion aspect went down the drain.
Personally, there is something else that quite annoys me about this game. Thing is, Stronghold Crusader was a standalone extension to Stronghold, which meant that a lot of aspects were simply copied over. For example, most buildings still had the same cost in wood, even though they're made of stone, which also makes more sense to use in a desert environment. Also, Arabian units felt very "tacked on", as they cost money instead of requiring weapons and armor. And even though the whole setting screams for two factions, all players had the same available buildings and units, with only the lord looking different.
Stronghold Crusader 2 not being an addon to anything else, I'd have expected it to fix these issues. But it didn't.
Furthermore, this game is a technical mess. There is no borderless windowed mode, no anti-aliasing. SSAO produces ugly scan lines all over the screen. Performance tanks once a game picks up some action. The AI is garbage, your allies will constantly demand goods from you from the first second. There are bugs all over the place, some that I noticed when it released 2 years ago. And with all that, it still has the graphics of an ancient game. Look at Company of Heroes and this, and tell me that one came out 8 years before the other.
Last but not least, I'd like to give a honorable mention to the completely horrendous art in the game's menus. The average 15 year old on DeviantArt could draw something better.

I've tried to use Nimble Writer time and time again, and, to be honest, I can never stick with it. Nimble Writer doesn't do anything that other writing apps already do and worse: at times, for free.
I'm not sure why is that. I can see that Nimble Writer is a good app, considering. It has interesting features. It just keeps feeling uninteresting overall. I gave it some thought, and that's what I believe might be the problem.
If compared with the all-famous Ommwriter, Nimble Writer has more features. But if compared with Focus Writer or WriteMonkey, Nimble Writer falls woofully short in its achievements. And that is even more accentuated if compared with Scrivener, its free (even if less user friendly) conterpart yWriter or Quoll Writer. All three apps are considerably more powerful handling full-size novels than Nimble Writer is, with a full-range of interesting and useful features. Scrivener is known for being a undisputable king in its category, but there are free alternatives. Nimble Writer could be one, but it isn't there yet.
Not only that, but I believe--and that's strictly a personal taste--that it needs a heavy redo on the interface. While we can customize, Nimble Writer has a very unnappealing interface as default, and that is very off-putting.
Also, what's basically a structural limitation, is that Nimble Writer isn't portable (obviously). Which might be a problem if you need to use it in different computers all the time (if that's the case, I would recommend FocusWriter, or even WriteMonkey (if, about the latter, if you're okay with Markdown only). Of course that's not a problem that you can change, but it's something that keeps dragging me back to other apps.
Bottom line is: if you're migrating from a generic word processor like Microsoft Word or Open Office, Nimble Writer will standout as a distraction-free writing enviroment. But if you had contact with other apps with the same purpose, you might feel as stumped as I do while using it.
Give it a go, if you must--Nimble Writer is cheap enough you can just test it.

Bell Ringer is an arena-based PvP game that can be played with up to four players. There is a single-player campaign of sorts, co-op and multiplayer [online or local]. Each player can choose from a total of five different characters that come with their own semi-unique weapons and move sets, Bell Ringer attempts to cash in on the popular “Super Smash Bros” demographic with its own rendition of the arena genre, but doesn’t quite succeed in doing so.
There’s a core issue with games like Bell Ringer, and much to the game’s credit, one major uphill battle it faced wasn’t even in the game itself, but the marketplace. However, we’ll touch on that towards the end. For now, let’s focus on the gameplay and issues plaguing Bell Ringer from ever achieving any kind of notable recognition.
Bell Ringer, like many games, came to Steam via the Greenlight system with high expectations according to the Greenlight page, which you can find here:
However, like so many games before, Bell Ringer offered too much and delivered very little. Customization, world exploration, a unique crafting system, world generation systems and item management alike were promised, but none of this came to light. What voters were given was a mere shell of what was promised. Bell Ringer comes with a handful of levels, five characters with a pre-defined loadout, no item management, no exploration, no procedurally generated anything and zero crafting abilities; it doesn’t even come with a story outside of what is written on the Greenlight page, but that’s just the start of it.
Single player and multiplayer are roughly the same, except in single player you fight through varying levels and enemies towards the final “boss” more or less. As mentioned above, there’s no story or plot to the game, making it pointless outside of achievement hunters looking to complete it. The characters are fairly similar, each with a few basic moves, one moderately deadly one and one completely broken special ability that instantly kills your opponent.
The problem with such similar characters, so few moves, and the aforementioned item management being a pipe dream, coupled with poorly designed hit detection makes certain characters way more preferable over others, making the game unbalanced, even with such a subpar roaster. Combined that with clipping issues in the terrain, random disappearing characters [whom don’t reappear] and clunky controls, the game was doomed from the beginning.
Level design and visuals fared Bell Ringer well, as the levels themselves are done nicely and the visuals are actually quite pleasant, even down to the character models and attack special effects. What is perplexing is just how terrible the gameplay is in comparison to the visuals. While not visually amazing, the difference is palpable.
As I mentioned in the beginning, the marketplace is flooded with games that are PvP oriented and while the consumer market is huge, the surplus of these mediocre games are even greater. Bell Ringer entered a highly competitive category that’s known for high demand for ingenuity and an even higher player-base attrition rate. With nothing to set it apart from the rest of the crowd and very little publicity from the start, Bell Ringer came into the match crippled and the poor controls, lackluster gameplay and terrible PvP roaster all but sealed its fate.


Overall, Bell Ringer would have been an interesting idea if done properly, but the overall quality of the game leaves nothing but a bad taste in your mouth when you're finished. There are plenty of games that simulate this style of play far more completely and professionally and it would be in your best interest to seek them out instead.

This is one of the best games I've ever played, for sure.  People are calling it a MOBA, and technically it is, but it's not at all similar to League of Legends, Heroes of Newerth, Dota/Dota2, Heroes of the Storm, Smite, or any of the other existing MOBAs out there.  It's different because it's entirely skill shot based, and you don't move by right clicking the mouse.  You move in a traditional esdf/wasd method, which adds a dimension to the game that's hard to describe.
On top of all of this, the weapon charge system, combined with the energy system, combined with the skillshot based HEALING as well as damage, makes the game truely balanced.  It's actually balanced 1v1 between healers and dps, which is a feat not accomplished by any other game.
This game is most similar to World of Warcraft arenas, if those arena games were played from a RTS perspective.  And instead of 20+ abilities in WoW, you're limited to a core 7 with a special 2, totaling 9 (including the ULT).  The abilities cool down quickly and seperately, and it's all about using the best ability at the best time and aiming it the best and being faster than everyone.
This is definitely one of those games where you can 2v1 other players if you're good enough, which is what everyone who plays at a high level enjoys about this game.  As opposed to many other games, you can REALLY suck at this game, and tbh it will assuredly happen to new players.  The question is whether or not they can overcome their initial badness at the game.
It's not meant for people who aren't good at video games.  You're going to get♥♥♥♥♥♥on the entire time.  But the good news is, is never verbally.  The community in this game is something to be said for.  The reason why this is, is because this game evolved from something called Bloodline Champions, a game that was identical to this but had NO following.  Just a small handful of hardcores, and as a result of that, they had to be really nice to one another because they saw each other every day and every night.  It seems like the core of those people have moved to this new game (and are 5+ years ahead of everyone else - hey am I one of those people? You decide) and have taken that culture with them.  No one is rude to one another with the exception of a few people.
Hope this review was helpful.

Death of the outsider serves itself as a "DLC" to Dishonored 2.  You assume the role of Billie Lurk, a character from Dishonored 2 who's goal is to figure out the meaning behind the Outsider.
Very similar in nature to Dishonored 2, besides a few quirks such as contracts and new abilities, there's almost no difference between the two.
Decent writing throughout which serves as the games strongpoint. The story of Billie Lurk is fascinating and there's so much lore to discover behind it.
Great voice acting. The rats talking to you, the guards familiar voice, a scared citizen, all lend in hand to what made Dishonored 2.
This is a huge issue. The first mission is a unique area although a very short lived mission. The 2nd and 3rd mission both take place in the same map with almost no difference besides a new loot spawn. The 4th mission is the witch map from Dishonored 2 and the 5th mission is the void. To make 2/5 missions on the same map with no differences is awful. The 1st and 5th missions are way too short, and the 4th mission is literally the same map from Dishonored 2.
Easily the biggest problem with this game comes the length. It's 5 missions which are all (besides the 3rd) relatively short, add up to a very short play time. On my first playthrough it took me 4 hours to beat without rushing and my stealth playthrough took about 7. To charge 30 dollars for a game this short is a crime.
A decent game that's very short and lends itself to be a clone of Dishonored 2. Maps that are reused. Nothing innovative or new except the introduction of contracts and new abilities. Get this on a sale or from a cd key vendor because 30 dollars is far too much for such a short game.

Although a lot of these reviews claim this game is broken and unplayable on Win7, that isn't the case, as a few minor tweaks (compatibility, run as admin., etc.) will make the game run fine. However, the game is by far one of the most unbalanced and least enjoyable games I have ever played.
Anyone who has ever played the Might and Magic series will certainly be familiar with a high level of difficulty, but in that series a thorough grasp of the game mechanics combined with  a few false starts as you acquaint yourself with the lay of land will ultimately allow you to complete the missions. To take another example, the excellent Age of Wonders series (my personal benchmark for strategy/rpg excellence) is often said to be punishing, but the fact is once you learn all the game's tools, it's a rich and highly rewarding experience and there's no reason why you can't complete missions in fine fashion.
Disciples 2, on the other hand, is simply an exercise in masochism. Yes, the missions can be completed, but not without an excessive and highly frustrating amount of bloodletting, dying, reviving, etc., as from the start you will find that EVERY enemy on the map is stronger than you. Nor does it get better, as your character's progression -- should you be fortunate enough to carry one from one mission to the next -- is minimal at best and hardly matters compared to the strength of the monsters. Buffers offer only the most marginal of enhancements to your troops' stats, costly spells bestow laughable gains (10 fire damage to 300 HP monsters, oh boy), and hard-won battles are rewarded by the most modest and least consequential of loot drops.
It's only been from sheer stubbornness that I've persisted to the second mission (halfway through and looking bleak, overpowered beasts everywhere), but frankly, aside from the so-so graphics and music, this game offers precious little in the way of enjoyment.

I'm old enough to remember getting the PC Gamer CD with the original Shadow Warrior demo on it.  And I do have quite a bit of nostalgia for those days.  But the trouble with playing those old games is that graphics, level design and user interfaces have progressed so much since they were released that they often feel unbearably clunky compared to modern games.
Enter the new Shadow Warrior.  It feels like this is the game that would have been made if modern graphics and sensiblilities had existed back in the days of Wolf3D, Doom, and Duke Nukem.  This is a simple game, where your goal is only to survive hordes of enemies and find the key(s) that will let you progress to the next level.  The levels are completely linear--if it appears that you have a choice of direction, then one of your two paths hold a secret waiting to be found.  Your primary weapon will be the sword, though occasionally you'll switch to the old standards of pistol, machine gun, crossbow, shotgun, flamethrower or rocket launcher for convenience.  You collect money, karma and ki crystals, which let you upgrade your weapons, stats and special abilities respectively.
By all rights this game should be boring.  Yet I enjoyed it from beginning to end.  It is simple, vulgar, politically incorrect, gorgeous, funny and thoroughly entertaining.  It's best enjoyed in bite sized pieces of an hour or two.  I paid $5 for it and wouldn't have felt cheated if I had paid $15.  Don't pay more than that, though.  I've become increasingly bored with modern shooters, but I fully expect to buy the sequel to this game when it goes on sale for $10 or less.
From a fortune cookie in the game: "Having sex is like playing bridge.  If you don't have a good partner, you'd better have a good hand."

I love the concept of the game, I love that you have to decide between getting more money, and getting home safely with what you got. And two, the artwork is gorgeous.
But the one thing that makes this so incredibly annoying to play, and has me considering whether it's worth even trying to finish: the phyics feel so "clunky", which is really bad, since the is essentially a platformer. If you try to jump into a one-unit tall gap, the game may decide you want to cling to the wall above the gap. Or trying to jump off a wall, and the game decides you have absolutely zero vertical momentum on that jump and plummet to your death. Don't even get me started on trying to jump up a wall with a one-block overhang or walking down stairs with mines around.
Or if you try to knock out an enemy that you KNOW you hit, but instead get killed by it because the game phyiscs decided that you missed. There are enemies and obstacles such as mines that require split-second timing in order to avoid, but with the character movement being so clunky, you often end up dying because of the lack of fine control.
Yes, it is a difficult game, but I want to die because it is MY fault "I guess I shouldn't have gone back in the house for that extra vault" or "I should have waited for that enemy to walk by before sprinting behind the door."
I DO NOT want to die because "I pressed jump, but the character just walked down into the spike pit" or "I died because first the character clinged to the wall instead of jumping down, and then decided to let go a second later when the enemy had turned around."
Also, the "proedurally generated" aspect is nothing to write home about. The level is usually playable, but the generated layout often doesn't "feel right", and ends up with illogically placed rooms and empty corridors with nothing in them and no incentive to travel through them. There are pits and gaps which there is no real way to get across without because the code placed an enemy in a 1x1 block where there is really no way to hit it or jump over it, so you are stuck with an unsolvable situation.
It's a bare-minimum of what you can do with procedurally generated maps, but perhaps I'm giving it a hard time because  I'm expecting more, being a software developer myself.
I want to play this game, I really do, but if I can't control the character to my satisfaction, I'm essentially playing a game of luck, not a game of skill.

Kairo is a beautiful game. It stands right up there with best artistic endeavors in gaming in the last ten years, and its tone is perfectly executed. Do not play this game in a room full of housemates screaming at League of Legends (as I did in my first attempt); in order to appreciate the mood, you should be alone and open to anything. Because, thought the game does not literally deliver EVERYTHING, it conveys the feeling that it COULD, and that is a mostly lost art in gaming, as well as literature and film. After fully completing every aspect of the game, I still am not entirely sure of the exact story narrative, and the writer in me hates that, but that same writer also appreciates it. How easy would it have been for the developer to just give us computer terminals and characters to explain everything? But that's why this is so great. It felt like I was really there, really trying to piece together something entirely on my own. If I were actually there, I doubt there'd be notes scattered about just telling me every detail about what happened. But the story, while integral to the setting in design, is not essential to experiencing the setting. I highly recommend this to people who loved Myst back in the day; who enjoy newer exploration-based environmental games like FEZ and Gone Home; those of you who have to be driven by saving the princess and killing the bad guys, however, might want to sit this one out. But I enjoyed this game immensely. Thumbs way up!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Kairo is one of the most uniquely atmospheric game I've played. It's visuals are simple, but expertly crafted, both eerie and gorgeous at the same time. The movements feel rather sluggish, and at best, floaty, and there isn't much incentive to replay the game once completed. Not to sound cliche, but Kairo really is about the journey and not the destination.
For $5.00 at it's full price, you are getting a quality product. I can not recommend this game enough, especially at it's low price point.

- Excellent aesthetics
- Surreal and eerie atmosphere
- Interesting puzzles
- A very unique game overall

Cons:
- Floaty controls
- Not a lot of replay incentives

After playing it for a few hours last night, it seems the game has already been polished up quite a bit from all the gamer site reviews I read before it launched. Aliens, while powerful, are not as aggressive as the reviews would lead you to believe, and the first affinity bonus for purity prevents aliens from initiating attacks against explorer units, and I also got a quest perk that protects trade convoys from getting attacked by aliens as well. So all I have to worry about are my military units. There is also a protective laser fence improvement you can build in your cities that functions similarly to a great wall but just for a couple tiles.
The AI is definitely more anemic that previous games -- I'm just playing my first game on standard difficulty, standard pace, standard size, standard everything. After a couple hundred turns, nobody has attacked me yet and I've mostly explored the world, with three thriving cities (but health in the red). I still have quite a ways to go for aquiring more advanced resources, like Firaxite, so I can build more advanced things. Currently working on getting health to the green.
I attacked and destroyed a outpost that spawned one turn before I settled on it because that irritated me. I had 3 military units right there, and was barely able to take it out in 2 turns, and while I didn't lose anyone in the process, a couple of them were on the verge of death. The outpost never attacked me on his turns, just retaliated when I attacked -- which I thought was odd. Because if he did, I surely would have been forced to retreat and would have lost a unit.\
I'm just starting to get into the epionage part of the game, and it seems well structured and interesting -- more fleshed out than in previous games. I also like the satellite component of the game -- can build a satellite that clears miasmas over ten turns. Researching a tech that will improve food output over its area and actually create new food sources over it's 60 turn lifetime.
One thing that confused me at first were trade convoys. I accidentally built a naval version first, not realizing it, and then couldn't use it for a long time. Even though I had explorered coastal cities nearby, it would inexplicably not be able to trade. I was initially confused that I could selected it as a unit, but couldn't actually move it -- but you have to use the establish trade route button to do so. Just seemed weird and confusing.
The game is better than I anticipated after reading a lot of 7/10 reviews. It can benefit from additional polish and patches, but I'm confident Firaxis will deliver. At the moment, I'd give it an 85%, and I think the review scores would have been higher if they played the shipped version. Though Brave New World is still the very best of all the Civilization games. I'd rate this one 2nd best.

I honestly do not see why people like this game.
Poorly optimized, extremely shallow gameplay, broken menus, crap controls, and somehow bad graphics for such an awesome engine like UE4!!

The Ugly:
- The character portraits and design: I can only hope they were intentionally going for that pre-teen deviantArt feel, but being ironically bad doesn't mean it's not still horrid. Comparatively, the pixel art for enemies is generally pretty nice.
-----------
The Good:
- Random Encounter System. Each area has a set number of random encounters. After you fight that many, no more will appear as you walk around, although you can still seek out as many enemies as you wish through the "Fight" menu option if you need one more level before a boss or such. This system is...interesting. It's designed presumably to not be frustrating for people who get lost easily, but I found myself often simply exploiting the system by doing all 20 Fights that a late-game dungeon had, right next to the MP-restore point, and then going about my merry way through the dungeon totally risk free, a far cry from my memories of, say, fighting my way through FFVI dungeons with very limited resources and the constant hanging threat of game-over.
- Other "ease of play" changes, like above, is that you can save anywhere, and health auto-fully restores for free after each fight, which does streamline things, but also feel like betrayals of the genre to me. Putting it in good however simply because I don't think my opinion here outweighs the majority of people who were likely quite happy to see these features.
- The Humor. It being a parody, a fair sum of the humor unfortunately relies heavily on pop culture references and meta-humor about the genre. If that's your thing, then BuyBuyBuy, but chances are you've heard 9/10ths of it before elsewhere and the other 1/10ths isn't that funny to begin with. Maybe it's sad that that's all we can expect, but it comes with the territory. Thankfully, it doesn't feel as forced as it could be, and it's spaced out enough for the dosage to be non-toxic.
-The truly funny moments come whenever it stops trying so damn hard to reference older games, and just plays with it's own setting and characters.
---------
The Bad:
- Lazy port. There's a joke about ports in the opening, which should be a good sign, but then there's no way to quit the game without either dying and returning to the main menu, or killing the game process manually. It also has a permanently floating window, so good luck alt-tabbing out while the game is open.
- The music.  Ruins music is good, town music is generic, the rest is♥♥♥♥♥and the battle music will make you want to tear your ears off by the end. Mute it, listen to War & Peace on Audiobook and you'll be more stimulated.
- The plot. They didn't even try, which is the one sin an RPG plot can commit that is worse than having an incredibly over-elaborate setting and plot. The fact that the setting here could have been very interesting is what really twists the knife.
-----------
The Mixed:
- Hard Mode is actually hard. Which I would normally put as a good, except that the difficulty curve isn't truly apparent until the back half of the game, by which point some players may feel like they can neither progress nor justify restarting. It is always possible to simply grind through in that situation, though a re-consideration of tactics is usually that is necessary.
- Character building. It's a fun system, could be expanded on but it's tight and simple as is. There is one issues however that I draw against it. Every level-up each character's build options differ, but there's no in-game way of looking ahead of each character's progression. You can know from the archetype that Mages should have high Magic, but there's no way to know ahead of time what skillset your mage will learn have or what mutations each skill can undergo. This may cause some players to consult a guide, and anytime any game pushes it's player towards doing so, it loses major points.
- Interesting Setting, but grossly underused. Similarly, almost all of the dungeons are incredibly bland, but the ones set in the pre-war ruins are a real treat to explore. It feels like there was so very much wasted potential there.
------------------
Final Judgement:
For me, it easily passes the rule of thumb: Dollar for every hour of true enjoyment. It's price however certainly helps with that.
Recommended for: People who want a very cheap short RPG that isn't in RPGMaker and generally doesn't have aneurism inducing dialogue. You get what you pay for on Steam, but with this price, you actually get just a little bit more.

I really want to like this game, it bring something new to the electronic tcg genre. Unfortunately it is plagued with problems and I am getting tired of waiting for it to get better.
Card balance is terrible; there are 8 factions,  yet every single competitive deck has at least a splash of Cult of Verore. I can understand why, they have all of the direct kill spells, and a very easy board wipe that has no counter play. Sorry, when you bring up that Mass Death has no counter play, the designers of the game say "just don't attack or defend from turn 6 onwards", thanks for the advice. This game's card balance is one of the worst out of all the tcgs, you just see the same decks with the same cards over and over again.
The user interface is buggy and slow. It is often impossible to understand what is going on due to being unable to click on cards to see their text. Games drop out often or just flat out stall, leaving you to have to forfeit a game to be able to load a new one. I highly doubt that the game will ever be optimised to be able to run on a tablet like they have claimed, the game is just too much of a memory sink.
Abilities and cards do not operate how their text is written, you often have to play a test game when you get a new card just to figure out what the designers mean. The timing of how cards operate is never logical. If you are playing against an opponent with a card you have never seen before, you have to loose to that card just to see what it does. When a new set comes out, the process of learning the mechanics of a whole bunch of cards happens again. You could look all the new cards up, but what is written on the card doesn't always represents what happens in the game. The latest set Ascension has some terrible offenders: Anti-Air Array kills incoming flying creatures, but those creature still do combat damage from the graveyard, the card Descension turns a creature into a demonic dragon, but has the Consume ability, despite not being mentioned anywhere on the card. I haven't played against all the new cards yet, who knows how exactly they all work.
Lastly I am going to talk briefly on the very touchy subject of pay-to-win. I don't know what you may consider pay-to-win, but I am going to only consider the most basic interpretation, that if you pay money, you will get an advantage in game. OK, so I was about two weeks into playing daily, I had got the hang of the game and started to play competitively. I stalled out at about 800 rank due to the people I was playing having better decks. I figured I had to get some better cards. I couldn't trade cards because the free cards you get aren't tradeable. I could buy a booster using winnings from playing games, but that takes about 47 games at a 50% win rate. I eventually relented and spent some real world dollars. OMG, literally overnight I went up to 1100 rank. Within the week I was sitting at 1450. I'm now starting to slow again and I have to decide if it is worth spending more money to remain competitive, especially with a new set with all new powerful cards that I can't afford.

This is my favorite franchise of all time. I've bought every game and bit of DLC released. Even the books and such. I have almost 160 hours logged in D1 and over 90 in D2, so it pains me to say that DOTO did not hit the spot for me. I paid $50 for a six hour game for starters. This just wasn't long or deep enough to warrant a full separate release. It should have been $20 DLC.
Spoilers may follow:
- The ending of D1 left me awed at the journey the game had taken me on. The end of D2 left me satisfied that things had been set right. The end of DOTO made me feel like I'd been trapped in a corner by a philosophy major who'd had too many coffees and wouldn't STFU. I was caught between apathy and annoyance.
- Way too many ♥♥♥♥ing cultists. Apparently stuffing levels with enemies was prioritized over actual challenging gameplay. There's no Jindosh beauty in this game. Not even close.

- Unlike other iterations of Dishonored, this one almost felt linear. There was still some range of choice, but not compared to previous titles. In some levels, previous levels were used, but even they were cut down!
- Unlike in previous games where the drama played out directly in the actual gameplay via animated cut-scene in DOTO it's mostly you do some generic Dishonored blinking around to a designated point on the map, complete the level, and then a non-animated cutscene takes the place of what really should have been the most dramatic moments of the game.
-Sorry, but Billie Lurk was not written well enough to be the protagonist. I found her voice acting flat and unemotive, and I'm not sure I would have cared anyway had it been better. Even Daud came off as flat and apathetic. The game spent the whole time trying really hard to be meaningful and deep but in the end it just felt disconnected, disjointed and sort of unsatisfying. There was no moment of triumph. No swelling of music, no joy to be found. There was just moralizing and whimpering and a story that lost its way. It didn't even have the balls to go full on "Evil Emily" ending. It was just "oh well, I'm a murderer woe is me." (Apparently the non-lethal ending is more cheerful. Even so, the other comments stand. It's still a short, shallow shade of the first two games. Would have been fine as DLC, but not as standalone.)
To sum up, this fails on level design seriously, story line out of what feels like laziness. The gameplay is sort of interesting and might have held up better if the levels had been more expansive and not the tiny space same over and over.

If you don't want to read, just like a summary: This game is amazing, 11/10 buy it now!
What can I say? This game is Dishonored at it's finest - the graphics are beautiful and it doesn't suffer from the performance issues that the second one had upon release. I get a solid 60fps on Ultra, and the game is great! The new powers are awesome and being a character other than Corvo or Emily is really refreshing and you rely on bone charms a whole lot more than you did in the previous ones and they are a lot harder to find usually, especially considering you don't have a way to detect them in the beginning and you get a power that can do it but it requires more manual effort than it did in the first two.
The game overall is much more challenging and includes a lot more stealth elements; having your assassins creed-esque crossbow in the sleeve means that silent takedowns are easier but there isn't any guns blazing violence. You have a teleport ability similar to those of Corvo and Emily but getting to ledges higher than you is sometimes a little more difficult, meaning you require more skill in jumping from object to object. You have an ability I am upset you didn't have in the original games now that its in this one and I hope they include It in the next one; you can impersonate other people for a short amount of time and it's fantastic, really one of the best stealth game mechanics I have ever come across before.
Swordplay is pretty much the same as the other two and overall it feel very Dishonored; obviously runs in the same engine as the second one and feels the same graphically - my one gripe is that even on ultra the faces lack refinement, but the environments and clothing are amazing as always. The story is great, really dark and going back to Carnaka is a treat - so is being able to talk to rats, yes, you can talk to rats.
I've only had a few hours in this game and I will update you on how it goes for the rest of it but if you love dishonoured then I cannot recommend this game enough, it is more of the same and its just what I needed. If you have never played dishonoured before but wanna get into it this isn't the game for you; the rest of the series is really cheap right now and if I were you I would pick up the first one asap and play though it all because it is just amazing!

Ever thought of owning your own Taxi business? Do you like games that are all about patience and following the rules? Then Taxi still isn't for you. If you can get around the game's lackluster driving, the big issue here are the game breaking glitches.
The driving controls are easy, up to drive forward, down to come to a stop and go backward. Left and right to turn. While the controls are easy, its just a little dull having to follow the rules. The camera is automatic and as you drive faster it will change from a near top down angle to letting you see in front of you. It would be nice if you could move the camera around to either soak up the sights of the city or peak around the constant 90 degree turns.
Since you run a legitimate business, any speeding will get you fined. Most of the speed limits are 30 or 40, so I try to keep it under 20. Does that mean kph or mph? The game never told me. Running a red light is a fine. Damage is a fine. Even playing the game as carefully as I do and learning how to be patient, it was a struggle to make money, even when I wasn't fined. In the game's defense, the speed limit and your speed are clearly marked, as is the street lights. What's really odd is the logistics of having street lights on the same side of an intersection rather than across. I suppose from a game standpoint it makes sense, since the camera looks down on you when you're stopped rather than looking from behind you.
You own a taxi service, but in the hour that I played it, I never felt like I ran it so much as drove around picking up fares. In your garage, you can buy cars, hire other drivers, repair cars, clean them, paint them, and fuel them. They're all useless add ons to a shallow driving game.
The core of the game is simple, you drive around picking up fares. Then you wait as they take their sweet time getting into your taxi cab. Once they're in, your GPS shows you where to take them and you just follow the red line. This red line appears on your GPS from where you start, to where you finish, so if you deviate far away from the red line, you need to hit the refresh button on your GPS to get a new red line.
If you can't find a fare, you can click on an icon that will show you to one. These are the more interesting fares. People with luggage that needs to stay on top of your car, because apparently your trunk is full of dead bodies or something. Some people need getaway drivers, so you'll need to avoid cops, but that's okay because the game glitches out where it doesn't spawn cars until you quit and restart the game. Another quest had me following a car, but there was no subtlety. I could follow so close that when coming down off of a bridge I rammed it. That's cool, my passenger didn't mind I rammed what was probably his friend's car.
Your fare has a happiness rating, break the law and the happiness goes down, but its so slight that its barely noticable. The further you drive, the more money you'll get, so always take the long route and your passenger doesn't care. If you want to drive around the city, when the person only wants to be dropped off around the block, go for it.
There are a few fares with time limits and those feel impossible, because you'll need to end up breaking the law and therefore there's no profit from it. So its better to waste time than lose money in the process.
One of the glaring issues with the pick up and drop off is how small the zone is. You need to stop in a narrow slot with no wiggle room. Its only a minor issue, until it comes to stopping in an area with a pot hole that takes up 50% of the zone. Your car takes up about 90% of the zone. So you have to take a hit from the pot hole.
You see pot holes damage your car, which has what I can only describe as a health meter. If your car is out of health, it needs to be towed back to your garage for a hefty fine, but the bigger issue is pot holes are like objects. If you run into them head on, that's fine you can go through them, but if you try to turn into a pot hole or nudge it with the side of your car, it blocks you. In fact I've seen my car ram a pot hole and come to a complete stop.
Each fare tends to be around $100 which is fine. The real problem is the expense of repairs and cleaning. Fuel goes down at a laughably low rate. You'd assume driving around 24 hours a day with no brake would have your gas tank empty three times, but no 24 hours of driving is worth 10% of your fuel. I'd say fuel and cleaning is reversed. Cleaning runs about $50 or so.
You can get your car cleaned, repaired and fueled at your garage, but there are places out and about when driving to have it done. The really cool thing is your passenger sits happily as you get your car repaired. That's super nice of them. I wish I could say easy mode lets you do that and hard mode doesn't let you do that, but there are no difficulties.
Another problem is my car would get damaged without me understanding why it was damaged. Did I hit a pot hole? No. Did I ram a car? No. Did I hit a sidewalk or a stop sign? No. yet it went down. Repairing your car from low to full health can cost $250 - $400. That's about 4/6ths of the money. To the game's credit, there are no shifts, you can drive around for days and days. Just like you can in real life! Hey someone out there has probably done it before! How else will you get from Alaska to Argentina in a week? Buy a plane ticket?
While your car will need repairs, there's no damage effects. So when you crash, that's okay your car doesn't crumple up. No one gets maimed when you plow into them. Street signs don't even fall over when you hit them. Sure your car stops as if you hit a building, but the signs are okay.
What you really came here for is to know about the glitches in a $5 game. There's nothing laughably awful, just game breaking. Such as the passenger that I picked up and the GPS didn't refresh to tell me his destination. So I refreshed... well his destination is where I picked him up. That's silly. So I drove around the block to get more money out of him. When I arrived back where I picked him up, there's no drop off zone. I was stuck with him. You can't tell a passenger to get out, you just need to make them unhappy, which is surprisingly difficult.
Then there was the glitch where my car was in pristine condition, cleaned, fueled and repaired to perfect health. Then I made the mistake of saving and quitting the game. When I returned the car was badly damaged and half clean. Maybe someone used it while the game was closed? No.... the save file glitched where it used my car's status from a previous save using the same slot. I still had the same amount of money from my real save, which was virtually nothing. So I couldn't repair or clean my car, because its 100% or nothing. You can't repair 10% at a time.
For all of the laws and fines, the cops don't care if you do a 3 point turn about in the middle of a 2 lane road, even when they're right there watching. If you break the speed limit after the game stops spawning cars or even people, they still care.
The city feels like a shining point to the game, but anything can be a highlight in a game that I hold such low regard. There's a bridge over the city with 45 degree on ramps. Its interesting. You'll never get lost with your GPS and instant garage traveling icon. In a perfect world, the city would be vast and procedural generated.
As for the music and sound, there's a music loop in the menu and your garage, but out on the road, you only have your car's engine to listen to. It almost sounds like what I imagine a gentle spaceship to sound like. Its a gentle sound, instead of an over the top 50s style spaceship sound or what the Jetsons would sound like.
So with all that the game has going for it, how could I not recommend it? Well you see I like actual business with my business games. There is a business, don't get me wrong, but after playing the game I wasn't able to buy anything for the business.

Ok so I pre-ordered this game because I love the series but I gotta be truthful to what I'm about to say.
I feel the pricetag is alot for something that feels empty at the end of the game.
I finished the game and walked away with "hm ok".
Now I wish the recommend this game part said "Yes + No" or a custom type of recommendation so let me explain why.
I recommend this to anyone who are fans of the series but I do not recommend this to anyone who would end up picking up and playing it.
Lets start with,
Pros:
Gameplay is great and feels the same as dishonored 1 and 2 in terms of doing different types of tactics etc,
Graphics are good but sometimes performance suffers even on my beefy PC,
The voice acting is top-notch,
The sections of the game are very lively,
No bloodflies to scare the crap out of you,
The new powers are brilliant.
Cons:
This should've just been some cheap DLC like brigmoire witches rather than a whole different "game" even though it uses the dishonored 2 engine and the same exact locations which are just revisted,
The story is way too short and doesn't really reward you with any "OMG" moments,
The missions seem lazy compared to dishonored 1 and 2,
You have 0 incentive to not murder everyone in sight as it doesn't affect the game ending,
You play as one character (while i thought you play as billie and daud kinda like corvo/emily),
It took me 3 hours (Though i did afk hour alot due to not caring if it was on or not) to complete it while collecting and completing any side quests/contracts on max difficulty,
You can easily run through this game if you don't care about killing,
The performance of the game in terms of FPS mirror dishonored 2 launch issues with fps drops,
Only 5 missions and one shouldn't really be considered a mission as its that short,
Only 1 new type of enemy aka the void version of the clockwork soldiers,
You don't get to upgrade your powers only more bones,
You only get 3 powers through the whole game until you get a certain weapon that is just MEH.
So all in all I'd tell you to wait for the game to be $10 as I feel I just wasted my money.
The only good thing about the game is it at gave me some time wasting for FIFA around the corner.
So my final review score is -
6/10 - Above average aka mildly mediocre.

While I had problems running it in the beginning (my computer is I7 - Win 8.1 - 64 Bit based) I found out that the problem was connected to the audio settings (have a look in the configuration editor) and its CPU Affinity (seems to have problems with more than one assigned to it...).
Disabling Sounds and Music and setting the application to use only one CPU (easytoolz => CPU Affinity) solved my starting issues and the app ran fine.
Having a deeper look into it however, the sound issues seem to be connected to the secondary buffer size (advanced sound settings). After increasing it to the maximum I could enable sounds and music too.
I don't recommend this game.

My hours on this are misleading because, like a typical author, I'll leave it open to think on something and then perhaps walk the dog, take a shower, go to the store, fall asleep...
I'm a published author, but I also ran a small publishing house for years. I edited and formatted several books, and I also create ebooks. That last one, creating ebooks, is the biggest feature that I love about Nimble Writer.
When you're writing, you're creating your ebook as you go. What you see is how it will look. When you're finished, you can export it as an epub and put any final touches in with Sigil or Calibre. It takes out a ton of extra work without sacrificing quality.
I also love the way I can easily export chapters for Microsoft Word. This enables me to send them to my editor as I finish going through them in later drafts. He sends me the edits back, I apply the changes in Nimble Writer, and keep truckin' along!
Finally (for my review but certainly not the features offered), I love that my files sync with the Steam Cloud. That added bit of security should anything go wrong is wonderful.

I'll try and be short as possible and describe how i got this game working on Win8:
First start with configuration editor that is offered to you by Steam when launching the game. Set resolution to 800x600 - when setting any other resolution, game wouldn't start.
Check "Use 3D" "Stretch to full-screen" and "Compatibility mode". Other settings do not affect game start or performance. Click on "Save" at the bottom of window.
Secondly, DO NOT change seetings in "Discipl2.exe" as this will just screw up game start. DO NOT set compatibility mode or "Run this program as Administrator" in here. Let the Configuration editor do all the work.
This is how i managed to start the game after half an hour of trial and error. This setting worked for me but it doesn't mean it will work for you. You may start the game with this settings but game might be choppy, laggy. If that happens, Alt+Tab and start Task manager. Click on "More details" if it isn't already on, and go to details tab, select "Dicipl2.exe", right click on it and set affinity to a single core. No matter how many cores do you have, leave only one checked! This is how i fixed choppy performance in SimCity 4. Since it's not lagging on my machine i can't confirm this will work, but it's another option that you can try.
In the end i would close by thanking Microsoft for making this new Win8 platform verry complicated for most(or all) older and newer games.
Game is definitivelly recommended by me if you like games like Heroes of Might and Magic and King's Bounty.

So from what I can gather looking at the lambasting this game has received, it seems most of the negative feedback stems from some ill conceived notion that this is a game about being a big badass mofo Space Marine chewing through Genestealers like gum. Basically kids who bought the game because they saw a Space Marine on the cover.
You can disregard those reviews.
This game is a near identical adaptation of Space Hulk, an early 80s boardgame that long predates 40k as we know it now. Space Hulk has a simple premise underneath all the fluff and theatrics of the 40k franchise: Do you have the tactical prowess to get your nervous,  bumbling Terminators from Point A to Point B without getting repurposed into a hat by the purple locals?
The game is all about space management: everything is based on a grid, and your big hulky terminators are slow as hell but have guns. Meanwhile, the genestealers are fast and there are always more of them coming, but they only have melee.
If a space marine shoots a genestealer, that bug is dead. If a genestealer gets in melee with a terminator, 8 out of 10 times that Terminator is getting turned inside out. You want to catch the genestealers out in the open so you can mow them down from a distance, while the genestealers want to ambush you and overwhelm you as you try to navigate long, narrow corridors.
The key to beating them is to carefully manage your squad's movement, placement, and keep them holding a perimeter at all times. Your terminators can only spend 4 action points a turn to either move/pivot, shoot, go into guard/overwatch or attack in melee if you're feeling stupid. You can kill dozens of genestealers in one turn, but it only takes one of them sneaking up on your guys to topple your house of cards.
If this sounds fun, intriguing, or strategically engaging to you, then congratulations, you'll probably adore this game. It's a lot of the strategic risk/reward planning one finds at the core of games like the XCOM franchise, and the genestealers here can certainly strike parallels to the ever so horrible Chrysalids from XCOM.
If this sounds terribly tedious, slow or boring to you, well then I just saved you a couple bucks.
Now that we've gotten that all cleared up, I can lay out the bullet points (from the perspective of someone who would be interested in this kind of game)
PROS:
+ It's Space Hulk. The missions are well thought out challenges that will demand you give it your all.
+ The graphics are respectable and work well in service of the board game. I hold this in point of contrast to the Space Hulk Ascenscion game , which while more graphically atmospheric, makes for a poor board game when you can't see where you're trying to place your terminators half the time.
+Some of the sound design is actually quite immersive, particularly the groaning noises of the ships, the boltguns firing off, and the crunchy noises your guys make walking over bug corpses.
+ It's Space Hulk. I own the board game as well, but sometimes you just want to play the game without roping someone else in or spending an hour setting up the game. This is a great way to get a fix without the hassle.
CONS:
- The kill animation/stingers while a novelty at first, can get a little tiresome at times when you're lighting up 7+ genestealers in one hall at once.
-The animations can take up your sweet time. There's options to speed up the animations which is fine, but then you gotta find a way to not get distracted by the sight of your terminators quickly waddling around. Seriously, it's like watching a line of ducklings.
-Music is kinda mediocre whenever it does play. I usually have a playlist going in the background when I play.
-The price. While it's true 30$ for a digital version of a 150whatever+$ board game is a fair trade, I can see how the price tag can put people uninitiated to the board game off.
-The actual melee/death animations for both the Nids and Space Marines feel a little piddly. If there is one thing I can say about the Ascencion variant, it certainly brought the violence of fighting murderous space bugs to life in a way this one didn't.
TL;DR: If you love the board game, you'll love this. If you were like me, I never paid the board game any thought until I bought this and realized how much I enjoyed it, to the point of going out and getting the actual tabletop version. Money well spent in both cases. If you're looking for what is essentially a digitized boardgame, this is the game for you. If you're looking for fast, frantic violence, you should check out Space Hulk Deathwing instead- for all it's flaws, it still looks pretty fulfilling on that end.
Normally this game is 30 or 25$, and I would say that price is rather steep for what is essentially the board game but constrained to single player format. Right now though it's on sale for 5$ and If you are interested in this game, THIS is the time to get it.
If you can get it for just 5$, you absolutely should. Worst case scenario, it ain't your thing and you only lost 5$ (and even then you have Steam Refunds now). Best case scenario, you just got all the fun of a hard to find 150$+ board game for 5$.

As a young novelist I can tell you that Nimble Writer is definitely a program that can take on the role of your main word processor. The layout of Nimble Writer is basic but not outdated, it has what you need;
- you can quickly check notes and move back and forth between your chapters.
- It allows you to make meaingful notes.
- Background is soft on the eyes so it won't hinder you from working for long periods.
- It helps seperate you from any distractions so you can focus on your writing.
- It keeps counts of your words, paragraphs, and characters.
It sounds good and it is good but it's 'not stand alone.' Nimble Writer is in it's young years and cannot meet all the needs a professional writer must have.
- You cannot insert images (which gives it no practical use for those making magazines and things of the sort.)
- There is no ruler to properly adjust your typing space.
- It does not have actual pages (Nimble Writer is actually a scripting "pad" that's been modified like with google docs.)
Let me elaborate on the not having pages. Not having pages is a huge deal. You cannot edit your page numbers; you cannot properly put headers; you cannot put footers; you cannot properly put titles.
Conclusion
Nimble Writer is good for writing but requires other software to properly format and edit your product.

First up, Nimble Writer is indeed rather short on feautures.  No grammar check, no thesaurus, and yes, I have found a few bugs.  Those cons aside, NimbleWriter is nonetheless a clean, compact writing program with a good interface that works as advertised.  There is a certain productivity that oozes from it for me, and I'm not exactly sure why.
The primary reason I've started using it is the organization of chapters and character notes into one file.  Gone are the days of Excel, Word, the internet and Paint all being open at once.  Now, it's just me, the dictionary/thesaurus and this program - at least for the drafting stage.
The ability to export to various formats doesn't hurt either.  Personally, I love that it tracks your efforts in terms of hours logged and words written.  I'm a sucker for metrics, especially when they give you a form of tangible credit at the end of the day. Would I use this program just because it has Steam achievements?  No way, but it sure doesn't hurt anything.  Pair the above with Steam Workshop, the fact that the devs appear responsive and you have a program that is at least worth a closer look. See youtube for a few impression videos.  Rating 6.9

Lets keep this one simple.  Its Assassins Creed.  You guys know it, im sure everyone has tried one of the games in the series at some point.
The story for this one is very interesting, Ubisoft seems to have changed gameplay up and made the game far more open world.  So you have the normal Assassins creed, parkour mixed with hack and slash fighting mechanics with a good and interesting storyline of the battle through the ages of the templars vs the assassins.
The story is solid making reference to historical characters and events, you even meet the real life characters that made piracy so compelling as a storyline throughout the ages.
After playing through this i feel that it was a much stronger game than every other Assassins creed game i played and i own the entire series.
What did i like about it?
The storyline while starting off dragging its heels a little was very interesting it almost felt like a movie to me.
Characters were fantastic i loved them all, the voice actors did a fine job.
The actual fighting on land was typical of any Assassins creed game here nothing new i found this average at best.
Ship to ship combat and travel was immense, this was the most interesting part for me at least.  Braving a tropical storm at sea while in a battle firing cannons at an enemy ship was breathtaking.  I enjoyed the fact you could attack any ship you wanted i felt this made the game more open and enjoyable.
Ship upgrades were a much needed addon and ubisoft delivered on this.  No more running from a battle with a larger more powerful ship later on in the game once you have the upgrades needed to take down such ships.
The deck battles after weakening a ship i found better than the land battles as it just felt right for the the time and location and scenario of the game.
The side missions as usuall were and interesting touch and i found myself constantly starying from the main story to chase these and complete them while not ruining my enjoyment of the game at all.
The graphics and sound effects were excellent but you can expect the same movements and similar textures to previous titles but dont be put off ubisoft once again have done a great job makign everything and everyone look good.
What i didnt like...
Average land combat although the flint lock pistols added some fun it can get repetetive quite fast and i found myself itching to get back on the water to take down a man o war spanish warship everytime.
The story seemed somewhat short, this is usually a case with most Assassins creed games they seem to end the story rather short.
All in all i enjoyed this game.  It was a very different approach to what im used to with the Assassins creed series and what i would say if you are considering this game its a no brainer really to just buy it and play through it at least once.

That rounds up my review i'll give this one 8 out of 10.

Kairo - Review
Gameplay:  7/10
Delivering a new and fun approach to puzzle gaming, Kairo give hours of fun with an ancient twist. The gameplay is simple yet effective, it delivers a challenging balance between the need to use logic and intuition.
Game ambiance: 6/10
There is little in the way of graphic ambiance in Kiro; odd geometries floating about with an abundance of fog. This is exemplified by the subtle use of sound and music. What it does have is a creative and well blended atmosphere between these elements to give a relaxing sense of space and mystery.
Reliability/Stability: 10/10
The game has had no issues to report.
Story/Plot: n/a
Concept: 6/10
The idea of using ancient Egypt in the puzzle genre of gaming has been around for a while. But it's never been done in this way.
Concept execution: 7/10
Creative, original, simple and effective; the execution of this game is almost dream-like. Unlike other puzzle games Kairo enables a challenging, stress-free, fun and relaxed problem solving platform to explore.
Textures: 2/10
Nothing special, but then nothing special is needed.
Modelling: 4/10

I love the central idea that this game is built around.  But I don't love the heavily flawed controls, and constant bugs and glitches. Just in the last few days of playing, I've encountered many glitches. I've gotten stuck in the scenery, I've had the Teleporter ability completely glitch out and freeze my character in mid-animation so I had to terminate them, I've had enemies somehow see me through solid objects and instantly kill me. When it plays well and how it's supposed to, it's really enjoyable, but when you die several times from glitches and terrain weirdness beyond your control, the gameplay feels cheap and unsatisfying.
The controls are not tight enough to serve a game which demands constant careful traversal. Sometimes I've slid down stairs onto mines, or had the jump button suddenly become unresponsive. Many of the commands sometimes feel like they're not responding. The game simply does not give you the control and polish you need for the level of skill it wants from you. I love the idea, the challenge, and the look, but the shaky controls, and frustrating glitches make it too flawed a gem for me to recommend. When I die in a game I want it to be because I screwed up, not because the game suddenly decided to get my character stuck in a wall.

As an Assassin's Creed game, Black Flag doesn't bring much new to the series. As a game on it's own, however, I found it to be one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I have had in a long time. The gameplay is essentially the same as any other Creed game, with the addition of sailing and advanced naval combat, which is marvelously streamlined and satisfying. The star, Edward Kenway, is a far more interesting character than in previous installments, and I found a lot of enjoyment in meeting and reading about the various pirates of history in the carribean.
Honestly, when I started this game, I cared very little for the simultaneous modern timeline story in which you play as an Abstergo Employee sifting through memories. I've always found Creed's ongoing story to be a little tedious. The more I advanced in the game, though, the more attached and interested I became; which is great, because that's how a game should be.
My only complaint is in regard to combat, and it's a small complaint. Occasionally when fighting larger groups of enemies, it can be very difficult to see the parry warning pop up, particularly when the enemy in question is out of your camera range. It was annoying at worst, but rarely an issue. Otherwise, combat was very smooth, almost on the level of the Arkham series's freeflow engine.
The music is absolutely fantastic, and features collectible shanties for your crew to sing while you sail.
I really can't recommend this game enough. Even if you dislike Assassin's Creed, but you like pirates, buy this game. If you like Assassin's Creed, you simply HAVE to own this game.

So, its time to write a first report based on the current state of the game. You should know however I only played a few TCG online and only 2 in RL. Maybe thats helpfull for other ppl without TCG experience.
I want to point out the 3 factors why I love this game so far:
- Interesting mechanics
This game is very different to other TCGs. Its a great advantage, IF you like this. You have to try it out (not only for 3 hours), than you can decide. Imo it has a fresh mechanic that enables various interesting aproaches and mindgames.
Be aware that you have "learn" some effects first, but they are rly well described ingame, also you can see this helptext every time you hover over the cards (also during a game).
Every game you wanna play longer HAS TO HAVE ITS STRENGTH IN THIS AREA!
If the mechanic is to simple, you wont play it that long. In this game, you discover interesting moves and synergies as you play erverytime.
- Great community
I dont know what decides how a community acts, but for this game the community is a big plus. You will need the ppl for two aspects. As there is a complex mechanic, its always good to get some helpfull tips, new ideas and such. This community will provide it. There are many friendly ppl who help all the newcomers if they have some questions or need some input for their decks.
Second, this is a trading game. Ofc not all ppl are the same, but I met so many ppl that not only provided FAIR trades to newcommer, no, they also made trades in my favor because I still have a rather small collection in comparism to others. This is the second important fact.
- F2P
This is probably the most important information for ALL F2P games. There is and will always be a debatte about the "fairness" of a given game in the F2P aspect.
First, you can start very smooth and will get ALOT cards as a new player FAST. You are also guaranteed to get some better (rarer!) cards during that periode. IF you are lucky, you get ever more rarer cards instead. However, as in every TGC, if you have 100 cards in the end, you will only have a few rares, no matter if they are "rare" "epic" or "legendary" using the ingame-terms.
Second, you always get free cards for login, daily wins and quests. Again, some of them are fixed, some of the prices are random (your luck decides!).
That means, if you start out, it compares to the fairest F2P games that are currently know. Why is there still a debatte? Because there is the midgame part. Imho this is the part where changes are needed. You have 3 problems after the early period (remember, this starts to happen after 150+ hours, THEN you enter the midgame periode.
First, level ups are getting more and more harder (you need more exp for every level) and the highest lvl is currently 50. I am at lvl 27 myself. If you are a more or less casual gamer with only a couple games a day, you will start to feel it. That means the free booster (15 cards) will come on a greater periode.
Second, the boosters with ingame money are fair priced, but again as casual it takes some time to get them.
Third, you can only trade with cards you have got with ingame or real money. So, you get less free cards, but you cant earn ingame money faster.
