I have no idea why there are so many negative reviews.  Nevertheless, the reviews were so bad about a year ago that I didn't touch it.  So I did wait until Dec 2015 to try it out after all the patches and changes that seemed to make it worth buying.  I race in iRacing, PCars, Assetto Corsa, FM, FH, and now RaceRoom.  The graphics inside the cockpit and looking out to the opponents is probably the best among these sims providing you have a decent PC and can max out the graphics.  I give it a 9.5/10 for graphics.  The physics are also very good since you can adjust many settings in the FFB.  So if you make a few adjustments, then I would easily say 9/10 on phyiscs.  And with all the adjustments you get for the feel, then nearly a perfect.    The gameplay is focused on DTM and GT3 in my opinion and that is pretty much why I bought it.  No other sims have anything really in the DTM class although I am hoping PCars gets into DTM more.  So if you like DTM, I can tell you this is the best sim for DTM.  I haven't had any issues at all and have to say the negative onslaught this game gets is just not accurate.  But there seems to be a few issues.  Like with the fuel and tire wear set to real, they don't seem to ever go down.  It's 100% all the time so I think that is a bug.  And the AI is annoying until you learn how to avoid them.  But this is one of the best sims out there in my opinion, especially DTM and GT3.  I just don't understand how people can spend 15 min on a game and slam the heck out of it.  Their connectivity issues and setup is more than likely their own setup problem.  Yes, it needs a little help with car setups too like adding tire pressure...lol  But the game feels and looks excellent,  It's worth the money for DTM for sure.
Update: 4/30/2016 - RaceRoom is Awesome!  I've waited a month after the 3/31/2016 update that massively improved the GT3 and Prototype physics.  The new physics and new FFB settings, new car setup, especially for GT3, ADAC GT Masters, DTM, and the new Audi P1 along with Nordschleife puts this sim to the stellar level in my opinion.  In addition, the fuel and tire wear now works finally.  Neverthelesss, the new FFB meter to check for clipping is very nice.  I am very critical of physics and so you know where I am coming from, Assetto Corsa and iRacing have the top slot with PCars a close second.  Race Room was just behind PCars.  Unfortunately, Forza just doesn't have the physics at these levels, e.g. you cannot feel the rubber on the road and utilze braking to control the cornering accurately in Forza Motorsport at least yet.  So Forza is last in the physics ranking among all these.  But I am now putting RaceRoom up there at the Assetto Corsa and iRacing level.  I am at the point of saying the physics in Race Room, at least for the DTM, ADAC, GT3 and Prototype classes, is possibly even better than Assetto Corsa and iRacing.  The sound in Race Room is also stellar if not the best among the aformentioned sims and I am not even using 7.1 yet just stereo.  Race Room does not get the recognition it deserves....another point is I am astonished it's onlyh using DX9c where all the others I've mentioned are on DX11 or even DX12.  So it blows me away they are getting this level of crisp graphics viewing the opponents cars and interior that they do....congrats Race Room for pulling that off.

This game should have been so good.
The aesthetic and art is fantastic, and is embellished by the great soundtrack. The exciting, tense gameplay draws you in and the somewhat unique risk/reward system is very compelling. The proceduarally generated levels ensure infinite replayability and are challenging, but sometimes generate inaccessable rooms or spawn things in such a way as to make the room impossible to traverse. The Swindle is an exciting, tense, difficult, beautiful stealth platformer.
This is all ruined by the controls.
The controls are
. In games like Mark of the Ninja, controls and actions are pixel-perfect. You know exactly what will happen when you press those buttons. In The Swindle, you do not. Will I grip onto that wall? Will I make the jump in time for the guard to not see me? Will I be able to jump down there? Will the wall slide work this time? These are questions that I cannot answer. I have genuinely seen internet flash platformers with more useable and responsive controls. It makes me very sad to say that, because this game could have been one of my favourite games this year. It's a terrible, terrible shame that things are this way, because if this game had Mark of the Ninja's controls it would be truly exceptional.
Also, no mouse control in any menus. Really?

This game is a faithful interpretation of the board game.
If that is what you are looking for, you will be happy with the end result.
The AI is acceptable, and the convenience of having the game handle dice rolls and special rules is really nice.
For lovers of the board game, I'd recommend the following settings:
1) set the animation speed to "fast"
2) turn off the extra combat animations (they are cinematic sequences that get a bit tedious)
3) turn off the over-the-shoulder camera view (a neat feature, but it clogs up the screen)
My ONLY complaints are (1) that you can "undo" combat dice rolls that occur on your own turn (breaking the value of some of the achievements) and (2) the inclusion of that RIDICULOUS ultra-grind achievement involving killing 40,000 genestealers (the completionist in me can't stand that kind of crap)

The Perfect Christmas Game:
Have you ever wanted to play a game as Santa? Well, slip on your red cap; this is the game for you! Christmas is under attack, and only you can save it! The Devil’s Basilisk is an evil machine that would make it impossible for Santa to infiltrate people’s homes and deliver presents. As such, you, Santa Claus, have devised a plan to restore joy to the good girls and boys. You are going to steal the Devil’s Basilisk. Commanding your elves, or “thieves,” you will jump, bomb, and hack your way to a Merry Christmas. Also, the world is run by robots.
The Swindle’s art and music are very festive, and set the mood for some platforming action. But don’t be fooled by vision cones; it’s not a Mark of the Ninja clone. This is not truly a stealth-game. More than anything, this is an arcade game. The rigid, deliberate controls recall games in the vein of Mario Bros, and Donkey Kong. Additionally, much like an arcade game, you are most likely going to fail in your first playthrough. Christmas wasn’t built in a day, and this game is challenging. However, unlike most classic arcade games, you do not have a set number of lives before you are forced to restart. Instead, you have 100 days (referencing the song “100 Nights of Christmas”) to reach the last level, perform the ultimate heist, and save the season.
Access to the last level is expensive, so before you can win, you will need to amass money- and they only accept British Pounds. Fortunately, after the apocalypse, the British Pound was the robot’s currency of choice. Robots cannot love; surely, it is okay to rob them. Using, your Santa infiltration know-how, direct your elves through the slums, banks, and casinos, to take them for everything they’ve got. Every attempted heist costs one of your 100 days, and a successful heist will bring you money and experience bonuses Fail, and one of your elves is banished from the Winter Wonderlands- Santa Claus does not accept failure.
Have you got what it takes to save Christmas?

Exciting and Frustrating.
Exciting:  There are lots of different cards with different powers, and turns are played simultaneously, so there is lots of tension and excitement and surprises.  This plays very differently than other cards games in which matches have more of a sense of grinding them out and focussing on small advantages.  Another plus during the Beta is that you receive lots of free cards (including one per day for simply logging in), so if this game catches your interest you might as well download it and start collecting free cards in case you like it.
Frustrating:  There are certain uber cards and uber combos, most of which are rare.  And at least during the Beta, a majority of the players I encounter are long-time players with good collections.  Therefore, it is not uncommon during a match for a newer player to be totally outmatched by cards and tactics that you have no chance of countering.  My hope is that once the game is published there will be a large base of players so that newer players will mostly play against other newer players. Another frustration is that, at least as of this writing, there is no replay function, which means that sometimes effects will happen and you will have no idea how or what happened.  The company says that a replay feature will be added.

I don't normally like trading or customizable card games, but for some reason I keep coming back to this game. I think it might be the cool animations on the cards when they do battle. Whatever it is, I haven't regretted getting into this game.

While I recommend the game overall for the new twists on development and growth (e.g. the tech web, policies, etc.) - I was very disappointed in this game from a graphical and presentation perspective.
It definitely scratches the turn-based itch, puts enough new spin on previous Civs to treat as a stand-alone product, and on its night of release already cost me sleep. (For the negatives read below).
Using a 30" monitor at x1600, the graphics actually regressed from Civ V. As noted by others, depending on the underlying terrain miasma, hills and other features can be difficult to see. The "new" interface is less intuitive, feels more clunky, and doesn't scale to the resolution as well either. While they tried to make a more alien 3D landscape, it still came off feeling a bit too flat.
In the grand scheme of things, most of my complaints are all minor or related to the overall polish of the game, but they are detractors that can leave the experience a bit flat and bland - as if something is missing. I understand the minimalistic approach to design, but the information should be readily available without requiring that I go digging in the Civilopedia for better details.
In addition, seems as if quite a bit of balance still needs to be done on certain choices and/or technology rushes - some of the choices are so blatantly beneficial, you have to wonder why the option was provided at all.

This game is still in beta, and there are some annoying bugs, but, it is free to play, and you get cards and in-game currency given to you simply by playing the game.
It plays similarly to other card games, in that you draw a card each turn, your resources typically increase each turn (No lands/mana here, you get Resources, increasing in number by 1 per turn, refilling at the start of your turn, ie: turn 1 = 1 resource, turn 2 = 2 resources, until you hit 10.)
The Good / Innovations:
Commanders (3 Characters you assign to be in the command zone of the battle field, able to be played like they are in your hand, but also able to be targeted by abilities/spells due to being on the battlefield. This adds another depth of strategy to the game, and takes a little luck out of getting a good starting hand.
Trading Post:
Got spare resources? Use them to draw a card, or increase your resource pool by 1 permanently. This also adds another layer of strategy to the game, but slightly diminishes that special feeling of certain playstyles that draw cards regularly.
Zones:
4 zones, Command (Commanders start here) Support (Think of the bench where your backups are, newly played cards and exhausted units go to this zone, some cards give/get bonus attack/health for remaining in this zone)  Defense (Area for characters that will defend you) and Assault (Characters you want to attack the enemy go here). The order in which your characters are placed in the zones, determines what order they will attack/defend in, and can be switched around for added strategy.
The Bad:
Issues that are acknowledged by, but not resolved by, the developers.
Don't bother with doing the game mode "Rift runs" (Ranked drafted matches where you can get your drafted deck for free if you win enough games before losing 3 times). Your opponent can just afk if they are about to lose, and the timer won't force their turn to end, and they'll just leave their computer on for days, if you exit the game, you get an automatic loss and they a win. It becomes a test of who will lose their internet connection first.
This issue has existed for months, with the devs calling it a bug (It clearly isn't from peoples reports and the fact it always happens near the end of a Rift match, even if it was, it's pretty major considering you pay for rift runs with either ingame currency or real money)
Ranked matchmaking: You get a rank, but it does affect the rank of your opponents, most of the time you will face opponents much more experienced than you, it's a tough road, especially when these people can exploit bugs to get more cards than you.
The community: is fairly infant, but I do hope it grows. Most people don't use the chat, nor reply to glhf/hello or ggwp etc. Some people take extra time on their turns (if they stretch it out to about 10 minutes a game, they get max currency for that match)
Level cap: Reach 50 and you no longer receive exp (required for some quests) and cards when you level. I think it's something being considered being removed, if not, it should be.
If you have friends who enjoy card games and can play with them, this is a great game, easy to learn yet hard to master, and has some innovations other card games could learn from.
If you mainly enjoy playing versus random people, especially competitively, I'd wait until the developers finally get around to fixing some serious issues, or you're going to have a bad time.
tldr: play with friends gooood, play competitively baaaaad (at the moment)

Excellent card game! I've played quite a few, and have been browsing around trying all sorts of them. This game is great - it has all the elements of other card games but plays pretty smoothly. The game has a lot of cool mechanics, each side is different and the deckbuilding is really cool with combining different sides.
Deck building:
You pick 3 commanders and then you can only include cards with that generals type in your deck. (Think mtg EDH). You then also get those 3 commanders as guaranteed cards leting you build a deck with a lot of strategy and not just luck of the draw.
Play style:
You play cards into a support zone where they are delayed for a turn before attacking, this zone is in play but they can't be attacked here. You have the commander zone which your commanders start in, and cards can never move in here. This zone  can't be attacked and your units in there have "haste" (move to atk or def zone). There are two other zones the atk and def zone where you put cards to do exactly that... atk or def. Each atk and def zone have hp - the def zone loses hp as your units die in that zone so you can't infinitely chump block. You have 3 passive abilities to help fix your deck - 3: shuffle a card back into your deck and draw a card, 5: draw a card, 9: increase max resources (income) by 1.
Game Modes:
Campain, Draft, Ranked, and I've read that 2v2 is "planned" format.
Downsides: It takes forever to get cards, packs don't give many cards and are very expensive. I like this game a lot however due to how long it takes to get cards I don't really play it other than the dailys and weekly quests. The game ends up being a pay to win game due to how long and difficult it is to get cards compared to the people who just spend money.

When you first boot up ArmA 2, it's hard to shake the feeling that you've played this game before. It bears more than a passing resemblance to the original ArmA: Armed Assault, as well as 2001's Operation Flashpoint. Not surprising given that Bohemia Interactive developed all three titles. But has ArmA 2 improved on the formula?
My personal answer to that is YES!
The single-player portion of ArmA 2 takes place in Chenarus, a fictional former Soviet nation steeped in civil war. As a member of the US Marine Corps, you are charged with backing up and stabilizing the current democratic-leaning government against communist insurgents.
There's no denying that ArmA 2 is the most ambitious war simulation ever made. Players could mess around with just the mission editor and lose themselves for weeks on end. But with its steep learning curve, the game requires a good deal of commitment. Not even mentioning ArmA 2 DayZ Mod, those willing to invest the time to learn all there is to know about ArmA 2 DayZ Mod, the glitches and the bugs are currently too much to take. Maybe once they've patched it up, there will be something more playable. We look forward to that day, because there's really something special in ArmA 2, cheesy voice acting and all. In its current state, however, if you are looking for a war simulator then i recommend you to buy this game!
Personally, i've spent hours and hours on this game. Everything from been chased by zombies in Chenarus to chasing bad guys as police or military. It's amazing how much you can do in this game.

There are so many competing visions of the future in media that it makes the fully-realized ones stand out all the more. After all, it's easy to envision a blasted wasteland or an ocean of shimmering glass towers but not so easy to envision how to get there. Technobabylon has no problem clearing both of these hurdles, establishing a thoroughly wired world of networked decadence built on the ashes of the old order. But what makes this title truly remarkable is how that is the very least of its narrative accomplishments.
Set in the advanced, AI-directed city of Newton, Technobabylon follows the stories of Latha Sesame, a Trance-addicted (think super VR internet) young girl from the slums and Charlie Regis, an investigator for the previously-mentioned AI's management bureau. Their tales dig deep from the introductory scenes of poverty and squalor on Latha's side and cold authority on Charlie's. Both are brought together in a very clever way as the plots involving them expand to encompass Charlie's tragic past and hand in what the city has become, eventually touching on the underlying conflict between the rigid governance of the present and the chaos that preceded it.
I know I'm talking about the plot in terribly vague terms but for a game that's around six hours long, there is an incredible amount of narrative twists and turns crammed in there. From humble beginnings trying to puzzle a way out of a locked room and investigating a murder scene, you'll be taken on a whirlwind tour through the wars of the old world, the AI dominance of the city, heartbreaking personal tragedy, blackmail plots, conspiratorial uprisings, and terrorist attacks. There's so much going on here that you're sure to get sucked into the story by something, and once you do it all starts to fit together in a masterful puzzle that may have more relevance to our present society than we'd like to admit. The dystopian themes are strong here and surface everywhere you look, from the gruesome extents that gene engineering reaches to the differences in food machines throughout the game.
What really sells the narrative here though are the characters that you share it with. Technobabylon features some of the best writing and voice acting to be found on the indie end of the spectrum, forming connections between you and people having to deal with organic computers in their brains and explosives in their bones. The natural, flowing dialogue keeps the game grounded even when the plot takes off, and I don't think the game would have worked half as well if not for the excellent deliveries of the entire cast. Charlie and his partner Lao in particular have a wonderful interplay that speaks volumes about their personalities and relationship from even the smallest conversations. And it deserves recognition that similar attention is paid to every character in the game, no matter how minor.
As an adventure game, Technobabylon limits your movements more than most but makes up for it with the aforementioned dialogue and equally clever puzzles. Interaction is simply left-click for use or pick up and right-click for examine, and there are never more than five or six items to juggle at a time. Figuring out how they work together is the challenge, especially with the introduction of some surprisingly deep side mechanics. Latha, for example, can enter the Trance which is a VR network interface. Using organic computing material she can connect to everything from vending machines to door locks and interact with them in cyberspace as you would any other character. Charlie also gets some neat gadgets like a future cellphone that can manage data and network connections, and a gadget called an AI splitter that I won't describe but is used in one of the most clever puzzles I have ever seen.
Still, each chapter is comprised of only a few scenes and usually revolves around a single central goal. It's not a bad way to handle the gameplay in light of the complex story it supports but it should be noted if you're more a fan of wide-open adventures. This one has also made me appreciate LucasArts-style deathless adventures all the more because in the few scenes where death is a possibility, it's not handled all that well. There's one scene where almost everyone playing is going to die at least once, because literally the most conspicuous object in the room is a crate and it will get you killed instantly if you try to interact with it at all. The art style honestly doesn't help this or the matter of finding items, as the chunky pixel style isn't a great match for the slick, detailed world around you. Still, these end up being minor gripes when viewed against the towering success of the story and puzzles. Technobabylon was a pleasant surprise, one that grew more and more impressive the further I delved into its secrets.

Fantastic HoMM-style turn-based strategy RPG built around Norse mythology marred by some poor game design choices. There's great variety between the races and each has their own campaign, with each faction having a distinct style. The combat is unique and feels like Ogre Battle but this is also one of it's biggest problems; similarly to Ogre Battle, if all of your units in a party die, they are gone forever. Your favorite hero and his units will transfer between missions so this means if one of your super-units dies you can potentially throw the campaign. The terrain control mechanic is a great visual representation of your area control but I find it downplayed in many missions because of a turn limit or boss rush. Hero customization is diverse and has more options than HoMM but they are slower to level up. Although it has aged poorly, this is a great HoMM alternative that is worth checking out if you're a fan of strategy games.

I have a very short attention span and had a difficult time focusing on my writing. I'd spend hours, even days on the same chapter--sometimes the same page--and among other things, that was KILLING my grades in school. Nimble Writer delivers exactly what it claims; a low cost, low profile, distraction-free word processor. I can focus entirely on whatever I'm writing and nothing else, but if I need some reference material, I can easily import it and drag it up right beside the document at any time without ever closing or minimizing it, and when I'm done with it I can just push it over to the side again until I need it. If I'm writing a novel, I can write character descriptions listing off anything and everything I need to know, and add pictures to them if necessary. It's a great program, with great support on the forums, and quite frankly I just can't recommend it enough. For $10 it's a steal, but if it ever goes on sale, you'd be a fool not to buy it up in a heartbeat.

While you have to pay for the program, in my honest opinion, it is so much better than when I was writing on Word.I generally have to type out my stories because my hands get sore really easily, but while Word has let me type up my stories for many years, I hated the brightness and I was always distracted.

The spellcheck works fine. It doesn't distract me like Word does where it puts a red or green scribble everytime I mess up somewhere. I can just continue writing and if I make a mistake, I can just check them when I'm done.

. Though, this program is fairly new on steam so there won't be a lot of options right now for you to choose. There is also a importer where you can take your documents and finish or fix them in Nimble Writer.
Overall, it's basic, non-distractive, and conveniant. If this is what you are looking for in a writing program, you should get this one.

Not recommended for anyone who still remembers and loves Alpha Centauri. This game simply lacks the charm of extraterrestrial exploration. It's not easy to pinpoint what, exactly, is wrong with it: maybe it's the lack of AC's narrative elements that popped up after each significant achievement of your faction. Maybe it's because we have nations again instead of factions. Or perhaps it's because the aliens are not menacing at all - once you've researched some basic upgrades, you can steamroll over anything but sea giants, and those are pretty passive. So BE basically boils to good old faction vs. faction warfare.
Plus, compared to AC, this game is very simplistic. Domestic policies with special bonuses and drawbacks? Not anymore! Because all players love Civ5 culture advancements that are strictly positive and boil down to "+5% to military unit strength", right? Of course, option to design your own units is also gone, as well as psi-combat. Everything is as simplified as possible.
And the most baffling design decision of all involves affinities: they are not mutually exclusive! So you can be a human purist who aspires to become a half-alien hybrid while modding himself with cybernetic augmentations to high heavens. And of course, descriptions (for example, in diplomacy screens) never acknowledge how ridiculous this monstrosity is. Nice work, Firaxis.

Before I begin, I have played for more than 0.3 hours, but I played in offline mod. Not very much though, this game made me bored faster than a math lesson can do.
Positives:
- Decent scripting I guess
Negatives:
- Pretty much everything
- Boring gameplay
- No storyline
You spawn in a world with absoutely no clue how you got there. You don't have a name, you don't have a goal, you don't have anything to find. The story is non existing.
Some games can be good even without a clear goal or a background story, but not in this case.
Not only do you have no goal, enemies or purpose in Kairo whatsoever, the puzzles are also simple but yet confusing. You can not interact with anything and you don't have an inventory, meaning that all you can do is move objects by walking towards them, or jump on random platforms in hope that something will happen. Really, really simple puzzles. And when I say it's also confusing, what I mean is, you don't really know why you are doing what you are doing due to the non existing story and the few hints you get doesn't really help that much at all.
Do I recommend this game? No. I don't recommend it to anyone.
People that love adventures, no. The game is as simple as it can be (including the soundtracks and gameplay in general) with nothing to explore or discover at all. You don't even have a purpose or anything to lose. Not even health (no, you can't even die in this game).
People that like puzzle games, no. Again, the puzzles are basic, yet confusing, and you don't really know why you are doing them.
People that love a good storyline, no. There is no story in this game at all.

The Swindle is the action stealth platformer you probably didn't know you wanted. With each district you unlock the rewards rise, but so does the dangers.
The Swindle is a hard game, one mistake may kill your current thief, but those errors are usually a result of your own actions... and greed. You can walk away with only a small portion of the current heists loot, but why do that when stealing everything nets you a hefty reward? Fighting your greed and urge to press on is often the hardest part of the game.
There is little hand holding, and a certain amount of trial and error is expected. There is a thrill the first time you encounter a new security robot and do not know what to be aware off. Though you can purchase upgrades, it never changes the fact that its your abilities as a player that determines if a heist is successful or not.
A good game that may infuriate you at times, but keeps drawing you back, there are more places to rob after all, and this time, this time it will succeed without a hitch...

The best game in the Assassin's Creed by 1000 nautical miles. I have the feeling someone at Ubisoft wanted to make an amazing pirate game and Ubisoft, being♥♥♥♥♥♥ didn't want to take the punt in creating an entirely new IP so they told the devs to tie it in to Assassin's Creed.
As a result, when on the open sea, the game is near perfect. One of the most beautiful games ever made. Naval warfare is brilliant, and provides a variety of options in all facets of attack. The sound design is spectacular, Whether it be cruising around the seas listening to your crew sing various shanties or the crackle of mortars raining down on enemy ships. The upgrades are well spaced apart and are satisfying enough to keep you playing for hours on end.
Unfortunately, there are times when you must come ashore, and this is when the game becomes just another Assassin's Creed. The same tired, easy combat system, the same clunky, counter-intuitive climbing system and the same enemies as always. The Story Missions are especially terrible, and often boil down to simply "tail the target", "eavesdrop on the target's conversation" and then "kill the target". It's terribly dull.
The game also feels it necessary to drag you out of the action at various points throughout to force you to play in the modern world. These sections are by far the worst parts of the game. You are ordered around by a man in your ear to complete various hacking minigames (all incredibly easy) to gain nothing but tidbits about the lore. Not to mention, these portions are all in first person with an FOV of about 60. I spent almost all my time during these segments simply wishing I was back on the Jackdaw.
The story otherwise is not terrible. Edward serves as an adequate protagonist, arguably both the most relateable and most likeable Assassin yet and he is surrounded by well-rounded, well acted supporting cast of pirates and sailors.
80/100
Would receive a significantly higher score if it were to cut out the modern segments, and the repetitive, boring mission design and be what it wants to be: a pirate game.

Love it.
I simply love this game.
To sum up my surprise with how good it is, I generally hate turn based games. However, I love the look and feel of Warhammer 40K so I decided to finally splurge on some of the games, and I don't regret it. This is my favourite so far. If I ever find this board game, I am 100% buying it, because it is just pure fun and enjoyment. The lurking around, the strategy, the being cornered by a line of Genestealers and mowing them down with a flamethrower, its all there and it's fantastic. I bought 4 copies of this game for my friends and I and do not regret it. It can be intense, hilarious, and downright unfair, but it's fun the whole ride.
This game has a lot of great aspects to it, especially the visuals. The way your Terminator walks around, the environment, the lighting, all of it is great. The color scheme as well adds to th overall experience of th egame, with some nice contrasting colors that pop out. The sounds in the game are great as well, with very nice voices for the terminators and weapons, just the sound in general is good.
Level design is great as well if you ask me. Every room/area has its own advantages and purpose, and this can b egreatly utilized to the player's advantage. It makes the strategy a bit easier to grasp and gives you the chance for redemption in every new area.
The only downsides to the game are a few bugs, the not-so-uncommon bad roll of the dice (which for me personally is a pro as it is hilarious) and some odd choices for the animations.
The only consistent bug I have found in the game is that occasionally a unit will be selected, then stay selected even when you finish using all their points. this is more common in Genestealers, as I will "END UNIT" and it will continue to stay selected and I will be unable to choose another unit. This has been solved when I select the unit as though I am intending to turn him to another direction, then wildly spinning and a new unit is selected. I can only describe this as annoying as it generally appens to only one unit, but it has happened in 2/5 games I have played online, so it could become a very infuriating bug in the future.
The animations are only considered odd to me for the Genestealers. Some of their movement is odd, mainly bevause they always act as though nothing is around them until attacking. This is a minor complaint as the quality of the animations are good, it's just odd looking at a horde of Genestealers staring down a Terminator and acting as though they are doing nothing, licking the air endlessly and generally being in their own little world.
Lastly is the dice rolls. Being a board game running off of a dice rolling system, you're gonna have some bad streaks. This however, has never infuriated me in any game I've played so far, as I and my friends find it hilarious. A large, probably 1-2 ton Terminator the size of the hallways he occupies is standing directly in front of a Genestealer. The Terminator attacks with his chaingun. He shoots dozens, even hundreds of bullets and misses, and it is hilarious. The idea of someone being that dense, so unable to fight yet being in the situation, is just the funniest thing to me. This is even funnier when considering you only have to be hit once to die, so say that rule is true, he only has to hit the Genestealer once, but no, he misses all of them. Oh, but he can cross-map snipe with the chaingun and never miss a shot. It's just when his life depends on it he can't fight. This may be a very infuriating thing to some players, which is why it could be seen as a con, but I find it hilarious and adding to the fun of the game.
Overall, I'd say this is a strong yes. It has gotten me into a genre that I previously thought I couldn't enjoy, given me and my friends something to laugh about, and offers a fun singleplayer campaign with cool levels. It's a great game, and I'd highly recommend it.
Just be warned, some of these games can last over an hour, possibly even two, but it's still TONS of fun!

I haven't played a lot of TCGs (not even Magic the Gathering), so I really don't know how to compare its gameplay with the others in the same genre. In fact, I have only played Yu-Gi-Oh! and gave up on it since xyz, tuners, six samurais appeared and became OP af.
This game can be really stressful while in a match due to its mechanics requiring you to re-arrange, bluff, plan, manage resources to fully make use of your turn, and when you're against a more experienced player, you'll always be thinking "omg, he might put it back to support zone... should I still target that card? cuz it might be a waste, but if I'm wrong, I could lose the game" This can be really annoying at times and I personally rage quitted some matches because it stresses me out XD
At one point, it will make you think that a faction is way op compared to another one, but I don't think that's true. Each faction has weaknesses that you can take advantage of. Maybe I haven't played long enough to actually see the unbalance between the different factions but so far, I think they're just fine.
The game is not pay2win. I haven't spent a dime yet, but I can say I am doing fine even if I use a deck filled with only common, and uncommon rarity cards. You don't have to spend real money to get the higher rarity/better cards, but might require a bit of a grind. Booster pack cost 5,250 Infinity Points (free in-game currency) which is a fair price considering they guarantee you to get atleast 1 rare. You don't like the rare you got? You already have the certain card? then don't be afraid to go to trade chat and advertise those cards you don't need. Chances are, there's one person looking for that certain card of yours. Winning a game (without totally running over your opponent) gives about 150 Infinity Points and 500XP. Every level up gives a free booster pack, but the cards are soubound. There's a free card for logging in daily and completing your first 3 matches of the day (cards from daily log in and match rewards are soulbound).
The devs, mods, and admins are active in global chat. The community is not bad. Ask a question, they would answer. I have no idea about getting support about bugs on purchases though, since I haven't experienced it yet.
There are still bugs (It's a work in progress since it's still beta). The cards are animated which is cool and the art is great too. The characters and the factions themselves have stories and they all connect to each other. The campaign though seems more like a grind to get starter decks than being a story of each faction.
To me, the game overall is great and I would recommend it. The developers seems to be working hard and It feels like they actually like developing it and interacting with the community. If you're in to CCG TCG then you should give this one a try.

Great adaptation of the board game. Involves a lot of random rolls, but quite a bit more forgiving than table top version, since you can "undo" your last move even after the roll.
In this version of the classic board game, player controls a squad of Space Marine Terminators of Blood Angels chapter, as they delve into the cavernous corridors of massive space hulk, infested with genestealer aliens. Each Terminator has 4 action points to spend on your turn, and literally every slightest move costs action points, including changing facing. Luckily, on every turn you get a common pool of a 1-6 command points that can be spend by your squad to do additional actions. Poor roll of command points can be rerolled once per round, as long as at least one squad sargenat is alive. Leaning to take maximum advantage of action economy is key to being good at this game.
Just like any other game based on dice rolls, the random factor can feel punishing to beginners, but the game is quite easy overall, I think I managed to do most missions in a single attempt.
Notable differences from table top is that you can't play as Genestealers in a single player campaign. Some weapons and powers work with slight differences (most notably flamer) and unfortunately video game did not include the new missions from third edition.
Overall, it is a light and enjoayble board game adaptation, especially if you are a fan of table top space hulk and having trouble bringing this massive game to the table regularly.

This game started out really well and had I reviewed it earlier it would be a recommendation but it has lost its way.
To its credit the simultaneous turns is a great mechanic and the payment model is really well done (not pay-to-win but payment does feel like you are getting something). Also the cards (mostly) avoid being ridiculous and thus having decks that will never be countered except by a deck built just for that purpose (a problem Magic hit years ago and never found a way to fix other than limiting card choices).
However, there are 3 reasons that you shouldn't bother with it;
1. The support is mediocre (which is a better than most I suppose). They are supposed to refund you if bugs cost you in-game currency but they have never done so for me.
2. They created a brilliant, immersive, fantasy world in which all the cards make sense. The races have their place and they all fit together well. Then they added Star Trek... No, really. So now your beasts from the nature themed faction can take on dudes with phasers... wait what? It's the most immersion breaking design decision I have ever seen in a game (and at my age, that experience goes as far back as the Commodore). It screams of a 'Trekie' designer desperate to include it just because they got the IP licence. And it plays about as well too.
3. The community. I have lost count of the number of times I have been flat out abused in private chat by opponents just for running particular combo's and/or cards that they don't like. I have reported each case and non have been banned. This includes some extreme language, bigotry, personal attacks etc. yet the devs take no action to control it.

For strategy fans (maybe RPG fans too), I think the game's worth buying.

Disciples II is strongly reminiscent of Heroes of Might and Magic III mixed with the Ogre Battle series of games, and the mix is succesfully engaging
Those familiar with HoMMIII should feel comfortable with the turn based play, isometric map, resources, town building and creature tiers. The primary difference is in the combat.
As in Ogre Battle, combat takes place between squads that meet up on the map. Rather than stacks of creatures, each member of a squad is a single creature with a health bar. A number of rules dictate the squad composition: A squad has a limited number of slots, a large creatures may take up multiple slots, some units can only attack from the front row, others from both. To this end it's greatly engaging experimenting with squad composition and placement, building countersquads, attrition squads, and so on. I recommend this to fans of either of the two games it resembles, or simply fantasy TBS's in general

I bought Nimble Writer without any positive expectations. $10, after all, is an acceptable loss to me, and what greater way to spend it than to experiment with different softwares for writing?
That was more than a month ago. I'm still using it, and as of now, I'm just a day away from clocking in 100 hours on it (I write 1000 words a day, which should translate to about 2-3 hours a day). Basically, these are the reasons why I'm still sticking to it:
- The simple GUI and anti-distraction scheme does work, at least for me. You could minimize everything, and maximize them only when you need them. Most of the time, all I really need is the writing space. Awesome!
- Customisable workspace. I chose the most subdued theme possible. When I started out, I wasn't used to the font, which was the only thing I like about open office and microsoft office. Guess what? I get to tweak them to exactly that. Moreover, as I'm writing a novel that's meant to actually be published (it's for a talent-search competition), I matched the width of the writing space to that of an A5-paged novel. I actually feel like I'm writing a novel for once! And I didn't even have to go from page to page, hah!
I plan to create a military-themed workspace to match my novel :)
- The formatting for the text (italics, bold, etc) are headache-free. No more struggling to italicising!
- Autosaving and cloud saving. Works better than Open Office crashing and trashing hundreds of words.
- Oh, and by the way, Nimble Writer's stable and lag-free on even my work laptop, which boasts a cutting edge 4GB Ram, 1.5Gz motherboard and no graphics card. I can't say the same for Open Office and I don't even have Microsoft Office anymore because of their tyrannical pricing.
- The development team can actually be approached, and they're friendly. Just as importantly, they're actively improving Nimble Writer as the days go by! As far as I know, this thing is actually evolving alongside me and my novel, like it's alive (Don't kill it with fire!). My suggestions are actually taken and next thing I knew, it was there...
- The statistics are incredibly handy to evaluate your performance. Believe me, serious writers do this all the time, and Nimble Writer's system is the next step. I mean, Stephen King would not stop until he got in 2000 words a day, and some writers even more. (hint: There's a homage to King in Nimble Writer)
- The achievement systems, courtesy of Steam. It's actually something of a bonus motivation for me. Even though I'm self-motivated, as any writer should really, but I'd take what I can get.
Of course, there are downsides to Nimble Writer. Here's to hoping the Nimble Staff will look into them soon!
- The statistics system could be thrown off by undos and copy/pastes. There was this once I accidentally deleted a chapter but thankfully I could undo it. The problem is, it threw the statistics system way off, and subsequently, the achievement system. (This was way back, so I'm not sure if this is still a problem. Haven't made this mistake for a month now.)
- I can't reset the statistics. (Last time I tried was about 3 weeks ago)
- There's no undo/redo button. Yes, I can use the keyboard shortcuts, but how many of us knew those? Even if it's the minority, we should also cater to them. Even Open Office does that. Let's just say I didn't need to use the redo shortcut yet *shameface*
- Last time I tried to export to .doc extension, I had problems. The result didn't work and couldn't be opened. (This was a month ago though. I've been caught up in a literary whirlwind that I haven't bothered to try)
- That said, my main concern is only exporting and formatting.
EDIT: So far, exporting into PDF works extremely well. There's nothing more I could ask from it, except perhaps to add in more features such as page numbers, styling, stuff like that.

For $9 this software isn't too bad. It has a lot of good ideas, and while not as fully featured (out of the box) as Scrivener, it does have a lot of the basic tenants behind it - and it in some ways I actually prefer Nimble over Scrivener, primarily due to its sleeker, simple and modern interface. Seriously, Scrivener looks and still feels like a clunky 90s application.
That said, Nimble Writer still has a lot of bugs to work out. Sometimes it fails to close out notes when I open a new Nimble document. Other times, it fails to properly resize the Notes/chapter area. Also, while for the most part Nimble Writer is distraction free, it is distracting when I have to stop to resize everything to accesss notes.
Overall Nimble Writer is a nice little package for writing articles, and literary pieces. It has all the stuff you need to store your notes and write your drafts in one place. And it's nice that it has native Epub export (which is why I bought it. I hate coding epub.)
As for script writing: Nimble Writer seems suitable for writing treatments and outlines, however for actually writing out the script I'm going to stick with CeltX. I write primarily comic book scripts and the occasional short film script, both of which CeltX is just much more efficient at, and And it's FREEE. But like I said, I didn't buy Nimble Writer for writing scripts, I bought it for general writing and epub export. Although, I'd like it if Nimble were to at least adapt a CeltX like system of character and item  tracking through out scenes.
I also like that this program has badges. I'm hoping they'll help motivate me to write more, as that's something I've been seriously slacking on lately.
Overall, this program isn't too shabby! I'd say give the Scrivener demo a shot first, and if you don't like it (or just can't afford it) then give this program a shot. Otherwise there's always the method of keeping track of your notes in EVERNOTE, and then writing your texts up in OpenOffice or  LibreOffice (Which was my usual method until recently...and of which all 3 are free programs as well.)

Let it be known I am already a fan of ccg.
That being said, Infinity wars has a lot to offer any strategy minded individual. As a ccg it has some interesting features, bearing familiar elements for those adept with ccg already. There are 7 main factions, a unallied faction whose cards can be included in any deck, and of course, the amazing Star Trek expansion.
Deck building is virtually unrestricted - a legal deck must have three 'Commander' cards, which determine the types of cards you can include in your deck, and at least 40 cards.  Each card has an affinity cost, and as long as you have enough generals of the appropriate type in your command slot, you can put that card in your deck. A maximum of three copies of any card can be included, but you can break that rule by also putting those cards in your command zone (protip). There are also unlimited cards, which as their nomiker indicates, can be included in any number.
Now where IW excels is that, while rare or epic cards can seriously affect the battlefield, some of the most effective decks I've run or come across use common, or even unlimited cards. I've had marked success in both ranked mode and tournament play, which are single pvp battles. These are further restricted by set types, including five different types of deck restrictions. Within these, if you are concerned about pay-to-win decks, there is even a merged deck mode, which shuffles both players card sources together, theoretically limiting the effectiveness of people with scads of cash.
However, the game is balanced enough (imo) to not require such drastic measures. The draft mode as well is extremely fun, and also (if you do well) seems to be the best mode of earning the in game currency. Drafting players select three commanders from 3 4 card choices, and then draft a deck from cards that will come up in the same 4 card options. This means 0 wait time, as you are not dependant on other players to make desicions, you just draft, and then can queue up for matches at your own convenience. 3 losses and you are out, but the better you do, the more you earn. Once you accumulate 3 losses the game offers you the choice to purchase your deck, with cost reductions based on how well you did, and taking your entry fee into account.
Anything purchasable in the game can be bought with the silver coins you earn from playing the game normally (infinity points) or by purchasing Lightmare points (terrible name) with actual cash. While grinding infinity points, apart from draft, is sloooooooooow, (more o's are really needed, but just imagine them) that is hopefully due to the fact that the game is still in Beta. No good getting people all jacked out too soon as of yet is the reasoning I figure. That being said, after beating the campaign mode, the tutorial/challange mode, and participating in 2 drafts, I have close to 600 cards. That's a lot of options.

Imagine you wake up on a stone platform. You havce no idea who or where you are, or even what's happening. Pushing a button on the wall causes a chime to go off and suddenly blocks of "water" are flowing up a cliff...
Welcome to every second of gameplay in Kairo, a first-person puzzle game somewhat akin to the "closed-room" Flash games you got so furious at as a child. There is no menu to speak of. No dialogue. No explanations. If you want to degrade yourself by using the "hints" provided, then you might have some idea of what needs to happen. Otherwise? Well...maybe if you hop backwards on one leg the door will open.
Don't get me wrong, the puzzles in Kairo are great! They twist and bend your mind in ways that few activities do. Sadly, this is somewhat diminished by the monotonous tone of walking through nothingness hitting the Escape key for your next clue. It looks like someone wanted to make a game of random puzzles, but felt the need to incorporate a storyline. This is fine, of course, unless you refuse to use any words at all - written or spoken. As the player, you end up with a small hint as to anything that did happen/will happen/is happening....then the game ends. Congratulations! You've solved 3 hours worth of puzzle game!
All-in-all, it was a good bit of fun. I bought it for $1.50, so it's hard to complain. But if you find yourself having to pay any more than that for it, I'd say take a pass.

is a narrative without words painting a picture of aloneness on a canvas made of staggeringly large geometry.
The art.
people who appreciate geometric abstraction, and like deeply mysterious Myst-style puzzlers.
I have never before played a game with such an incredible feeling of scale.  The place is enigmatic, it is stunning but, more than anything else, it is *overpoweringly huge*.  Figuring out what you are supposed to be doing is part of the experience of this game, so don't be put off by what appears at the outset to be random acts of geometry.  There is meaning and purpose to this place; it just takes some time to start to piece it together.  This is a different kind of narrative.
For me the strangest part of the experience of Kairo is that at the outset you are in a place of geometry and void, with no personality or sense of place; you are cast adrift with no instructions whatsoever, completely alone in a place which amplifies aloneness.  You aren't even sure what the game is, let alone what the game world is all about.  But by the end you feel like you know this place, you understand it, it is familiar and you are at home here - which, given the way the game ends, is the ultimate irony.
There is a story here, but one told without words, and it is a magnificent story of great scale and great aloneness, and it is masterfully told.

This game is pretty crazy. Somewhere between fascinating and terrifying, wondrous and foreboding. There are no monsters or even imminent threats really, but still your entire surroundings feel so ancient and so much grander than you that it creates an incredibly ominous feeling that never quite goes away.
As you interact with the world, huge abandoned structures come to life, and though the scenery changes and the paths are made clear, you never really know what’s going on under the surface. What do these huge contraptions actually do? Where is it leading? And how did all of it (and you for that matter) end up here? You get the sense that you’ll never really know, because it’s all just too ancient, too alien for your understanding.
The entire experience is rather chilling, and if you let yourself really become immersed in this world, you’ll probably find yourself making some pretty strange sounds, like I was, and laughing at points about just how uncomfortable it actually makes you.
The game isn’t perfect. There are bugs, but those tend to add to the strangeness of the environment in a way. One noticeable fault I had was that the footstep sounds are the exact same no matter what your pace is. This may sound minor, but it is rather noticeable at times when you are really taking it slow to take in your surroundings, which you will probably do quite a lot. Still a minor complaint in face of everything that’s really on display in this one.
I bought it during a Summer Sale at $1.50, and I would probably recommend it at a fairly higher price-tag even still.

The game has a lot of potential. I played 30 hours into it. It has a very steep learning curve. I began to manufacture items to build a bigger ship when I was hit by an inventory bug that crashed the game any time I used the 'R' key to open up a storage or factory inventory box. This made the game completely unplayable. Somehow the game even carried the bug over to new games that I created so I could not simply start over. Also, the game has some very convoluted builing mechanics. For instance, when building a turret that can track the enemy in every direction you will be required to use at least 3 different ship cores. Each ship core must be entered into, parts of the turret placed on that core, then docted to another core, exit that core, enter core 2, place blocks, doc core 2, exit core 2, enter core 3, place blocks then doc your turret on it. The big issue with this is not the inital building but if the turret takes hits and loses some blocks (which it will), how do you remember which ship core to replace the broken blocks , armor, or gun barrels on? Are those ship cores barried far under several layers or armor blocks for protections? Good luck. The game does allow you to download blueprints which does help some with this turret issue, but if you lose blocks, again you have to start removing armor, power modules, and other stuff off the turret to rebuild it. I still have high hopes for the game but in its current state, I can not recommend it.

I've been a Stronghold fan since the begining. The original Stronghold was one of the first PC games I ever played. Crusader was one of the first games I ever wasted months of life addictively playing. And it's been all downhill from there. Stronghold 2 and Legends were both horrible. Stronghold 3 was respectable attempt at a game, but still it fell way, way short. And then we come to this.
Stronghold Crusader 2 might be one of the biggest letdowns of my gaming life. Firefly has officially ruined their Stronghold franchise. They nuetered Castle Building. They threw troops out of balance. They took the balance out of the economy. Building up your economy is so quick and lacking in challenge that its turned tedious and boring.
The game almost completely lacks a "story mode". The campaigns they do have are a quick joke. And, from what I think I'm observing, All of the single player campaing content is offered as 6 dollar chunks of DLC. It shouldn't matter though, because stronghold is all about skirmishes right? Well they've screwed that up aswell. Their maps all suck. Even the maps that echo some of my favorite Crusader maps are completely ruined. The only maps that are any good are player made, and at least we get workshop to facilitate that(this might be the ONLY thing you could call an improvement over the original crusader). Seige equipment and the whole "seige camp" approach over the old engineers guild is garbage. Seige units suck and their too expensive, but simultaniously present themselves as the only way to take on a well built castle which leads me to another thing. You produce way too much, and way too quickly, for the frankly tiny troop caps ive experienced so far. I was, in my second attempt at a skirmish, able to produce enough resources to churn out armies as big as the 250-300 what ever unit cap every 5-7 minutes or so(limited only by how quickly peasants become available). And yet that same army doesn't stand a chance against even a computer oponent unless you pick at them with archers and seige quipment for 15 minutes first. Which the latter makes sense, but if I'm producing resource as quickly as I am, I want to be able to use them to throw 2-3000 unit army at someones walls and watch the world burn. But no.
In short, don't buy it, even if you want to complete your steam collection like I did. This game is garbage. You will not get 3 hours of quality entertainment out of it. And it will stain your respect for Firefly and the franchise.

Another gem from the Wadjey Eye Games studios.
Set in the future you start playing as an unemployed character who just wants to be in "the Trance" (what the 'net has become). Sadly she's booted out as someone locks her in her apartment. So you work to break out.
Following this opening you're introduced to the other main characters of the game: Regis and Lao who work for CEL which is the game's version of the police. You're tasked with investigating a building where a murder might take place in a little while, as predicted by the central AI of the city.
The controls are intuitive with left-click being action and right-click being "look at". You do have an inventory, accessed from the bottom right of the screen, though you never end up carrying too many items. I will say for me that MOST of the puzzles in this game were fairly logical, with the game providing enough context and ideas for you to work out solutions for yourself. It also helped that, on a few occasions, I couldn't leave the scene I was in without solving all the problems so that narrows down where the solutions must be.
The main puzzled I struggled with involved me having to leave the building i was in to talk to a man who had appeared outside with no indication. The character was not there when I went in the building. Once I had done that, the rest of the puzzles dropped into place.
I enjoyed exploring the world these characters exist in and seeing this particular interpretation of the future. It's not an interpretation I would care to live in however.  Although I would like to explore "the trance".
A solid addition to the point-and-click adventure game genre. More please!

This game deserves a positive review. Back when the game launched it belonged to a different company and was a pile of garbage, as a result the reviews were mostly negative. New content, new features and fixes - basically all you'd ever want from a racing game is slowly coming to RaceRoom.
RaceRoom used to be very DTM / GT3 focused but nowadays there are a lot of different vehicle classes available. Prototypes, touring cars, open wheel, GT3 and even some older ones. The game has pitstops, a good selection of tracks and very competitive AI. The driving feels great and the force feedback is fantastic. Graphics are solid but more importantly it runs with high framerate.

- Weather
- Day / night cycle for endurance races
- Pit strategies
- A racing line that rubbers in over the race
- Better damage model
- More tracks and vehicles (Le Mans, Silverstone, Sebring are my favourites)
- Proper triple monitor support

Amazing. Somehow this program has nearly surpassed most of the generic writing softwares out there, at a fraction of the price.
The fact the interface is uncluttered and clean means I can write things with little to no distraction from the thousands of icons that programs such as Apache Openoffice and Microsoft Word have ambiently filling the screen, doing mostly nothing. The function to have images/references in the same window is also amazing, so I don't need to keep opening and closing things to look at sources.
The customisibility of Nimble also helps massively. I struggle to read the generic "Black text on white background" motif many programs have going without an option to change it, so Nimble's default beige text on charcoal background helps massively in being able to read my own work.
My only complaints are the file types in which Nimble can load/save in. The fact it cannot save into well recognized file formats such as .word or .RTF means I have to copy and paste it into Wordpad or Apache Openoffice to safe it into such a format, which is rather inconvenient. The formating is also rather confusing in terms of how it works. The current way in which format works is comparable to a forum using HTML to format forum posts, which isn't ideal for a writing software. One of the biggest priorities I think that need fixing is the formating, as its essential for any writing software.
Once Nimble Writer irons out all it's issues with file types and formating, I feel it could genuinely will be the perfect writing program, but even now, its more value for money than many of the big writing programs and definately worth getting.

Breath of Death VII: The Beginning (BoDVII) is a classic 2-D turn-based role-playing game (rpg) developed by the company Zeboyd Games with emphasis on combat mechanics and tactics.
+ The 16-bit-style and general layout of the game provides a retro-feeling.
+ Various entertaining allusions and references to rpgs from the ‘90s.
o Relatively short game that can be finished within a few hours.
- The musical background lacks variety.
+ Fast paced battle system with round-based combat mechanics.
+ Easy character development with branching level-up system.
+ Employs an interesting combo system with multi-character combination techniques for special attacks.
o Party size is limited to a maximum of four characters.
o Encounters in an area are limited (with a manual option to have additional encounters).
- Next to the protagonist there are only three recruitable characters.
+ Creative characters offer amusing dialogues and slapstick humour.

- Lack of coherent and fluid story telling.
- No voice acting during the entire game.
Zeboyd Games has created with BoDVII a short and entertaining game experience. It pays tribute to the classic rpg genre and successfully mimics the basic mechanics without overstaying its welcome.
Despite its title, it is the only game of its "series", and the previous "six" do not exist. The title is simply a parody.
The game has no Steam achievements.

If you had asked me if I wanted to play a "bug game" a couple of days ago, I would have said no. But this is so much more than just a game about bugs. This game is really beautiful, and I really like its style and feel. You explore an ancient bug kingdom underground, trying to figure out what happened to it. The artstyle is really nice, and the colours, music and sounds work well together to set the mood of the game. I really enjoy exploring the world and fighting all of the different enemies you encounter on the way. If you like platformers, you'll probably really like this game.
I play the game on pc, and I found the controls a little difficult to get used to. When you get used to the controls, the gameplay will be really smooth. The only thing I dislike about Hollow Knight, is that I've gotten stuck multiple times in the game, trying to figure out what to do or where to go next. I haven't finished the game yet, but I think I I'd love to play it again when I've finished it. If you know what the key events are and how to get (to) them, you won't waste as much time trying to progress the story as I have.
Overall, I would recommend this game! If you like platformers, exploring and beautiful art, you should definitely give Hollow Knight a shot!

The Swindle is a procedurally-generated, real-time semi-roguelike solo heist game. You break into randomly-generated houses swarming with robot security guards and attempt to steal all the cash. Eventually you can move up the socio-economic ladder and break into richer buildings like banks and casinos. But it's all moving towards one goal: hack into the AI that is about to be unleashed on the city in 100 days.
There's two levels of failure in this game: You can trip the alarm, or you can die. If you trip the alarm, you get a frantic little while to scarper before the police show up. If you die, you lose all money on this heist and a day towards the deadline.
It's an interesting game. Not as refined as, say, Spelunky. The platforming is a little awkward, and occasionally the level can provide you with an impossible house. There's a nice upgrade tree that you need to climb, but probably cannot get it all before the deadline.
There's lots of great little elements. The heists themselves are neat, with steadily increasing dangerous foes. The atmosphere is great - footsteps change as you go from rooftop to floor, and the rain pattering on rooftops dulls as you go inside. And my favourite, Big Ben chimes when it hits the top of the hour in the real world!
The controls and feel need a bit of polish, but overall it's quite a neat game. It's a good colleague and counterpoint to Spelunky - a campaign rather than a run, upgrades instead of items, patience and care rather than running to the finish.

Playing the game actually reminds me of "Excerpts from Expert Judgement on Markers to Deter Inadvertent Human Intrusion into the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant", which you can google and peruse at your leisure. What they talk about on the site is: after we dump a bunch of nuclear waste somewhere and seal it off, how do we signal to future generations that they should stay away? Given that the half-life of the waste in question is 10,000 years, about as long as recorded history, this poses a significant problem: how do we communicate with people who will likely be nothing like us, and have a very limited understanding of our language, society and history; how do we tell them that they should not hang out in or excavate this nuclear waste dump? The expert judgers come up with a series of sculptural and architectural edifices, things that imply danger and will last millennia, and each one is more bizarre, desolate and brutal than the last.
A lot of what I see and do in Kairo feels like I'm interacting with someone's answer to that kind of question (although not about nuclear waste, specifically), which is extremely cool.
It doesn't hurt that the puzzles are very good. Gameplay is mostly about observation, testing interactions and figuring out how things work. It's kind of like Riven in that regard, and so far I haven't run up against any versions of classically lazy puzzles. Which is to say: no sliding tile puzzles, no finding the bauble and sticking it into the mcdooly, no one-on/one-off puzzles where you try to get everything to sync up as on or off. The first step of every puzzle is figuring out its rules and its pieces, and then trying to understand what the end goal is. It's all very seamless, very understated, and very rewarding.
Highest recommendation.

Ladies and gentlemen allow me to inform you that Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen was not the only interesting title released on my birthday (January 16) this year. Of course it received the majority of the headlines and the water cooler discussion – online as well as off in gaming circles – but Fair Weather Studios’ first entry on Steam is well and truly worthy of your consideration. Unfortunately, for the most part it has been completely and utterly ignored. It’s a real pity. The game does a lot of things right and the majority of those who have played and reviewed it on Steam have walked away leaving positive remarks on the game.
Bladestar is yet another SHMUP, or an arcade action shoot ’em up, to add to your library if you’re a fan of the genre. Those who love the genre know that the really good ones are easy to learn and quickly become difficult to master. That is absolutely true here. In fact, I may have never seen such an easy shooter to begin with making it ideal for those who are interested in the genre but have been scared away from the tough as nails titles.
The majority of good games in a genre also have a point of difference that separates them from other games within the genre. The point of difference in Bladestar is one that I have enormous appreciation of. Instead of having to gun down as many enemies as possible your sole job in successfully completing each wave is to collect as much plasma as possible. Failure to do so will doom your home planet. This is introduced to you very well in story mode as the opening levels are without enemy fighters but there are traps in the form of asteroids that need to be avoided.
You may feel that the $9.99 asking price is a little high for a first time indie developer. You may be right. However, there has been a lot of effort into the game and the quality of the game is at such a level that I feel that you would be getting your monies worth. However, if you were to wait for a discount or a bundle you’d be getting an absolute steal. There is still time, however, as of posting this spotlight for you to take advantage of the 25% off Lunar Sale pricing. If you’re a SHMUP fan you’d be crazy not to pick it up at this price.
If I could offer one point of advice to the developers it would be add those those in game achievements to the Steam Achievements feature on Steam. That way not only are going to attract the card hunters – kudos on that – but also the achievement hunters as well. In game achievements are nice but to actually have them on Steam means as much if not more.
Bladestar is a great little SHMUP that I would highly recommend to newbies and die hards of the genre alike. Easy to learn but difficult to master. With more play time I can see this becoming one of my favorite games in the genre and certainly my ‘go to’ for some time to come.

Infinity Wars (IW) - is a great dCCG!
I found it quite innovative in comparison to more traditional collectiable card games (such as Magic The Gathering, HEX, Shadow Era and others). It's easier to see how it plays or try it by yourself then to describe it!
A great art, animated cards makes this game highly enjoyable!
Also a lot of game modes available: Academy (which learns you the basics and more advanced rules of the game), campaign (8 missions per each faction) rewarding you with starter decks and even more cards, AI battles and different PVP modes, quest system also rewards you for your in game progress!
Though IW still in beta, the game is still under constant development and sometimes some bugs could occur and some issues in the game could be noticed (For me the UI should be more user friendly for example). But I am sure it will become better and better.
Really waiting this game to be released for mobile devices (iOS, Android) so could play it when not at home.
As a conclusion, this title has a great potential and I could recommend it for every TCG player.

Dishonored: DOTO (That's what the cool kids called it) is a shorter, 5-mission expansion from the Dishonored series. As Billie Lurk, you must save Daud and combine your strength to kill the "black-eyed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that started all this."
The game still uses VOID engine like D2, so performance-wise was the same. If you can't really run D2, chances are you won't find much luck here. Other than that it runs pretty smoothly with a i7-6700T and GTX 960.
It is a shorter game, like the Brigmore Witches and the Knife of Dunwall, however personally I think the contracts and the new powers really made up for that. The "talk to the rats" mechanic is really interesting and I like it more than the heart, to be honest. Displacement is a neat twist on Blink, and can be extremely handy in combat situations. Contracts are optional objectives you can do inside a mission to get extra cash, and it really makes you feel like a mercenary taking odd jobs.
I wouldn't spoil the story, but they DO EXPLAIN HOW BILLIE LOST HER ARM EVEN CORVO/EMILY ALREADY WENT BACK IN TIME TO FIX THAT GOD DAMNIT, which is a nice touch.
Overall, if you love Dishonored, get it.

DOTO adds onto Dishonored 2, letting you reexplore a couple areas from the main game whilst giving you plenty of new places to explore. Story is solid, although it follows the same sort of narrative as Brigmore Witches in my opinion. Completed in just under 7 hours, but there is still a lot of replayability. The areas you explore are large, filled with lots of nooks, crannies, and places that harbor secrets.
As someone who has invested a lot of time into the Dishonored series, and considers it to be my personal favourite game, I recommend this stand-alone DLC. It gives you a nice end to the series without feeling cheap or rushed.

Selenon Rising is a sci-fi noir styled mystery visual novel developed by Fastermind Games, and published on Steam by Sekai Project. It’s available on Windows, Mac OSX and SteamOS/Linux via SteamPlay for $5.99, and includes both Steam achievements and Steam trading cards. Published episodically in four installments, the first episode is currently available with the rest being included as DLC for the same price, to be released in the future.
Lex parsimonae
The story revolves around Violet, a psychic agent of SPECTRA, working for the Bureau of Human Protection under the supervision of the Selenon; the all-powerful beings ruling the Earth from the dark side of the Moon. For the most parts the story is well-written and captivating, yet some scenes manage to feel more or less a filler that adds really nothing to the story – maybe because they don’t achieve the deeper character development they aim to do, and just end up making those scenes feel a bit rushed. There is also a whole lot of back story available in the in-game dossier, presenting more information about the world and people of Selenon Rising to those interested in that.
It takes about 2.5-3.5 hours to clear the first episode, and assuming this will be the case for the remaining three episodes as well, it can be said that overall this is shaping to be a decently priced title. The obvious problem with episodic content is that the next installment will be released when it will be released: there is no definite release schedule available, so the closest thing is “upcoming months” listed on the store page.
Visually Selenon Rising is competent, and the black and white backgrounds help create the feeling of a somewhat depressing “retro-future”. The occasionally used more draft-like drawings for the CG’s are quite nice, but I would still prefer to have the styles matching each other better to keep the overall art direction consistent. Animation used in some scenes is really nice, and it brings life to those moments.
For the most part, the audio work in Selenon Rising is magnificent, and it really fits the theme and helps set the mood. However, I found the music used in interrogation to be pretty much the exact opposite of this: it’s quite loud and fast electronic music that seems to be completely misplaced. I can kinda see what the developers were trying to achieve with such decision, but I do not feel that it fits the game at all.
Wait a minute!
The main gameplay aspect in Selenon Rising is the interrogation mechanic, which is pretty similar to that of L.A. Noire, and I mean that in a good way. The player is able to listen to what the suspects are saying, and then either question them, doubt their emotions or present evidence that contradicts what the suspect is telling. This mechanic may sound a bit complicated, and to be frank especially when dealing with judging emotions and shooting down interfering emotions it can get pretty hectic. It’s not overly hard, but will probably lead into few confusing situations, and might be completely off-putting to some players.
But it does add a nice element of interactivity, when one has to search the scene for related items, and then use this information when confronting a suspect. There is a way to turn on an outline for the important items on the scene, making it easier to find everything that is needed. Those really into point-and-click games might be happy to just keep it off, which is the default position.
In conclusion
While Selenon Rising has few shortcomings, none of them are too much to make skipping the game necessary for someone interested in a mystery visual novel with interesting gameplay mechanics. That said, I am completely opposed to the episodic release method used more and more nowadays, as it leaves too much open questions in terms of continuation of the series. Still, assuming that the rest of the content will get released in a timely manner, and that they’re all around the same length, is Selenon Rising definitely worth the money.
