Breath of Death VII is a throwback to the original Dragon Quest back in late 80's.
If you have played that game then youll feel right at home when playing the game. From the graphics to the music.
Outside of nostalgia, this game also address some of features thats so annoying on that game and add some new features to keep the game up to today's standards.
If you have played JRPG back in late 80's or early 90's you must be familiar with the ridiculous encounter rate. This makes games in that era very hard and pretty bloated. You playtime is basically consists of 95% battling random enemies.
Here you have a very low encounter rate and there is even a limit. Exp and gold drop is very benevolent. This makes the game easier to get into but also serves as double edge sword since you can basically finished the game under 6 hours.
But this is perfect for us people who works for 8 hours a day and just want to have some fun and feel some sort of progression in the game even though we are rarely playing it.
There is also a character cuztomization here. When you leveled up you have 2 choices of stats/skill growth for your characters. Adding replay values to the game and makes the game more interesting.
The battle system is done through 1st person view with your run of the mill command such as attack, skill or magic.
THere is also a combo system. The higher your combo count the harder your finisher will be.
But there is a catch, Enemy will become stronger as turn goes. SO you have to kill them ASAP.
Oh yeah you also regain ALL HEALTH and some Mp after battles depending on your performance. Making the game even much easier.
Overall this is a good game. It's easy to get into. Very easy difficulty wise (i recommend playing in hard) and have good and silly dialogue albeit very scarce. All of those negative reviews about this game is basically some random kids expecting this game to have high end graphics and serious and awesome storyline of epic proportions.
No it's not. And the devs never advertised the game like that nor the tried to.
But if you are looking for some retro fun and that feeling of nostalgia then go get this game.

Selnon Rising is a sci-fi noire visual novel by the same people who made Icebound. While this game is episodic, the first episode has shown a lot of promise and I was able to get 3 hours worth out of the first episode. You play as Violet, an esper who's special power is being able to read people's emotions. She is out to work on a new case with her partner, Blue. After completing what may be a simple murder case turns out to be much more and starts Violet on her journey to her decision on how to save humanity.
In the game, you are met with a couple of investigation scenes and interigation scenes. During the ladder, it's much like L.A. Noire with its system of presenting evidence and doubting someone based on their testimony with their emotions when you can't present something. Out of these parts, you can pretty much expect the usual with visual novels and choices. Similar to Mass Effect's renegade and paragon system, you will be forced to pick choices that will make you allign either towards blue (Law), red (chaos), or stay netural. I only did one playthrough and stayed relatively netural, so I'm not sure what changes there are between the three allignments.
For the first episode, I found myself really lost in the world. There are so many questions you find yourself asking and thankfully albeit slowly, the game does give you some answers. There are a few surprises, one even made me scream at my computer. GG writer, gg.  For the price, think of it as a Telltale game. There will be 4 episodes and while I'm not sure about the price, it'll likely be around the same price for a TTG game, If you like a sci-fi detective visual novel, then you can't go wrong Selenon Rising.

Fantasy Mosaics 16 is a milestone in the series: finally, you have 6 colors in a grid. Is 6 colors a good news or not? Will it facilitate the game or will it complicate it?
Just for reminder, this is how my review for the 14th game began.
"Fantasy Mosaics is a series of nonograms (also known as griddlers) games released for iOS and Android before being ported on PC and Mac. I know that because I've added the whole series on Neoseeker. That's why when I saw it on Greenlight, I voted yes, despite the fact that it's just puzzles after puzzles."
And while it was the first game released on Steam, the 14th was coming from a long way, as it was introducting a fourth color. I don't know how it was before, so, the change of numbers was really experimented with the 16th game.
And it's not really making the game easy unless two or three colors are just plain to place. However, I found myself to choose more often which tile is colored at the end, when the rest of the colors were placed correctly and don't give a clue to where to place the last tiles. It has worsened with the 17th game but before reviewing it, let's just speak about Six Colors in Wonderland.
Nothing really changed. In fact, it's just two colors added at once but the mechanisms aren't changing:  you have a series of numbers indicating how many tiles are used for a drawing in the column or in the line. Sometimes, it's easy as the whole line or column is concerned but at other times, it's really a matter of making your brain work: if for example, three tiles are needed and known, you know that the tiles just next to the beginning and the end can't be used for the column or the rest of the line.
And that's it. 20 levels of 5 drawings, which means that I've solved 400 nonograms (yeah, I finished the 17th game and I've just bought the 18th), which I didn't realise until now. As usual, the plot isn't really developed for the penguin family. Besides, the 15 hours in the game is just showing that I've taken my sweet time... or reset puzzles because I'm challenging myself to have no mistake (and no use of hints). That challenge made me forget that bonus can be found under a colored tile: allowing more mistakes, hints and well, I didn't really pay much more attention. Besides, as far as I've seen, your "garden" or "landscape" is developing without needing a perfect score. Each level is rewarding you with an object, an animal, a structure or anything else. Sometimes, it's not even making sense but as we're clearly in a fantasy world, I suppose that it's making sense in that universe.
The drawings aren't really connected to each other but it's still great to discover them and to see if you managed to guess them or not.
I can honestly say that Fantasy Mosaics 16 is a challenge for people who loves using their brains, however, as usual, the full price is for me too high. Let's be honest here: 10 bucks for no real innovation is too high and while I've spent my money with the launch discount (-30%), I suggest you to wait for a better price.
And in the end, yeah, adding two colors can complicate some drawings. Be warned!

I got the key from the developer to review the game.
Bladestar is a simple and to the point shoot 'em up and, while it does nothing to standout from the average, it manages to be competent in what it does -- with the exception of the very obfuscating backgrounds and poor choice of colors throughout. This makes it fall into the "No" category, but it may still appeal to fans of the genre.
Presentation-wise, it tries to be a more modern, realistic looking game, against the many 8/16-bit games that most people are saturated with. Most of the models are nothing to write home about, once again being rather generic. The alien ships are the exception, which look pretty cool! Unfortunately, they're only present in the third stage of the game.
It has a nice lighting system, which surprised me when I saw my ship actually casting shadows onto other ships and responding to explosions and the like. The problem is that it only affects ships, which, let's be honest, is barely noticeable in a frantic shmup!
A minor complaint I have is regarding the visual effects on power-ups: for explosions, shields, etc. the particle effects fit with the general theme -- when you pick power-ups, on the other hand, a few pixel-y particles are created, which seemed like a weird choice... not too important, but still something to be fixed.
Still in the visual department, here's the game's biggest problem, to me: the backgrounds.
First off, they're just a couple of static layers with parallax -- nowadays, something more could surely be done! The backgrounds simply loop, which is very obvious when you see the same huge planet scrolling for the fourth time.
The real problem, though, is how they always make bullets incredibly hard to see, and even to distinguish between different color-coded weapons and power-ups.
Each level has a theme. For consistency, both the backgrounds and the enemies' colors are the same. While this makes some sense, it also throws visibility out the window!
The first level was okay. The others, however, were all a problem. The third level had green splashes on the background, which blended with the enemies' green bullets. The fourth level was in a debris field -- where most of the obstacles in the level were debris as well! I often got hit because I couldn't distinguish a real obstacle in front of the background...
The weapon pick-ups come in different translucent colors, making them blend with the backgrounds as well. This is a problem, as you'll often either pick-up a type of weapon you don't want, or pick up a weapon because you didn't even see it!
It was by far the biggest source of frustration I had with the game. Not being very appealing, visually, is fine with me, but when it obfuscates the screen in such a precise genre, it bothers me a lot! Hopefully, the devs can fix this! Tone things down a bit.
The music didn't really stand-out to me. It was simply background music, in no way connected with the game.
The sound effects were serviceable as well, nothing too wrong with it. The levels seemed a bit off, at times, with some explosions being much louder than the other effects (mostly the end wave explosions), but  nothing that bothered me too much.
Separate sliders for the music, voice and sound effects are always welcome, which the game had!
Control-wise, the game is pretty good! I played with a controller, and it responds well to the analogs, actually behaving like one!
The menus are not controlled with a controller, but a couple of clicks and you're in the game anyway. Would be better if it existed, but hey...
It's very straightforward, you move and you shoot. That's about it. There's an auto-shoot button, which is good! For the most part, I had that on, but the later levels did require finer control!
Onward to the actual game, now.
You control a ship that can only have one weapon at a time, out of 3 available. You can also have up to 2 drones at your side, each of them adding a bullet. There are 2 types of shields: one covering your whole ship, and small spheres that orbit around your ship. The former is destroyed when you're hit, while the latter can block bullets and stay strong, only being destroyed when it collides with an obstacle. All of these drop during the levels.
To beat a level, you don't actually need to destroy anything. There are little blue orbs that fall randomly that you need to collect X of to end each wave. Each level has 10 waves + a Boss fight. Needless to say, you actually do need to kill the bosses!
This little mechanic changes things a bit, but not enough to seem meaningful, in my opinion.
Weapons have different levels. Whenever you pick up a weapon, its level is incremented, and they max out at 8-10, if I recall correctly. This is an interesting thing. If you focus too much on pick only one type of weapon, you may have problems later, if you pick up a lower level weapon! On the other hand, if you want to balance them all out, you have to play slower, waiting for the weapons to drop.
There are various types of enemies as well. Some shooting ships, asteroids, and mines. The mines I've found the most interesting, gameplay wise.
With asteroids and ships you know what to expect. Mines, on the other hand, come with 2 types: EMP and ... bullet-shooting mines, for lack of an elegant word.
EMP mines destroy all of your ships if they're destroyed. The other mines explode into bullets, one in each of 8 directions.
Higher level weapons not only do more damage, but also have a larger spread -- which refers back to my previous point of not wanting to shoot in later levels. Something, it's best to play safe, keep your shields up and dodge for a while! Moreover, it also gives you a reason not to have drones/orbiting shields. These will explode a mine when they hit. As you can imagine, they also make avoiding mines far more difficult, if you're in a tight spot.
So, once again, in later levels, I had to change my style significantly, by not picking up drones nor shields, for more maneuvering space!
From what I've written, so far, you can certainly see the potential! It's simple, but it does have a few elements working together, leading to interesting strategic choices. Unfortunately, the visibility was a huge issue. For example, I often blew the bullet-mines up without even seeing them (leading to a chain-effect). You can see things going wrong fast.
That, with the levels being crowded (read: difficult), it was infuriating, at times!
Finally, the progression and upgrade system.
Something I disliked quite a lot is how your power-ups/weapons always reset when you beat a level. I mean, if I beat the first level, I should be able to carry things onto the next one, right?
The upgrade system is also very, very lackluster (to the point of making me wonder if should even be there). When you beat a stage, you have 1 point to spend in: 1 (of 2) more lives; +1 level on one weapons when you start a level; +1 wave orb, etc.
Seeing that in each level you'll collect probably around 10+ weapons, starting with +1 seems a bit... pointless?
You'll also have 4 or 5 points to spend, max. It's ... barely noticeable, unless you spend every point in one single weapon!
Then, you also gain experience points. These can be spent on more lives (max of two), a "secret" level, and ship skins.
Why not have a more fleshed out upgrade system with which to spend experience? I don't understand.
Of course, the levels would require a different kind of balance if the upgrade system was actually meaningful but... that's the point of upgrades, isn't it? Because, as is right now, you can experience the full range of your ship's abilities in the first level! After that, there's no "exploration" anymore, and it boils down to a precise grind to beat each level (which is valid, but, in this case, it seems like the two approaches are conflicted).
The game has potential, but there are conflicting design choices, and the visibility, once again, "killed" things for me.

Breath of Death VII is a first attempt at making a game. A bit of a messy one, but it was made by two people so... what the hell! I'll admit, I'm not the biggest of JRPG fans out there, and so this game definitely has a least-common-denominator effect on me as a gamer, but as far as JRPGs go... this game has some serious flaws.
For one, the game can feel very much like Final Fantasy XIII- where you walk down long corridors, run into random enemies, and deviate from the path only a little bit (but it can be a little frustrating at which path will take you to potential treasure, and which will take you further towards the boss... and away from the potential treasure). However, Final Fantasy XIII is better than Breah of Death VII (Oh, god, it's come to this. Next I'll start saying that I actually like Transformers) in the sense that the characters had unique interactions... and I'm trying incredibly hard to say that with a straight face. What I mean to say is, that there was a little variation in FF XIII's gameplay during the long, boring corridor walks. But BoD VII has one conversation per dungeon. Period. And I feel like making my same criticism that I made towards Soul Gambler. This game shouldn't be too difficult to have little bits of banter and fun conversation between characters, to pace the adventure. But it just turns into walking... and attacking.
But what about attacking? Let me tell you about Breath of Death VII's strategy in their game. Hit, hit, and keep hitting until they die. Until you get to the one bugger who doesn't take that. And you then realise at that point that all that "free choice" you had during those level-up moments were actually not as free as you suspected. I just figured that each bonus would be balanced with another, and they are most certainly not. There are highly essential spells and attacks you HAVE to learn, and if you choose the incorrect ones (the ones that break your oh-so-special combo meter... you're screwed). This is a massive flaw in crafting an RPG that flows with the player, but instead demands the player pay close attention to what the game wants you to choose. Yes, I know, an RPG-er needs to pay strict attention to their bonuses, but a game should accomodate to the player's decisions. Or else the game sucks. Like Final Fantasy XIII sucks.
"But what about the other elements of Breath of Death VII?" you may ask. "The sound's good, isn't it?" Yeah, sure, sound's fine. "And aren't the graphics great?" Well, that's where I'd have to stop you and kindly let you hold my holy frag grenade as I sprint away from the conversation entirely. No, I don't hate 8-bit graphics. I personally think that older NES and SNES game graphics age far better than older 3D graphics like N64 and PS2. And I think the game's graphics on it's sprites, portraits, enemies, and world is just fine.
So what's my problem with the graphics? The blackness. Beyond the dungeons there is a lot of black nothingness extending for what I'd expect to be all of eternity, which makes me feel all the more... isolated in the game. And not in the "I'm alone in a cave, and filled with suspense," kind of isolation. I mean the, "Well, that's where the wall ends, because the designers couldn't just repeat a bloody rock texture," kind of isolation. And when you fight enemies, there's no backdrop or really any animation to it. When you travel down stairs or out of towns, there's a neat pixellated background animation for that. Couldn't the designers have done something to make the battles less... spontaneous-feeling? And add a bit of color to the battles? It just feels like lazy desing to me, that's all.
So, finally, it comes down to story. I'll dedicate this entire blank space to the substance of Breath of Death VII's story in these paragraphs -> (                                                 ). So, yes, there's basically no story. You find a ghost, you go on random adventures! Something about crystals! I think! The story ambles where it wants to go (and, for the most part, is relatively linear)- but heavily caters to the heavily game-reference-laden dialogue. I believe every conversation I had with every character had some sort of other video game reference. And a few made me laugh. Such as the little conversation Dem (by the way, Dem Bones? I laughed at that name when I first saw it.) had with Sara- where he just looked at her, and she said "I'm fine"- and the game announced my relationship with Sara went up 10 points. I hadn't laughed so hard before in a game. However, the rest of the references in most of those conversations made me realize a sort of... predictability in the game. It goes from reading clever, witty dialogue to a game of "Spot that Reference!", where the entire conversation hinges on some Zelda II "I Am Error" joke.
I don't hate Breath of Death VII, much like I don't hate broccoli. But if you invited me to a dinner party and offered me sweet corn or broccoli? I'd pick the sweet corn, because I prefer the taste. But I wouldn't look at you strangely if you took the broccoli. Just as I don't think anyone who buys Breath of Death VII is mentally challenge. For a game made by two people, it's decent. It just happened to balance a bit to the "I don't quite like it" side of my video game scale.

I'm mostly going to agree with other reviewers: "The idea is great, the execution leaves much to be desired." After several hours just getting to the mid stages of the game, I feel the game is starting to show it's cracks.
Now let me start by saying that this game is meant to be really hard; if you're spotted then that's it, the alarms will sound and you have to make a run for it while doing a quick mop up, there's no hiding to get the alarm to go away. The heist has been compromised, run. You die in one hit, die from tall falls, pits become commonplace and enemies tend to be abundant. Dying costs you your run and a precious day on your 100 day limit to try and claim The Swindle to yourself, if you try and quit the game if you've had a bad run the game will dock you a day anyway. It's unforgiving.
This wouldn't be too bad if the procedural nature and certain design elements cause the game to go from unforgiving to unfair. The game will constantly generate scenarios for you in which you're SOL because it's neigh impossible to get through or that you don't have the required skills to deal with said situations. The latter will happen CONSTANTLY, especially with areas of the map that you can only access with the expensive teleport ability you have no hopes getting before the middle of the game. I've started many a heist where most of the loot was in areas I just couldn't access due to not having the right hacking ability or the teleport, neither of which would have been accessible to me at that point in the game so it effectively wasted one of my days. I love that the levels are never the same, but there's no book keeping to make sure that the player isn't screwed out of most of the loot because of a lack of abilities.
Finally, there's certain design elements I think are jarring. Of the enemies I've encountered so far some of them seem really poorly thought out. For instance, in the second heist area you'll encounter caterpillar enemies which you can take out but their spikes will STILL kill you if you jump on their corpse. Now if you're careful, that doesn't become much of an issue, but they can be in narrow areas that if they die on them you've just denied yourself access to that area because there's no way to get around. There's flying torches which look flimsy but take four hits, more than any other enemy including the large brute guys. Your wall jump goes higher than your regular jump+a double jump does for some reason and save for the starter upgrades everything is ridiculously expensive. The difficulty also shoots up very quickly and leaves things to a lot of trial and error trying to figure out how enemies operate; tutorials are short bursts of text when you begin a new mission which isn't enough for some things.
Now, with all of the bad out of the way, the game has a lot going for it, the art and sound is fantastic (the soundtrack rules) and the gameplay hasn't been done before. It's certainly unique and I think with a bit of polish and adjustments to the difficulty this would definitely be worth it's weight in gold. I have to recommend the game for it's style and fresh gameplay but buyer beware, it's hard and it's going to lead to a lot of frustration.

Nimble Writer isn't a perfect piece of writing software, nor does it have to be. Let's put this in perspective:
Ommwriter: $5.11
Nimble Writer: $9.99
Scrivener: $40.00
Microsoft Word: $6.99/mo or 139.99 for unlimited access to the whole Microsoft Office Suite
I'm not really sure what some Steam users were expecting. Nimble Writer has more features than Ommwriter, less than Scrivener, and Microsoft Word is overpriced garbage. Seems reasonable. If you're a professional writer, $40 for Scrivener is a pittance. However, most of us don't need and won't use a lot of Scrivener's features. Ommwriter is especially great for writers who are easily distracted, but it's bare bones. Nimble Writer is for writers in the middle or for people who just want cloud support. Don't let any jackass on Steam tell you that you need Scrivener to be a good writer. At the end of the day, the software is just supposed to make you want to write more. It's not flawless - I did have a (mostly) empty file get corrupted when I tried to save it - but if you don't like Ommwriter and don't want to spend that much for Scrivener, this is a very sensible alternative.

I blindly stumbled through, hoping against hope that at some point, the confusion would clear up. It did not. I ended the game more confused than I started it, with a healthy helping of disappointment and bitterness to boot. Some may call the graphics abstract, unique, or elegantly minimalist; I call them lazy. They look unfinished and bland, as if the developers simply couldn't be bothered to polish them, and tried to pass this off as artistic choice. There are tantalizing hints of a story that never emerges, only a few little morsels here and there which, like a can containing only three potato chips, provides just enough taste to make you want more, only to be disappointed that you can't have any more. And no, the ending doesn't make anything clearer, or anything of that nature. If anything it'll just confuse you more. I sincerely regret spending my time and money on this game.

Unforutnately, in it's current state, I can't recommend this game. Which is disappointing because I really, really like this game. I love the setting, the music, and the design. Please bear in mind that these problems I'm having are, for the most part, subjective.
First, the controls are not as responsive as you would need for this genre. Comparing it something like Spelunky, Super Meat Boy, or Mark of the Ninja this game, unfortunately, does not come close. Which brings me to my second point.
You don't have much control over your character. For instance, you cannot control your jump height when you're either clinging or sliding down a wall. This is incredibly important when trying to take out enemies that have been generated in an area that's difficult to get to. Sometimes the jump will accidentally put you in front of a window sounding the alarm. The controls, I feel, is the biggest hurdle for me to get over.
The randomly generated levels can be irritating. I've experienced mission 1 that does not yield enough money to get the hacking skill. This skill is what will net you most of your money in the early game and is an imperative skill to have. On more than one occasion, without being able to see the entire layout of the building in the early game, if you don't have the double jump, a triple window can really screw you over and force you to terminate your current employee and losing your XP bonus. To mitigate this, however, you could get bombs. Again, these are subjective complaints.
Lastly, I don't like that there is instant death from fall damage. Personally, I don't think this is something that's needed in this platformer, but hey, I'm not the developer.
If you do decide to buy this game, regardless, make sure you get hacking from day one. Be careful with your jump. Learn how it works and what you can do to work around it in order for you to be successful in your heists. Take your time to understand the enemies' pathing. Find the right cycle to strike and remember to be patient.
TL;DR - wait until you hear about an update outlining a "fix" for the controls or if they address something about their random generation.

After playing Hex, Scrolls, Hearthstone, Solforge, Duel of Champions, Conquest of Champions, and other new digital card games, I have to say that Infinity Wars is the best of them all. It strays the furthest from the MTG formula (unlike hex) without turning into a tabletop strategy game (scrolls/coc), and without oversimplifying the game (solforge/hearthstone). The addition of simultaneous turns and the division between attacking/defending/standby/command zones and their units makes this a really, really fun game with lots of opportunity for mindgames. There are a lot of strategic choices to be made in this game.
The other great part is that it is also contains all of the key components that make for a great digital card game:
Can you use one copy of a card in multiple decks? Yes.
Can you trade with other players? Yes.
Bots? Yes
Draft? Yes (and AI drafting practice!)
Campaign? Yes.
Leaderboards? Yes.
Game modes? How about a whole separate set of cards for playing with a Star Trek theme, future themes on the way, and queues for Star Trek games, standard deck games, mixed/"infinity" deck games, merged deck games (both players combine decks and draw from combined pile), and you can queue for all of those modes at once with different decks for each, or play draft...
Cross-platform? Mac/PC for now, upcoming iOS/Android, possible WP8/Linux support
Pay to win? Hell no! This game THROWS CARDS AT YOU. If you finish the campaign you are a loaded, deadly weapon. Unlike other games in the genre, doing something as simple as finishing the single-player portion will give you a deck for every faction in the game, plus the bonus cards you earned along the way for leveling, making achievements, etc...You will be able to immediately make decks for any faction to your own design, no grind required.
Shiny and fast to play? Yes and yes.
The only drawback is there are still a few beta bugs in the system, rendering bugs or deck-picking bugs during campaign, but they're all easily worked around and FAR from anything that should stop you from playing this game.
Play this game.

Kairo is an interesting, if ultimately slight, atmospheric puzzle game.  The artwork is all rectangles and circles and simple geometric shapes.  The music exists simply to generate atmosphere.  There is no "plot," but rather a series of puzzles that are to be completed simply because they exist.  The puzzles are generally fairly easy, although there are no real instructions and most of the puzzles require you to use your surroundings to figure out what to do.  In addition the "secret" puzzles are a pretty big step up in difficulty and will likely resort to the user having to consult a guide.
All of that said, the game succeeds with what it's trying to do.  The atmosphere is engrossing and engaging and the game is neither too easy or too difficult.  It's really a shame it was only 3-4 hours long, 'cause I think it could have been twice as long and not worn out its welcome.
Rating: 8/10

Stronghold Crusader 2
Stronghold Crusader 2 is the simplest of RTS games. It is the follow up to the critically acclaimed Stronghold Crusader and builds up on its predecessor. Stronghold Crusader 2 features all the elements you would expect from a game of its genre but nothing intuitive enough that you would be really amazed by.
The singleplayer campaign is labelled as only a learning campaign but is unable to fulfil even that job. You play either as Saladin’s or King Richard’s forces against the other. The campaign does nothing else but pits large waves of enemy troops before you can keep up with your production. It is based as a multiplayer skirmish game and it suffices the job. In Stronghold Crusader 2, you start  by building your economy and building your troops. You need to attract to come and live in your keep by making buildings such as Inns and Temples. Once you set up the castle, you need to protect it and try to demolish your opponent’s at the same time.
The maps available in Stronghold Crusader 2 are so small that you can literally see the other player’s progress at the same time. There are multiple choke points but these maps are prone to get very quickly rushed and that tactic is the only thing you will see players doing in the multiplayer. The no. of unit types available to you are very basic. There was not a single unit which I had not seen before in a RTS game. After the castle is set up and your economy is building itself, it remains but a match of who will produce faster. The only satisfaction comes from destroying the enemy castles with your siege weapons as your army can’t really get through the walls by itself. When you do demolish your opponent’s castle, it gives you a sense of achievement which is where the game shines the most.
The visuals of Stronghold Crusader 2 are average to poor. There is no real variety in seeing units crashing against units. The building designs are  fairly simple but it looks really good once you have set up your keep and it is churning out units. What really makes Stronghold Crusader 2 fall is the amount of bugs it has. Enemy units plainly running in through the walls, frequent crashes and freezes are only some of them. It is wrong for me to expect them to patch up as it has been nearly 2 years since the game came out.
Even then if you can look past the bugs and other problems, what awaits you is a fairly Run of the mill RTS game which may provide you with a couple of fun hours.

Space Hulk is exactly what its name suggest – it’s a conversion of the board game that came out in 1989, was released as PC game in 1993 and finally got more love in 2014:
I won´t elaborate too much on the gameplay, since the amount of the luck required renders that gameplay pretty much irrelevant in terms of comparing it to other PC games. It may be that this chimera of board- and videogame is not better than the boardgame. Or the target audience is different from what I am looking for.
Space Hulk has many interesting features, like a shoulder camera that shows the point of view of the selected Marine. A very nice touch! You can also play different chapters, which adds to variety. Most importantly: It is close to the boardgame. Added are a fitting soundtrack and a nice tense atmosphere. The game wins on this side as you can see. Sadly, it is not enough to warrant a recommendation.

Has to walk the plank!  It is just not cutting it in comparison to other PC games. I will keep it as a relaxing timewaster for in-between, but that is just me. Every non-warhammer 40k enthusiast should skip it.

Cyberpunk games are rare, good Cyberpunk games are VERY rare. Technobabylon is a rare gem with interesting puzzles, great old school graphics, and a fun plot. If you're a fan of old school adventure games or Cyberpunk in general, purchase this game!

About one-third of the way through, I'm finding this to be an excellent point-n-click adventure game with a compelling story and atmosphere. The puzzles are well thought out (so far) and the developers have done an excellent job avoiding outlandish combinations, a major weakness of many games in this genre.
The story, game design, art, voice acting, dialogue are all top notch and easily exceeded my expectations. And the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Surprisingly, Technobabylon kind of seems to have flown under the radar. It deserves more attention and love from discerning gamers of the unhurried variety.
Highly recommended, a 9.5/ 10 for me in this genre and style. After completing, will edit this review to revise and add to these impressions.
Update after completing Technobabylon:
-----------------------------------------------------
The game is as good, solid and well thought out as in my initial impression above. If not more. Game design is particularly good, there is coherency and no dead ends. The puzzles are excellent and satisfying- I never had to consult a guide. The writing is first class and thought provoking, with many science and technology themes explored.
On an ending note, Technobabylon gives many opportunities to interact with characters, and they should be seized to appreciate the story that much more. As before, a splendid 9.5/ 10.

Technobabylon gets it right where many AAA games fail. Mystery story that will suck you in like a black hole, only to spit you back out to reality, tired but satisfied. Suprisingly relatable and believeable characters, decent puzzles that are neither too easy, but also not too hard (if you can use your brain, that is) make the story-flow smooth and enjoyable, all in lovable oldschool graphics. Despite plethora of other options - few games deliver like Technobabylon.

Absolutely amazing adventure game.
The best part of this game was easily the characters. A wide variety of characters with distinct personalities, and each with actually pretty good voice acting! To top it off, this game does something many others fail to do. This game actually had diversity in its characters. Characters ranging in age, sexuality, gender and nationality, and all of them well written. You even get to play as two characters that ARE NOT an old white guy (and hey I loved Dr Regis despite that).
The story was really gripping and interesting, the gameplay was simple but it worked better than many other adventure games, and the all the visuals were wonderful. The music wasn't too great but it wasn't annoying at anypoint.
The only real issues I had with the game was some simple bugs, that were more an issue of the AGS engine than anything else. Characters clipping through walls during animations, elevators getting stuck, that sort of thing.
The puzzles were, up until one bit in the very last section, sensible and fun. At no other point did I hate a puzzle for making no sense or give in to looking it up.
Highly reccomend this game to anyone who likes cyberpunk or adventure games.

A game I bought with few expectations, and now one of my favorite FPS experiences of all times.
Shadow Warrior is an old school FPS which, in my opinion, manages to get it all right.
The visuals are nice, with large levels filled with secrets, which environments varying from regular street, through mountains and ships, all the way to the shadow realm. Exploring the levels is fun and rewarding, and the 17 chapters offer a suprising amount of content considering modern FPS standards. The blood effects are also great, which is important because you will spend the game chopping off limbs and sinking tons of bullets into demonic flesh.
Which leads me to the action. Which is bloody (pun intended) amazing! Both the guns and the katana feel amazing, comlimenting each other, and with the addition of a small pool of magic spells and weapon skills, the combat offers a lot of variety. The game even encourages you to fight with a vide variety of moves by granting you additional, bonus upgrade points at the end of a fight based on how creative and fast you were. Enemy variety is ok, with only a few types being really annoying.
What surprised me the most was actually the story, which unfolds in two separate storylines. The main one is of Lo Wang and his quest to piece together the Nobitsura Kage and prevent the Shadow Realms from being destroyed, and the other, revealed through flashbacks each time you defeat a boss, reveals a rather tragic, and towards the end, surprisingly emotional, tale of why the Shadow Realm is falling apart in the first place. The flashbacks are presented as gorgeous 2D animations, and are a joy to watch.
The story is carried by fantastic writing and even better voice acting. The main character is a jerk, but a badass jerk you just can't help but like. The dialogue between him and his companion demon Hoji is just fantastic, and his one-liners are some of the best I've heard in a long time.
Finally, I would like to touch upon one last brilliant element of this game. The fortune cookies. They are hidden in the levels, and the reward for finding them is 5 health restored and a fortune. These fortunes are amazing humorous takes on popular culture and well known sayings, each better than the last.
I honestly can't think of anything this game does badly. There are so many additional little details done right, of which there are too many to mention here, but as a whole, every moment is either action-packed, or funny, or even emotional. I was never bored or displeased, it's so much fun to play, and definitely worth the buy.

Selenon Rising leaves me with a feeling of "nearly there."  The characters are interesting, engaging, and easy to identify with.  The character art is suitably attractive and expressive.  The music is atmospheric and follows the action well.  The setting and story are both very intriguing.  The interview mechanic was challenging and fun: the "correct" solution was not always obvious, but always made sense in hindsight.
Selenon Rising has a lot going for it, but stumbles in places as well.  Some of the transitions are a little awkward, some of the scenarios not adequately set up.  This was mostly an issue early on, and the payoff for sticking with the game is pretty good.
The price seems right so far, maybe a little steep for the amount of content in episode 1.  Value for money will depend a lot on whether subsequent episodes will be released free, at a reduced price, or at the same price.  A demo, perhaps including the early Grange scenario, could encourage interest since it is difficult to communicate what the game is really about without one.

Selenon Rising is a scifi + noir visual novel in which you will follow Violet, an esper who has the power to read the thoughts of people. In Episode 1, you will dive into life with her, and you will quickly start to question who your true allies are. Alongside the "regular" visual novelness of this game, you will also need to perform investigations. This will start with you looking through an area to find clues, and then you will end up using your powers to try and get the truth about something out of someone. This happens twice within Episode 1, and both times will really make you think about what it is you need to choose for a situation.
I overall enjoyed my time with Selenon Rising, and I only really found one issue while I was playing it. During some text boxes, there will end up being far too much text for the size of the box, causing it to go out of that box. Other than that, the art and sounds are absolutely fantastic, and I really enjoyed how much the investigation parts made me have to think out what I was doing.
Disclaimer: I was provided a key by the publisher for review purposes.

Let me start by saying that I beta-tested this game, so there may have been some edits or changes I wasn't aware of when it was released.
As far as the game is concerned though - I love it!

I would like to recommend this game because I liked so many elements within it. However, I can't recommend it as I didn't personally enjoy it.
However, since this is the first review of Selenon Rising on Steam, perhaps people should wait for some more positive reviews, as I feel sure that there would be people who would like a game of this nature (but it seems that I'm not one of them), and they may have a take on the game that is completely different to mine.

If I see any reviews or other information that make me re-evaluate Selenon Rising, I may give it another try.

Early Impressions:
Civilization is one game series that is so well loved and respected that expectations and very high every time new game comes out. I've read reviews at IGN and PC Gamer and both reviewers liked the game but have some reservations.  Those reviews seem somewhat paradoxical.  They complain that the game is too much like Civ V while simultaneously saying the large amount of new material made the game difficult to get used to playing.  I have only played for 1.5 hours so far but I believe that the game is great.  If you liked Civ V and were getting board with the music and tilesets then this game is for you!  It's also for you if you like the futuristic setting; a portion of Civ gamers that really only care about "historical accuracy" (such as it is) will probably not like a game that doesn't take place in Earth History.  While this game is great and while it builds on the success and innovation of Civ V, it is its own beast.  It has many new features including interesting faction affinities, many choices to make before you even begin playing, semi-intelligent alien life forms, and synergy bonuses for unlocking multiple different virtues.
Bottom Line: The game retains all the aspects that made Civ V fun while simultaneously introducing lots of new and exciting elements that make Beyond Earth its own game.

I get a lot of quests that bug out . . . and also ones that can't be completed (have to build a specific building in a city that can't build it for example).
Still, it is a very fun game and there are lots of gameplay improvements over Civ 5.  It won't be long, however, until it's basically just the same game after the excitement of the new stuff wears off.

The Assassins’s Creed series has always taken us to different historical periods of time, with great success we have been witness of events that shaped humanity’s life and course of history, this is something I always liked about these series. Meeting and talking to important characters, the combination of fiction and history make a great combo of storyline, and AC Black Flag is not the exception.
Our new hero is Edward Kenway, a mere pirate with delusions of greatness and endless treasures so he and his wife won’t have to work for anyone ever again. So he leaves home, country and family behind to pursue his dreams, acting out of egoism he travels to the Caribbean, heart and core of the pirates between 1714 and 1726. But this is an especial case, Edward is not an assassin, just a simple man that finds himself in the middle of this war between Assassins and Templars, he doesn’t care about it, money is his final objective, though some events will change that, small yet significant ones that will make him take sides and support the assassins and finally become one.
While gameplay hasn’t changed that much, the stealthy kills and different ways to eliminate your targets tend to be overshadowed by the main protagonist here, naval combat. It feels so great to engage all sorts of enemy ships, the system is quite simple, while advancing further in the story, and you get to engage new and more powerful ships, like schooners, frigates and man o’ wars, the latest being the most powerful ships in the game, with hundreds of cannons and almost invincible hulls, for this your own ship, the Jackdaw, must be improved by buying more cannons and better hull, at the same time you can also change its appearance. While destroying and boarding enemy ships you gather resources like cloth, metal and wood that serve to improve the jackdaw, also every time you board a ship you have three options, you either repair your own ship, decrease the wanted level or you can send the ship to your own fleet. This makes the concept of boarding and attacking other vessels exciting and rich, pretty satisfying.
In the case of the fleet, you can clear your way to send ships to trade and that way getting money, this is some sort of mini-game where you fight enemy ships and at the same time you clear the trading routes, making it easier for your fleet to sail in peace, it is not strictly necessary to deal in this kind of activity, but it is a good way to make easy and fast money (reales). Another cool characteristic related to the naval combat is the fact that sometimes enemy fleets like the Spaniard and English ships will engage in combat, you can either watch them destroy each other or attack one side weakening the ships or just attacking both, testing your luck and skills.
On the other hand, the way you kill enemies, tailing them and facing multiple foes have not changed that much, though some new tools have been introduced, like the blowpipe with berserk and sleep darts, which make it even stealthier for you to get rid of enemies or just have fun by making them go crazy and fight, also using your environment has improved a bit by using trees and foliage for surprise attacks.
I must say AC4 is one of the most beautiful games in the series, it is breathtaking at times, full of detail in the sea and under it, the cities look great, with a lot of vegetation around, and the jungle side of the map is awesome. The sea is the main protagonist, of course, we spend most of the time aboard the Jackdaw looking for big ships to board and resources, so the sea is mostly everywhere and it looks awesome, great waves effects, storms that affect everyone, not just us, waterspouts and wild changes in the water make it hard to maneuver at times.
Also, the vessels look spectacular, every little detail put into the ships’ characteristics is great, you can see the passion the ships were created with, splinters, holes on the hull, the smoke every time you fire the cannons and the sails being affected by the winds, top notch graphics. As well as every little island or old ruin, everything screams details. A beautiful game.
There is nothing bad to say here, the music is brilliant, every time you board an enemy ship or when you first touch ground on a new city, every song depicting the atmosphere of such activities, top notch sound and music.
The voices are equally great, the acting is awesome, believable characters, great dialogues and accents, from the less important NPC to the main character such Blackbeard, Hornigold, Edward, Kidd, pure passion in the voices!
While other games in this series had minor things that were annoying at times or simply atrocious, like camera angles that made it hard to play at times or NPC’s popping up out of nowhere and textures loading when approach to, on AC4 there are not that many negative features, we have the usual tailing missions which are a bit boring sometimes, or the amount of fillers that are thrown into the storyline just for the sake of making the game even longer, we can collect animus shards, treasures and different shanties scattered all over this big map, the thing is that these side activities tend to be fun for a while, after 20 hours of gameplay, you just forget about them. Besides this, there're not many bad or negative things worth mentioning, I could say the game is bug free for me, some insignificant crashes, but that was all. No problems with performance either.
When everyone was talking bad about the AC series, and especially after AC3, everyone fell in love with the new turn of the series, this game feels fresh, maybe not on the side of storyline and the war between Assassins and Templars, but for gameplay. From this turn of events we can see that the series has potential for more interesting historical events throw into the mix with fiction. In the beginning, you might not feel sympathy for the main character, but in time Edward builds charisma, he is a nice character, full of nice lines, humor and a personal story that shows a great potential, not just because of the piracy theme, but because he is part of a series of events of games in the series that occured after his life.
It was nice to get to know more  detail the whole historical background for Nassau and the Caribbean in that time, the post war events, the new found colonies, like Havana, Kingston and other minor cities, what I mean is that we do not just play a game but we can also learn about the time and different conflicts that shaped part of our history.
AC4 is full of critical and touching moments, like the ending, the dreams of gold and a free nation for free men away from the tyranny of the crown. Recommended for fan of the series and even for non-followers of the games.

First off, I'm not gonna be like these other reviewers downvoting instead of not recommending because of a problem they had with Uplay. I've played the game and finished it, and put alot of time into this game, therefore I am actually gonna talk about the game, and discussing about what Ubisoft did right and wrong.
It's definetly the most unique Assassin's Creed game out there. It shares a few elements from the other ones, but makes its own mark with its setting... 18th century Carribean. The gameplay is incredibly easy. All the enemy types are the same, and even though the animations are well done, they get boring to look at pretty quickly. Enemy AI is also pretty bad. Sometimes an enemy will see you, and then all of a sudden go back to patrolling. This is franchise has one of the easiest stealth systems ever, and Black Flag shares that curse. Enemies can't hear you running, enemies can't see you clearly sometimes, enemies walk across dead bodies sometimes, the list goes on. It's surprising that after five games, not even counting the PS Vita and PSP version, they can't add a simple little crouch button that games in 2004 had. Scaling also feels dumbed down and much easier. There's nothing special about it anymore, and there's a lack of interesting buildings.
Now... being a captain of a ship. Something an Assassin's Creed game has never aimed at. It's got it's share of good and bad. The good? Steering feels immersive. The atmosphere of captaining your own ship, and having a loyal crew of members working for you that all want the same thing. It's done well. Everyone's happy, having fun, but always ready to follow orders. Ship battles are also fun, but there's no real strategy involved. Jumping on to the enemy ship never gets old too in my opinion. There's no better feeling than "I've disabled you ship, now I'm gonna jump on, kill your crew members, and force you to lower my bounty level!". Hunting whales, dolphins, and sharks is cool the first few times you do it, but it gets boring after a while and doesn't feel too useful. Same with diving missions, it's cool at first and actually has it's own little stealth system, but feels useless. The world is also HUGE! But... the islands are small, and there was never any feeling that I ever wanted to explore any of them unless they had a collectible that I wanted at the time. There's only four islands that have full cities, the rest are either for trading or they're empty.
Edward is also probably the most unique character out of all the previous Assassins. The previous Assassins wanted Revenge, Freedom, Justice, Answers. Heroic type things like that. Edward? He wants to become rich and famous, which is fitting for the setting. His character model is also super badass. But despite all of this, he's not that interesting of a character. Bad thing's in his life happen, but somehow the player never really feels for him (except for maybe in the end). The story start's out right in the action, which is nice, but after that it sort of starts to lose its meaning. Of course, there's also the story that goes on in the modern day. I don't have many good things to say about it. It's unwanted and unnecessary. It's like immigration: an incredible boring and long process that you don't want to do, but it needs to be done for you to progress. Even though I'm not saying alot of good things about the story, don't get me wrong. It has it's moments that I wouldn't want to spoil for you, but it's taken over by too much bad.
Graphics and sound aren't too special in this game. Facial animations aren't the best, and the lighting isn't too great either. The resolution for texture's aren't that low, but they aren't very high for you to be amazed either. Voice acting is good, but the quality of all the other sound's are average, some even subpar. There's also some bugs. I didn't deal with too many, but I dealt with enough where I have to inform it. Nothing gamebreaking though. And no, I had no problems with Uplay.
Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag doesn't do much to impress. Here and there, it's got some good things, and it captures the pirate aesthetic, but it's overtaken by a boring storyline, easy gameplay, a few bugs, some "meh" sounds and graphics, and there's really not much to do in the world.
If you are thinking of buying this game,
buy it when it's on sale, or find a good price and buy it for the cheapest price you can find.

This game has finally done what every other online tcg should have been doing from the beginning; every single card is animated. I actually enjoy just looking through and appreciating the awesome art work and watching the cool little animations. I also really love how every deck feels completely broken when it goes off; It's a total power trip!
One of my favorite and most unique features is when you play a location card and your side of the board transforms to match it; it looks awesome! The different factions each represent different deck strategies that you're probably familiar with. The flame Dawn Army is your Big Red Aggro deck, playing a lot of fast creatures to win the game before your opponent can stabilize. Genesis Industries is a robot synergy deck that lets you play cheap guys who eat each other to get bigger. The Warpath uses really cheap big guys to smash through your opponent's creatures and in to the win zone. The Cult of Verore is a control deck that makes it's own creatures stronger by killing yours. The Descendants of the Dragon is a turbo fog control deck that uses all kinds of defenses to frustrate your opponent until you literally win the game by draining his morale or playing a giant unstoppable dragon. The sleepers of Avarrach is one of the best, coolest and most viable zombie decks of any tcg I've seen. Using recursion and graveyard effects to help you amass an overwhelming horde of the undead. The Exiles are demons who reward you when you discard cards from your hand or sacrifice creatures. All in all, you should DEFINITELY check out this game; if only to see the cards.

i love this game!
I have been playing CCGs since Magic the gathering 4th edition came out.  Most recently I played a big name digital card by Blizzard, which i was very disappointed with.  Infinity Wars is the whole package.  Fun gameplay, fantastic card animations, and a HUGE library of cards.
Now some specifics:
1) there is a fantastic campaign mode that quickly gets you starter sets for every faction in the game, enabling you to quickly begin trying all the factions out to see what kind of decks you might like.
2) I felt like I was always unlocking new cards.  after only playing for 4 days I have over 600 cards.
3) There is never any need to spend real money on this game.  you can unlock every card just by playing the game.
4) You get a random card just for logging in every day.  that card can be any card and rarity.  from common to legendary.
5) Theres a reward for playing 3 games in a day, and weekly quests as well.
6) You get rewarded for playing against your friends.  More xp, more in game currency, and more cards.
7) This is the first digital CCG I have played that actually feels good to play on the computer.  In fact the game itself would not work as a tabletop game. Thats because...
8)  Each player plays cards at the same time!  Let me explain.  each turn you have about 2 minutes to spend your resources to summon you characters, use special abilities, attack your foe and defend yourself.  Once you have done everything you want for the turn you simply push the "end turn" button. While you have been doing everything listed above so has your opponent, so when you both push "end turn" the uniqueness of simultanious play really shines.  every happens in a specific order for both characters at the same time, allowing for bluffing, tricking, trapping and utterly destorying your foe in fun new ways not possible in traditional card games.
Now for some of not so good things about infinity wars:
1) this is most definatly still a beta version of the game.  it crashes, it gltches, cards will be covered by other text, some cards abilities act a little wonky.  the game still has some bugs for sure, but even with its technical issues it is still worth playing.
2) the card library needs some work.  when you go in to find a card there are some helpful search options to find what your looking for, but there needs to be more.  there needs to be an option to look up cards by special ability and by resource cost.  you can llok up cards by faction, by type of card, and by which set of cards its from; but with the amount of cards in the game there needs to be a better way to narrow it down.
3) This game needs more players!  I dont know how many people are currently playing, but there have been a few times when Ive tried to play some PVP matches and it took 3-5 minutes to find someone to play against.
4) It seems to take lots of in game currency to buy anything.  it costs 5200 points to buy a boster of cards that comes with 15 cards.  you get at most 75 points after playing a bot, or 150 for beating a pvp match.  if its your friend you both get 150 win or lose.  you need to play 70 bots minimum to get a booster or 35 pvp matches.  In my opinion you should be able to get a booster in half that many games.
so there you have it.  dispite some flaws that will hopefully be worked out as the game nears official release this is still the digital CCG to play.  Fast, fun, and unique in a way no other card game has every been.  Hope to see you on Infinity Wars!

I was skeptical to begin with but this turned out to be one of the best adventure games I've played, I would definitely recommend it.
+The puzzles are logical and don't involve the usual inventory spamming so endemic in this type of game. The signaling is great and if you get stuck you can usually get a decent nudge in the right direction by talking to everyone.
+The game is broken up into ten chapters and each chapter takes place in a relatively small area with a limited inventory so things never become overwhelming.
+The voice acting and dialog are great, though they start out a little shaky (this may be to do with the fact that chapters 1-3 were made years before the rest of the game was finished). As the game progresses you'll encounter loads of memorable and well fleshed out characters oh my yes.
+The world building is excellent and though there is quite a lot of technobabble in the dialog (it's right there in the title) it's incorporated well enough into the story and puzzle that it doesn't feel gratuitous.
-My only major criticism is that the last chapter is LITTERED with bugs. I didn't encounter anything that prevented my progress but I stopped trusting the game at that point and when I got stuck I presumed it was because of a bug not a puzzle.

If you're a fan of old school point-and-click adventure games, this game will not disappoint you. The writing is so good I barely have to add the phrase "for a game" to it.
The use-item logic puzzles are quite good, too. I rarely used the walkthrough to get past difficult parts. Most could be figured out by just reasoning through it. Invariably, there will be a time (or two) where you look up a problem only to find out it was an element in the environment that you didn't recognize. These moments are rare.
The story presents you with authentic moral choices which actually matter insofar as you care about what's happening because the characters are very well drawn. If you are confused about someone's motivations, then it's because the writers meant it, not due to poor design.
The game isn't long, but that's a feature, not a bug. I didn't feel like this game was wasting my time and will definitely play another by these developers.

I've enjoyed other Wadget Eye games, but I was surprised by how much I liked this game--the story was intriguingly complex and involving; the world was interesting and well-realized, and the characters had strong motivations and made interesting choices.
The gameplay was mostly fine, marred a little by slow sections at times, but mostly by hunt-the-pixel puzzles.  Seriously, it's 2017; hunting for objects on a screen without a way to highlight them should be universally understood to be bad game design at this point.  Once I actually knew where I could click, the puzzles were usually fairly straightforward and reasonably satisfying.

The only thing I can concretely say is that Litil Divil is some form of dungeon crawler. The game was clearly emulated from an older time so I’m sure the full color manual that was sold with the original game really filled in the blanks, but as a standalone title it feels like all there are are blanks.
It took me almost 2 minutes to figure out how to get the game to begin once I was at the start screen. I still am not entirely sure which key actually did it. Once dropped into the game I quickly figured out the arrow keys move.. easy enough. I walked 3 steps forward to be assaulted by a troll. Okay back up and figure out how to attack. I proceeded to press every key on the keyboard to no avail. Another 4 or 5 minutes later I realize that you actually have to press right, while against an enemy and then press the ‘X’ key. I don’t think it could have been more unintuitive. Regardless I pressed onwards to be dropped into a old school type dungeon crawler, a revelation that had me rather excited. After figuring out how to enter rooms (forward and ‘Z’ clearly, because thats the obvious go-to for object interaction) I poked my head into a few and each time was presented with a wild scene with no clear objective and no idea how to interact with the world to even be able to begin some trial and error.
Deep down I believe that Litil Divil may be a fun little game, but it’s torn down by the fact that digital delivery platforms don’t account for the original way to introduce players to a game world: manuals. Good Old Games does an awesome job of this by providing PDF downloads of said manuals. If Steam wants to keep pushing out ports of old DOS era titles (which it absolutely should) there needs to be a system in place for users to have clear and easy access to the media that was expected to be provided along with the game itself.
It's cute, but as many old games on Steam it crashes too often to be playable. :-(

Pros-
Excellent gameplay, the same as the previous games except with less reliance on powers now, since you only have 3. I thought this would be a bad thing, but it is not. Each of these powers is essential.
Lot more variety of gadgets, as well as nonlethal ones
Excellent level of polish- no bugs, no frame rate problems, and well voiced and acted
Contracts: Act as side missions in each level, and you get paid for completeing them at the end of the level. There are quite a few in each level, with some being simpler than others, and they are sometimes separate from your main mission, and at other times can be completed in the process of carrying out your main objective if you do some extra stuff in the process.
Cons:
Short. Five levels, two of which are the same one at different times of the day. It is half the price of a regular game, but then again, this should be an expansion like the Knife of Dunwall and the Brigamore Witches rather than a standalone. But the length of the game is shorter than those two DLCs put together.
The enemies are the same, character models are the same, the location looks very similar and uses the same assets, the animations are the same, bonecharms are the same. It is not a new game by any means, but feels very much like the knife of dunwall and brigamore witches
Token characters and poor story. Billie now has a lesbian lover whose picture she keeps and talks to about her in the past tense. its hardly ever elaborated yet the game tries to get you to feel some sort of sadness for their relationship. It just feels like they decided to throw her in to meet some diversity points. This is especially annoying since Billie was obviously in love with Anton in Dishonored 2.
Daud is now Asexual and has no interest in sex. This is read in a Penny novel, but one that accurately describes the events after the assasination of Jessamine Kaldwin, including Daud's thoughts and such, so it seems like this is canon. It makes no sense once again, except to appease those who clamor for diversity in games. It feels forced, and takes a great character and  turns him into a caricature.
Billie keeps talking about a dream in which her hand is hacked off, and during the start of the game she has both hands. Yet she meets the outsider who gives her a mechanical hand? This is never clarified and I am still confused about what exactly happened.
No explanation for why she suddenly gains powers despite not having the outsiders mark. No introduction to your powers. You are just tossed in with her saying a line when you use each power.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
My main worry with this game was that it was going to be as unoptimized as Dishonored 2 was when it came out, and still is in some cases. But thankfully, this was not the case. I have finished just the first mission so far, and it runs perfectly, without any of the stuttering and jagged looking edges in Dishonored 2 that anti Aliasing would not fix completely.
As far as gameplay, it is excellent. I love the new story, despite being somewhat peeved that I would not be playing as Daud, but Billie Lurk. The first mission shows a great deal of polish and has that same fleshed out world that made me love the first game, with side missions now showing up as contracts, although they work in a similar way. COmpared to the first mission in  D2 and Dishonored, this was a lot better, and did not feel like a mission I just wanted to get through to get to the good part of the game with all the powers and runes. So far I am very happy with the game, and I hope the rest of it is as polished. It took me about one and a half hours to finish the first mission, but that is because I reloaded multiple times and got the ghost and merciful achievement, and spent my time exploring every bit of the level.
I'll likelly change the review as I play more, but as of now, this game is a solid 9/10. If you liked Dishonored, this is definitely something worth picking up. I only wish Dishonored 2 had shown this level of polish.

A game I bought with few expectations, and now one of my favorite FPS experiences of all times.
Shadow Warrior is an old school FPS which, in my opinion, manages to get it all right.
The visuals are nice, with large levels filled with secrets, which environments varying from regular street, through mountains and ships, all the way to the shadow realm. Exploring the levels is fun and rewarding, and the 17 chapters offer a suprising amount of content considering modern FPS standards. The blood effects are also great, which is important because you will spend the game chopping off limbs and sinking tons of bullets into demonic flesh.
Which leads me to the action. Which is bloody (pun intended) amazing! Both the guns and the katana feel amazing, comlimenting each other, and with the addition of a small pool of magic spells and weapon skills, the combat offers a lot of variety. The game even encourages you to fight with a vide variety of moves by granting you additional, bonus upgrade points at the end of a fight based on how creative and fast you were. Enemy variety is ok, with only a few types being really annoying.
What surprised me the most was actually the story, which unfolds in two separate storylines. The main one is of Lo Wang and his quest to piece together the Nobitsura Kage and prevent the Shadow Realms from being destroyed, and the other, revealed through flashbacks each time you defeat a boss, reveals a rather tragic, and towards the end, surprisingly emotional, tale of why the Shadow Realm is falling apart in the first place. The flashbacks are presented as gorgeous 2D animations, and are a joy to watch.
The story is carried by fantastic writing and even better voice acting. The main character is a jerk, but a badass jerk you just can't help but like. The dialogue between him and his companion demon Hoji is just fantastic, and his one-liners are some of the best I've heard in a long time.
Finally, I would like to touch upon one last brilliant element of this game. The fortune cookies. They are hidden in the levels, and the reward for finding them is 5 health restored and a fortune. These fortunes are amazing humorous takes on popular culture and well known sayings, each better than the last.
I honestly can't think of anything this game does badly. There are so many additional little details done right, of which there are too many to mention here, but as a whole, every moment is either action-packed, or funny, or even emotional. I was never bored or displeased, it's so much fun to play, and definitely worth the buy.

Billie is brutal as hell. I love it.
Okay serious review though:
NB, I have a pretty solid gaming computer, and I'm playing on medium settings. I have experienced 0 technical issues thus far. I understand a lot of the negative reviews are from people who are having issues running the game -- PLEASE check the required specs before buying because this does seem like a serious problem.
Pros:
* Billie has a much smaller pool of powers, which leads to a much more deliberate and stealth-heavy gameplay style. As Corvo you could always fight your way out and it was super fun, but playing as Billie is TENSE in a way I haven't encountered in a long time.
* Big maps, lots to explore.
* GREAT dialogue/writing. ♥♥♥♥ the haters: easily the best writing I've seen in a Bethesda game, pretty good writing fullstop. There's even occasionally these little poetic flourishes that I would love to see more of.
* Genuinely challenging in a way more games need to be. Play smart or you're gonna die.
* Despite the short length, there's a really satisfying progression/customization system with the bone-charms. Instead of runes, there's just increasingly powerful and interesting bone charms (much more than in previous DH games) that add a lot of variety to the play.
Cons
* Short. Probably 4-6 hours if you're burning through the plot, 6-8 at normal speed, maaaaybe 12 if you're a completionist.
* Doesn't seem as replayable as DH1 or DH2 -- the limited powerset means you're probably only gonna play the campaign through once or twice. High Chaos/Low Chaos, done.
* Lots of reused assets (even whole maps like the Conservatory) from DH2.
* Have encountered a few scripting bugs that really shouldn't have made the live game, mostly relating to moving between zones -- there's contracts that require you to knock somebody out then dump their body in x, but then you can't get the body to x because it requires a new map to load and your kidnap-ee disappears.
Pro OR Con depending on what you want out of it:
* Graphics identical to DH2. Don't expect it to look any prettier, but don't expect to need a new graphics card either.
* This is NOT an action game (see below)
* A lot less forgiving than other DH games. Billie has 0 ability to tank, even by the standards of an assassin, and screwing up WILL get you killed. Her movement skill is slower and doesn't go as far, her face-steal barely lasts long enough to make it useful -- you have to plan methodically to have any hope. It's much more of a traditional stealth game in the vein of Thief than a stealth-action hybrid like the other two.
Hell, let me elaborate on those last two points (and the first Pro). I am an old♥♥♥♥♥man, and I remember Stealth games of the 90s. If you got caught by a single random guard, you had decent odds of making it out alive (if you got it over quickly). Two guards? RUN. Billie plays like that -- she hits hard and fast, but one solid hit will take her down. Billie MUST stealth, and her abilities play into that very heavily: she gets no combat boosts outside of equipment upgrades, she knocks herself over if she teleports into somebody, and she has Foresight, which is probably the best stealth/recon tool I've ever encountered in a game. Even with the twin-blade and some of the beefier late-game bone charms she's still a total glass cannon. Billie is not meant for front-on assaults at all: she's meant for
1) avoiding combat all-together and
2) meticulously planned surgical strikes
She's so fragile, you start avoiding even unecessary assassinations, in case somebody is watching. When violence does happen, it's fast, tense, bloody, frightening. If there's two guards standing together, you better learn to wait until one of them leaves before you go for the throat. It kinda reminds me of the recent Atomic Blonde: the fights play out like close-combat between a (highly trained) woman and a (decently-trained) man would play out IRL -- to win, the woman has to tilt the scales, and fight fast, dirty and brutal.
There's a real tension and desperation to the way Billie handles that I haven't seen in literally decades. You will spend five full minutes lurking on a drainpipe so you can drop down and kill one measly guy without being noticed. You'll hear that musical sting that means you've been rumbled and just immediately bug out because there's no way you're winning a fair fight. You'll run, find somewhere new to strike from, spend another ten minutes planning while swearing under your breath.
If that sounds boring to you, this isn't your game. If you miss the days of Thief: the Dark Project, this is right up your (heh) alley.
EDIT: this has been rewritten quite a lot, as I've now completed the game. Initial review was first couple of hours, this should cover everything.

A game that completely flips what you'd epect from a regular video game, The Stanely Parable's whole gameplay bases on the idea of what would happen if you don't listen to the oniptient narrarator and chose your own path instead. While you can do exactly what the narrarator tells you to, the real experience of the game comes from doing the complete oppisite. Explaining the game anymore than this would be a diservice to what the game truely delivers. The game does have a demo, but if you're worried that playing it would ruin the full experience you won't need to worry! The demo and the full game are totaly different from eachother. But each both provide hilarious commentary on the way Video Games work in their own ways.
As for replay value... Ehh... After finding every possible outcome, you really have no reason to return. Unless you want the achivements, or just want to revisit it every now and again. The games intention is not to really keep you coming back often. However, this should not plant a sour taste in your decision, the game is still worth going back to now and again for a good laugh.
Completely clever no matter witch path you choose, The Stanely Parable is something you should check out for yourself!
