When I first started playing R3E it was a total mess, I was quite surprised given the pedigree of the guys behind it.
However, as time has gone on and with every single update it has improved to the point where it can be considered as a must own title for both arcade racers and sim racers alike.
Sure, the starting F2P content is dreadful and if you're going to base an opinion on that content, then you might aswell not bother, to be quite honest - Spend a bit on a decent pack or, as R3E calls them 'experiences' (Any of the modern DTM 'Experiences' will do) where you get a selection of cars and tracks and I can guarantee you that this will put a smile on your face.
I'm not a hardcore sim racer, but I do use full manual including clutch with my T300 wheel, I race in various other games ranging from pCars, through Assetto Corsa and Game Stock Car up to iRacing - This seems to sit somewhere in between pCars and Assetto Corsa, in terms of physics (In my humble opinion). This isn't a bad thing when you also consider that it has arguably the best AI outside of rFactor 2, while also being a bit more forgiving to those of us who aren't aliens.
When I think about the main reason I recommend this, it comes down to this:
Every other popular racing game currently on the market does something better than this does, rFactor 2 has better physics and better AI, iRacing has better multiplayer, pCars has better single player career, Assetto Corsa has better graphics.
BUT, for all of the above excelling in different areas, nothing else quite ties it all together as well as this does, and thats good enough for me.

Look at Civ5, it's vibrant, entertaining. You can spend hundreds of hours in it and chase that "one more turn"- fix.  Civ: Beyond Earth is just ... boring. It's a solid game as such but there's just no 'flesh' to it.
Firaxis can make good games, it's just a shame that they require a DLC of some sort to become good.
The patch released just recently made things even worse. The AI gets a tremendous boost to research, production and resources in general. It's not fun or challenging, it is frustrating to the point of it being a futile endeavour.
This game had so much potential and yet it feels like a half-arsed mod that could've been made for Civ5.
I cannot in good faith recommend this game in its current state. If you find it in a bargain bin under 10€ and if you have nothing else to play, then I still wouldn't recommend it.

I only played the first and second AC. The first was a clumsy mess of a game but very innovative. I remember thinking to myself "Can't wait to see what they do next, with all issues solved. This is going to be the go-to formula for AAA games in the next few years". I guess I was right, AC 2 did solve all its issues and expanded on the original. And this did became the go-to formula for AAA games even to this day.
Then, after many years without playing an AC game, but playing plenty of sprouts of AC, like Batman, Just cause and many others, I gave AC another try with Black Flag. Heard great things about it, so why not. I don't remember exactly how AC 2 felt when playing, so my main parameter for comparison comes from Batman games, and I don't know if Batman really improved on the formula or if this AC took a few steps backwards.
About free running/climbing. The level/missions' design certainly doesn't respect the limitations of the system. The game makes you chase enemies through narrow streets, so you will find yourself climbing a wall that was exactly perpendicular to the direction you were running because you brushed against it. Then the game makes you stalk people, but you can't rely on this movement scheme will do what you think it should. When you are two levels above the guards and want to drop to the second level you might end up doing a somersault with a rolling finale on the guards' feet instead.
The parkour system is actually impressive, with glitches here and there, like getting stuck at small steps and not finding the occasional edge, but it's the level design that simply doesn't know what it can do well. On the sea there is a similar issue. It's all very fun, sailing through storms, attacking other ships, upgrading etc. Until the game decides to throw an escort mission. Oh god. An escort mission. On a ship. What else? underwater level? slippery ice level? (retro references :P) And this is yet another example of mission design that doesn't seem to respect the mechanics a whole lot. Sure, you can finish this level, but not with skill. You will play again and again until you know where the ships are coming, just like you did for the chase and stalk missions. It's not the kind of level design that makes me happy. It feels like a chore.
Does all of this break the game? not at all. It does make it frustrating about half the time. In fact, it feels like AC1 all over again! I remember feeling exactly like this, admiring the potential and wanting to see what comes next in the series. Only now I'm not that curious anymore, specially after I heard this is the best of the series since AC2.

Monoliths, glyphs, runes, buttons to step on... Kairo.
For every step you take in this lonely world, you find yourself seemingly stuck and lost within yourself as well. Film grain covers your field of vision as you navigate the towers, solving a wide plethora of puzzles, from simple navigation of a simple maze to interpreting a star map just to open a door to running on treadmills, Kairo does the puzzle genre justice by infusing complex and mind-boggling puzzles towards a simplistic, minimalist world. The colours are beautiful, the gameplay is relatively solid (although I personally find the movement a little too sensitive) and this is really immersive by itself (if you play in a dark room with headphones).
A drawback for me personally was that I found myself getting lost most of the time, that I was unable to have a good view of the puzzle I'm trying to solve. Like a rat in a maze, I could not see the big picture of the puzzle and I had to keep walking in circles trying to figure out what I've done, even resorting to sketching out some rooms on a piece of paper and drawing the various interactive elements on the paper so I can figure out what in the world is going on. It does interrupt the flow of the game for me sometimes and it was a little distracting to the overall feel of the game.
In short, despite the few rough edges of this work of art, Kairo is really a beautiful gameset (with its fair share of really, really creepy elements and depictions here and there), really meant for the casual player to play and enjoy this surreal world, while unraveling a terrible tale that led to this place. If you're a puzzle nut and you enjoy creepy, lonely worlds, Kairo really is the place for you to be.
Eurogamer has succiently highlighted the deep spine of Kairo. "Kairo is mysterious and elegant and powerfully distinct. Like Fez and Minecraft, it will work your way into your dreams if you're not careful."
Play at your own risk, because Kairo does leave impressions in your mind as you play it, with the wide rooms and chilling images (when you stumble upon some seemingly "dead ends") and huge, huge glyphs.
To this casual gamer's opinion:
Kairo: 7.5/10

Some of the problems that irked me back then and are still in the game:
*Stupendously complex repair system; the sun burnt away a logic block in the smack middle(why sun? WHY?!) of your ship and som linked weapon computers? No blueprint? (Why would we autosave your creations? On your computer? Don't be silly) Have fun unraveling that mess.

*I'm repeating myself, but good luck finding any relevant info to a problem you have, on forums people nab back and forth at each other, making it impossible to know who's right or wrong, if they even come to any kind of conclusion. Wiki's are either woefully outdated or woefully unhelpful.
*you saved  a couple of blueprints for your turrets --with no thrusters and no own power supply-- and a few mining ships and scouts --with no offensive weapons-- Oh guess what, PIRATE ATTACK, with inert turrets, harmless mining ships and scouts that all just want to cuddle you! Before reading this review I would like to announce that I have playedt around 50 Hours in the nonsteam Client. Also this is a long♥♥♥♥♥review.
This is a great TCG, To start with you get a free card or even a booster when you log on, and after 3 games you get another card/ booster. You also get a booster every time you level up (A booster of 15 Cards) and your 1st 10 levels are faily fast to obtain. You also get a starter deck for each faction for getting 5 levels into each campaign and a booster for each mission finished. You also get a faction booster (Generaly 3-5 Cards) every time you level in a faction.
So right away you get a hardfull of cards within the 1st few hours of gameplay. Not to mention if you were to buy the boosters with real world money they have great value (In my opinion) It also only take a few hours of gameplay to get a large booster with ingame currency.
Now for gameplay.
The gamplay in Infinity Wars is like gameplay that I have never tryed in a TCG, when building a deck you have three commanders and those commanders limit you to what factions you can use in your deck. Turns are done at the same time with one player having prioraty in a turn for spells and attacks to go first. you also have two ways to lose a game, one being health and other being moral. health is lost by you being attacked directly and moral is lost by losing creatures.
There are 3 battles zones. (Attack, Defence and Support) Attack zone is used to attack your opponents fortress. Defence is used to defend your fortress and the support zone is were most creatures are summoned to. while creatures are in the support zone for the most part they cannot be attacked and they cannot defend. but there are many cards that get around this.
The 7 factions in Infinity wars all have there own style of play. one faction may be a direct assult to the enimy base while another will use more spells then creatures. another relys on its grave to grow in strength.
over all this is a great game I would recommend it to anybody who enjoys MTG. The game also has a great community that will be happy to answer any questions you may ask.

I got this game because I was in the mood for a good-old-fashioned shooter, but I was tired of all the "retro" pixel or SNES graphics that seem to plague this genre. I understand this is an old-fashioned genre, but I like flashy graphics and I want to have my cake and be able to eat it too!
I am pretty pleased with this game overall. I have an older laptop (still runs with Vista) and this game played very well, there may have been some lag with the bosses, I'm not entirely sure, it was ever-so-slight if it was lag. And the game feels like a pretty solid shooter. Lots of fire on screen, lots of moving targets to hit and avoid, powerups to collect all while the game gets increasingly faster and more difficult.
This is a more old-school type shooter difficulty-wise as it is fairly unforgiving with one-hit kills, no more than one shield able to be stored at a time and no mid-way save points, so if I don't beat the boss of a level, I start all the way back at square one for that level. I do like that each wave is randomly generated, though, rather than just trying to remember a certain pattern to beat each wave every time.
The weapon system took a bit to get used to. Three different weapon types randomly appear throughout each wave, and the more of each specific weapon type I pick up, the stronger that weapon type becomes. However, there is no way to choose between the different weapons, so every time I pick up a weapon I am not currently using, it switches to that specific weapon. This makes for a game of go for the "good" weapon upgrades whilst trying to dodge the "bad" weapon upgrades (defined by personal preference) all while at the same time trying to collect the blue resource, dodge asteroids and enemy ship fire, and gain bonuses. But at least there is unlimited fire with each weapon type, as I hate having to be stingy with my ammo.
I really like the graphics though. They are sharp and colorful and pleasing to look at. Sometimes it's just nice to have a little eye-candy while destroying everything on screen. The music is nice and fluid as well, and I enjoy the rock music that plays, signalling the boss fights.
I'm also glad that this game comes with partial controller support (you still need your mouse for menu options) as I found it easier to play with the controller than with the keyboard and mouse. It seemed like there was some slight drifting when I played with the keyboard, the controller felt more solid. Although I would have liked a help page that told me what buttons did what. I had an issue with pressing "Pause" instead of "Options" whilst in-game because, when paused, I could not go back to the main menu, but when I pressed optons, then I could. Even though both of those buttons bring up the same options menu, when the game is paused, the "Main Menu" button is disabled for some reason.
All in all, I got this game to be a fun, old-school shooter with pleasing eye candy, and I got exactly what I was hoping for.

This is a fun scrolling shooter that is worth trying.
The game involves collecting little blue balls to beat waves.  There are a variety of power-ups to pick up in your quest, and various enemies will try and kill you and get in your way as you pick up things.  The game starts out pretty easy, but really starts to get tougher around World 3.
This is a shooter that has an old school feel despite the pretty 3D graphics.  The most important thing in a game like this is control, and happily your ship controls very well.  Movement felt natural and I quickly was able to figure out the weapon mechanic.  Your ship can only take one hit.  No life bars, just one hit.  You can pick up shields, and you get extra lives.... but every moment is very edge of your seat due to this mechanic.  The bosses are an interesting change of pace from the normal waves, but you need to figure out their pattern quickly due to how easy it is to die.
All that being said, I found time really got away from me playing this game, and before I knew it I was happily blasting my way through giant packs of green aliens.  The art is great.  The voice acting works, but doesn't stand out, and the music was fitting for the style.
The options are bare bones but functional.
Overall I had a blast playing this game.  It is different from your normal shooter.  It reminds me more of Galaga than anything released in the last 10 years.  Very satisfying to blow up the enemies.
If you like shooters, especially "old school" shooters, this is one to try.

Now, right off the bat; credit where credit is due: there is a lot of work that was put into this. This was clearly someone's passion project. Either that or someone's first stab at making something so cohesive and interesting. It was a valiant effort on the creator's part. And I want to stress my appreciation for the talent and effort put into this. Even if I can't really sink my teeth into it personally. From the art to the lore to the voice talent, you can tell that people really labored over this; that much is evident. However, there are some parts missing here. There are some ingredients missing from the soup,
Technobabylon is a story about a futuristic world that couldn't care less. Cloned babies, overbearing artificial intelligence, zero privacy, escapism, nuclear war, and the ever present looming threat of scarcity masked as abundance. Everything is here and accounted for. What I can give Technobabylon credit for is how it presents its setting. It doesn't bother to bombard you. It gives you clues about this world you're experiencing. And aside from a set of very specific situations, it isn't required that you care at all about this setting. The characters themselves clearly don't. That's a little more believable in my opinion. If we all lived in the dystopia, I'd doubt that anyone would care after so long. That's natural for these characters, and this is shown in game. Kudos.
Now, I'm going to have to take those kudos right back, because for these steps forward, Technobabylon makes some very curious design choices. I know it's the future in all, but this game has a bizarre fixation on fitting in some heavyweight rhetoric in the wrong places. What do I mean? Well, early in the game we learn that one of the major characters underwent a sex change. Wowee. And this is just mentioned in passing. Never comes up. Never adds much to the character other than a moment of, "uhh.. ok?" If anything this soured my vision of one of the characters right off the bat. Why would I care about a character's gender? Or past gender? Especially if this point was treated with none of the tact and meaning that a subject like this usually requires.
Later in the game we're introduced to a homosexual couple who have a synthetic housemaid who's strongly implied to be assisting them in the bedroom. Did I say strongly implied? I mean outright stated. Now, that's fantastic and all, but this is just dropped and left to sit there. The most we know about them is they like Paris. That's about it... Again, no investment. No meaning whatsoever. Strike two. The last straw came late in the game when I witnessed the fastest devolution of what could've been mildly entertaining dialogue into what was essentially akin to "mind your pronouns." Apparently the distinction between gynoid and android is very important? Also, points for me reacting almost exactly like the villain did.
Contrast this with the only straight relationship in the game: Regis and his wife. This relationship isn't impactful because its straight, its impactful because it plays a significant role in these character's motivations. It plays into the plot a lot more. It actually contributes. In fact, this point would've remained entirely unchanged if it were a homosexual relationship anyway. I feel like the game tried to make it a point to include these things but ended up making them completely insubstantial as a result.
As far as the rest of the game goes, I can say everything blends together more or less. It does the setting well, like I said, but failure to utilize this and make something meaningful just leads to more disappointment. The characters are serviceable. So is the plot. It really comes down to how predictable you like your point and click games. I could guess the big twist about two hours before I actually completed the game. And while I'm throwing stones, the last area and the ending are so horribly contrived that it ruins anything the game was trying to set up. Some special thread of voodoo magic is tying these character's fates together. It's up to Regis Philbin and two other people to save the world I guess.
For what it's worth, this is an alright experience. I wouldn't recommend it for a few reasons. The later half of the game suffers from lack of direction, and it all trails into the worst parts of the game. Puzzles fall into two categories: immediately obvious and impossible. Out of the entire cast, Regis was the only one I was vaguely interested in. The entire rest of the cast was more or less forgettable or boring. And the big top off is the ending. For the asking price, this is an alright game to put some hours into. But honestly, I just don't regard it as exceptional.

Okay, I know what interests people the most when it comes to a new Dishonored game that is powered by Void engine - is performance any good? Well, I played at Very High settings at 1080p resolution, with Vsync on, and I had 60fps pretty much at all times. i5-6600 CPU, RX 470 8 GB GPU, 8 GB DDR4 RAM. Graphics are very good, with dynamic lighting and shadowing, radiosity and all the other great things. It's not photorealistic, of course; the game maintains its art style that has been characteristic to Dishonored series ever since the first game.
Level design is what you'd expect from Arkane game - lots of alternate routes around obstacles. You can pay your way behind closed door, steal the key, climb in through the window... Always look up when playing this, there's always a ledge to climb up or pipes leading across the room with enemies. The first level is pretty big, with bone charms, supplies and various messages scattered around it. Attention to detail is definitely noticeable.
For €30 this standalone expansion has lots to offer and is worth the money. Definitely recommending this if you're a fan of Dishonored series.

A game that completely flips what you'd epect from a regular video game, The Stanely Parable's whole gameplay bases on the idea of what would happen if you don't listen to the oniptient narrarator and chose your own path instead. While you can do exactly what the narrarator tells you to, the real experience of the game comes from doing the complete oppisite. Explaining the game anymore than this would be a diservice to what the game truely delivers. The game does have a demo, but if you're worried that playing it would ruin the full experience you won't need to worry! The demo and the full game are totaly different from eachother. But each both provide hilarious commentary on the way Video Games work in their own ways.
As for replay value... Ehh... After finding every possible outcome, you really have no reason to return. Unless you want the achivements, or just want to revisit it every now and again. The games intention is not to really keep you coming back often. However, this should not plant a sour taste in your decision, the game is still worth going back to now and again for a good laugh.
Completely clever no matter witch path you choose, The Stanely Parable is something you should check out for yourself!

I played the original board game back in the day (late 1980s) - and it was one of the best board games ever devised. I played the previous Space hulk video games (Space Hulk on Amiga and Space Hulk vengence on PC/PS2?) and they too were excellent.
I bought this Space Hulk video game (and I bought it on iOS for my iPad too) pretty much as soon as I saw it - and I rarely buy games not on sale.
This version of Space Hulk was very close to the board game.  The initial build of the game was OK(ish) - good core gameplay, but quite a few flaws that needed to be (and were) sorted out with later patches. As this Space Hulk was so close to the board game, I was dissapointed that the original board game expansions (Deathwing and Genestealer) were never added to the base game as DLC, but you can't have everything I guess.
The game mechanics are solid, there are a good set of scenarios linked into a story, the AI opponent is competent and - most importantly - the scenarios are well designed and balanced. If you play well you will win (probably, unless you have some very bad dice rolls). If you play badly you will lose (and lucky dice won't save you). Only downside is you can't play scenarios as the Tyranids against the computer's Terminators on solo.
Personally, so far, I prefer this Space Hulk to Space Hulk:Ascention. I've played this Space Hulk through start to end on iPad, and again on PC, but I'm just not as keen on the added complexity/customisation element of Ascention.
Overall its an excellent game, particularly at the price it often appears on sale.

I am a rather frequent writer and I do write a lot (my novels average some 100,000 words). I've used OmmWriter for concentrating and Scrivener for just regular novel-writing, and this thing doesn't measure up to either.
Concentration-wise, OmmWriter trumps this thing. This interface is a general simplified version of your average word editor; OmmWriter takes up the entire screen, toolbars included, so that it offers minimal distraction when writing. Nimble outdoes the Ommwriter in text-editing UI by a far margin, but when it comes to just distraction-free writing environment, this isn't a very able editor.
Organisation-wise, I've found Scrivener to be well worth the price, which is 4 times the price of Nimble. Scrivener offers everything from dictionary to wikipedia to name generator, not to mention colour-coding documents, sticking them in hierarchial folders (no limit, I believe), highlighting, back-up, templates for settings and characters, exporting formats from manuscript with Courier font to .mobi (lets you add table of contents, cover, and everything else an ebook needs), adding images, adding pdfs, managing sources... plus it does all the things Nimble does, including word count, word target, full-screen, e.t.c. It even allows you to take snapshots so you can do massive re-write, then roll back to the original if you don't like it. The only benefit of Nimble, possibly, is cloud sync, but you can just save on dropbox for Scrivener and that'd solve the problem. I can't imagine why I'd want to encrypt it, so I can't really say much on it.
If this had... oh, I don't know, about 40 add-ons, it'd provide a competitor for Scrivener. As of now, there are seven, and two are for exporting to WordPress and
, both of which Scrivener does without a hitch. So if I'm recommending a quick writer with minimal distractions, I'd recommend the OmmWriter and Sigil (for compiling to epub) at a super-hefty price of about 5 dollars. If someone's seriously considering writing a novel with notes, research, plotlines and character sheets, I'd advise them to dish out the $40 and buy Scrivener instead (or $35 at student discount, I believe).
I kind of wish this thing had a trial, instead of forcing people to pay the full price when they don't know the full functions, which aren't listed. I really, really want to return this.

I have one observation and one complaint.
Observation:
This comes with an encrypt your story option.  The instructions direct you to reset your encryption key by deleting it.  But, oh, by the way, make sure not to delete the key before you decrypt your story first.  You did?  Oh, well then, I need to you open Windows to the folder where your story is saved.  Now lean forward to your monitor.  Put your lips directly on the filename you saved your story under.  I know you don't have a touchscreen; just trust me on this.  Put your lips right on the filename.  Now gently but firmly kiss it goodbye.  You ain't never gonna see it again, Bubba.
Yeah, there could be a bit of refinement there.  Maybe add the option to the program to reset the key (which the program would then do), but prohibit doing it while the story is encrypted.  That might save some tears.  Just a thought.
Complaint:
Once I save my notes on a character, there's no way (that I can find) to edit them again.  They're saved and locked in for all time forever and ever.  After all, characters never go through changes over the course of a story.  Or series.
Most likely this is either an interface problem (in which the user can't find how to do it), or an oversight in the development of the program.  This is, however, a significant issue.  Notes can be edited after saving them, but not a character (which is a special kind of note).
Finally, it would be nice (and may be possible with the right addons) to create different kind of notes.  What if I want my character to list a race, color, height, weight, etc (Skippy the 3'4" purple and pink polka dotted goblin boy of 12 months old).  Or, I want to create a robot.  Or my characters are planets.  Yeah, pretty planets.  With colors.  And sparkles.  Okay, I'll lay off the acid.  But my point stands.  Not all "Characters" are human.
A note type for organizations or groups would also be nice.
Anyway, my two cents (or $8.99 as the case may be).
-----
Update 4/21/15:  After a bit of back and forth (See the comments on this review for details), there is a workaround for the complaint since it was a formatting issue on my screen.
And I can create new note types easily with a text editor in the NoteModels folder quite easily, which addresses my other concerns.
So that makes it a very nice package.

So, yeah, how do I describe Kairo?
First, the puzzles. While they start out easy, later in the game, they are really counter intuitive(At least the devs had the idea of including hints).
I was stuck on the last "world", not even because I was stuck on a puzzle, but I simply didn't knew what puzzle was left to do.
Not to mention the optional puzzles that lead to the secret ending(which is just stupid and feel more like a filler than rewarding) are even harder and are simply undo-able without a guide. Also, they require backtracking.
The graphics are both basic and good, and the game run very well on low end computers(Even with shaders on). Though the environments are sometimes too lazy and blocky. The ambient music is also great, and give a mood to each "room".
The "story"... Okay, I just don't get it. Kairo use a lot of morbid symbols, post-apocalyptic pictures, etc, but it never feel more than an assemblage of tropes("Oh, look how creepy is this place! So creppy, huh???") rather than a mysterious story. So don't buy this game for the story.
In short, if you are okay with using a guide/the hints for the puzzles, then you could buy it.

Infinity Wars is an easy to learn but complex card game that focuses on winning in either two ways, destroy the enemy fortress (which has health) or kill enough of their minions and deplete enemy morale to zero, forcing their retreat. You choose 3 commanders, of whatever faction you wish, but depending on which cards you want to use, you will need a minimum amount of that factions commanders. An example would be having a specific faction card, lets say (Genesis) that requires you to have 2 of its factions commanders. For this card to be in your deck, you need 2 of those 3 required commanders to be of that faction, in this case Genesis. This allows for unique deck creation as you can have 1 commander from 3 different factions, allowing you to use faction cards with a required commander cost of 1, making it a unique and versatile deck. Or if your like me, use three commanders from the same faction and gain access to its extremely powerful cards.
Very noob friendly with a long and informative tutorial that is completely optional to do, but I would highly recommend completing the first two sections to make sure you understand the game. The third is for more advanced play, and can take upwards of an hour to complete, due to learning how to use special game mechanics.
To make sure you aren't getting destroyed, multiplayer VS people is disabled until you reach level 4, which will take roughly 1:30 - 2:00 hours to finish.
There is a long campaign that is interesting and very fun, which allows you to play every faction in the game to better learn its playstyle and get comfortable with the cards they command. Or if you feel like killing computers for that much wanted experience, just play the AI over and over until you reach the required level.
No Pay 2 Win, you can pay for decks and booster packs with real money or use the in game currency to buy cards. (like most online TGC) If you do choose to sink money into IW, the prices are very reasonable and you get a good amount of cards added to your collection.
Low player base, as its probably not very popular with the current kings of cards being MTG and more recently, Hearthstone.
If you were to ask me to explain Infinity Wars in a sentence, it would be (Its like the middle grounds of Hearthstone and Magic: The Gathering: animated cards, complex at times, simple to learn and very fun to play)
Personal Rating: 4/5

I very much recommend StarMade to anyone who might be thinking about buying it. This game is amazing, and you can build incredible ships, even if it takes a bit of time. The devs are active, and a new update comes around once a month. Unlike games such as Minecraft or Terraria, which allow for you to easilly build settlements and defeat enemys, in StarMade, building any sort of perminate structure is hard, because the Pirates are always tracking you, and can be very hard to defeat or even run away from if they show up in large fleets. (Before you attempt to take on the Pirates, you should have a reasonably powerful ship.) Another great thing about this game is the crafting system. If you want to get a single block of Green Advanced Armor, you have to make a basic hull, then make paint, then combine those things, then create standerd hardener, then combine them, then create advanced hardener, and conbine them too. And crafting takes time, so producing stuff in bulk while you hunt around for other things on a planet such as ores or crystals is a good way to pass the time.
All in all, this game is one of the best I've ever played, so if you like sandbox games and space, you should defiantly get this.

This game is easily one of the best indie games I have played to date. It has it's flaws, and, of course, the very occasional bug, but what game doesn't?
This game sets the tone with a very dark, sad world, with very sombre themes and time-worn characters throughout. The varied areas each supply different challenges, and the fluid gameplay makes for a very difficult, but very rewarding game.
It has the same 'learn by dying' mechanic as Dark Souls, where if you die, all your currency is left in the spot of your death for you to get when you return to it, and it helps teach you where dangers are, what a boss is capable of, without making you 'lose all your lives,' rather restarting you from a checkpoint and trying again. There is no real loss in dying, unless you die on your way -to- your money, but even then, it's not a major loss.
This game gives little hand-holding. A short tutorial area in the beginning will give you a brief overview of what you're capable of, and the first town gives you a nice hub to return to, but beyond that, the game does not give you any direction on what to do, beyond areas that require new abilities/powers to reach. You ahve to figure out where you need to go, and explore.
There is only -one- part of the game I dislike, and it is a late-end game dungeon that requires lots of precision platforming to traverse. It can be extremely frustrating, given the game's unforgiving mechanics, but beyond that one area, this game is a marvel in Metroidvania gaming.
There are even plenty of things for the 'completionists' and 'collectaholics' to grab, ranging from grubs to save, pins to enhance your abilities, mask and vessel shards to increase your health or magic meters, and 'soul' energy, to power up a dream nail that requires lots of exploring to fully upgrade. The game has everything for every player.
I would give this game a firm 9/10. There are a few flaws, and, given the game's difficulty, it can discourage new players, but I would recommend this game to everyone and anyone willing to give an indie game a chance.

You set off into the aftermath of a bug apocalypse—a nearly desolate kingdom, It's civilians scattered, missing, and dead. To be put in a world with no background of who you are or what your purpose is, you delve deep into the depths of obscurity, facing off against creatures who want nothing else but to kill you. Despite the turmoil setting, the atmosphere of the game is truly beautiful. The art style is endearing, the music is well-orchestrated, and the combat is original.
Hollow Knight pushes you to go explore the vast world to your hearts content. This 2D action-platformer focuses on exploring an undiscovered map, slaying a magnitude of enemies, obtaining skills that allow you to backtrack into previously inaccessible areas, and unlocking hidden secrets.
I absolutely love this game and would greatly recommend it; one of my favorites of all time.

I love point & click games and I love cyberpunk. Those are two excellent reasons to love this game. But I have more to say about it.
Point & click + cyberpunk is a rather common combination, these days. For example, see Read Only Memories, Void & Meddler, Gemini Rue... All these games are good, but Technobabylon is definitely the best I've ever played.
All characters are very interesting, full of surprises.
The scenario is clever, unexpected, easily believable, easily understandable, and full of interesting moral dilemmas.
There are two great endings. It's very hard to say which one is the best.
Musics and graphics are both beautiful. Voice actors are great.
As in most cyberpunk games, there is a queer side, but it is not too invasive, unlike in many others (see Read Only Memories and Void & Meddler, for example, that can be annoying here). This aspect of the game is balanced correctly.
When you'll finish this game, your first thought will be: "when do they create a second episode? I want more!"

Originally very good review, however the developers balance is making me change my feedback on this. Original review is still below the line.
Originally the balance within Battlerite wasn't perfect but it was somewhere balanced. Since then 3 new champions have been released and a few balance patches have come out.
These new champions seem to have just been put in the game with very little attempt to make them fit and instead they have been ridiculously strong since release with no attempt at balance.
Jumong for example, remains the most broken ranged dps in game. Literally everything Jade does, he does more effectively and with higher numbers. A couple of weeks or so ago a patch was released declaring it was going to nerf Jumong, what actually happened was they removed invulnerability from his Q and sped up his right click.
Whilst the Q nerf was a step in the right direction, he has the exact same thing still on his Ex-Q so it was utterly pointless if you know how to play the game at all. Literally all it changed was instead of pressing Q you press Shift+Q. Oh and they buffed his right click speed on top of that so overall it was a buff pretty much. Fans of the champ tend to cry that Ex-Q uses energy so thats balanced, however very rarely does anyone use Jumongs energy for his ult anyway and the only other thing people use is his R which still does silly damage and only costs one energy bar.
This has now carried on to Pestilus who is just plain silly at release.
Existing champions have had many questionable changes made too. Lucie for example remains one of the top picks as does Taya simply because they are constantly way too strong despite awful balance attempts.
So many games fall down horribly at this hurdle and unfortunately it seems Battlerite is going to follow. I find myself playing less and less with each update because the balance is getting more and more unbearable.
Many of the hardcore fans pretend not to notice major balancing issues simply because they play the unbalanced champions themselves. Reddit constantly has posts like this, often recording 1v3 videos then claiming they are fine.
Healing spam in particular is the most poor aspect of the game. Certain healers literally spam heal themselves so much its impossible to deal damage unless you stick to them with multiple players. The attempted balance was allowing 3 heals with a few seconds gap before it recharges, however this is completely negated when all they do is heal and run.
I can vouch for this myself as I climbed very high on ranks just doing this same aspect. At this point all balance in the game is a ♥♥♥♥ing joke, Taya is like Sonic on crack, Pestilus heals more damage than you can hit him with unless you use two players and the entire thing is just a horrible steaming pile of turd. I play less and less with each patch because it just gets worse.
Overall I will keep an eye on this game but it seems to be plagued with the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ balance as Smite, with the devs concentrating on the same aspect of releasing new content rather than fixing old. Very disappointed.

Not very often that choose to review a product on steam, unless its really bad or really good.
Battlerite is one of the few games I have played that has really impressed me.
For an early access game, it feels more complete than many other games in the same category. It is one of those games that you can jump into, play a quick few rounds then jump off before/after work. Whilst I hesitate to compare, think LoL but without the farming.
Champions in this game require some time to learn and skill to play, rather than no brainer builds. Many people like to say its a MOBA but without the farm however realistically it plays like a combination of Smite and LoL with a mix of any deathmatch style game thrown in.
Take Smites aiming system for abilities, combined with the viewpoint from LoL and the fun from deathmatch in something like Overwatch and you have Battlerite. That's pretty much the best analogy I can come up with.
Skills can be missed very easily, battles are short and fun and the community isn't as bad as a lot of games at the moment. That being said, its not perfect.
Often in standard games you will find people who have no idea what they are doing, as per your usual online game however this becomes annoying when matchmaking puts you with this same person 5 or 6 times in a row. I mean come on, with a player base this large you can't find ONE other person to match me with? Even the enemy teams remain the same players many times over.
Other downsides are the lack of interesting outfits for your character and a lack of any meaningful development in game. Most outfits right now are just recolours and nothing more and there is 0 champion progression at all, levelling up basically just adds currency and at level 10 an avatar.
Champion balancing is generally very good, some feel a little stronger than others but since the game relies so much on being able to play the champion its usually down to the player rather than balance.
Whilst this game is early access and I am sure these issues will be fixed with age, I cannot help but judge the game as if it were a full release because of how polished it feels.
I would give this game a 8.5/10 in its current state. Some may feel that is a little high but I really feel like this game has done something interesting and well. It definitely has potential and is worth the money.

This game makes me feel like I was inside the dreams of a weird engineer/architect. It is great how it can give you so much with so bare materials. You walk around huge constructions, trying to make sense of it. And then you realize you are the life inside these dead empty endless halls.
Kairo begins with a throne in the middle of nowhere. You're alone, there's nothing. But "nothing" becomes something tangible, you begin to think about nothingness. You enter this nothingness, this void, and find many things there. Things buried, forgotten. Other thrones, kings, or perhaps other times of the same reign. But you are the king of a dead and empty realm. Are you alone. There is a world out there and you do not have access to it. There is life, and all you see are images, codes, machines, mementos.
Could the machines drive you back to life? Where does this light leads? Where does this flow leads? Where will you go? Who built it? For what purpose? Where are you really? Maybe in a hospital bed, waiting to wake up. I enjoyed every minute of this trip. I did not understand almost anything, but what I did was enough to make the trip worthwhile.
This game is about second chances. You move from a lifeless place to a garden with flowing life. It is really about coming back to life, so it is another game that helped me recover. It is amazing how this message is there without the need of any word. It is a memorable experience.
Positive points
* A very trippy and weird experience.
* Logical puzzles that you solve without any instruction.
Negative points
* Very easy to get lost.
* Looks empty and random.
* The above are all part of the experience...

POSITIVES:
~~~~~~~~~
You can build anything from a tiny little drone to a massive bohemoth that annihilates everything in its path... a little outpost through to a monstrous city station.
Your creations can have jump drives, jump drive inhibitors, several different types of weapons which can be customised for different effects (punch, pierce, explosion, etc), different colours, rate of fire, range, etc by connecting them in different ways.
Your creations can fly, they can mine, they can repair, they can destroy, or any combination.
Drones, fighters, bombers, corvettes, destroyers, carriers, battleships, alien creatures, force fields, seriously this game gives you a massive choice of toys to build and play with.
Role Play / PVP / combo suitable
Great community
Game constantly evolving and changing and improving.
Almost every part of it is fully customisable - you can even create your own set of blocks and textures with unique behaviours and crafting ingredients and resource trees.  It's not easy to customise some of the features, but it is possible to customise pretty much everything, and most of it is super easy to edit.
NEGATIVES:
~~~~~~~~~
Block based.  Seriously blocky.  They're bringing in LOD blocks that break this up a lot, but it's still seriously blocks blocks blocks.
Bugs galore, but to be fair the devs put a great deal of effort into squashing them, and they're doing an outstanding job of it.
Physics are limited.  For example if you blow a hole in the middle of a structure both separate bits are still part of the same object and will spin together as though they were attached.  It's not a big deal but it does destroy the realism of it.  Also space friction.  Uggh.  I think that can be adjusted in server settings like most things, though.
Missiles are points, not objects.  But you can make actual torpedo objects that fire and explode on impact (but they're basically ship entities by themselves).
Explosive warhead blocks need serious buffing to be effective.
Very Memory and CPU intensive.  Optimisation needs a lot of work.
Unrealistic resources.  Forget gold, carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen.  Bring on a bunch of random♥♥♥♥♥resources that you need to remember in order to gather for your desired crafting goods.
OVERALL:
~~~~~~~~~
This game is tidy.  It has a lot of freedom to build what you want without the clunkiness of similar games like Space Engineers.  It does however have a less refined finish especially on a smaller scale, and is a real RAM and CPU gobbler.  Don't even bother unless you have an above-average computer.
The devs are keenly focussed on improvements and bug fixing, and the game is in a constant state of improvement, giving it a constant supply of new parts to play with.
If you like space building sand boxes this is one of the giants.  Enjoy responsibly.

It's no Magic: The Gathering, but Infinity Wars is a solid, free-to-play digital TCG. Being digital does allow Infinity Wars to do some pretty cool things that aren't possible with physical TCG's - like simultaneous turns and actively creating cards during gameplay. The simultaneous turn system adds an interesting, poker-esqe level of strategy. It allows you to guess, or force, your opponent's moves rather than simply react to them. There are several factions from which to build decks, but each faction seems so lazer-focused on a single mechanic that there is little room for building a "unique" deck. This will probably improve as cards are added over time, and it doesn't keep the game from being fun in the meantime.

More of a sequel to Hard Reset than Shadow Warrior, and it's all good.
People who played Hard Reset might remember that the basic abilities you started with were stale, but by the end of the game you'd have expanded your arsenal to a wide variety of unique weaponry. Shadow Warrior wisely starts Lo Wang out with just about everything the player needs to have fun from the word GO and brings back the odd blend of monster kiting so that you can blow up environmental hazards, like cars, explosive barrels or electrified objects, to create a cascade of explosions and bloody chunks.
Lo Wang is a big idiot, but that's what makes him fun. The dialogue is surprisingly casual and made me laugh plenty of times in the midst of the demonic invasion. The voice acting is great and his cluelessness and comic book fantasies are both endearing and hilarious. The end of the story took a tonal one-eighty that was too heavy handed after the casually kitchy tone, but it sure beat the utter cliffhanger that Hard Reset ended on and resolved the story of the vengeful spirit and constant companion, Hoji, and Lo Wang.
Probably my favorite bits of dialogue were the set of whiny, pained lines tied to taking too much damage... A constant reminder that Lo Wang is still comedically human despite becoming his own original character.
The game still has some similar UI pitfalls retained from Hard Reset by allowing the player to craft their game into a boring one... A quick recap on Hard Reset: You started out with practically nothing, and you were presented with an upgrade tree that could route the player into using very boring weaponry for a very long time if they didn't experiment with unlocking alternate-fire-modes that vastly changed the behavior of the weapons.
There's an unintuitive paradox between picking what I think are important passives, and the immediate reward of unlocking the ability to use all the Sword Arts and Ki Powers. For example, FIND MORE MONEY is critical to feeding into your ability to unlock more fun weapon upgrades... Especially their ALTERNATE FIRE, which is tantamount to unlocking a new basic ability... Otherwise, you're left with a passively powered-up toolset that would probably get stale.
All in all though, it's a fun game that has some odd quirks (Lo Wang can't swim, some checkpoints are poorly placed later in the game, and dashing off of a ledge can apply deadly fall damage).

I haven't beaten this game yet, although I can feel the end drawing near. From my experience so far though, this is easily one of the best metroidvania games I have ever played. The action is tight and controlled, with a slow progression curve that grants ample time to master each new ability. Unlike a lot of games in this genre, the Charms system offers a lot of room to customize how you want to play. Want to kite enemies with enhanced mobility and a long blade? Or tank hits with a berserker riposte? Or AOE blast enemies with shamanically enhanced magic? All options, building on the same simple combat system. The game can definitely be difficult, with demanding bosses and hordes of enemies, but keeping calm and reacting with experience is always enough to win a fight. Dying isn't even more than a minor inconvenience (usually), especially if you're willing to pay the price to auto-restore your shade.
The game doesn't really guard any of its secrets behind unreasonable, wiki-mandatory veils. It just asks that you pay attention and be inquisitive. That being said, I am positive I've missed stuff because there's hardly a room or hallway without something to pay attention to.
It's just a really solid action/discovery platformer, with a compelling story and beautiful art. I bought it on a whim, but it's probably one of my favorite games in my library.

Technobabylon has an amazing narrative setting and will impress you with its very down-to-earth take on cyberpunk philosophy, technology and social themes. On the other hand, the game itself is only average for a point-and-click adventure. Fortunately, it lets its narrative parts shine through it.
Being a cyberpunk fan, I bought Technobabylon hoping to experience a good cyberpunk story, and in that regard, I was more than satisfied. The game's strongest point is definitely how clever, well thought out and realistic its narrative setting is. Throughout my experience, I kept thinking that if I was transported 50-100 years in the future, I'd be hearing about exactly these issues on the news. I particularly enjoyed how social issues and ethical decisions in technology are at the forefront of this story, in a way that is completely believable. This game is definitely a love letter to the cyberpunk genre by someone who has reflected a lot on it, and that person has my warm thanks for it.
As a game however, Technobabylon has its share of drawbacks.
In terms of atmosphere, the art is not so appealing, although the portraits during conversations are really nice. The overall art direction is functional and supports the theme. Voice acting is ok. Music fits, but is not inspiring.
The story is really great, but would be more appropriate for a book/movie. I find it loses some of its luster here because it's really convoluted. It showcases multiple protagonists, antagonists and secondary characters, goes back and forth between past and present, and jumps from one character's perspective to the next all the time. This could have worked very well if it had been delivered more gradually, but because this story only coalesces at the very end, you spend 80% of the game quite confused by it.
And this is made especially a problem because of the difficulty of the puzzles. They are not difficult in the sense of requiring great intellectual feats to solve, but rather in the sense of "how on earth did they want me to guess I should do this sequence of things to reach this scene's not-even clearly stated objective". Granted, I consider myself a casual in terms of point-and-click adventures, in the sense that I want the story to unfold with a good flow and the puzzles to be easy and intuitive. This is how I generally felt with Gemini Rue for example, another cyberpunk point-and-click published by Wadjet Eye. But here, in every single scene, I found myself stuck, not knowing how to advance to the next part. I had to make generous use of a walkthrough to move through the game. After reading the solutions, I often found that there was no way I could have thought about doing that, and so it reduced greatly my enjoyment and desire to even try in the next scene. The other downside of this difficulty was that all of my brainpower went into trying to solve puzzles, which made it much harder to focus on the strengths of this game: it's atmosphere and story.
To conclude, if you are a fan of cyberpunk stories, you should definitely try this game; you'll be greatly rewarded narratively for it, especially if you don't mind using a walkthrough. If you don't care for cyberpunk and are primarily a point-and-click adventure fan, there are definitely better games out there for you. I guess hardcore point-and-click fans who love difficult puzzles might enjoy it.
Thanks, Technocrat Games, for a great story!

Technobabylon is one of these games that I bought on sales and let in my library for weeks, asking myself if I will ever play it. I finally did, and it was one of my greatest experience in point-and-click.
The one thing that makes this game GREAT is the vision of future it embraces. It isn't yet another utopia/distopia, it's a blending of plausible, mature extrapolations of nowaday's tendencies in technology and social life. You will find many things to think about, dream or fear about, in this game's vision of our future. News and secondary characters strongly participate in creating this wonderful atmosphere.
This game acted on me like a wonderful book, when you appropriate the author's universe and make it your own, thinking about it for the rest of the day, talking about it with collegues, friends and family. If you like science fiction, you'll LOVE Technobabylon.
One more thing: beyond the incredible story and atmosphere, the point'n'click mechanics are great, and the puzzles are always logical. You don't find solutions by trying - like - the potato on the ceiling, you know what I mean, point'n'click players! And it is very well balanced. Go play it now, the developers deserve it :)

Set in the future, humanity has been wiped out by nuclear warfare. The undead remained, who rebuilt civilization. All was well until evil invaded the lands. You assume the role of Dem, a skeleton hero and silent protagonist. Dem meets Sara, a historian and mind reader who forces her adventure on Dem to uncover the secrets of the past. Join Dem and Sara on their journey as they meet new friends and combat evil foes along the way.
This is your standard turn-based RPG gameplay. There's really not much else to comment on. You roam around, a random encounter happens and battle ensues. You can use your basic attack, a more advanced “Tech” attack, magic and even use double team or “Unite” moves with someone in your party. As you advance in the game, meet new party members and acquire better weapons and armor. You'll also level up and learn new attacks. This game breaks the fourth wall constantly. You won't have to question what type of game you're playing. It will be sure to let you know that you're playing a turn-based RPG with it's constant references to the typical happenings of these types of games. That's one thing I loved about this game. It adds comedic relief to an otherwise serious genre. I mentioned that Dem is a silent protagonist. He doesn't verbally communicate, but the game allows you to read his thoughts. Sara is also able to read his mind so there is still communication, which adds to the light-hearted narrative.
Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of turn-based RPGs or is trying to get into them. This is a tribute and love letter to the classic JRPGs of the past. The gameplay is fun, the story keeps you interested and it's use of satire gives it charm. It's a short game, but for the price, I can't really complain.

SUPER IMPOSSIBLE ROAD is an intersting take on the infinite marble track survival game. The concept itself isn't new, I have a very similar game on my tablet that I bought for $2, but it's a fresh and genuine take on the formula.
First off, I can tell that this is either the devlopers first ever game, or he is still in school and has used his knowledge to make this game, that being said, this shouldn't be taken as a bad thing, as one can see a well excecuted first attempt.
Some pros and cons of the game are:
Pros:
Interesting take on an existing fromula, with some interesting innovations
Mechanics are solid and in-game controls feel robust and well managed
Challenging without being fustrating
Lovely asthetic and and visual appeal, even if it still needs some polish
Excellent and enjoyable soundtrack.
Haven't encountered any game breaking bugs or glitches so far
Cons:
The biggest issue with this game is the lack of content, not nearly enough to justify the $14 asking for this game. (The game is in early acess though, so take it with a grain of salt)
Menu navigation is a bit clunky and some of the normal menu controls aren't the same here (For instance, Space is select instead of enter)
The game is lacking polish in areas. The game's opening window/configurator commonly seen with Unity games is lacking a cover screen, control remapper, or graphics presets (Although most users won't nesecarily see this window, it does seem a little off that the game has leftit baren when most other games fill it with something)
The tracks for the levels seem almost untextured, definately more room for smaller details and variance in level design.
Level design needs more work/variance. While the game is challenging without being fustrating, you soon find yourself hitting the difficulty celeing fairly quickly. The infinite survival mode soon becomes predictable and survival becomes less about difficulty and more about not making mistakes.
Keep in mind that his game is still in early acess, and will no doubt improve immensly with future updates. The game is fun and challenging, while providing an innovative take on this style of game. It's enjoyable enough to stay in my library and I eagerly wait to see what lies ahead for this game.

With the BE expansion pack coming out soon, I thought it was finally time to update my review.
I'll start with the good: CIV BE plays on the classic Civilization formula. If you have played and enjoyed a CIV game, and aren't expecting some kind of revolutionary new gameplay, you may be satisfied with BE. Kudos to Firaxis for putting together an excellent User Interface, not-too-obnoxious tutorials, and a very playable experience.
Firaxis has also supported the modding community, and thanks to the effort of modders, this game kept my interest longer than it could have in the "vanilla" version. Thanks to everyone who helped with unofficial patches & adding onto the base game.
That said, there isn't much new to be had in CIV BE. The affinity system works much like religions/wonders in other CIV-style games.
I was disappointed with how long it took to fix the launch bugs with BE. First and foremost, users with 120hz/144hz monitors were locked into low resolutions (720p). The official word was that, since this was a minority of users, the issue wasn't a priority. I'm happy to say that the issue seems to be fixed today, but for the three months I played, all of that time was spent at a lower resolution and so I can't endorse the graphics of BE.
Graphics aside, gameplay is pretty "meh." If you've played a Civ-style game you have played BE. The affinities are nice, but they are basically the only way to customize units. I would have preferred more in-depth options to specialize my military.
The quest system is interesting until you realize that most quests are simply A/B choices - and the majority of those have only one right answer. Would you rather have 1 extra trade route at every city forever, or +1 energy from each trade route? Don't worry, the answer will be pretty obvious by the time you start. Unfortunately, the AI will cripple itself by making the bad choices in some quests.
Units are somewhat bland. Firaxis didn't bother reskinning the units, so each player's armies look identical. Flags next to the unit names are used for identification, but since factions share similar flag icons/colors, scanning through the map could be a pain (Which faction had a star in the flag? Oh right - all of them). Some useful mods will change soldiers' shirt colors so you can tell at a glance who is who.
What I found most disappointing really, was the diplomacy system. All factions share the same dialogue and, based on affiinity, the same strategy. Three affiinities, three playstales, one personality.
Verdict: CIV BE has the personality of a cardboard cutout. The addition of Quests/Affinities can't substitute for real innovation. If you MUST play CIV in space, there are better alternatives. I could reccomend this game at around $10 - 15 USD price point.
Some alternatives to try:
Warlock I or II: A fantasy-based CIV clone with a much gentler price point and lots more to do with the military/research(spells). Warlock games also lack in-depth diplomacy systems, but make good with much more interesting battles. Warlock I in particular is a great bargain, as it is not too terribly different from II.
Endless Legend: Another fantasy-based strategy game, but breaks the mold a little from Civilization titles. Possibly the best strategy game out there right now, and polar opposite of BE: customization galore, interesting quests/objectives, bursting with character. Professional reviews and multiple GOTY awards say more for EL than I ever could. As a nice touch, EL gets frequent updates/bugfixes.
Endless Space: The debut game from Amplitude, creators of Endless Legend. If a sci-fi setting is your thing, can't go wrong. Endless space is set on a galactic scale, so you are doing away with traditional hexes altogether. Despite this, lovers of the 4X strategy formula will be quite at home with an experience that is both in-depth and easy to learn. The only draw-back for me is that the AI goes off the handle and has a tendency to "cheat" in higher difficulties. Look out for Endless Space II coming out possibly in 2016.

As someone who was turned off by playing the original Shadow Warrior, this completely took me by surprise. One of the few instances where a reboot is better than the original, both in gameplay, level design, writing, and voice acting.
You play as Wang, a cocky, loudmouth mercenary hired by Orochizilla, a multibillionair that owns everything. He's tasked with buying an ancient sword that is said to be able to vanquish demons. However, the deal goes sour when the seller refuses to sell to him, and gets even worse when the demons start invading and steal the sword. With the help of a ancient spirit that will go unnamed in this review, Wang must recover the sword and save the world.
Writing in this game consist of well written casual racism that can be easily looked over because it's hilarious. Wang always has something funny to say, and your spiritual companion offers witty dialouge to clash with Wang.
Gameplay is some of the best I've encountered in a fps in recent years. Along with your guns, you have supernatual powers thanks to your spiritual companion. You have multiple ways to combo your enemies, said enemies are different and offer interesting challenges, and you have to look for and conserve supplies to upgrade your weapons and take on the bigger baddies. One thing I like about this game is that it had actual boss fights, something you don't normally see in FPS games. I'm a sucker for good boss fights, so that's a plus.
Preformance is also a huge plus. On my budget hardware pc, I was able to get a constant 60 fps on high settings. Props to the programmers.
Overall, I recommend this game if you want to have a good time. I got this game for $5, but I feel like I should have paid $15. Get this game if you can.

The Swindle has a fantastic idea -- work your way up through randomly generated heists, starting from the slums and working your way up to banks -- and surrounds it with creative visuals and gameplay, but some occasional frustrations with design and mechanics do tarnish the experience somewhat.
First, the good: the art style is fantastic. Every new robot sentry brings a creative touch that is always tied to how it functions in relation to gameplay, whether it's the huntsman-looking sniper or the sherriff bot wielding a six-shooter. I also enjoyed the variety of upgrades that the game offers to you; while there are a few essential upgrades early on, for the rest of the game every single path felt viable. I never felt like any of the upgrades I chose were a complete waste, but I ALWAYS had my eye on an ability or trait that was just out of my reach. If only I had a triple jump...or just one more bomb...or a longer range on my remote detonator. This, along with the 100-day limit, keeps the game moving and gives you an incentive to progress.
And that brings me to what seems to be the most controversial element to this game: the 100-day limit. Each heist, successful or not, ticks off a day from the countdown until you have to complete the final swindle. And if you hit zero? That's it. You have to start from the VERY beginning. The restrictions on the final mission are similarly harsh: if you fail, you have to raise the exorbitant starting fee ($400,000) all over again with your remaining days. While I understand these decisions from a design perspective -- giving the player unlimited time would undermine much of what goes right about this game -- softening the blow might have been a good idea. Surely there are ways to not force a player to start completely over without losing the high-stakes tension of a countdown. It's especially painful since the early heists are a slog once you have to do them again, earning menial cash to buy back dozens of lost upgrades.
Now, that said, I still recommend this game so long as you know what you're getting into. If you can get over that hump -- the ever-looming knowledge that you may have to start completely from scratch even after completing/failing 100 missions -- there's an extremely rewarding experience here. Just be prepared to take your lumps.

Does the phrase "procedurally generated steampunk heist" pique your interest at all? Then I seriously recommend you give this game a try. You should know what you're getting into; The Swindle doesn't hold your hand at all and expects you to lean through trial and error. Mostly error. You will die a ton at the beginning, and probably every time you come across a new enemy type, and definitely whenever you get overconfident or greedy. That said, it is really rewarding to pull off a heist perfectly, or to escape by the skin of your teeth after you screw everything up. Either way, there is an incredible tension and a wonderful balance between reward and failure.
If you tried this game out at first and were put off by the rediculous upgrade prices, know that the dev has seriously reduced the costs of the first tier of abilities so you can buy the double jump and other basic tools after just a few hiests. It's a huge improvement in my book.
The art and music are just fantastic. I love the design and feel of the world, and the soundtrack just ratchets up the tension. The music transition when you are spotted is excellent and makes the mad scramble to get out in time all the more heat-pounding.
That said, this isn't a perfect game. The controls could be tighter, and sometimes that will kill you. Usually deaths feel fair, but occasionally your theif will do something you did not intend at all. The procedual generation also leads to impossible situations or impassable obstacles from time to time, but most of these could be overcome with the right upgrades. Neither of these complaints are game-breaking, and honestly I see them as part of the game's punishing charm. Part of improving is learning when a room is just not do-able and getting out while you still can.
Finally, from what I've seen this game comes from a great dev that deserves your support. I reached out to him with a minor bug and he got back to me within minutes to suggest possible fixes. He's already updated the game four times since release, including those upgrade tweaks, and seems to listen closely to feedback.
With all this in mind, I highly recommend The Swindle. It can be incredibly frustrating at times, but it is the kind of frustration that compells you to try just one more heist. This time you won't mess up. This time you'll be patient and careful and get the payout you need. This time you'll - oh god, there's fall damage and you £20,000. Oh well, just one more go. This time you won't mess up...

I mostly see people who aren't part of the minority groups at hand talking about this, and honestly, the only way you could make any kind of insightful critisism of a minority character is if you ARE that minority. I know we all like to think that we can think through every puzzle in the world whether it's race or gender, but I've had to learn over a long time that it's definitely not as simple as just thinking objectively.
As a white person in New Zealand, I do all I can to advocate against racial violence, because I'm never going to experience having my rights as a white person being subtly exploited on a grand scale, via laws implemented by other white people back when you could sell human beings.
Any opinion I have on Lao's writing or characterisation as an East Asian character are never going to be as good or in depth as those of any given Asian person, because I just don't know what it's like to be Asian. Even just under the general title of 'transgender' I'm sure you can hear a million different feelings and interpretations on Max Lao, from people with massively different experiences and perspectives. With this in mind, that's why I roll my eyes when I see people who aren't transgender talking smack about the presence of trans characters in media. If you want to help keep damaging or stupid characterisations out of games, any of the people writing those reviews will probably give you lots of stuff to look out for (see: the trope of being outed against one's will).
WITH THAT BEING SAID. I loved Lao. I love how her backstory is revealed, I love how she is the one who CHOOSES to reveal it to Charlie on her own terms, and I love how for once I got to play a game that doesn't decide to have a protagonist who can probe the trans character with invasive or demeaning questions *cough Dragon Age Inquisition cough*. Obviously those interactions have their place, but Jesus, we get it already. There are more interesting conversations to see about a character being trans than just that. The world will not suffer for having one less game where a character gets interrogated on why she chose to be a girl.
As anyone who's still reading has probably guessed at this point, I'm transgender myself, but I don't know what it's like to be raised as a boy and then try and carve my way from there. It's a hugely different experience and there is a lot to Lao that I honestly can't really say whether it's done right or not, I just wouldn't know.
And I mean even aside from all this, it's really a pretty miniscule plot point, so I don't know if I missed anything but there's not really a whole lot of room FOR a problem. This makes it seem like it was a humungous part of the game and it really wasn't, as with a lot of other minority appearances, re: the interracial gay couples I've seen someone get massively upset over. As well as a robot that they claimed to be gay, with no supporting evidence. But that's none of my business.
There's not really much I can say about the other minority appearances in this game, other than 'they were there'. It would've been a really cool opportunity to have a disabled character that wasn't a villain, but again, I don't really know much more about that - maybe we'll see that in the next installment from these guys!

Technobabylon looks very polished for the engine it was made in. The visuals are the first thing that draws my eye. It's futuristic landscape and location both in the physical world and virtual are incredibly eye catching. In this adventure you play a detective on the trail of a serial killer and a net junky who has been suffering a series of unfortunate events if you will.
Starting off you aren't exactly sure how these two character's stories seem to connect and that's an underlying mystery as they both have missions of their own, crossing but for the most part independent of one another. The story itself while is not hard to follow does have a lot of science and a bit of technical jargon mixed in but nothing too hard to follow. Each chapter is great at giving you a piece of the bigger picture without completely confusing the player and I appreciated when I got to experience past events that helped explain our main detective's state of mind. This all leads to a natural progressions of things and events that come together so smoothly. When you have that "aha" moment it just fits and everything makes sense.
As with most adventure games you have your fair share of puzzles. The beginning is where I was most frustrated because it confused me how I would take a physical object into the internet realm but after that initial segment puzzles were a bit easier. They required a bit of thinking. A lot of moving my mouse over random stuff to see if I could click it and a lot of paying attention to my surroundings and conversations. There's various puzzles in each chapter and usually you're putting your detective skills to good use. I found the final set of puzzles particularly clever and fun to figure out because you had to utilize all 3 characters to solve it.
This game by far has the best representation of online interactions, even a torturous little mini-game by the name of Gravball, which happens to be human Pong. I must have spent the better part of half an hour trying to beat the computer legit. Even with the game being linear I never felt like I was stuck in an area for too long. Things never got stale or boring. It's rare that an adventure can keep my interests straight through. And I didn't think it suffered any of the pitfalls that other games seem to possess.
So in short you've got a beautiful, fast paced game with intelligent varied puzzles. Decent voice acting and music which never gets stale. I think Technobabylon is one of Wadjet Eye's better games and if you're a fan of futuristic, science-y detective games then you should definitely put this one on your "to play" list.

As almost everyone has noted, the game overall is fantastic; there are a surprising amount of negative reviews, however, almost all centered on the supposedly clunky and unreliable controls. This, to me, is like complaining about Dark Souls because you can't cancel any moves. If it were easier to walljump up from under a ledge, or take a flying leap over spikes to hit a guard before he turns around, or fire your EMP at just the right moment as you crash down on top of a sea of baddies, then this would not be the game it is, and I, for one, think it would be far worse. Likewise, if failing to perfectly execute such complex moves didn't have such dire consequences, it would not be the game it is. If the controls made no sense - like, if they were inconsistent, or it wasn't possible to learn the timing given the animations - then I could understand the hate, but I guess a lot of people just didn't know what kind of a game they were getting. My prediction is that a lot of the people who are leaving negative reviews are gonna return to the game, get used to it, get better at it, and love it like they should.

First of all: The Swindle is a
game to play, a truly well done combination of stealth and platforming within a rogue-like mechanic. And don't worry if you are, like me, not a big fan of hardcore stealth games: this one has exacly the right amount of stealth so that you cannot easily rush through levels but you don't have to be planning each move for ten minutes either.
As a steampunk crook, you have a hundred days of heists to prepare for the big one. Through these 100 days, you will, ahem, "earn" money from every (procedurally generated) house you visit, and then use it to buy upgrades that will make you much better at your job. Those upgrades range from athletic ones, like double or triple jumps, to gadgets like bombs or bugs to help you steal more money, to ones that make the police take more time to appear when you set off an alarm during a heist. Which you will do, like, millions of times.
And yes, you will get caught. And you will die. A LOT. And you will curse at everything around you. And then you'll say to yourself "okay, just one more heist". And twenty heists later you will still be there, telling yourself that it will be just one more, and still playing. Remember Spelunky? Well, yes, that.
The graphics, the music, the whole ambientation of the game are just fantastic, and add up to the great feeling of immersion The Swindle has.
Don't be scared of reviews mentioning that controls are bad: even if that might have been the case for some people on the release date version of the game, sucessive patches have made them much better. In fact, the tweaks that are being added little by little by Dan Marshall on every patch are making the game even better and more fun to play while making the learning curve much gentler for first-time players.
So, long story short:

Well made. Controls tight. Looks and sounds great. Can get pretty hard, but almost never unfairly so. Has a bunch of bugs. Some of them really adorable, only couple not of the creature kind.
Dark Souls-esque metrodivinia where from Dark Souls it takes it's story telling (and bit of the story as well).
