Being (or at least drawing heavily from depending on your interpretation) a roguelike does mean you will die. You'll be beaten by guards, you'll be shocked by generators, you'll set off alarms and be crushed by the security shutters and you'll misjudge distance and fall off the roof.
The combination of procedurally generated levels and difficulty scaling (though new areas and new enemies) really comes together in making you use the most of your skills and tools. With your increasing income from successful heists you get access to more powerful tools to increase your options in facing the more secure venues.
The tools and upgrades themselves are all useful, from remotely detonating mines from a safe distance to being shrouded in steam for several seconds to evade a patrolling steambot. There are a lot of different enemies in the game and with each new area you unlock you'll find a large amount of new enemies that ensure you have to adapt your playstyle to get all that sweet cash.
Lastly the art and atmosphere is really pretty with each area having a distinctive style, not to mention all the little touches like when the grime and moisture effects on the screen (that thankfully don't go too far and obstruct your vision).

Minus points.

Online games are hard to find without DLC.
Plenty of online servers are empty.
Overall, this game is great fun.
I would recommend downloading the barebones version to start with, if you enjoy the couple of free cars and tracks then it's well worth considering buying some DLC.

This game seems to confuse "challenging" with "cruel". It presents you with obstacles and challenges that require specific gear to overcome (gear which you probably won't have when you first encounter them), never tells you how exactly you screwed up, and on top of that includes a ticking clock mechanic that as of my fifth attempt at the campaign has made it impossible to win the game proper.
On top of that, your thief's lack of a health bar makes it impossible to track damage-over-time things, or things that I believe are damage-over-time things as shortly after they happen my thief will drop dead for no reason at all.
And now the Top 5 Reasons Why You and I Died in The Swindle:
5) Miscalculated how long that drop was and fell to your death.
4) The police hovercraft dropped in and deus ex machinegunned your sorry♥♥♥♥♥
3) Miscalculated how far a jump would take you and subsequently got spotted and clubbed to death (meaning hit once).
2) Some enemy feature which you were not aware would result in your death resulted in your death.
1) Elroy Blues' word for "lies" when discussing them with his brother Jake (see "The Blues Brothers" for details; great flick).
I kid you not, this game keeps inventing new and creative ways to royally screw you over, from blowing up a security console that you thought your bomb was far enough from to not touch, to putting enemies with ridiculous lines of sight on a single block so they keep going back and forth with no way to effectively deal with them, to enemies killing you when you swung first at point-blank. The game's lack of tutorial on the controls and enemies means that you'll also encounter many, MANY things that will take two or three deaths for you to fully figure out how they work, and since the game only gives you 100 heists to make money from before Game Over, those are deaths you cannot afford to have happen to you. I'd think that as the Master Thief that you are (as declared by the opening text) you would've done your homework on these kinds of things so at least you'd go in knowing what you're up against.
But you don't. This game takes a lot of bad cues from Dark Souls 2, from the ticking clock ultimatum to the lack of any significant amount of health to the heavy penalization for dying when dying is the only way you can effectively gauge what enemies do and how they can kill you. If any one of these issues were addressed, particularly the latter two, I would probably enjoy the game a lot more. As such, I can't recommend it.

A legit, comedic 16-bit era RPG with most of the garbage cut out.  Breath of Death VII knows and loves RPGs of yesteryear, and seems to have learned from mistakes of the past and delivered a breezy, straight forward, but still satisfying adventure.  Everything from the snappy (and eventually skippable/fight-on-demand) turn based combat to the ability to save anywhere makes progress relatively painless.  Humor permates throughout, and even with a few references and self aware jabs it thankfully avoids being juvenile or overly meme-y.  That doesn't undercut the staples of the genre, either: battles can be difficult unless you (quickly) do some grinding and there's a learning curve to the characters' abilities and roles.  Nothing seems insurmountable or overwhelming or cryptic; it's just a good time all around.  My only complaint is the envirnoments can be overly maze-like in same-y looking areas (the last level in particular), but that's just a matter of puzzling out the lay of the land or grabbing some graph paper if you're crazy.  Other than that I highly recommend Breath of Death if you're the least bit curious of old school console RPGs.  It's not going to steal your money or time, and will most likely put a smile on your face.

I only play this game 4player-splitscreen and it really surprised us! It is totally addictive, and you only need a few rounds to get the hang of it. Yes, it is basically a racing game, but we realized that the racing game fans in our group did not have a huge advantage, which is good. Actually, everyone of us won some rounds and that's got to do with some key features:
First, all tracks are random generated, which is necessary for this game, since you can't lean any track. Second, the idea is to take shortcuts wherever you can, because it is much faster than to stay on the road. This is a concept of risk an reward... sometimes you are 4th and go for it, make that awesome huge shortcut just before your screen fades and are back in the picture. On the other hand you can be first and afraid of losing time risking a shortcut and not making it to the road again... so the game balances itself. Sure, you get a good feeling for where to take shortcuts and get better doing it, but since the tracks are always random generated, everbody has good rounds as well as bad rounds where nothing you try seems to  work.
The current content is enough to enjoy maybe half an hour to an hour at a time and to keep us coming back. I really would like to see more parts to customize your ball, maybe some additional environment. It's still early access, though, so there might be coming more.
At least - and I can't say that for a lot of EAccess titles - this game looks awesome and gameplay is polished and flawless. I think it is a really addictive and fun 4-player game, especially as we didn't expect it to be that good!

Well, I suspect this review will be building over time.  I started with Battlerite (BR) a long, long time ago.  With a game called Bloodline Champions.   It never quite 'made' it, and wasn't even on Steam for the most abyssmal longest time.  The game went through so many iterations and ended with a strangely game breaking level and traits system.  Well, ended in terms of casual players.  For many years dedicated fans would continue to play knowing that BLC had something unique and unreproducable.  Especially a feeling you would get when a fight was real, and your heart is beating so fast because it is you vs that one other person.  You will know what I am talking about if you play this game.  We play this game because it challenges us like no other game can.
Now the first thing you need to know is that it is a top down mouse and keyboard fighting game.  It is primarily based on skill shots and timing(?).  What this means is a completely new type of Multiplayer battle that brings to mind, 'WOW Arena' fights in which abilities can change the course of every battle dynamically and in fresh unique ways every single time.
If you approach BR as a fighting game you will understand the premise quickly.  But imagine a fighting game with healers and support characters.  There is a reflecting bubble for projectiles that when used correctly is incredibly satisfying like landing a max hit combo.  Another character has a shield that reflects, which can turn a losing battle into an interesting and inspiring come back, and a heal that links your teams spirit.  Another character shoots a gigantic beam of light that heals your team and damages the enemy.  Each hero has their own signature fighting style.
Also it must be stressed that point and click movement which is predominant in the most popular mobas is very limiting technically.  I respect that skill but it is a huge waste of energy..
The game's artwork is reminiscent of an aztec sort of temple look.  The battlegrounds glow with suffused energy and there is a 'clock' that visually gathers energy as a rune is spawned.
Knowing the skins and cosmetics in BLC I think that they will not disappoint in that department.
In my short summary for now, you should buy this game immediately even in early access.  It is a fully loaded fighting game.  The developers slaved a long time over BLC and it never got the props it deserved.  BR is a great game that needs to be shared by the community simply for the sake of fresh gaming experiences, that we all love and appreciate.
9.5/10 recommended.

Many have describe this game as Minecraft in space. While I respect such an description, I daresay that it is not the most apt way to describe Starmade. Many of the limitations of Minecraft (no such thing as entire structures that can move, a lack of symmetrical building assistance, voxel shape outlining, to name a few) are not present in Starmade, making this game, in effect, superior to Minecraft is many aspects (though subpar in others).
The most alluring aspect of Starmade is the ability to build what you want. If you want to make a small shuttlecraft to simply explore space, that can be a viable option (as long as you stay clear of pirate outposts). If you want to take as much time as you need to build the most massive ship with the best defenses and weapons the game has to offer, that is, not only within the realm of possibility, but highly likely, given enough time and effort. If you want to simply screw other players over by making a one-person faction and claiming systems left and right, then yes. You can be "that guy" on the server. If you want to make a huge space station that can accommedate any size ship and have a shop to make money hand over fist, then go for it, Mr. Ferengi!
I personally love the approach Schine used in building. The ability to place an ENTIRE row, column, or chunk of blocks down in one click makes the ship/station building experience much more enjoyable, as you don't need to spend tedious amounts of time building something, one-block-at-a-mind-numbing-time. The symmetry grid also helps to alleviate the grind of building. I myself use the symmetry grid very often, as it saves time when you are building one side of a station and want the other side to be completely identical.
The block system works out quite well for the game, though there are some flaws with some of the blocks/systems. A few of the blocks have outdated descriptions (shield capaciators, for example), while others have incomplete descriptions (punch-through module block does not state what effect it gives a weapon). Power blocks can be somewhat tricky to use as their benefits are greater when placed in a straight line rather than grouped together in chunks. For some (not all) players, this causes builds to be very long or have awkward shapes. Schine is currently looking into the current power system, and pitched a proposal on a revamp. We will have to see how that plays out.
Which brings me to another point: Schine listens to their players and interacts with the community on a regular basis on their website. They listen to their complaints, compliments, suggestions, etc. and are very professional about it, taking everything in stride.
However, by far, my most favorite feature in Starmade is the blueprint system. After you have spent a week working on that ship of yours, and you have it exactly how you want it to be, you can then save it as a blueprint. Then, take said blueprint, and upload it to the Starmade Dock. There, others can download your ship and use it in their own game/server. They can rate it and suggest to others to get it, as well. But, the fun doesn't stop there. Schine every now and again hold contests for builders, and the winner of the competition can get their build added to the base game, making it so it appears in-game without the need to have the blueprint downloaded (one perfect example is a derelict medical station created by a player that was added to the actual game). And, with the right tools, players have even created 1:1 scale models of famous space ships, such as the Millennium Falcon from Star Wars, or the USS Voyager from Star Trek.
The one thing to keep in mind with Starmade is that it is still Early Access and in alpha testing phase. There WILL be bugs and glitches. There WILL be changes to how some of the blocks work, as well as new ones added and others removed. Change is inevitable. It's the nature of game development.
All in all, Starmade is well worth the price you'll pay. It's still in development, so there will be many more features that will be added, as well as something that will be changed or removed. If you haven't bought the game yet, then do it. If you don't want to buy it, then keep an eye on it, as something may be added that will turn your head and changed your mind.
In Starmade, the stars are not the limit, only your imagination.

I write this review as the game is still in Early Access. I say that not because I plan to go easy on the game or something, just as a heads up to those that will consider buying the game. I've always maintained that "Early Access" is not an excuse for how good or bad a game is. Once you put it on the marketplace, you're fair game... in my opinion.
Super Impossible Road is a racing game. There's really not much to say about racing games in general. You control a ball. You can modify your ball to have the stats that you want it to have but let's be real here, does anyone ever care enough to min-max perfectly? If you do, please send me a message, I need to know what's going on in your head.
The tracks have gates on them which fill up your boost bar. Using boost makes your ball go a little faster (obviously). Where this game differs from other racing games that I've played is that you can jump off the track to "cheat" your way to finish line faster. That's why the game's tagline "Winning is cheating". Now you can't just jump off the track and free fall to the finish line for victory. The game would be too easy in that case. Upon leaving the track, you have five seconds to return to the track. If you fail to touch the track in that time, you will automatically respawn at the last boost gate you touched. Which means that you have to be really careful about deciding when to 'cheat'. Otherwise you may waste up to five seconds. If you see the writing on the wall that you're not going to make it, you can force respawn early.
The tracks can be fairly complex. At this time, while there are only three 'tracks', the tracks are procedurally generated so it's like having an infinite number of tracks? There's also a daily track where you can compete with people across the world for the top score.
The game is aesthetically appealing (to me) with that 'Tron' feel. I'm not the biggest fan of EDM so there's only one or two soundtracks that I like but it definitely matches the feel of the game. Excellent job.
While the game does have multiplayer, it seems it only has local multiplayer. Perhaps they will change that as it is still in early access. You can still have CPU racers and you can even race against your ghost. So it has some rudimentary tools.
Anyway, at the time of writing, the game is priced at $12. While I do like the game for what it does, I don't think it's worth $12 yet. Do it if you want to support the creators but other than that, I'd wait for it to go on sale or something for $5 or $6. I'm not the biggest fan of racing games so I won't dump too many hours into it, but in my opinion, it does look promising.

(I really play a lot of card games..)
But this one is above most of those I played yet.
The game is still in developpement. The menu is not always intuitive. There is often bugs.
But, in my opinion, the game system is amazing.
Each player have a deck of 40 cards and 3 commanders. The commanders are regular creatures but they start in the game. You can use their abilities but you can't use them to fight until you play the on the battlefield like other creatures.
You can put your creatures in three zone: Assault, Defense and Support. The creatures in Assault will fight the creatures in the opponent Defense and deal damage to his fortress if you can. The creatures in Defense will prevent the opponent's creatures in Assault from damaging your fortress. Creatures in Support will be out of combat and protected from some spells.
So, your fortress have 100 health but you also have 100 morale. You lose morale each time one of your creatures dies.
And, each player moves and play spells at the same time. You must anticiapte your opponent moves.
There is many factions in the game and the cards you can play in your deck depend of your commander's factions. Different factions will give you more variety while three commanders from the same faction will give you stronger cards of that faction.
You will soon unlock starter decks for each factions. These decks are obviously weaker than most of the decks you'll see online but they are still very fun to play (at least against AI) because each faction have excellent synergy together.
Even better, each factionis better than somes and weaker than others, like a rock, paper, cissors game but with eight factions.
In my opinion, this game is among the best cards games even if some parts still bug. If you love strategic games, I highly recommend you to try this one!

If you're a myst fan then this will be right up your alley. Stepping out into to the monolithic environments of Kairo is akin to stepping out onto that dock in myst for the first time. Kairo is able to conjur up an atmosphere of loneliness and mystery that really sticks with you the whole game. While basically a walking simulator, there where times that I was simply awestruck by the towering structures and deep shadows the dominate its barren landscape. Aparrently it has oculus support as well, which put this first on the list of things i'm going to play when I finally have the funds to join the VR club. Kairo is also a very decent puzzler, requiring you to pay close attencion to your surroundings in order to peice everything together. While a few of the puzzles can get rather abstract, I never found myself stuck becuase of a handy hint system you can use to cheat if ever need be. For the price you can get it at, this game delivers a unique experience that you won't find anywhere else. I'd highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys atmosphere and immersion, and doesn't mind being stumped by a puzzle from time to time.

I got the game on sale for about 1.00USD$ and I'd say it is worth (or more near) that.
4.99 is too steep for its general quality when compared to games with higher budgets for sale at similar pricepoints.
The trailer may make the game look a little more complex and polished than it really is (especially in regards to graphics, they look way worse in the actual game than what appears in the trailer..) but what is present is a solid top-down shooter. With full controller support, a dodge button, and equipment and skills to unlock, it presents a "full game" for its price. A lack of any kind of camera control (it follows directly above the player) may be irksome to some, and does make the animations appear a bit more stilted than they may need to, but it also keeps the action proceeding simply and smoothly.
You can level up, unlocking skills (higher health / shields / more ammo / higher dmg etc..) and you find and unlock a plethora of guns which are available later for loadout customization. Grenades and medkits add further complexity to the gameplay, however it largely is a "what you see is what you get" kind of game (and its budget is readily apparent..) It has a certain charm if you're a fan of sci fi / alien type scenarios, and the gameplay itself is fun as you survive further levels into the derelict space facility, while fighting off a variety of enemies and bosses.

This PROBABLY could have been a bit more involved, but I'm no designer and have no specific suggestions.  After having my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me by both the Pan-African Union as well as feeding dozens of brave colonists into various alien maws, i can say that the changes and wrinkles are unique enough to make this game worth the price of admission.  The manner in which tech evolves is far more interesting.
Of particular note is the tech web.  Technological growth is no longer linear, but asymmetrical.  It's no longer a race to nukes or gunpowder - my ground troops were overwhelmed by units i couldn't even build, while I brought war to a standstill with atmospheric bombers that the enemy had not even conceived of yet.  While many techs are necessary, you are able to be far more specialized in terms of your mode of advancement and it makes for a much more interesting route to victory.
Some will say that this is a civ 5 reskin.  Their objections are not entirely without merit - the UI and basic theories are more or less xeroxed.  The flavor and the small tweaks, in my opinion though, make for a unique experience.  Get it, play it, love it.

I really wanted to like this game. I absolutely love "artsy" games like this. However, there were several problems that tainted the experience for me.
Puzzles - They are counter-intuitive. While some puzzles make sense and are easy to figure out, others don't. For example, the puzzle at the back of the light house where you step on certain blocks seemed entirely random.
Movement, view, and mouse control - The extremely smooth movement in combination with narrow point of view made me feel sick to my stomach within 10 minutes. The lag between when I moved my mouse in comparison to when the character moved certainly didn't help, but that may have just been caused by my machine.
Broken pause menu - Again, this may have just been my machine, but during the pause menu, there was no way to select any options. I could only exit the pause menu by hitting escape. When I wanted to quit the game, I had to alt-tab and force close it. Being able to access the options may have been able to fix my previous complaint.
Empty textures - Textures and objects seemed empty and incomplete. I know that is the art style this game is going for, but it still seems very unpolished.
Sound - In games like this, sound effects and music need to take advantage of the atmosphere. I found most of the sound effects were cheesy and took away from the experience. For example, the cheap MIDI gong sound whenever you made progress in a puzzle is just awful. A lot of the time, there was too much silence, or just unvarying static, that could have benefited greatly with ambient music. During the few moments that ambient music was present, it seemed immaturely written and distracting.
I think that covers about everything I found poorly done in this game. Luckily, I bought it on sale and obtained a foil card so I have already made my money back. I really do want to enjoy this game and am disappointed that I didn't, since it seems like an interesting idea and I liked the lonely atmosphere. I will try it again if/when there is ever an update to see if any of these issues were fixed.

First, make sure you can play this with a mouse and keyboard. Game controllers are unusable in this game (e.g., the aiming reticle disappears if you're not using a mouse, making aiming effectively impossible).
That said, if played with a mouse and keyboard, this has the potential to be a fun little top-down shooter. The action is fast-paced, the limit of vision based on physical obstacles makes for a bit of "fog of war" effect that keeps things interesting.
Unfortunately, the game is ruined by a really awful "save game" system, where, if you do not end your game on an odd-numbered floor (????), you'll have to start at the last odd-numbered floor - in my case, I ended my game on floor 2, but the game made me start over on floor one. Not only that, the floor I restarted on was significantly more difficult than the first floor 1 I played - significantly above the skill level I had been able to upgrade my character to.

I have to write a review for this game while it's fresh in my mind.  Kairo is every bit as fun and eerie as you would want a 3D puzzle game to be.  Do yourself a favor and play this game alone and uninterrupted for a full immersive feel.  There are no verbal cues - as in you will never have another character speak to you, and you will never hear your own character talk.  There aren't any written cues or instructions beyond symbols you find (and of course the gentle hints in your menu screen, should you need them).  It's all about using the landscape and the machines and puzzles to your advantage - to a visual person like me, this was a wonderful experience.  Each different area in the game has its own color scheme and chosen background music and sounds from one of the game's tracks (the music is great for the game and ranges from "Fairly soothing and enlightening", to "I feel like someone just shoved ice down the back of my shirt").  In terms of graphics, it's not exactly, say, "Skyrim" in terms of detail or texture - but that honestly works well for the game.  The maker of this game knew what he was doing and while it's a little rough around the edges in some regards (I guess) the game is -solid- in the graphics department to me.  It feels like the great machines are actually working next to you.  That you're standing next to sources of great power, or that you're standing next to a row of...  Well you'll see (I really do love the architecture in some parts).  I completed the main storyline and some of the extra content without any help, but admit that I did need some help from the Steam Community to unlock the rest (there is one particular "bonus" puzzle that actually demands that you seek outside help in order to solve it).  Lastly I want to talk about the storyline - There is a lump that forms in the pit of your stomach once you start realizing where this game is going and the gravity of what has already happened and the gravity of what you might actually be doing.  It was mentioned already, but once you're done with the game (as it contains heavy spoilers), check out "The Secret of Kairo" on Electron Dance's blog if you want to read into some good theories behind the game.

Im a big fan of the Civ series and plaid the crap out of Civ5 with my buddies, that being said I was totally stoked to hear about this game and I wasnt disspointed. Sure it was hyped up alot and maybe didnt end up being the BREAKTHRU ZOMG new spin on Civ ever conceived but alot of the new mixed in with the old in my opinion came out with a fresh yet familiar game that I could excited about playing, enjoy the additions and not feel totally lost right out the gate.
So whats the same? Happiness, Gold, Culture are all still things there just named Health, Energy, and... I think culture lol
Trading over Land and Sea is still in the game, Diplomacy works just like Civ5 (Including most of the old dialog which kinda peevs me but I can look past that). Can Still spy on folks with the right tech researched, and a few smaller things that just make the game Familar and easy to jump into.
Some things that have changed: Quests: Researching tech, time elaping, dynamic events, creating buildings, putting points into your Affinty or Virtues all these at least have the ability to drop a quest on ya. They can chain into 4-5 parts in some cases or might just even be a "Build this to get = X" deal. IMO this was a nice touch and really adds flavor to my otherwise bland Civ game experience. Affinity is the new Ideology, letting you pick from basically "Human Supremecy", "Terminator", or "The Na'Vi from Avatar" and shape the way you deal with your new world by either Embracing the Old, the new, or pure symbiosis. Virtues are the new Policy and come in 4 types with 3 tiers each that reward you bonuses based on how many choices you've made per type, per tier and accross all tiers total meaning min/maxing a type has its benefits but mixing it up can make things interesting too without sacrificing bonus's. Your units also can be upgraded via combat as before but also thru your Affinity and change in appearence to reflect such... Going Purity? Your gunna have some shnazzy Tanks and Pwr Armor, Going Harmony? Prepare to watch your dudes ride into battle on a flippin Alien. Beginning Loadouts when starting a new game also give you a feeling of having more of a say with your starting package before planet fall besides the usual "Well, has to be next to a river... need to have that strat resource outright..OK PLANT IT". Finally but certainly not the last of the new stuff just crunched for space.. ALIENS, they be the new barbarians. They have Aggro now meaning you attack them they become aggressive but avoid them long enough and they might forget your there, keep poking the Hornets nest and they will send a Dune worm to your base (No Foolin).
Since its barely a day old theres bound to be glitches or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that will be patched, its also Vanilla as far as this Stand Alone goes so of course there wont be 20 Civs to choose from or stuff like that... Look, Civ5 wasnt what it is now until after Gods and Kings / Brave New World came out and fundamentally changed♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as we know it. So Expect that this game will also see similar changes in the future as it progresses and enjoy the ride! I never give games a perfect score so this one will get an 8/10, if you love Civilization, love turn based strategy, Like SciFi then give this game a try, if your worried about paying this much for a game your unsure of then DONT BUY A GAME JUST CUZ OF THE HYPE: This leads to you being one of a few dozen people worldwide who post bad reviews on this game with a couple hours playtime complaining about how nothings changed, your bored to tears and you wish you didnt buy it. No ones holdin a gun to your head to buy this game, this game type is not for everyone but for those that enjoy it a great deal then I think you wont be dissapointed

I think I oringinally saw this game on one of the Gawker blogs, and the art-style and concept were interesting enough to make me buy it on Steam.
2D gameplay remeniscent of "Mark of the Ninja" but the procedurally generated levels add an interesting twist.  Yes, sometimes the levels are "broken" because you haven't got the skills to open a locked door or make a door with bombs.  Sometimes a level locks one of the money terminals away in a sealed room you have no hope of reaching.  Sometimes enemies are in places that make them impossible to avoid or take care of.  I've definitely had my share of controller-twisting-frustration moments, but part of what makes "The Swindle" fun is that some of those are (maybe) the game's fault, and many of them are obviously my fault: hitting LEFT instead of RIGHT, misjudging a jump into a spike pit, etc.  Failure isn't just "the game is broken," it's frequently "I need to do better," and that's a great way to do gameplay.
A lot of the stuff I would have whined about was recently fixed: the upgrade tree makes it obvious what you can and can't buy at a given moment.  The scrabble move is easier, so a lot of the early levels where you haven't unlocked skills are more navigable.  The first level more consistently gets you enough money to buy the essential hacking skill.  The prices for a lot of the "essential" initial skills/upgrades have been adjusted so you don't get to day 50 before having more than a thousand pounds handy.

Sigh, Technobabylon.  A game that many people call one of the best new adventure games.  It's really not.  It's very nostalgic and a great call back to the adventure games of the past, but that's where it belongs in the past and not now.  First off, this horrendous pixel style needs to stop.  It's bad, real bad.  It looks ugly, trying to copy the pixel graphic style of games older than Kings Quest 5 is just not something I want to see.  I assume some people do, but I have no idea why.  At worst it should have the clean visual style of the Moneky Island remasters games.  I know this studio loves their pixel graphics, but harenking back to the terrible graphics of the past is not the way to go.
You play the game as 3 different characters.  A senior detective on the police force, who is kind of this old curmudgen who hates technology and dislikes the direction the future has taken (also he is from Texas...apparently in the future Texans have no accents).  His partner, a young female detective who is a computer expert and is very much on board with the direction the future has taken and all set to accept her AI overlords.  Finally, a young female hacker, who is addicted to the internet and spends her entire life in the internet...hacking?  Of these three i liked the female detective the most and really just wanted to play the game as her the whole time, which is unfortunate because she probably has the least amount of time in the game.
On the up side this game is far better than Gemini Rue.  The voice acting is better, the puzzles are better, the environments are better.  I really thought the voice actors did a fine job, certainly not the best job, but a fine job.  The puzzles are a lot less pixel hunty than Gemini Rue which is great.  However, the puzzles also aren't very good. They certainly don't take a lot to figure out.  I only found myself stuck on the very last puzzle in the game which involved a wrench and I had to eventually just give up.  I'm pretty confident i would never have figured it out as it required me to do something that I didn't even think was possible.  The rest of the puzzles are mainly easy, because their are very few items in the environment to click on, so most of the time i was just stumbling into solutions without even thinking.
Really, though I can forgive basically anything so long as the story is good, which is also where this game fails the most.
So yea, that's Technobabylon, another mediocre adventure game from the studio dedicated to making classic nostalgia adventure games.  Sigh, I feel if they just embraced the modern developments and story telling techniques games like Life is Strange have made they might be able to accomplish something very special, but instead they like to just lie back and copy what has already been done and like the main character in this game they shall always be stuck in the past.  Still, I enjoyed my time with it, just get it on massive sale, or you know just buy Life is Strange the best adventure game ever made.  So #worth $3

A sci fi point n click adventure straight out of a Gibson novel. I loved every second of it, despite a few puzzle hickups where online walkthroughs had to help me.
Written and directed, created and voiced by only a few, yet on the peek of what can be done in this industry, I would say it´s a masterpiece in it´s own right. Let me further explain why:
- One of the lesser impressive things are the graphics. You can literally count the pixels because of the pixelart. The unique touch in this game´s visual design lies less in its color scheme or art design but more in the story and characters that it has. It´s not the prettiest at all, clearly a reasoning with the creators budget. It keeps true to the atmopshere and visual response etiquette of such games though and delivers all it needs to for what it wants to achieve in order to suck you into the world.
- Didn´t encounter any bugs in playing this roughly for 19 hrs. Completed. Experienced one issue though, audio controls in the options menu don´t control the speech volume which has to be set through windows audio mixer instead. Naggy but alt tab works easily. Everything else just worked as it should. High quality for the few people that worked on it.
- Now here it all comes together into why it´s such a masterfully crafted game. Not only are all characters shaped with unique and likeable or understandable/reasonable personalities and motives but they also all have their own useful role in a complete story with twists and plots/schemes. The theme of the game builds upon that and combines these characters and the well written dialogues and philosophical scaffolding under the sci fi transhumanistic topic it´s made for with such detailed plotting, it blew me away at times. I literally was blown away each anew that characters in a video game could even be written and thought off as such diverse and well build figures. Usage is smart and they clearly preferred having less useless characters but instead craft a lot well done ones into their storyweb together with good humor and cheeky sarcasm. Love it. You could literally fill a whole wikipage just with this game and create an own universe out of it. Genetics, cannibalism, morals, old vs new standards, transhumanism, synths and robots, consciousness and cloning, gengineering, AI and selfawareness, religious terrorism, nuclear fallout and it´s aftermath, VR, organic computing, etc and much more, it´s all in there to feed the sci fi nerds mind. Psychological and emotional drama with decisions. You also can decide from time to time in certain situations how an outcome will play out. Of couse with different endings too. The game has it all and works like a well oiled machine. It even introduced new stuff I didn´t think of before and made me curious like: Wetware and AI splitting. It leaves you thinking after finishing it. And it will always become a conclusive whole. No stupid hidden secrets, no stupid easter egg story details, old school straight up masterwork of writing. It´s pretty mature with gore and darker topics throughout. No children allowed. Thank god.
- Your usual point n click adventure, let´s you think outside the box, combine tools or hack systems with wetware, use CI splitters to swap out modules of personality and memory. Less hammer on nail, but creative stuff where a casual adventurer with no brain for technology will often just trial and error. PnC veterans though will have a smooth and enjoyable non stressful ride. Except for a few situations where the game really was unhelpful in even giving me hints in what to do, I had to get myself some walkthroughs. And those scenes really blew. In total only 3 though. Not much in a game of 10 chapters with 14hrs of gameplay, if you take away my idling and fooding.
Loved every second of it. Get it. ♥♥♥♥ watch dogs, ♥♥♥♥ binary domain,♥♥♥♥♥effect, sci fi is done like this!

This is a good looking 2D game, for sure. I really like the steampunk-meets-Victorian-era-London art direction. There's some CRT scanline effects that are fitting for the overall aesthetic, but not overused. The player protagonist and enemies all look good IMO. My only complaint in the graphics department is the visual arc that's represented in the animation of your melee swing. You don't always hit what your avatar's weapon goes across (if an enemy is above or below you for example), even though visually it looks like you made contact.
A good platformer will make your character's deaths feel like your own fault. The Swindle doesn't feel like that at all. I've died
too many cheap deaths that were caused by a control scheme that's just not up to par for this type of game. I've been spotted by enemies that should never have had a chance to see me not through lack of skill, but because my character didn't move in a way that you would naturally expect him/her to. It's truly frustrating, because this could be a real gem of a game were the controls better. Hopefully the developer(s) can improve upon this aspect of The Swindle. Having only recently discovered the Stronghold series about three years ago, I feel like I am coming to the series as somewhat of a neophyte. Take that as you will. It's true - the games after Stronghold Crusader (now HD) are not very good. Stronghold and Stronghold Crusader are great games, if you can get past the somewhat annoying pathfinding. At times, enemy tactics get a little stale as well. These are problems with the originals, and they remain issues with Crusader II.
With Stronghold Crusader II, the spirit of the first two games really shines through. The added benefit of full '3D' rendering is that it's a bit easier to find a pesky enemy who's slyly hacking away at some random bit of wall. It's also successfully merged the wonderful gameplay and customisability of the original games with its new perspectives. Yes, things are *different* at times. There are fewer units, buildings cannot be placed in the same fashion (i.e. a fletcher will not change its shape when butted up against a wall), and there are arguably fewer construction possibilities overall. However, this does not detract massively from the immense amount of fun the game provides.
The game runs very well on a very modest set-up (this was less the case when it was first released). The Steam Workshop is a great place to find user-created maps, etc. On the whole, it's a really fun game - even better when playing with a friend. What I miss from the originals is the single-player economic campaigns. But, that's why I own the originals. Anyway, grab it on sale and enjoy!

I haven't beaten this game yet, although I can feel the end drawing near. From my experience so far though, this is easily one of the best metroidvania games I have ever played. The action is tight and controlled, with a slow progression curve that grants ample time to master each new ability. Unlike a lot of games in this genre, the Charms system offers a lot of room to customize how you want to play. Want to kite enemies with enhanced mobility and a long blade? Or tank hits with a berserker riposte? Or AOE blast enemies with shamanically enhanced magic? All options, building on the same simple combat system. The game can definitely be difficult, with demanding bosses and hordes of enemies, but keeping calm and reacting with experience is always enough to win a fight. Dying isn't even more than a minor inconvenience (usually), especially if you're willing to pay the price to auto-restore your shade.
The game doesn't really guard any of its secrets behind unreasonable, wiki-mandatory veils. It just asks that you pay attention and be inquisitive. That being said, I am positive I've missed stuff because there's hardly a room or hallway without something to pay attention to.
It's just a really solid action/discovery platformer, with a compelling story and beautiful art. I bought it on a whim, but it's probably one of my favorite games in my library.

Star Made
Star made is a voxel based space shooter/ builder. Essentially it could be described as Minecraft in space. Like Minecraft everything is made of blocks (except some objects witch are shaped like wedges), however unlike Minecraft, structures such as ships and planets have their own gravity, meaning a player standing inside a ship they have built will move with the ship. The game can be purchased on steam here

The “goal” of the game is to mine planets and asteroids, scavenge ship wrecks, and trade with other factions to build up the resources (the blocks) needed to build your own Ships, space stations and bases. Ship building is a particular focus of the game, with the ability to add shield blocks, thruster blocks, gun blocks, and more to improve your ships shield, mobility, offensive capabilities respectively, being a key part of game play, with a focus on balancing the different ship systems for the best ship possible, while still having a ship the looks good inside and out. Building is made easier with the use of advanced build settings, access by hoping into the ships control cube. The advanced build settings allow for placing multiple blocks at a time, and the use of symmetry tools which allow for truly immense builds to be made with relative ease. The control cube is also the means by which the ship can be piloted, much like any vehicle in any other game.
One of the games highlights is the dog fights. Nothing is more thrilling then using the ship you have work so hard on in battle. Firing your custom laser canons at your enemy, watching your shields health slowly tick down with every hit you take, praying to god you have enough shield, before your tracking missiles reload and are ready to fire, wiping out the enemy ship. Then you have the reward of scavenging the blocks from your kill, and adding them to your own ship, allowing you to take down even bigger pray next time.
One of the games draw backs is the lag online. Online playing with friends, taking down ships with real people and having a crew of even a fleet with several human players running around each ship is great. Your friend might be manning a turret on your ship, or flying alongside you in his own. However the servers are currently not up to the task and lot of lag or not being able to connect is common. And single player can become quite dull, as there is less of a sense of competition against bots.
Another drawback to the game is how complicated it is, the building system of adding blocks to change your ships stats is surprisingly sophisticated. Weapons fire in different ways depending on how the blocks are placed together and they can be further modified with other support blocks, rail systems are used for docking ships to ships, and logic systems can be built to allow for complicated automatic systems, and much more. This means no two ships will be the same and will all have entirely unique strengths and weaknesses in combat, such as weak stealth ships or slow moving but heavily armed battle ships, but unfortunately it does mean that the learning curve is very steep for someone wanting to master ship building, and fully understanding how to build a good ship will take tens of hours of both game play and watching tutorials, this complexity understandably can turn a lot of people off the game even though you don’t need that much knowledge to make a basic ship that can fly and shoot. The complexity issue is further compounded by the fact that there are frequent updates changing how things work and rendering old knowledge useless. But on the flip side these updates mean there are always new features keeping the game fresh and fixing bugs.
Ultimately star made is a solid concept of a game that is constantly improving; some people may find the building overly complicated and the game boring as a result. But I personally enjoy the level of uniqueness and customisation this complicated building system allows for. And the satisfaction of walking the corridors of a ship I’ve built, or using it in a high speed dog fight is more than enough to make up for the games current floors in my opinion. I’d give Star Made 7.5 out of 10.

For a free card game, this one's pretty cool.
I just totally dig the animated cards. It's something most digital card games could have, but only few actually seem to do. heh, and effects like having cards with flying ability float... it really breathes that extra bit of life into those card games.
As for the game itself, it's pretty straightforward. There was this youtube tutorial... but I totally skipped it. I'm not fond of video tutorials, rather have a written guide. But neither was necessary, it just takes a few rounds and a test build deck to figure out how things work.
There's also a few tutorial matches you can play to learn the ropes.
Gameplay;
This is a multifaction cardgame; meaning that, much like MtG with their different elements, this game has different factions. And ofcourse each has their own way.
The way you choose your factions is by giving creatures of that faction a commander position. This allows them to be on the table and use abilities, but they're not directly on the battlefield. Some cards seem to need more than one commander and only a max of 3 commanders allowed, so for the really powerful stuff you'll need to choose.
Resources on the other hand are automatically added; rather than needing resource cards, you get incremental RP each turn in the game.
The "battlefield" consists of a commander field, support field, and combat zones (defense/offense).
You can freely move your creatures around each turn, even their attack order can be sorted. Support field is where you can place creatures outside combat, it's also where most creature cards start.
Player turns go in 2 sections; preparation and turn resolve.
Basically, each player prepares a set of moves, and then that turn is set into motion.
Rather than turn based and being able to interrupt the other players' turn to use instant abilities, they have to be prepared up front. This does make it harder than waiting for the right card, you also need to be sure your target will become or will stay available when you aim for them.
Apart from PvP, there's also a campaign available. It's best to start off there with the first few levels of each campaign, as you get a starter pack from each one.
-
I haven't been playing much yet, so I can't say much about the balancing issues some people have been talking about.
Either way, as this is still a beta, I'm sure eventually the whole set will get balanced eventually.
All'n all, it's been pretty good so far.

Call of Duty is a first-person shooter taking place during World War II.  During this actioned packed Campaign, you will not only fight enjoy the Campaign and story line of the American Assault, but also the British and Soviet soldiers.  For a game that was released in 2003, Activision and Infinity Ward brought a lot of realism into the game. As you assault forward into and behind enemy lines while a relentless barrage of artillery fire and mortar rounds impacting around you, you will find yourself taking cover to overcome shellshock and regain awareness.
The American Campaign
-	Brings you and your fellow comrades into the invasion of Normandy. Lack of sleep and male nourished, you fight your way through towns and villages eliminating all German enemy forces, securing the areas, and continuing your venture into the depths of the Nazi Front. Following your success in Normandy, you make your way to Bastogne, Belgium. (9 Missions)
The British Campaign
-	While the American Forces are assaulting the western front, British soldiers are assaulting the eastern front partnered with 1 Canadian Division.  Starting their mission near Benouville, British troops capture and defend key bridges the Germany Forces are utilizing to transport tanks into the central and western Forward Line of Troops. Following their success, British elements are tasked to take out Planes and most importantly, a German Naval Vessel, the Tirpitz, near Norway. Nearing the conclusion of the mission, British forces are tasked to destroy German Rockets in Burgsteinfurt, Germany. (7 Missions)
The Soviet Campaign
-	The first Soviet mission takes places during the Battle of Stalingrad.  You are unarmed and taking relentless machinegun and mortar fire. Once successfully ashore and the machinegun fire has been suppressed and eliminated, you find yourself flanking and neutralizing a German stronghold. During this campaign you are elected to take charge of a tank and maneuver throughout a Village, eliminated German Panzers. (10 Missions)
In conclusion this game was fantastic to play, everything from the realism of shellshock, ability to eliminate targets with a distant well sniper round, and assault bunkers conducting room clearing and hand to hand combat.  This game offers non-stop action-packed fighting to always keep you on your toes for 26 intense missions total and a variety of weapons. I would absolutely recommend this game for the simple fact or how engaged your will be at every moment.  The campaign does not take very long to beat but you will sure have fun playing it. This is a small, excelent exploration game. The art is very minimalist and surreal, very blocky in a braod sense, on purpose, and each screen or level is dominated by a color, which permeates everything in said level.
The puzzles are mostly "positioning" puzzles, in which you solve them by standing in a specific position or having to take certain path (but they are very logic and easy to understand), by having to push here and there some objects, just moving against them (there is no "action/manipulate" button), or by pressing some buttons in certain order. The atmosphere is mostly relaxing, but there are a few spooky or strange moments as well.
There is no rush, no sense of urgency, so you can stroll at your leisure through the many blocky landscapes. If you try to solve all puzzles by yourself, it could take about 6+ hours of game. If you follow a walkthrough, you could rush through it in a couple hours, but it would be a shame. There is also no manual save, but the game saves often as you reach a new area or solve some puzzle or find something noteworthy.
This game is ideal to relax or slow down a bit. Higly recommended

A great ride from start to finish, 'Technobabylon' hits all the right notes both in terms of being a great scifi/cyberpunk tale and as a point an click adventure. The story is tight and paced well, the characters are engaging and well written and the puzzles blend into the plot with general seemlessness.
Not everyone will be on board with the pixel art style and AGS engine (which is frankly starting to show its age even in 'faux-retro' titles like this) but it's hard to complain about stuff like that when it suits the storytelling style so well and there's obviously so much love put into these environments and characters; it's really remarkable what the developers have done within the constraints of the tools they're working with.
I found the difficulty of the puzzles somewhat on the easy side and there was never a point where I had to reach for a walkthrough, but then I'm a genre-veteran. The game pretty sucessfully (and organically) limits inventory and number of spaces to explore, and the characters around you are usually dropping subtle hints in dialouge as to how to proceed which keeps things moving. There's more than one way to solve a number of the challenges too which is a nice touch.
So, if you're looking for something that'll keep you busy for 10-15 hours and maybe spark off a few neurons as you wonder where technology is taking us as a species then you could do a lot worse than take a trip to Newtown in 2087. I feel there's a lot more exploring to be done in this world and I'd love to spend more time with these characters too... sequel? Please?
On a side note, I'd like to give this game extra-special props for being one of the few games (or pieces of media period) to do representation of minorities in a really great way; two of the PCs are female non-caucasians and a major character is trans. The game and dialouge never hammer any of these points or use them as cheap ways to stir controversy and all come across as individuals. It's really great to see people from many different racial backgrounds and sexual orientations in roles both heroic and villanious and to be able to interact with them without these identifiers being the defining aspects of their characters. Many writers and devs could learn a lot from Technocrat in this area.

I like Space Hulk the board game and this is a mechanically true implementation of it.  As such, it will likely be most appealing to individuals immersed in the Warhammer 40K universe and who are familiar with the original game's mechanics.  SH uses the Third Edition ruleset and scenarios.
The main weakness, for me, is the Genestealer A.I.  The computer is very easy to aggro and will always push ahead with its blips, rather than holding them back as lurkers ahead of the marines' line of advance.  This makes the original 3e campaign fairly easy to complete with careful play.  The DLC campaigns seem to recognize the A.I.'s weaknesses and work to compensate for it by forcing the marines to be more aggressive through time limits and other stressors.
I found the game to be achingly slow on a non-gaming laptop, but it motors along at quite a nice pace on a dedicated platform.  I turned the animations up to the fastest setting and that was fine.  Sound effects are decent (storm bolters, in particular, pack a wallop).
Pick it up on sale if you like the original board game and the price is right.

Whether the idea to make a racing game about cheating was an accident or a stroke of genuis remains a mystery.  What I do know is that it's freaking fun.  I was the kid no one liked to play Mario Kart with becasue I always focused on the chincy spots to use boosts and cut across as much track as possible.  Now its not just an exploit, its the principal mechanic.
Falling off the track and landing 50 feet ahead may not sound like much, but when you get 5 seconds of freefall that refreshes every time you so much as graze the track, magic can happen.  Granted this is a curse as much as it is a blessing.  Without passing through gates to progress your respawn point, an incredible run ruined by one bad bounce can send you back to the starting line and irredemably far behind.  That's just the thing too, bouncing can and will happpen, and mastering it can be tricky.  Sometimes you bounce straight up and time out just hovering there, other times you get pitched impossibly far to the side where the road simply isn't.
Then there's the tension, and feeling of panic.  Much like hearing the warning of Mario Kart's blue shell which puts your blood on ice, seeing an opponent fall ahead of you and skip 30 gates is terrifying.  Suddenly your killer lead has evaporated and you need to start getting risky to catch up.  You take jumps where you normally wouldn't, you expend your boost trying to keep up only to blackout and respawn.  Disheartened you look at your position and realize it still says 1st.  This is a frequent occurence, just because they passed you, doesn't mean they're ahead of you.
Couch co-op gets competitive as hell cause you can see when your friends are taking jumps and you start reading their path to see if they can catch you.  Races are short enough too, unless you dial up the distance and complexity of the course so rotation of players usually isn't an issue.  If you don't have local friends, beating thr AI is plenty of fun, and there's a survival mode with leaderboards that are frankly insane.
When online multi happens along with the career, this game is going to become huge, at least I hope.  A dedicated dev with a great idea, I'd hate to see it fall flat.
All this is bundled with a sweet soundtrack and stunning visuals.

Hollow Knight, Hollow Knight, how great a game you were until you forgot what game you were.
So why am I giving this a negative review?  Because Team Cherry doesn't know what this game is.  At first it seemed like a solid Metroidvania that was plauged by being too open, and not giving many hints if any where to go, or what to do.  This is not a good thing, but it isn't really had either.
But then you progress further.  You get to the arena, you get to "optional" bosses, and suddenly it isn't just the atmosphere of the game that feels like dark souls, but the actual punishing enemies that don't forgive even small mistakes.  Well you know what?  Get gud.  Practice, learn patterns, try different charm load outs, it is rough but you can play through it.
Then you get to the end, and the "optional" areas.  Suddenly Team Cherry thinks this game is Super Meat Boy and you are expected to go through room, after room, after room, of no room for error, extremely hard, pixel perfect at time jump puzzles.  This isn't get good anymore.  There were jump puzzles before, but not one, after another, after another, that required wall jumping to hit an enemy, double jumping in the same jump to the other wall, bouncing off an enemy, wall jumping to an oposing wall, then dashing over another enemy to bounce again, all while timing your dash stop perfectly or overshooting to hit spikes, or undershooting to land on a saw.
It gets stupid.  Yes, that's right word for it.  Stupid.  It isn't fun to play, it feels totally out of place with everything else in the game.  It took a game that hard flaws, but made up for it in atmosphere and fun factor, and removed the fun factor.
Atmosphere alone isn't good enough.
So here is my advice.  Don't be like me.  Don't play these "optional" content area's (read: required to see the real ending, so not optional at all), beat the game without them.   Then just go watch the real ending on youtube.  At least then you can still like the game instead of hating it like I do now.

It's been such a long time since I played this, and I played the Xbox version way back when. Playing it on PC for the first time is wonderful. I didn't remember much about the game, so a lot of what I'm experiencing feels new, and nostalgia for this specific game isn't a factor, but nostalgia for this era of shooter design is.
Call of Duty feels intimate in a way that most other shooters can't do. You get verbal and written briefings, some even through you character's diary. The briefing often includes clueing you in to the overall strategy of the Allies and your small yet significant place in that strategy. The battles you fight aren't the ones that make headlines, but are the backbone of the offensive. You capture small towns and estates, and defend key points like bridges. The battles are small but feel personal, especially because your teammates' names show up when you point at them and the name changes in color to reflect their health. When Call of Duty goes for a dramatic moment, it doesn't wrestle control away from you. Rather, it fades in some melancholy orchestral music to fit the moment.
Call of Duty can play more run-and-gun or stop-and-pop depending on the difficulty level and the environment you're fighting in, with indoors being more of the former and outdoors being the latter. Weapons are still reasonably accurate even without aiming down the sights, which feels delightfully old-fashioned and is something that I dearly miss. Controls include leaning and going prone, both of which are useful in the game's indoor and outdoor battles. Sprinting is absent but that absensce isn't really noticable thanks to tight level design. Infinity Ward prefers to make a lot of short levels, something I prefer over a game with few long levels. My patience hasn't been tested by superfluous dialogue, cutscenes, or other ways to artificially inflate the length of game.
Quite simply, Call of Duty is a marvel of old-fashioned game design, built on the foundations of some of the best shooters ever made, then given its own identity as a shooter that sits confidently on the line between realistic shooters like Red Orchestra and Rainbow Six, and run-and-gun shooters like Quake and Half Life.

Kairo just seems like it was made for VR. The best way to describe is it is a Myst like experience where you travel through enormous rooms and areas that are large puzzles to figure out. There's no weaponry, no enemies unless you count the puzzles and you pretty much cannot die (falling off ledges just puts you back on the ledge). Each room is dominated by a simple color scheme and the architecture is large and blocky as giving the environment an ancient feel.
When played on a normal monitor, the simple graphics and plain architecture might seem like a negative. However, you activate VR, put on the Rift and you realize these graphics are now a strength. Just as Valve Steam Dev Days demo showed, so long as you keep latency low and frame rate high even a simple environment will seem real. Kairo delivers on this concept in spades. The large throne rooms, invisible maze arena, hollow pyramids, giant light orb and many other breathtaking sites fill this game. The slow pace and not too mind bending puzzles mean you're seeing new areas yet have plenty of time to appreciate each one. The sounds are different for each location and all are relaxing and never seem to be over bearing or painfully loud. There are a few cases where the sudden movement of the environment surprised me, but never did I feel the need to pull out of the game. The presence is strong and even with lengthy gameplay I did not notice much if any in the way of nausea. The frame rate seems great throughout with only one room (the one with four treadmills) showing lag.
Like Dear Esther, I play this game standing up and do the fake foot walk to aid in my immersion. The look is not tied to the control movement so it's easy to look around and enjoy the environment as you travel through. Its very easy to get drawn into the game and forget that you're in your room playing a game.
People probably have missed that this is a VR game as it does not seem to have the "VR Support" tag in the Steam search function. I've written the author and asked if he can get that added. As I said, for only $5 you're getting several hours of a great VR experience. A perfect game for those that prefer relaxed gameplay over the horror or shooter style games currently listed with VR support.

A wonderful story, full of intrigue where your choices decide how it unfolds. The game has two game modes: Classic and Casual. Casual Mode in essence allows you various cheats such as undoing a choice, having all choices available and unlimited healing before fights. For me personally the real fun was in playing Classic Mode which has none of the luxuries of Casual Mode as every choice truly matters. The immersion is greater in that mode as you will experience the finality of every choice. You will feel the adrenaline. You will feel the joy when you overcome a challenge, but also the sadness when you make a wrong decision. It is not easy at all and you will die many times, but each time you learn, become more knowledgeable and therefore better. If there is one point of critique I have, it is that the 'Fitness' dice roll at the start of the game is incredibly important up to the point that if it is not high enough in Classic Mode, then you might want to make choices even far more carefully than before or you might want to restart your character in order to beat the game. Nevertheless it is a great and well written story.

Not the greatest entry in the long-running CYOA series but an entertaining one at least. If you're the kind of person who likes to roleplay as a thief, or assassin, or generally as a rogue then you'll want to look into buying this one as its focus is on the underworld and the gritty nature of medieval. Whilst this book isn't as punishing as others, like the Forest of Doom and Deathtrap Dungeon, there is a moment where you can instant die if you happen to make a single wrong choice.
Though what I love about An Assassin in Orlandes is that it's stylised to my personal interests in what I seek out of a CYOA book. The choices, the setting, the items you'll find and characters you'll meet add up to create its own world fit for your imagination as that burglar, or thief, or assassin you tend to be. There's little sorcery in this, which might disappoint high fantasy lovers, but given the style this is it is forgivable.
Most importantly, I found the storyline to be linear compared to other CYOA books out there, where it feels more akin to an on-rails experience than decisions being made that totally change where you are going next. This doesn't mean that all your choices are pre-determined, as you can make some that will make getting out of certain situations easier, but it feels like there is a parallel consequence if you decided to bring x item, and left y behind. This also plays into the linearity of the story where specific items are only helpful in specific situations, rather than decking out your character to make willy-nilly free choices. What I really love about books like House of Hell, or afore mentioned Deathtrap Dungeon, were the splitting paths in the story and having your items be more of a general use than a direct choice. In An Assassin in Orlandes, it feels this element is stripped and you're being guided through.
Having said that, I tend to love these mystery, crime-driven stories that are dark and gritty and focus on that cloak and dagger style - so that helped a ton when it came to liking this one. I did enjoy my time, there are some great choices that will bite you in the butt later on, and other lacklustre ones that feel like padding; to delay the inevitable. I'll definitely recommend An Assassin in Orlandes to fans of CYOA but go in with caution that this probably isn't as open ended as you might expect, but expect a great mystery and some storytelling here.
And if you really love this, there's an overview world map in the bonus section as well as chunks of lore ready to immerse you.

An Assassin in Orlandes by Tin Man Games is a text adventure/choose your own adventure game that mixes the dice rolling of RPG with the path-choosing style of CYOA (Choose Your Own Adventure) books.
If you’ve read my previous review I’ll be repeating myself here, but: Mixing dice in with this means you will also be rolling for stats, and that most fights and encounters are purely luck based. That said, I quite enjoyed the mix of these two game styles, it makes for very interesting gameplay that mimics the board RPGs quite well, and reminds you very fondly of CYOA books.
If you’ve never read a CYOA book, it works like this: You reach a point in which you’re given two or more choices, and it indicates what page to turn to continue the story on the proper path. There are several different endings, some failure, some death, and a ‘true’ one.
Controls are simple: You just flip pages by clicking and click choices as they appear (some might be obscured if you are missing an item or certain knowledge, but otherwise you're free to pick and choose). Should you need to, you have a bookmarking function to return to a previous point in the book, maps, etc.
At the start of the story you may also pick up the difficulty. Unlike The Forest of Doom, this one offers only two settings: A regular difficulty mode and a “casual” (cheat) one. The cheats are the same as in Forest: you can heal yourself or uncover options you might have not had otherwise, in order to get through the book.
The story is better written than in The Forest of Doom, though the main premise and how the character comes to be in troubles is still lacking a bit. Still, it’s a story I would definitely recommend for a younger audience. The fight style I found a bit more confusing than in the previous game, but it was otherwise equally luck based and mostly simple to learn.
The graphical aspect of the book was a bit more typical, but the images (in black and white) were so much nicer to look at, and the maps were also much better drawn.
Would I recommend it? Yes. But again, I’d recommend you grab it for at least half price.

What is An Assassin in Orlandes?
An Assassin in Orlandes is a gamebook in video game form. If you know the Fighting Fantasy books by Steve Jackson and Ian Livingstone (not to be confused with Ian Livingstone, the Illuminati card game designer!) you will know how it plays. If not, here is a small summary.
You are presented with a lot of text that describes your situation, then you choose your next action from a set of several possibilities. Often, you are constricted by having or having not a certain item, or you must fight or check your fitness.
At first you roll fitness and vitality.
Fitness is determined at the beginning of your game. I recommend to keep on restarting (more on this in a bit) until you roll at least a 4, preferrably a 6. I got very lucky, having rolled 6 for fitness and a high vitality. Vitality is rolled with 4 dice, fitness with 1 die, and a set number is added to each roll's total (I think 26 for vitality and 6 for fitness). Vitality can be restored in some ways, and it is not that important, but fitness is essential. Rolling a vitality of anything that is not trolled (you should try to get over 40 vitality, but anything over 36 should work well) and a fitness of 6 is what you want for almost all of the game (there is one artwork where you must follow a set of actions that includes a failed fitness roll, but you will want to do that after finishing the game).
So in short: Vitality = 4d6 + 26. Fitness = 1d6 + 6. You need 10+ fitness for all achievements, and 12 is absolutely recommended, even if vitality is low then.
After you are done rolling your initial stats and assigning yourself a name that you will never see again, the adventure begins. So you are in a tavern and can decide if you want to get drunk, talk to the barkeeper, or leave the tavern. All ways eventually lead outside, where you witness an attack against a young nobleman. The game follows its main path linearly, but branches off at the side paths, enabling you to get some better equipment or helpful items - or into dangerous battles.
The battle system works on offense, defense and vitality. The vitality is hit points, offense and defense are each the number of dice you roll for yourself or opponents when attacking or defending. The highest single die counts, in case of a tie the next one, etc., but I don't fully understand the system even after beating the game.
So you remember me recommending 12 fitness? You can use fitness in the battle, and it seems to jump back to the previous value when you win, but the advantage is really small and you have to do a fitness check each time.
The fitness check consists of throwing two dice, and you pass if the total is lower than your fitness value. This gives you at 12 fitness a 1 in 36 chance to fail. Unfortunately here is a huge weakness of the book: Almost each time you fail in the story, it is a certain game over. There are a few exceptions.
You can make up to three saves (called bookmarks) when the game is started. My first playthrough attempt failed because I set the bookmarks too early. Of course, this is part of exploring the game. So you start the game, set the first bookmark (to save your fitness and vitality) and explore until you know what is a good course of action. And this goes on that way. Eventually you run out of bookmarks and want to restart.
Wait, how do you restart?
You can only do so after getting a "THE END" message, which appears when you die or when you win the game. So if you want to get 12 fitness you will need to die a few times, which is annoying because it takes a while. And - minor spoiler - you need 10+ fitness for one achievement, so you will want to reroll if it is too low.
There are 23 artworks to find (24 if you include the title page), and when you found all you are awarded with an achievement, which is most likely the final achievement you find. By that time, you will have won the game already and tried a few different approaches to sidetracking. Without a guide it took me around 2 hours to beat the game in classic mode, but as I said I got lucky with the initial rolls. I then used a guide for the last few artworks and another achievement, bringing my platime to around two and a half hours.
And that is it, after seeing everything once, there is no replayability. Sure, the time will depend on how fast you can read, or if you get bored, how fast you skip pages and make decisions. The story is in my opinion your standard fantasy story, and the ganeplay is unbalanced in terms of fitness, but rather easy and forgivable for the rest, showing that it is aimed at beginners of gamebooks. If you look for the classical situation where you missed one item somewhere along the path and now can't beat the final boss three hours later... this gamebook does not have it.
So, this is a gamebook for beginners, and if you get it cheap or in a bundle, you should give it a try, if you enjoy the genre.
Recommended: For gamebook beginners and achievement enthusiasts

I have to say, Technobablyon is the first point and click adventure I've really enjoyed.
All of the puzzles are SMART. Not just "click random thing on random other things until stuff happens". You can actually THINK about the puzzles, think about what could actually solve them, then work towards those solutions, making for satisfying gameplay!
The characters are also smart! They're different, wrong sometimes, make mistakes, but they actually try to think and understand what is going on. I enjoyed all of the protagonists.
I'm happy to say that every time I got stumped on a puzzle (with one minor exception, mentioned below), it wasn't because the solution was bizarre or counter-intuitive, it was just that I hadn't thought about the actual facts of puzzle the right way.
The major downside is the ending (spoilers).
A minor flaw is it sloppily scripted (lots of weird bugs that you can cause, nothing game-breaking but obviously not been through thorough QA, like the door lock lights disappearing (not turning off - literally disappearing) after you go through the door and return, or Lao being able to hand her wetware to Regis but not get it back).
It's also unclear that there is an entire third floor in the Trance, making the final part of the puzzle a matter of luck or blind guesswork.
But the big part is the endings are unsatisfying. Either you force a person into slavery, or you force them into being someone else's agenda and to go through an invasive mind-altering procedure without their input. I would have been much happier if there was a third option, where you can actually respect the autonomy of the AGI and let it free without compulsion. Or at least if you can ask Central what she thinks of her options.
