My main gripe about this game is how ridiculously important it is to use overwatch. Setting up good overwatch is 90% of the game. You terminators each have 4 actions, plus there is a pool of command points all your terminators can draw from for extra actions. Firing at a genestealer takes one action and has a 31% chance to hit and kill it. Additional shots at the same genestealer have a 56% chance of success. Thus, firing twice on your turn would take two actions and gives you a 31% and a 56% chance of killing a single genestealer.
Now if you point the terminator down a hallway that covers several squares and spend 2 action points on overwatch you get to shoot at a genestealer EVERY square it moves. So you might have one shot at 31% than several shots at 56% against one genestealer on one game turn. And beyond that, if you kill it (which is the most common situation) the other genestealers that come down the hallway that turn get the same treatment from the same 2 action points.
Now there is a game mechanic that has your storm bolters guns jam regularly, but they will automatically clear them at the cost of one command point each time if you saved points from the last turn. This does little to take away from the power of overwatch and basically forces you to save command points instead of spending them on your turn.
You might argue that it’s a game design thing and my dislike for such a powerful overwatch is my preference and doesn’t make it a bad game. I would argue the reason it’s a horrible design is it makes the melee characters in the game nearly worthless. The odds of losing a melee character guarding a door are astronomically higher than losing a terminator overwatching a hallway. So much so the melee characters are barely useful and can block line of sight for their gunwielding brothers.
I would argue that the biggest factor on the challenge of the map is based on how many storm bolters you get.
Another smaller annoyance is that opening a broken door is a 16.7% chance for most actions and a 33% chance for most melee weapons. So it’s not out of the ordinary to watch a terminator miss opening a jammed door several actions in a row.
Another complaint is there is the only thing that makes a campaign a campaign is you need to finish one map to open up the next. There doesn’t seem to be any repercussions to how many terminators survive as long as you finish the map. There is no tally on remaining terminators like in the opening movie or even a page telling you how well your campaign is progressing. Your campaign progress is only what maps are available to play.
For such a simple game they could have spent more time on making the tactics more interesting than just setting up overwatch. If you are a turn based combat fan and/or a 40k fan you’ll probably find a few hours of entertainment here, but this kind of thing has been done a lot better by many games.

The Swindle is a very good game, that I am very, very bad at. The Swindle requires patience, timing and skill. Traits that I am sadly lacking. But I am learning. I'm getting better.

The Swindle is a steam punk accidental death simulator in which you guide a motley crew of thieves to their inevitable demise, and each death is more hilarious or frustrating than the last. Your mileage may vary.

The overarching goal is to steal the Devil's Basilisk, an omniscient survellaince device that Scotland Yard are planning to activate in 100 days time. Each time you venture out on a heist, the doomsday clock ticks ever closer to game over. Why yes, you can actually fail in the Swindle, and many of you will do so on your first run.

Each day you will go to work, statrting off in The Slums, pilfering money from the poor London folk until you acquire enough upgrades, skills and forged documents to take on richer, and more secure locations such as casinos and banks.

The procedurally generated levels ensure that you'll never burgle the same establishment twice, although you will start to see general themes and patterns in the level layouts, every heist is a fresh and unique challenge. For the most part, the rules of each level are laid out in front of you, the enemy's fields of vision and capabilities are clear to see at a glance. Patrol patterns are consistant, and security cameras scan specific areas with precise timing. Patience is key to progression, watching for a weakness that you can exploit and then doing so will net you consistant rewards.

Interestingly, some levels may even be impossible depending on the upgrades you have acquired thus far, I'll get into upgrades a little later, but it's a very real possibility that you will be unable to 100% many levels in the game if you are not prepared for every single eventuality.

It's a risky design choice from Dan Marshall, but it highlights the problems that you will face throughout your financial reallocation career and encourages you to delve into the progression system and have a good look for tools that may help you out in the future. It also teaches you a very important lesson: Abandonning a heist is very much part of this game, in fact it is as much a part of The Swindle as any mechanic or feature.

Your thieves are not warriors, one hit, one mistake, and they are dead. Risking a gauntlet of guards, landmines and spike traps to hack one more terminal may not be worth it. Grab what you can and get out alive and the multiplier is integral to this.

For every successful heist your score multipler will increase and this nets you a juicy cash bonus at the end of every level. The more successful heists, the higher the multiplier so sooner or later you'll reach a stage where you really REALLY don't want to die. The Swindle makes you care about the lives of you little tea leaves and the exponential increase of risk/reward is the reason for this. It's a stroke of genius. Giving in to the temptation of hacking one more terminal is potentially fatal, but if it's a casino terminal worth £50k and then combine that with a triple multiplier... it's awfully tempting isn't it? Just bear in mind that carelessness and greed are your bigest enemies in The Swindle.

The problem for me however, is than in games especially, I am careless and I am greedy. I want ALL the things and even now, will try and clean out a level whether it's a good idea or not and I believe the this game has been constructed to deliberately punish gamers with that kind of impulsive habit. I love the Swindle I really do, but not necessarily when I'm in the same room as it. Sometimes I do have to literally walk away or switch to playing something more forgiving. Like Dark Souls.

Luckily, there are several abilities & tools to mitigate one's incompetance. You can unlock multiple jumps, the ability to cling to walls, a remote detonator for mines, dynamite to blast through walls and EMP device and much, much, more. There is an incredible depth in how much you characters can improve. Luckily, your upgrades carry one from one hapless thief to another as I dont think I could take having a thief with £500k investment in him getting eviscerated by a robotic Bobby.

Ah yes, and that brings me to the police. No, not the godawful band with Sting in, I'm talking about London's robotic law enforcement. Normally when you get spotted in a stealth game, that's it time to restart, in The Swindle the game turns into a frantic platformer where everything is trying to murder you adn you have to get out before the cyberfuzz turn up and REALLY make your life a misery. Or do you have a couple of seconds spare to grab a few extra quid on the way out?

The way the music kicks up a notch when you are spotted is delicious, as is the music in general. The score really is excellent and you can see for yourself how gorgeous the art is in this game.

The Swindle is like a splinter in my head, I find myself constantly thinking about it like on the next run Ill do this differently or I'll prioritise these skills. It's infectious and magnificent in equal measure. It is something rather special indeed and scrathes that "just one more run" itch perfectly.

In conclusion then, I really, really, really, want to buy Dan Marshall a pint.

Being a thief is hard, especialy if you rush in without some sort of plan. Smash a window, grab the loot and get out. That sort of thing. Well, this will probably get you killed.
It's all about being patient, calculating your jumps and using your abilities as best as you can.
And that's exactly where The Swindle is a brilliant game. Each ability is usefull. Some don't seem that usefull but it's all about how you play the game. Knowing where the computers are seems like a waste of resource when it's that or a tripple a jump, but information makes the job easier. Tripple jumping to, sure. If you are unlucky and face a lot of empty void between too ledges.
Anyway, managing your money, establishing "the best buying plan", min/maxin risks and rewards while in missions, figuring out how to get that heavily guarded chest...it's not just a action game, it's a puzzle action game. And with procedural genereration of terrain, the same situation is hardly encountered again.
As for how it's proceduraly generated, well, don't expect the same few rooms over and over. There will be similarities but a small underground map can be as easily encountered as a huge 3 storys with a one tower or two. The map are diverse, there may not be enough sort of level but the increasing difficulty and payout rewards make them just the right amount.
One last thing, the music and sounds are good. It's just what you would expect of a steampunk era, and even more what you would expect  for a stealth steampunk mood.

Short review:
If you're really into Space Hulk/ Warhammer 40k, or have a friend you really want to play this with, you might as well get it no matter what.
If not, imagine a tower defense, where your towers can move, but miss all the time and might blow up due to sheer bad luck and gameplay is generally slow. Still sounds fun to you? Well, if you're enough of a masochist, enjoy, otherwise, better keep away.
The experience of the game:
If you play any Warhammer as a tabletop game, with a friend, or fellow players in one room, every move, every single dice roll can build up sweet tension, your strategy vs. your opponents, your luck vs. theirs and every time one of you makes an awesome move or seems to beat the odds, it can be hillarious.
The game might translate the mechanics perfectly, but no matter what, it can not translate this feeling and at least for me, this is doing a lot and seems to turn the whole game into an ok puzzle at best and a boring random number generator at worst.
Sometimes there might be a positive feel to it, if you pull of a good move, strengthening your position, or barely getting out of a tight situation. But, most of the time there is no feeling of achievement, when just another one of the hundreds of generic enemies you encounter dies, nor if you complete a level, really. On the other hand it can be rather frustrating, if the randomness turns against you big time, like a single enemy running down a hallway, all overwatch shots missing, the bolter jamming 4 times in a row and then your unit is dead and the whole mission might fall appart. Bad luck, rinse and repeat?! Meh.
In addition to that, both visuals and sounds are just bad. Again, if it's tabletop, your imagination might fill in cool effects and so far, no graphics engine can beat good imagination. But, if a program shows you, how your unit is shooting the wall, while an enemy in the hallway next to it falls in a weird splash of red, that might be funny the first time, but in the end is just, well, really bad. It's pretty much the same with moving animations, first time it might look funny when your terminator is awkwardly wiggling backwars around a corner, but at some point it's just awkward. Also, it's good that you can crank up the animation speed, otherwise i might've died of boredom just watching unit movement.
So i prefer... playing anything else.

I've clocked up about 11 hours in The Swindle so far, and I've not even come close to reaching the halfway point of the game. This is mostly, I'm not afraid to say, down to my incompetence, which this game isn't afraid to remind me of. Regularly.
To describe the core of the game - steal as much cash from each procedurally generated level as possible, without dying - makes it sound simple and repetitive, but that's sort of the genius. Your goal and the way you achieve it often is simple, but your one small mistake will cost you and you will hate yourself for it every time.
"I just need to drop down, whack that guard and the jump over those spikes," you think, just before mistiming your initial drop, getting spotted by the guard, and jumping into those spikes in a state of panic. Of course, you then try and make up for that mistake by doing something more risky next time (you need to make up for that lost cash somehow!) and, well, you can probably guess why I've barely scratched the surface in 11 hours.
There are a huge amount of upgrades available for you to vary your approach and tactics for the inevitable sixth and seventh playthrough, which often leads to those confidence-dashing moments, too. Y'know, just as you found that perfect combination of upgrades that means that this guy is no longer a threa--oh, he got me.
I've read a few comments saying that it needs a tutorial of some sort. It really, really doesn't. The controls and the mechanics are as simple as they come, it's the real understanding of how you use the simple tools you're provided with, plus those you 'provide'* yourself, that brings the real fun here and that would be taken away with any sort of guide. If you really want help, watch 10 minutes of someone else play it on YouTube and you'll know more than enough to get going.
Basically, it's infuriatingly brilliant because it's always happy to give you the perfect opportunity to♥♥♥♥♥♥things up, just as you think you've got a handle on it.
* I mean steal. You play a dirty, dirty thief.

Super Impossible Road is an awesome, fast-paced racing game.
You control a very cool looking ball-vehicle-thing and race down a randomly generated track. Tracks are incredibly twisty, turny and bumpy. They remind me of audiosurf tracks, or rainbow road from Mario kart. Racing down these is a blast.
Even cooler though, is that you have the ability to roll off of these tracks and skip ahead. Since the tracks are constantly going downwards, you can simply fly off of the edge and land somewhere below. You have a set amount of time to do this, or else you'll respawn back at the last gate you past through. This adds a great risk, great reward mechanic in the game, where skipping ahead could gain you the lead, but not timing the jump properly could cause you to fall behind.
There are multiple gates throughout the levels, that once you go through serve as a checkpoint, and will fill your boost meter. You may use this boost while racing down the road, or falling through the air to make sure you land back on the road in time before you respawn.
There are a decent amount of game modes to keep you interested.
There's the basic racing mode where you can customize the amount of local players, AI difficulty, track length, track complexity and the environment look. There are currently only 2 environments as of the time I'm writing this review. It's not important that there aren't many, as they're completely cosmetic, but I like that the option is there. They give the game a fresh look every new race.
There's also a survival mode where you don't get any respawns, and simply try to go as far as possible without dying.
The time gate mode has a timer constantly ticking down to zero, and you are required to go through a special type of gate in order to gain some time back.
Currently both of those game modes are singleplayer only, so I would really love if more players would be able to play those together in the future.
There is a career mode and online mode currently under construction, but I can't comment on them as they aren't available in the current build I'm playing.
I'm very happy to see that the game gives you a lot of graphical options to tweak, which is very nice. Sadly, on the other hand the game doesn't control as well as it should with PC controls. Playing the game itself is fine with a controller or keyboard, but the menus are SLIGHTLY frustrating to maneuver. There's no mouse support in the main menu, which can be annoying. I'm hoping the simple stuff like that will be fixed, because I don't really have any problems with the game itself.
It's a great idea for a game, well executed, and I honestly can't wait to see the online mode available. The music is some pretty decent techno to get you into the moment, and compliments the look of the world quite well.
Overall, it's a really fun, and unique idea for a racing game!

Starmade, to be overly reductive, is Minecraft in space.
Starmade is a voxel-based space game that takes place in a procedurally generated universe.
Players have complete freedom over what to build and do.
1.)When I say you can build anything, I mean anything. The various block shapes allow for more diverse shapes than a fully cubic world would allow. Functional blocks also make your designs have a purpose that extends beyond the aesthetic.
2.)The developers stream Tuesday and Thursdays 4-6 EST, and communicate with the community
. The fact that you can play the game for free is testament to the fact that the dev team actually values creating a great game (not to mention how long its been in alpha!).
3.)There are a whole host of multiplayer servers, and customizing the servers to suit a group's playstyle is easy. Sector length, mining yield, what ships pirates use, and so on are all completely customizable in server configs.
4.)Being able to actually build functional ships brings a sense of purpose to any construction project. Your ship isn't just a centerpiece, it's a colossal avatar of destruction/stealthy perma-cloaked spy/kingpin of the mining industry. Each block has its own contribution to the whole.
1.) When playing multiplayer, lag and latency are issues, particularly for people with lower-end CPUs. Large collisions, overlapping spawns, or interacting with planets really at all will lag servers enormously. However, the devs do work to solve performance issues, just recently releasing a patch that nearly eliminated online lag with large amounts of missiles on screen.
2.) Any story is self-made. To the credit of the devs, space is a busy place, with various factions fighting it out and trading with the player. It's unfortunate that interactions with factions does not go beyond that. Randomly generated quests, or even some preset ones in combination with some simple lore would do a great deal to flesh out the single-player experience. However, this game/genre isn't really supposed to have an engaging story-line. Those looking to be immersed in a single-player story should look elsewhere.
3.) Arguably, there are some balancing issues (no reason to use pulse weapons; what is a warhead). However, the game is still in alpha and the devs do change the balance in the game frequently in order to find the right mix.
4.) Though the complex nature of the building system keeps the game interesting and adds an element of skill through optimization of ships, the lack of any real, advanced guides in game hold back new players from learning much. Also, due to the rapidly changing nature of the game, youtube tutorials often can be quickly outdated (docked power, weapon rebalancing, how shields and turrets work).
If you are a fan of creative construction, then the pros clearly outweigh the cons. For those looking to recreate their favorite ships, fly them around the galaxy, and terrorize pirates, this is your game. The Mulitplayer community is mostly friendly, or at least active and passionate about the game, and playing online in a faction is a lot of fun. Once this game is fully balanced, optimized, and released, I completely expect it to be a wonderful experience online.
For now, I would rate Starmade a 7/10. It has all the right tools to be a paragon of the creative genre, but is held back by low popularity and performance issues. Once more people can and are playing Starmade, I would rate it 9/10 for people who enjoy these types of games. Definitely a great game, and I encourage anyone who can to contribute to its development process. Those who simply want to try it out always have the option of playing the entirety of the game for FREE as well.

Final Review 9/5/2014
Honestly, I'd like to say that I had a whole bunch of information to drop upon IW's release, but I don't. Release for this game was not so much a bang but a very timid whimper. My honest opinion is that it felt rushed if solid, giving it a very mediocre launch.
There are no big changes so I can't find my revised review changing all that much. Several much-needed card fixes were implemented, but that's not what should set a gold release apart. The truth is there's no point in adopting this game at all as it sits, if you played beta you're not missing anything. If you have to pick up this game might as well wait for 2015. That's when most of the launch features a TCG should have wil be implemented.
The game is barebones at the moment. It didn't launch with any kind of card recycler or revamped rewards system. The developers think that's fine, I find it a grind. Even something as basic as a tournement mode didn't make it into release. The truth is they're still on a player-to-player system and, you guessed it, serverside matchmaking won't be making it until the year after release, and dysincronizations and endless turns are still very much a reality. Current plans for IW 2015 make this feel like Beta Mk 2 not Ver 1.0.
I'm out of room. Can't recommend.
Revised Review 5/5/2014
----
So, I decided to give the game a more in-depth review at the behest of some of the developers. My main review is mostly still intact, so I'll detail where it changes and my new experiences with a month worth of play. Despite what Steam says it's over 40 hours (I dont' play with Steam in online mode a lot).
Like I said before the game has potential that's almost all it's working on. I saw that patch .96 was live so if convention is to be believed it's very close to release, so I don't buy that, "It's beta" excuse everyone from the developers to the community likes to foist on you. It's way too close to a 1.0 version for that to be a sufficient. Still, if you're a person who like to play games based on the promise of what they might be (a la Dwarf Fortress or something). I'm not really going to convince you. I'm here to report on what exists. I can't critique things that don't exist.
The AI is horrible (They've "got plans"). I beat the most difficult AI routinely and draw it out if I'm lazy. I think I lost once to it because I wasn't paying attention. You can beat the AI with just about any deck you can put together. The campaign serves as less of a story and more as an extended tutorial to get you cards.
The bugs and glitches are still pretty bad. At .96 you'd expect most of the core modes to be at least pretty solid, but Rift Run (there version of draft) didn't work right for about two weeks I was there. Every patch seemed to make the game worse. While they'd fix some things they'd introduce two issues for every issue they fixed. Some people tell me that's "how development goes" but I'll let you realize who paradoxical that is.
Speaking more on the modes. Rift Run (again their Draft) is actually an exercise in how much money you're willing to pour into it (thankfully not real world money). At one-thousand Infinity Points (the free currency) it's actully quite cheap to at least make sure you have ideal commanders, cheapinging the spirit of the mode.
The factions: The game is pretty strong, it still feels really random to me, but you learn a few tricks. It still does feel like you're throwing cards. One faction (their first post-core faction) is basically unplayable by itself and is generally in need of reowrking. It's been through one already. That gives me pause to invest in the next non-core release, Ascenscion.
The only way to get free card packs after a while becomes leveling up. Which is fair. They don't have to give you free packs for everything. You get a few single cards for weekly quests and the fee card for your daily login and first three games of the day, which makes sure you get a card for participating, but the leveling up is purely geometric in scale (one more thousand exp to level up) in scale. You get one pack no matter how much it actually took to get to the next level. So the rewards remain the same while you're doing more work for the same thing. That naturally make leveling up a grind. If you're the kind of person who can do PVP all day long with no change then more power to you.
If found the community by in large hostile if you didn't toe the general opinion. Any critique of the game is met with "It's in beta' again remember they're at version .96, that's almost release, or it's met without outright nastiness, which I suppose is just the nature of the beast when you're dealing with anything over the internet. The inablity to take and evaluate criticism is only going to hurt the game in  the long run. They'll probably say bad things about me, but I don't really care.
There are a few other small issues that give me pause to invest anymore time into the game. A sale was held on a deck recently. The sale was in LP (Lightmare Points the real-money currency) and not Infinity Points. I asked around and that wasn't something done before with both currencies being slashed for the sale. That smacks of riding the P2W line. So be careful if you do decide to adopt this game.
All in all, I still cannot recommend this game. It's an okay TCG and it's probably the best F2P digital traiding card game I've played recently, but remember that the lesser of two evils is still evil. These are my opinions, but I did not enjoy the first time I played it, and I did not enjoy the month I spent for this review. There came a point where I wanted it to succeed, but if I'm going to play a game I don't want to feel like I'm just hitting my head against a wall, which is exactly what Infinity Wars feels like, except the wall has spikes.
I'll be making a final review when it hits release. Though my expectations are markedly low.

While this game has a lot of potential it falls down in a few key areas one would expect a trading-card game to flourish in. Turn length is painfully long and busy, and their are far too many mechanics to keep in mind as you play. Including what order your creature cards are in and where they are on the zone.
While the simultaneous turn mechanic might seem like it speeds up gameplay the uneeded general complexity of the game at large keeps it from being effective. Also, the simultaneous turn resolution (though there is initiative to keep in mind as well) gives the game a painfully random element beyond simple luck of the draw. It felt more like I was throwing cards at a brick wall and seeing wich ones took rather than leading an army in a grand strategic victory. Instead of skillful counters and repostes it feels more like you're constantly punching in the dark at one another.
In this regard the mechanics of the game shine a light on a dominant strategy that shouldn't be so dominantly effective in this genre as to be the go-to strategy: The rush. Rush decks are the majoiry and the game tends to punish slightly slower than rush decks. It makes the game feel stale and samey.
That being said collecting cards is fun, and the game does offer up many rewards. If you can get past the cumbersome mechanics progress feels nice. The cards are animated with looping gif-like pictures on each and every card which is pretty, but also fees gimicky. Battles aren't fought in any cenematic way. Cards bump into each other doing their damage. The factions are fairly distinct and the art is nice with shades of Warhammer 40K in a blend of sci-fi-coated fantasy.
The game is in beta now, but as a representation of what we can expect it leaves a lot to be desired. The lovely if pointless card animations and promise of what are supposed to represent battlefield style engagements are marred by stilted and random mechanics. There are no doubt better card battle games one could be playing.

Well, I suspect this review will be building over time.  I started with Battlerite (BR) a long, long time ago.  With a game called Bloodline Champions.   It never quite 'made' it, and wasn't even on Steam for the most abyssmal longest time.  The game went through so many iterations and ended with a strangely game breaking level and traits system.  Well, ended in terms of casual players.  For many years dedicated fans would continue to play knowing that BLC had something unique and unreproducable.  Especially a feeling you would get when a fight was real, and your heart is beating so fast because it is you vs that one other person.  You will know what I am talking about if you play this game.  We play this game because it challenges us like no other game can.
Now the first thing you need to know is that it is a top down mouse and keyboard fighting game.  It is primarily based on skill shots and timing(?).  What this means is a completely new type of Multiplayer battle that brings to mind, 'WOW Arena' fights in which abilities can change the course of every battle dynamically and in fresh unique ways every single time.
If you approach BR as a fighting game you will understand the premise quickly.  But imagine a fighting game with healers and support characters.  There is a reflecting bubble for projectiles that when used correctly is incredibly satisfying like landing a max hit combo.  Another character has a shield that reflects, which can turn a losing battle into an interesting and inspiring come back, and a heal that links your teams spirit.  Another character shoots a gigantic beam of light that heals your team and damages the enemy.  Each hero has their own signature fighting style.
Also it must be stressed that point and click movement which is predominant in the most popular mobas is very limiting technically.  I respect that skill but it is a huge waste of energy..
The game's artwork is reminiscent of an aztec sort of temple look.  The battlegrounds glow with suffused energy and there is a 'clock' that visually gathers energy as a rune is spawned.
Knowing the skins and cosmetics in BLC I think that they will not disappoint in that department.
In my short summary for now, you should buy this game immediately even in early access.  It is a fully loaded fighting game.  The developers slaved a long time over BLC and it never got the props it deserved.  BR is a great game that needs to be shared by the community simply for the sake of fresh gaming experiences, that we all love and appreciate.
9.5/10 recommended.

Being an old MTG competitive player this game definitely peeked my interest. But I was still a bit skeptical b/c being from a company I had never heard of I was not sure if it was actually going to be another "pay to win" set up, for the more casual players. I was very happily proven wrong when it came to the "pay to win" scenario. A lot of times in TCG's the most difficult part is acquiring the more hard to get cards: Epic, Legendary, Mythic cards etc. Well what Infinity Wars does to help you acquire cards is give you a booster each time you level which is incredibly helpful, as well as offer an in game trading option with other players.
Also for those of you that enjoy drafts, this game does it right. It is similar to MTGO and Hearthstone where as you pay a buy in to draft, but achieving the buy in amount is very easy to get. You could play against bots for half an hour or play in ranked matches, or even play with a friend to earn in game currency to quickly buy yourself into a draft. My favorite part about the drafts is you have a chance if you are successful enough to get your drafted deck for free, but you also have the option of purchasing the deck regardless of your success in the draft as well.
For those Hardcore TCG gamers out there that want a competitive ranked ladder in either draft or constructed its here in this game. And yes even though it is still in the earlier stages it is very well thought out, and adds a very unique gameplay experience to turn based strategy. The community in this game is very interactive and friendly as well. The global chat within the game allows you to converse with other players about strategies, trading, and practice.
Overall if you enjoy TCG's I highly reccomend "Infinity Wars". A very fun easy to enjoy gaming experience.

Interesting little game. It walks a bit of a line between games like Antichamber, Myst and Fez, where the environment is all you have to direct you through the puzzles and the world. While the visuals and puzzles are interesting, I don't think they match up to the standard of those three titles. There are a few great ones scattered and some secret content hidden throughout, bringing a game that is overall pretty fulfilling for a puzzle gamer. The later optional puzzles in particular are really quite difficult and I was unable to complete most of them without external help, speaking as somebody who completed Antichamber and all but two puzzles in Fez without needing to do so.
The sound and visuals work well together to build a nice atmosphere; the screenshots on the steam store speak for themselves. The mystery in the game starts to build up quite nicely as the game goes on, although I felt left wanting more of a final payoff.
A decent title for 4 hours or so, but only worth getting if you have already played and enjoyed both Antichamber and Fez, as I would say they are better games with similar audiences. It is not easy to find competent examples of freeform world puzzlers like this.

I love me a good choose-your-own-adventure, and the Assassin series is a solid option for those looking for a lot of charming little split paths. Orlandes in particular I feel is a better put together tale, and although the choices you make have less impact, it's a fairly well written story. Just keep in mind that this is a two part series, so to get the full charm and see the series miniature example of developer evolution, this isn't a bad place to start. The story follows your share of tropes and leads us off on a very gentle cliffhanger. The use of old school dice to determine encounters and sneak detection is a nice touch, and going on the highest difficulty will garuntee some roadbumps along the way and some surprising challenge for a choose your own adventure story, which definitely extends it out a bit.
The story is fairly standard, all being said, but what is important is that it's an enjoyable little journey. Is it worth the 10 dollar asking price? That's...tough. Even with all the branching paths, Orlandes is a short novella at best. The sequel, which has the same asking price, has a ton more content. On sale? Definitely worth the buy, but the price tag as of now is hefty. Orlandes is one to keep an eye on, and it will probably elicit that nostalgic feeling, even if it doesn't quite capture the charm of its predecessors.

Breath of Death is a retro-styled RPG solo campaign game. It features a fast turn-based combat, graphics reminiscent of 8-16bit RPGs, many dungeons and locations to delve and many more features. Its also a parody of other RPGs that came before, hence the the ridiculously long title that is apparently part of a series of games. I can’t imagine what game they could possibly be poking fun at with the title. The game takes many chances to poke fun at itself, at other RPGs and the characters as well. They also like to break the 4th wall from time to time too. But it all fits into the universe somehow without feeling awkward or thrown in. The campaign itself is around 4-6 hours with additional modes and difficulty levels to keep you challenged
There are quite a few interesting features to the combat and leveling up system. The leveling up system was fairly deep but simple to understand in this game. You had two choices anytime your character leveled up and each choice had its trade-offs. It could be that the one spell hit all enemies but for lower damage or you raised specific stats. This kept things simple when leveling up and I rather liked it. The leveling system seems to end at level 30 though and after level 30 you just get a simple stats boost. Which I actually like that the end of the leveling system is reachable. Some games have the end levels at such a high level you have to do a ridiculous amount of grinding to get the spells you want. BOD, thankfully, avoids doing that.
The turn-based combat system has a combo count system. The higher your combo count from attacks, the more damage certain combo-breaking attacks did to the enemy. And you have a pretty wide array of spells to choose from. However, some of these spells included combo breaking so you had to plan out how you were going to attack your enemy as well as keeping your companions alive. You’ll need to pull off those combo-breaking moves at the right time too because as each turn passes, your enemies grow in strength and hurt harder and harder every round. So this prevents you from using any sort of tanking strategy, you’ll have to take them down quickly.
Overall though, I didn’t find the combat system as satisfying as I would have liked. It was challenging enough, but I felt like it was in constant conflict with itself. Reason being is that in order to regenerate your magic points, which are needed for your techniques, was difficult to do. You couldn’t regenerate your magic points without either visiting an inn, finishing a battle quickly or find a save point. There were no potions to recover them. So even if you try and conserve your magic points, this can get you in trouble as the monsters hit harder and harder each turn. The conflict, to me, is that your only viable spells in this game are damaging attacks but so very often you needed to use very costly spells in order to survive all the monsters. This could lead you to getting stuck in the middle of the dungeon if you ran out of magic points all of the sudden. I felt like there should have been something added to make the techniques more interesting, rather than they just be primarily damaging attacks, healing or stat boosting abilities. Lita did have some techniques that let her bind or put enemies to sleep, but far too often the enemies would resist or be immune to it, so I quit bothering using them as the game progressed.
Breath of Death VII has fairly basic settings, unsurprising for a 2D game. It only supports 1280x720, 640x360 and fullscreen mode stretched. As BoD is light on effects, there isn’t any other visual settings to customize. The game does run superbly though and is very well optimized. Remapping and controllers are supported as well but not mouse inputs. It’s also got a reasonable soundtrack for such a "budget" game. I didn’t encounter any crashing or bugs during my playthrough.
Breath of Death VII: The Beginning is an interesting jRPG. There’s plenty of amusing references and humor to keep a somewhat dry story going. The battle system isn't my favorite. I feel like their efforts to refine the jRPG typical battle system has created conflicts. However, it does make sure you’re paying attention but can be frustrating at times. If you're into jRPGs, this is one to check out. It’s short and refined to a polished shine. Plus, its ridiculously cheap as it comes comboed with Cthulhu Saves the World. If you’re not wanting a 40 hour epic, give Breath of Death VII: The Beginning a try.

As with most JRPG’s you can find a wide variety of armour and weapons, each with their own special abilities. The only feature that separates this game from any other JRPG is its combat. Ultimately all this normally does is forces you to use the spells that cause the most damage, and subsequently use up the most of your magic points. After the battle is over your characters will regain full health and a portion of their magic points back. This seems cool at first, but it gets pretty repetitive. First, I want to say thank you. Thank you for putting bots into your game let alone bots with ranging difficulty. You have no idea what that means to a player like myself. Steamified has already featured a number of promising multiplayer titles that are local multiplayer only or if they do have online multiplayer that the game is dead on arrival because the developers and publishers don’t have the marketing budget to get a large enough playerbase for their pay to play game. Therefore if you’re going to have a game that is primarily a multiplayer game please include bots. They make a game that could otherwise be pointless to be developed – even if the concept is sound and the gameplay exciting – playable until such a point as your game has an active community or you make a group of like minded friends who are able to party with you.
This alone gives Bell Ringer a glimmer of hope. It’s not going to be DoA due to the inability to get a game going. However, that alone doesn’t mean that it has a saving grace. The game itself still needs to be good and polished if it is going to gain any sort of community at all. I personally believe that the March 6th release date is pretty optimistic. The game still needs a fair amount of work. For instance, the game will not recognize my Xbox One controller. The game states that it comes with full controller support. I would suggest that that it is partial at best – I have read others who have been able to use their controllers. The keyboard controls are average at best and downright scary at worst. If you want to have the ability for players to enjoy your title local co-op you need to fix the controls all of the way through. I know that the devs are working on this but we shall see how it progresses.
Another issue that I have to take issue with may be in part because I found the controls dodgy and that’s the difficulty level of the bots. Even the bots on the lower end of the difficulty spectrum tend to kick♥♥♥♥♥ A friend of mine who played the game is a fighting game genius – to the point where he has done extremely well in professional tournaments – and he agrees that the game needs to offer newbies a glimmer of hope and that he didn’t always win as comfortably as he generally would. On the higher difficulty settings this would be a beacon for action players of his level but if you’re new to the game and unable to sniff a victory there is a likelihood that you will give up before putting the time into get to the required level.
I’d also like to see more characters on release. Give the game some diversity. If I play a series of 5-player games it would be nice to see a round where there’s at least one different character in the mix. But that may be a wish list item rather than a realistic one.
The sound and the graphics are very generic. Too generic. But good sound costs money and it’s clear that this is a shoestring budget game and that a lot of resources would have gone into developing the AI of the bots, etc. to make the game playable which I would argue is more important than the aesthetics. However, I’d like to see them improved. The music on the menu systems is great and I’d like to advise that you incorporate some sort of soundtrack into the game to help hide the generic fighting sounds.
One final suggestion to the devs is to please reconsider your choice of trailer video on the Steam page. Yes, gameplay video is very important, but I believe firmly that you’re not doing justice to your game or advertising it very well with that trailer. Cut the menu crap out. Get to the gameplay. Add some music or something to it to make it sound and look more exciting. Right now it’s just a few people playing the game – people that we do not know and do not have a reason to care about. Perhaps do a character trailer where you show off each character. If you have an animator then give each character a comic book style story so that we have a reason to know and care about each fighter. Are any of them bad? Are any of them good? Are they anything but generic? What is their background? Why are they in this battle? Which characters are rivals and why? A relatively basic story trailer would add more depth not only to the trailer but to your game. It’s all a little plain and generic right now and you have room to grow.
If I have to say “yes” or “no” for right now then I’m going to give a cautious yes but that’s solely because of the bots. After playing a number of local multiplayer or dead online multiplayer games it’s a healthy sign to see a developer ensure that their game isn’t going to meet the same unfortunate fate that those games have.

Imagine, if you will, a sitcom. It's a sitcom about a topic you really like, so you check it out. You know these sitcoms where the laugh track is the only indication that something funny just happened? This is like one of these sitcoms, only without the laugh track. The title is by far the funniest part of this game. There are lots of jokes or, more accurately, things the devs thought would pass as jokes. The formula seemed to be as follows:
- Take classic JRPG trope.
- Put said trope in the game, with a note saying "think of funny subversion later".
- Get bored and work on something else.
The game ends up playing straight all of the things it's supposed to subvert, with a few schoolyard level jokes tacked on where there was space.
Now, imagine watching said sitcom (why are you doing that again?) with a controller in your hand. Imagine that every few seconds, the image freezes, and the only way to continue watching is to press the "A" button between four and seven bazillion times. "Silly me", you exclaim. "I forgot to turn on the difficulty!" So you press the difficulty button on your remote, and you find out that you are already on the highest possible difficulty. You start the game over on "easy", thinking that maybe there's a bug where the highest difficulty is actually the easiest one, and indeed, switching to easy has a significant advantage: You only have to press "A" between four and
bazillion times because the enemies have lower health now. Anyway, save for boss battles, the difficulty is of virtually no consequence. You have lots of fancy special moves to use in fights, a combo count to build up, mana points to manage, which is all fabulous except for the complete lack of a bloody difference it makes. There's just no incentive to get into all these intricacies of the battle system when you fare just as good spamming your basic attack over and over. After each battle, your health is fully restored, so it doesn't even matter how often you're hit, as long as at least one member of your party survives.
"Well then", I hear you say, "the battle system may be an unfortunate abomination of nature, but when I watch
, I have to hit my telly every few minutes to get a clear image too, so that's okay as long as I can enjoy the story." First off, go get a new television set. Second, to enjoy the story, there would have to be a story first. I haven't finished the game (in much the same way I didn't finish pouring that bucket of battery acid over there on my head), so maybe the story picks up somewhere after the two-hour-mark, but I doubt it. So far, it's been: "You're a hero. Supposedly witty comment. Go east and kill something. Unfunny joke. Now go north and kill something else." You get party members who are supposedly parodies of some kind. One wants to be a vampire! It's funny because everyone hates
! Why aren't you laughing yet! Said party members provide the crucial addition of being able to push the "A" button more often per round.
To summarize: I do not recommend buying this
game. Want a funny video game? Go play Monkey Island. Want a nice, retro JRPG? Go play the first few Final Fantasy. They even have a few jokes in them, which is more than I can say about this. Want to donate two quid to charity? I guess this would count.
I can't say anything about the bundled game, "Cthulhu Saves the World", because frankly, when I think about "playing" a second "game" from the same people, that bucket of acid suddenly seems oddly appealing.
Just my two
dollars, which I will never get back.

For me both games' exciting parts come in overwatch: will your weapon jam and leave you exposed to the superior melee skills of the genestealers? I am a turn-based board/table-top gamer at heart and I love game mechanics.
The fear that my men will get slaughtered and hence the greater excitement comes from SH due to the fact that only command points can be used to unjam your weapons in overwatch. SHA is easier as weapon jams come from weapon over heating that you can mitigate: (1) by obtaining in game skills gained by experience points (2) by practicing 2 or 3 man fire & movement team tactics (3) by using movement zones to get to killing zones ... (4) by finding a weapon's cache with Storm Bolters that have an additional 5+ heat capacity before jamming (if you are lucky like me} .
SH discussions about great suggested modifications to SH can be found, guess where? ... in SHA! And how do I know that, because I read the discussions silly and I play the games. As a person who has bought over 1200 games on Steam, and has bought more than 1200 not on Steam (I support game developers like I know you support fine art), and when have I been burned ??? When I don't do my home work ... when I don't read the forum discussions ... when I don't check out MetaCritic or do web searches for other reviews ... when I don't look for outside support and mod communities, ... and for me, most importantly the developers web sites and blogs.
And guess what, depending on how you are bent ... you may find a personal gem that has a big o' red thumbs down on Steam with mostly negative reviews with maybe barely 30% percent positive reviews ... I know I have some ,,, and one of them is on sale with Steam keys but not on Steam ... check out out
Final word (and as always a quote), if you are a shooter, platformer, action gamer both SH & SHA may not be your cup of tea. The best game of this type of genre is XCOM: Enemy Unknown using full game controller support right here on Steam or if you prefer on your X-Box ...

Much like the iOS game, this is game is inspired by the shortcuts you would find in rainbow road on mario kart. You race down a winding path with no edges and attempt to get down the farthest or the fastest (depending on mode)... to do that youll be flinging yourself off the edges and aiming for the track below to gain a huge advantage. They balance this by allowing you only 5 seconds off the track, meaning you have to pick your shortcuts carefully.
This game is VERY early access at the time of this review, with online multiplayer and career mode being absent. The modes and local multiplayer it does offer though I do feel justifies the price.
Survival mode is much like the iOS orginal in that you are just trying to get the farthest down the hill,  speed isnt a factor. This mode is great for high score challenges with friends.
Racing mode is a new addition, and like the name suggests youre racing down a predetermined length course against ai or local opponets. When online multiplayer is completed I expect this to be the main mode I play.
And time atack mode, which has you going through gates every 10 check points to gain more time to go farther. In my opinion this mode goes against the spirit of the game but it does offer an interesting challenge as the check points get farther and farther away.
All in all its far superior to its iOS counterpart, the controller support alone accomplishes that. A game where you spot your landing like this just doesnt work great when youre tilting your screen around. At 8 bucks I feel like there is enough there right now to justify the purchase, but waiting for updates and a sale may be your best bet if you arent sure from the trailer and this review.

Have you ever felt like commanding a small squad of troops that sound like they are wearing refrigerators, then by all means buy this game.  Your warriors of the emperor die in battle against what look like horrible 1950's aliens again and again, yet strangely it's so wonderful to hear them shoot away.
So, lets do it:
Pros:
Terminators.  If you know your 40K, you know they are awesome.
First person view on the corner (can be toggled off if you don't care, but honestly I love it)
SLLLLLOOOOOWWWWW walk, considering the weight of the units every step feels very purposeful.  If it bothers you, there is a toggle where you can turn off this feature and they walk pretty much like a character in CoD (Movement is pretty fast at that point).
A good solid difficulty, worthy of Space Hulk (alot of 40K games give Space Marines way too much epicness... but this game makes you fear melee against genestealers)
If you get the DLC you have 2 sides with quite a bit of variety in strategy.
Cons:
Your troops will annoyingly move in ways you don't intend.
Overwatch is nice, but previous point makes the skill somewhat useless if you get unlucky with placement.
Due to the randomness of dice roll based games, situations where you obviously have the advantage can still go wrong.  Not to knock the game per say, just a warning that there will be times where you think 'Oh there is no way that genestealer can run through 3 tiles of flame and melee my captain and win.' But it does.  And you cry.
Would I recomend this game?  Yes.  I love 40K based games, and played Space Hulk on the Sega Saturn way back.  I will say this game is much better (god the melee in that game... was horrible...) but something needs to be said for a first person game in this universe.  This game is interesting, with quite a ton of frustration and elation... think darksouls the strategy game almost.  It is amazing.

A great mix of Spelunky, skill trees, stealth and steampunk! You have 100 days to gear up for the big heist by breaking into buildings to hack computers to steal money in order to buy upgrades to help you circumvent the increasily secure buildings with a variety of new enemies at every turn. The levels are procedurally generated so you have to be equipped to handle any number of situations.
It's a tough game that will require multiple play throughs because you have to learn about all the new obstacles and enemies as you encounter them and as you're figuring out the systems you're rapidly running out of time. I barely made it to the 3rd "area" in my first run before I ran out of time and had to start over again.
But as you improve it's a lot of fun trying to get that one really strong run where you're figuring out the best way to most efficiently purchase upgrades while also unlocking new areas. Do you save up for a new tool or do you risk going to the next area knowing that hacking even one computer will give you more money than three computers from the previous area?
I still haven't beat it but I've come oh so close and happily started a new game hoping that the next run would be better. If you're looking to beat a game in one sitting this isn't for you. But if you want to play a game that you gradually get better at playing and optimizing how you unlock your skill tree as you play then by all means play this game!
Once you get into the groove of successful heists it's very easy to get into the "one more try" mentality and easily burn away hours at a time.

This is the third time straight I threw my keyboard away in frustration.
Don't get me wrong, this is an amazing game, very smooth control, various enemies, big exploring world, amazing art and music, all the essential parts of a masterpiece. However, somehow a few features in the game design really ruined the experience. Game like this expects players to learn and improve from all the challenges and feel satisfied in the process, but somehow I was buried only in frustration. In short, I was expecting another castlevania, but this game is a harsher version of dark soul in disguise.
1. Healing. At the very beginning, I enjoyed the healing mechanism a lot. Very smart design, give you good sustain in fighting minions meanwhile train you to control pace in boss fight. It was until I started to run into mini boss and multiple fast-hitting minion combos, did I learn how incovenient it was in fight.  If you look at dark soul, drinking potion slows your movement meanwhile allows you to survive maybe another couple hits. Here you have to stand still for almost a second to recover one hp. If the healing is interrupted, you waste your soul. In a fast-pace fight, healing no longer serves as the important "oh-crap" button. You make a big mistake, this run is ruined.
2. Recovering from hit. After you get hit, the time you are immune from next hit is very short. So if you are cornered, facing multiple charging enemies in a low archway, you die in a couple seconds, without knowing what just happened or how you can improve next time. In the end, I gave up finding a skillful solution, but spammed attack and magic and bid on enemies die faster than I do. Combining with the first point above, this makes first time encounter of enemy/terrain combination very punishing. Usually, you will die.
3. Introducing mini-boss. It's the most brutal way I've seen to introduce a new enemy: You walk into a room with no warning. All of a sudden, all entrances are locked, and a brand new enemy jumps out and spams new attack patterns you never see. It's basically a surprise death-cage that ensures your death. Death itself is ok, but imagine if you have only 2 hp left, 1000 Geo in the pocket, and are struggling to find the next rest point, this is probably the last surprise you want to encounter. Castlevania series are good examples actually. They either mark it loud and clear: here is a boss, or allow you to retreat and fight another day. Been forced into a death duel with severe punishment and without notice is very frustrating.
4. Rest point. Previously we mentioned, in this game, you die a lot. Thus rest point is very important. It establishes a solid starting point from which you explore the surrounding, and helps you control time and Geo loss upon death. Thus player missed a rest point or cannot access to a rest point can be a severe problem. Unfortunately in this game, it happens. In Greenpath, I stumbled into boss before I find the neaby rest point. In City of Tears, I died a couple times (yes, death cages), lost all my Geos before I reached the central rest point with 2 hp. The rest point requires 200 Geos (more or less) to active! I died again when collecting those Geos, and had to re-run half a map. On those deaths I did't feel challenged, I felt unfair and frustrated.
5. Map. In this game, if you don't find and buy map for a region, the map is disabled. Before you rest, the map doesn't update your progress. Designer might think it's a good challenge and achievement, but to me, it's extra salt in the wound.  The first time I explore a new map is my most vulnerable time, new terrain trap to worry about, new enemy pattern to learn, estimate if my resource could support me to the next rest point (which I don't know where). Disable the map only make the process harder. A more helpful setting could be, player could explore and record map freely, and if you find and buy the map, you get a detailed version with rest point marked.
Any of the above issue alone shouldn't be a big problem. But combined together, it results in my miserable experience:
stumble into a new area (no map)-> explore deep into the area, resources half drained, get some decent Geos in hand ->
cannot find new rest point, start to concern if I should return to previous point and save the Geos or risk forward -> get caught in death cage and died ->  run map again to pick up the Geos, since die again means losing all Geos, I don't dare do a speed run, but carefully clean the path and proceed -> should I challenge the death cage without a nearby rest point? -> change route, get caught in another death cage and died -> repeat
I stumbled into Crystal Peak through the dark tunnel, explored about half of the area, didn't find the map or rest point, died 3 times, lost Geos once since I cannot locate last death place without map, and finally decided to retreat from the area. Then I know I am done with it.
To Developers:
Sorry I really want to enjoy this game. It's the most polished metroidvania indie game I've ever played.
Yet comparing with original castlevania series, the game system makes it too punishing for me.
And some personal thought: A few well placed shortcuts/secret tunnels would be a plus for metroidvania games. But a dozen iron gates block the way with switch on the other side in a single map just irritates me.

The first gamebook by Tin Man Games on mobile previously, and certainly my favourite among the franchise, A nice plot-twist saves the plot from being a run-of-the-mill variety.
The story flow is good, and choices in the book made sense (eg. if you don't know where to find someone it's game over). It might be annoying to some people to have managed to make it so far into the story, only to get a gameover because they didn't have x item or y information, but it feels realistic and adds to replayability (especially since gamebooks from this company have more than one path to choose from when travelling from one point of the story to another).
Also, just note that most, if not all of the gamebooks from this company has an encounter early in the story that can make or break the game (gameover) far into the story.
There are beautiful, well-drawn illustrations scattered in the book relevant to the story passage at the time they appear. Music is pretty pleasant and didn't break immersion when reading the text.
I like how the achievements are mostly there to hint to you that there are still parts of the story you haven't seen or experienced, rather than just placed there for overachievers.
Give it a try if you're a fan of gamebooks and a good story, try to give this game a try.
Can't wait to play the sequel. :)

This is a straightforward digital adaptation of an old choose your own adventure book. If you're nostalgic about that style of book, you'll get a couple hours of enjoyment from this game. The problem is that, outside of nostalgia, the choose your own adventure books haven't aged very well.
If you don't know the genre already, you read a few paragraphs of text, then you either make a decision, you roll a "fitness test," or you fight something. If you hear "decisions" and start expecting Telltale Games style moral choices you're going to be disappointed. Most decisions can be summarized as "you're running down a hallway, do you turn left or right?" That could still be interesting in a puzzle-y way, but there's typically no reason to prefer one direction over another. The fitness tests and combat can be summarized as "you roll some dice, and then you either succeed or you die." There is no meaningful strategy on the combat and if you fail you just die and have to redo the combat until you succeed or switch to "casual" mode and skip over it.
These types of gamebooks were fun back in the day, and I enjoy them in a nostalgiac way; but there's no reason to play this other than nostalgia. If you want a fantasy game, I'd reccomend you look up the old D&D games on
instead.
EDIT: Almost forgot. The other reviews mention it, but I'll repeat it. The achievements are broken for a lot of people, and the developers haven't, to my knowledge, said when they'll be fixed. If that's important to you, keep it in mind.

A choose-your-own adventure with dice.
~2 hours of story, more if you explore every story branch. Steam achievements are currently not working.
It's a book, but it's not. That can be positive (sound effects and music) and negative because you have to roll the dice to progress and you can't just leaf through it afterwards. Storywise, you're on a typical RPG adventure, you'll roll for combat and fitness checks every corner and die a lot. Which means you start over, maybe try a new path which still leads you through similar choke points until you die again. I did this 3 times on three different days because when the game makes you stop reading a story because of a virtual dice role that is frustrating, and then I switched the game from "classic" mode to "casual", which means it now works more the way I want it: I can just bypass the fights and checks and read on as if I'd won. And then I skip through half of the story which I've already seen in previous attempts (except the game can't skip like some Visual Novels do, you have to leaf through it and dice through it page by page) and get the rest of the humdrum fantasy campaign: betrayal, sorcery, nefarious doings that our hero thwarts, but not really anything in the way of character development or in fact anything that would make me think or feel.
High point of the writing was the time I died from a piece of timber that was floating towards me while swimming in the river. True, it was fairly menacing, with sharp bits and nails poking out, but still it must've been really determined, or the water was just flowing much faster for that piece of wood than it was for me.
So, I don't exactly recommend this; I've seen free visual novels that were better than this. If you do play this, choose "Casual Mode" when you start out; contrary to what the instructions say, it plays exactly like classic mode except you get more bookmarks and some "cheat" buttons - you could resolve not to use them (and only use 3 bookmarks max) and see if you make it, and if you don't you won't have to start over.

When i got ‘Shadow Warrior’ at its release in September 2013, i thought it was one of those titles, which only wraps it’s original game by 3D Realms in a new graphical enviroment. The thing i have totally ignored is that there is an actually well thought shooter behind the cheap one liners and mediocre graphics.
You play Lo Wang, a hitman/ninja under contract of Zilla, who is leading a huge corporation, who orders Wang to pick up a sword for two million dollars, but as soon you arrive, everything goes south and you find yourself in a Kill Bill-esc swordfight. At this point the world is overrun by demons and destroying the area you are in, where you end up half dead in a burning house, that leads you to meet Hoji, a mysterious and weird demon, who was with the man you supposed to buy the sword from. You both agree to work together to get the sword back to give him the chance to return to his old home: The Shadow Realm.
With a story arc like that, you immediately feel like in an 80s B-movie, which the game perfectly set the tone in this way by starting off the game with Wang sitting in his car, jamming to Stan Bush’s ‘The Touch’ and Flying Wild Hog (the developers) bombarding you with cheap one liners, which Wang not coming up with on his own, rather to his knowledge of comic books and his affection to B movies himself, which I, in my first playthrough attempt, totally ignored, even though it helps the tone of the story a lot, because it still has a chance to change it’s pace to a more serious tone, which it actually did and did well. I got super drawn into the progression of the Wang’s trip to ‘hell’.
Since Lo is a ninja, he is good with a blade and since the katana — called the Nobitsura Kage — you were supposed to pick up ends up in your hands, you are going to use it in all its capabilities, which becomes a main portion in the game, where you learn via picking up KI stones over time a bunch of skills. The way to execute those abilities are pretty easy to learn and execute, but being very similar to each other that you may end up looking up which one was which, but did not hurt the overall experience at all. I was very surprised by how fun it was, even though you will never encounter a blade on blade grinding sword fight.
Wang is a hitman as well, so he knows how to use guns, which you pick up the typical variety of weapons throughout the game that are upgradable through money that you can pick up in the levels. They feel pretty basic and not really satisfying, but i can forgive that, since they are not the main focus and in context totally fine, but i wished for that extra ‘oomph’, that Shadow Warrior couldnt deliver.
You are also able to learn passive abilities, resulting in things like more HP, damage resistance, more stamina and so on by collecting Karma, which you get by killing enemies and by chaining kills together, multipling the score of the staged fights.
I really liked the variety of enemies in here, giving every monster and human a distinctive look and feel, keeping ‘annoying’ types at a minimum and thanks to the game’s self awareness can’t hold itself back to comment on them, too, which was a nice move by Flying Wild Hog. But the time you actually have to fight them, it is a fun and challenging experience. The way it introduces new enemies to you is very good to understand, giving you enough time and chances to understand every enemy’s capabilities and weak points.
Sadly, even with it’s pretty neat animation work troughout and really good lighting effects, the game will/has not age(d) well, thanks to its pretty basic visuals in the level enviroment department. Some areas feel way too stretched, copy-pasted and boring, which could be the result of trying to hide the many secret areas (that not only are being extra Karma pools or Ki stones, even some levels mapped in the original Shadow Warrior’s early 3D artstyle, giving a nod like some other games did before, but definitely nice to see). Don’t get me wrong. The game looks pretty good, but its not blowing your socks off.
The sound design was fine, i did not get angered by bad sound choices here, more a bit confused that the video cutscenes are a bit lower than the actual game, but not by a huge margin. Everything sounds pretty solid, so there is nothing to complain about.
All in all, this game is not only an oldschool game with new shoes on, it’s an improvement with very good 2013 gameplay mechanics, an actually very cool and interesting story with a fun main character and sidekick, which lets you forgive it’s mediocre graphics. The only thing that holds me back to play this 9 hours and 30 minutes trip is that i won’t keep the sword in the New Game+ (here called EX mode), which is a huge bummer. Otherwise, if you like skilled based shooters, this one is for you and i can not wait for the second one to arrive.

This is a great game, with a lot of polish, which is let down by a few minor flaws which unfortunately, impact the enjoyability quite a lot.
I wanna start out by saying, I really enjoy the gameplay, its punchy, fun, the controls are solid(despite a couple of bugbears), the upgrades all very cool, a diverse range of enemies/locations, and different ways of tackling each level.
However, the first thing anyone will notice is your 100 day limit, which I was first put off by. As I got into the game I warmed to the idea, even with there being no New Game+ or what not.
Heres the first issue, the start of the game is a SLOW SLOG. Its great the first time around, as you open new stuff and work out what you want, but on subsequent playthroughs it becomes more than a chore, if becomes infuriating.
You will be rerolling a lot too, as your time ticks down and you realise that there is no way you are going to make it.
This is another issue, the idea might be that you need to race to the end, but all too often you get 3/4s and just shrug and say 'bleh'. You know you aren't going to make it, and have to go through all that slog again, before you can get to the cool bits where you are nimbly jaunting around.
The main reason this feels like a slog, is due to the fact you are going to feel cheated. Quite often.
At the start it will be things such as being placed in buildings you just cant escape. Fine, you arent outfitted for it, but your only option is suicide. Its particularly frustrating when you hit two or three in a row.
The enemies will sometimes spawn in such strnge ways, and once again early on that it makes stuff impassable. Enemies that will appear on single blocks, with a mine on it also, with a camera above it. Thats one example and by far not the worst, where it feels less like you dont have the skill so much as... well there werent enough variables set up for building the levels.
It all too often also feels as if the AI bugs out, floating cameras move slowly for most parts, then sometimes will turn on a dime, in a split second.
You cant get out of the way, and thats another GG.
There is no rhyme or reason to their patrolling either, nothing you can guage, and often, you will spend five minutes just waiting... waiting for the cameras to all align.
I remember reading that the dev hated tropes of stealth games, this one is the worst, and then some. You simply cant read certain situations, and have to just sit on your hands.
The controls are fairly solid, yet then in minor places fall short. The biggest example of this is when you run into a spike pit, with a roof directly overhead. Sometimes youll make the jump, other times youll smash your double jump to oblivion and still fall in. Tbh, I think there should be a variable not allowing a spike pit in this situation, its just kinda ridic.
Youll also often find yourself in a situation where you will cling to a wall at a bad time, you are lining up a jump attack or what not, and you dont THINK you are close to the wall, then bam.
All of this mixes into a milkshake of frustration, where it steps over the line of so many Rogues before it. In all the games of this type I love, I never feel cheated, theres always something to push me to try again, and the knowledge that the next time I will progress a bit further, with the aid of extra exp, or cash, or whatever.
The opposite is true here, and the fact is you avoid going to new areas due to a lot of these things. People seem to stick to farming Zones 2/3, which once you work out how the bonuses work seems a legit strategy.
By putting a time limit on it, and not giving any boosts on subsequent playthroughs, most people wont see the majority of the game. Thats a damned shame.
I've been fairly critical here, so I want to reinforce that I really like this game. It has a lot of heart, the fact is I just dont know whether it will have enough to keep bringing me back.
The dev has said they are happy with how it stands, and have no plans for adding an unlimited mode. If I could at least aim for a mode that let me just continue to enjoy and play through the gameplay (thats really why Im here, not the story, as good as it is, sorry) I think I would be happy.
But the thought of having to do that slog over and over? Often because I feel cheated? Eh...
This is one of those games that seems like it could have done really well on EA, with a wider demo giving feedback. Im not sure how they tested this, but it feels like it is a mere month or so of tweaking/feedback away from absolute brilliance.
As it stands, its just pretty good.

Absolutely incredible. Gameplay is similar to Civ V only better. There is a lot more decision making that makes you feel as if you were actually in charge of a civilization, and the results have real, almost tangible effects on the game. I felt like I was discovering a whole new world the entire time and really strategizing my resources and decisions, whereas Civ V, I often find myself in the same worlds making the same decisions. Here, the victory combinations and outcomes are endless. My favorite component of the game are the quests. It gave me something to do and incentives to build improvements, fight aliens, go on spy missions, etc. Similar to the quests given by city-states, but self-paced (no turn limit), no diplomatic pressure, and better rewards.
AI is much better. I played for about 185 turns and no one declared war on me. I also didn't feel as if someone were nagging me every two turns. There are no city-states, per-se, but there are stations you can establish trade routes with and the benefits are much better (more science, culture, etc.). No one begged me for money, either, which was nice. There was lots of room for expansion, even on the standard map, so border issues were almost non-existent, save one time I discovered artifacts near Brazil. You also get to choose missions for your spies and what they can steal (if they succeed). Alien personalities were pretty random and I had a few explorers killed, but not as much of a nuisance as the barbarians in Civ V. Never felt as if I had to constantly protect my workers or colonists, and they didn't pillage tiles nearly as often.
Few drawbacks: 1.) Resources and their management. Rather than relying on the a few basic improvements/resource types (quarries, mines, plantations, etc.) there are a lot more resources (which I liked), and most of them have specific improvements that need to be discovered by exploring the tech web. Thus, resources take a lot longer to obtain, are more scarce and harder to trade, and can drastically effect game play depending on your location and what type of victory you're aiming for 2.) I was a bit confused as to how expeditions work. I did a few, but there were times I would bring my explorer to an expedition site and couldn't do anything. This could very well be a big that requires what I imagine to be a small patch, but nonetheless it was a bit off-putting. 3.)The miasma was an inconvenience.
Overall, the strategic value and adventure in this game off-set these things. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys any games from the Civ series and anyone looking for a strategy game that really puts you in control. Still haven't finished the current game I'm on (I believe I left off at turn 185 which put me around 2900 AD from what I remember) or tried multiplayer, but I can't wait to see what else this game has in store. Overall score: 92/100.
