This game, what it tries to do? Wonderful.
Tries, being the keyword. More often than not the controls are sluggish, your character doesn't respond. There's no way to easily fall off the edge of a ledge, instead prompting you to begin sliding down it - which is ruinous for most runs.
You can be having a perfectly fine run, killing all the robots as you explore the house - only for yourself to realize that every computer is underneath four layers of concrete, disjointed from each other - which effectively makes the level entirely worthless because Computers are the main way you net cash. Thank you random generation!
The start of the game is -very- rough, where if you don't do the first area for at least 10 days, and buy Hacking for electrical doors, as well as double jump - you'll face many warehouse missions (I wasted six days in a row, on three different new games) where you simply cannot enter the facalities at all, or if you can it's begging for immediate death. In an effort to keep things fresh, there's lovely randomly generation - you more often than not get scenarios that are simply unbeatable, where computers are swarmed with two robots on a 1x cube, with spikes on either side of them with a camera scanning the room - and the computer to turn off said camera? Is the room directly past it. Where every window inside is guarded by a camera, that you're lucky at best if the controls work with you well enough to allow you to break through it, and jump onto a wall out of it's Line of Sight quickly enough.
This could be construded as 'They're just whining about the game being too hard!' but it really isn't. There's very simple things, and very simple mistakes that you'll be cursing at yourself over, and over, and over again - suddenly realizing you're on Day 20 with a handful of upgrades and fewer results from broken levels, half-broken controls, and awful enemy AI. Sure, I can be immediately noticed while I'm falling off the side of a window at escape velocity. Sure, the camera that saw me with less than three pixels wide of Line of Sight (It's clearly and physically marked) knew for certain there was a burgalur.
It has heart, but the mechanics just aren't there. They need to be tweaked and refined. Maybe if there's some updates? That'd be great. Before then? It's fun, before you hit your first randomly generation mission that calls for an immediate and outright alert, or death to get -anything- from, resulting in yet another wasted day.

The Swindle (2015)
Developed by: Size Five Games
Release date: 7-28-15
Retail Cost: $14.99
Story:
•	Set in a cyber-steampunk future in London, 1849 you have 100 days to keep Scotland Yard from activating their new AI system (think Big Brother) that will end your life as a master thief.
Gameplay:
•	A steampunk and stylish side-scrolling stealth-based platformer
•	You will absolutely, positively want to use a controller for this one
•	Even with a controller this game is pretty darn difficult! But fun.
•	Procedurally generated levels; not really a roguelike but had a lot of RPG flair to it
•	Start from the ground up; sneak around and steal the cash needed to buy upgrades in order to pull of heists in more challenging maps for bigger rewards
•	Levels change as you replay them and do amp up in difficulty on subsequent playthroughs.
•	If you don't make it back to your airship (yes, airship) alive you lose any money you found in a level.  There are no rewards for failure to be found in The Swindle.
•	Unique randomized characters - If you fail a mission your prior character is "terminated" and replaced with a new one.  There is no loss of your already purchased upgrades.
•	Upgrades are useful and can be quite expensive.  You really earn your way up the ability ladder in this game. (*ahem* Buy the $100.00 Hack upgrade first)
•	Over 50 skills and tools to upgrade each with different prices
•	You start out being able to blackjack cops when their backs are turned.  If they catch you with their flashlight the alarm goes off and you have to bail.
•	Falling to far and dying is a very, very real threat.
•	You have 100 "days" (Mission attempts) to complete the last heist AKA. "The Swindle" but you have to work through the first 5 missions and earn clearance to get there
•	You can get in an inescapable situation.  If you fall into a room and can't double jump out because you lack that ability, for example. The only option is to self-terminate and start the next day with a new thief.
•	Sometimes the procedurally generated levels are a little... weird.  This part of the game could use some fine tuning and it could be great.
•	Would be nice if the skill tree showed skills you could afford as the menu is difficult to navigate.
Graphics:
•	The main appeal of this game is it's art direction and setting.  Everything looks really cool, is true to the genre and is animated well.
•	I really enjoyed each new character that was generated.  They all look really unique and fit in with the overall aesthetic of the game.  I even had fun with the new names that they were given.
•	If you liked how Don't Stave looked then The Swindle is going to be right up your alley.
Sound:
•	FX: The sound effects in The Swindle are really, really good. The crack of your blackjack is satisfying and the alarms going off is nerve wracking.
•	Music:  I was really impressed with the score in this game.  The music is suspenseful and when you get caught it is super exciting.  It amps up the gameplay to that next degree.
•	Voice Acting: The is no voice acting (at least in the levels I played) in The Swindle, but it doesn't detract from the experience.
Final Verdict:
•	The Swindle is a very fun and often frustrating game to play.  So of course I really loved it.  You get really invested in surviving when your entire paycheck is on the line!  Its a neat take on the genre and I think it holds it's own.  It is priced appropriately and seems open to a lot of new content opportunities if the developers choose to go that direction.  I can't wait to see if I can actually make it to the last level!
I was provided a copy of The Swindle for review purposes. My opinions and recommendations are my own.

Don't listen to the reviews saying even die-hard fans should stay away, it's one of the best 3D Stronghold games in the series. A mostly decent castle rts with a few holes, some losses, but  many new features (including achievements).  I don't understand why some reviewers tore it to shreds, have they really played all of the Stronghold games?  It's definitely not complete trash and better than most of the lesser "3D" Strongholds for sure.
Gameplay: Overall, the game objective remains the same - build your castle and economy, make troops, conquer the enemy through a series of skermish trails.  Like Crusader I, the sequel also focuses more on wartime than peace-time - so you will find more war and defense buildings and less economy peacetime buildings. Too much disappointment, the Fear Factor system has been removed...seriously, what the hell? Production is stuck at slow as hell now.  Economic management has been improved with the lovely "automatic trades"  at the market and finer tuned popularity management with supply adjustments all made in a single window.  You can also see your daily production & consumption levels of popularity supporting goods to be sure the production meets the need. Troops vary from many familiar to several new troops as well.  New troops include some most-powerful "leader" troops that will boost the defense and attack for certain troops around them - Sergent for Knights, Slave Master for Slaves. A few favorites from Crusader I were unfortunately replaced with new troops too .  Keeping them all and adding on would have been better...I miss the underrated rock throwers.
Difficulty: Difficultly has been taken up a notch as Enemy AI loves to rush your castle early.  Even the weaker known AI such as The Rat will provide a greater challenge.  Some players say the enemy AI cheats more too and spawns many troops regardless of how bad their popularity and economy are doing.  Mastering stategic defense early is utmost importance, troops (towers & crossbowmen) must be made before much of the economy.  Popularity responds significantly faster to your economy now with negative and positive ratings immediately affecting your peasants - i.e. the moment your popularity drops, workers start leaving in seconds!!  Also castles are more expensive to build with stone walls costing 7 stone each and stone curtains being 3 stone...stone stocks too low sir!!
Performance:  The game runs fine until your castle starts filling up with tons of buildings (Bakers, Brewers, Hovels), peasants, and troops.  Then even systems with a Radeon R9 3GB+ will have frame rates of around 25ish.  This isn't a bad console port and they really should optimize the code further.  It's not horrible  and I still enjoy the game plenty regardless, but it is funny that my system also runs Fallout 4 around 45-60fps on max graphics... Many of the major glitches and flaws noted by early reviewers are now patched up and gone, however I do still rarely see the "crusified troops" glitch where they walk in a frozen T position for a bit or also troops getting stuck on the stairs. Also the audio for catapult rocks hitting stone structures and walls is overloaded and WAY TOO LOUD.
Visual:  The graphics are similar to Stronghold 3 and perhaps even better. The animations are about the same too.  The enemy AI FMVs have been completely redone with entirely new and goofier looking characters for classic familiar foes and many new adversaries.  The interface really varies from a crappy low res title screen of an assassin (come on, looks like crap) to a nicely done very zen feeling skirmish trail amongst the stars.  Some recycled troop graphics from Stronghold 3 for sure.
Audio:  A mix of half recycled, half new when it comes to effects and music - perhaps more new.  This is typical for Stronghold games.  Music really varies, but I feel it is not randomized enough and many tracks are rarely heard while a few are played too often.  Classic familiar AI features new voice acting that is a complete joke compared to the much more intimidating classic voice acting.  The Pig now says things like, "No No No, that's ma land!" compared to "I WILL CRUSH YOU!!! I WILL KIWWLLL YOU!!!." The Rat is also more dull and bore with phrases like, "My father didn't like ya, I don't like ya either." Blah.  The newer non-familiar enemy voiceacting (mostly arabic tyrants) does seem to be higher quality and more charismatic charm though.  Lionheart seems decent enough too actually.
Conclusion: A worthy castle sim gameplay for many new and veteran fans alike but nothing perfect or AAA.  Die-hard fans shall enjoy the new features plenty to make up for the loss of some favored features.  It's not the best RTS and there are flaws, but it's still pretty fun and easily to get lost in for hours.  Firefly always releases these too early in development, but I luckily began to play after much of the final development.  I'd say grab it on sale, and definitely wait for the DLC to go on sale.  The main game is tough and should offer plenty while waiting on the DLC.

I have played this game with a couple of different friends via the online multiplayer.  It can take a few tries for the other person to be join the game.  This game requires a lot of coordination between the two players.  It helps if you have a voice chat going while playing.
How hard or easy this game is really depends on what rooms you initially get.  Some are relatively easy, and other can take many attempts to get right.  For example, one room has a bull where both players are wearing "attention hats".  When you turn a hat on, then it will charge at you.  You turn it off before it gets to you and get out of the way for it to kill stuff for you.  The trick in this room is for each person to take turns calling the bull.  Once you have it down, it feels a bit like a coordinated dance.  Even so, the final two bugs that need to be killed by the bull are tricky since you do not have much space to navigate in the last area for that room.  My friend and I died several times before we finally got through that room.
Once you get through five rooms, you get to an intermediate area and then can do the next route.  At first the routes are randomly chosen, but once you do enough rooms, you can start to choose the path you take.  Each room is fairly unique in requiring different types of coordination.  Some rooms have more of a puzzle nature figuring out the right sequence to get through the room, while others require more team coordination.
Overall, for what this game is, it is pretty good.  It is only for playing with one other person online, preferably someone you know and can work easily with.

The Firefly team has been slowly going downhill, backwards. Even if I had not started with Stronghold 1, I would not
reccomend this game.
- Difficulty. The programmers confused cheating with difficulty. What this essentially means is the moment you have finally breached the castle walls, the AI will instantly spawn a very large amount of troops to flood you, then instantly repair the breach.
- Economy. While you certainly have to tend to yours, the AI does not. Destroying farms, mines, quarries, food, does nothing to slow down or stop the AI. While it appears they are spending money, they are not and can always afford anything.
- Rushes. The campaign is an exercise in defending against rushes. Remember the cheating thing? Combine that with a rush. Takes 30 seconds for a fully grown AI to be outside your castle with catapults, torches, and enough to kill your Lord, meanwhile your fletcher has not even gotten to his workshop yet.
- Defensive ability. All you have to defend yourself are walls. That is it. No moats. Hoarding is killed by a couple arrows, and arrows tend to simply pass right through it. No real way to create a defence besides building more walls. Walls that have to constantly be tended to due the the sheer catapult rush the AI throws at you. No engineers to help either. And Walls are super expensive to build, which wouldnt be an issue if I did not require so much time to tend to them.
It wants to be good, but falls flat. Play Stronghold 1, 2, and Crusader 1.

[This gets more comprehensive as I go, I swear.]
Shadow Warrior places you in the size 5's of Lil Wang, an aspiring tattoo artist, working as an intern for a vaguely communist law firm. Your boss sends you out on a coffee run and to see if the Soul Edge is still on sale at the local Trader Joes, only to find that the manager stole it, and a 55in plasma when they canned him for taking panty shots of ladies in the restroom. After a brief and harrowing stay in the stores dog kennel, you find the guy dead, a victim of his own clumsy handling of a Baby's First Meth Lab, and blows himself up to death, and dies. But, also being messed up from falling through the roof, his demon bro, Hojo, decides to aid you on your coffee run. And also something about his world being on fire 24/7. Hojo lives in east LA. So you, Wang, make a deal to save the planet California, in exchange for Hojo not letting you burn up in the exploded guest house behind Trader Joes. You agree, and then the rest of the game is you skull-murder-f**king 2 dimensions into oblivion. I didn't pay much attention to the story, to be honest.
The murder everything mechanics are meaty, and the sword feels like you're actually ace at it, even when you're just blind-fire swinging at a crowd. The enemy types, while not many, are diverse and require you to adapt to defeat them. They come in Chump, Flying Chump, Suicide Bomber, Giant Elfromancer, other guy, and Shadow of Colossus. Frankly, there wasn't any one point where I was bored. Even though I beat it on filthy casual setting there were spots that got a bit intense. The level design is pretty darn good, with secrets and hidden homages to the classic 1967 version (called 'retro zones') that feature pixelated lewdness. Which is comical. Humor goes a long way with me. The dialogue and voice acting is [mostly] great, and the banter between Wang and Hoji cant get to be a riot. I like that the satire was constant, being self-aware without breaking the '4th wall'. Audibly, the music and effects are great and mix well with the environment and situation (e.g. battle music / idle music) Visually, it's pretty impressive and runs like silk on my mediocre-a$$ hardware, so fps drops weren't an issue during big, gory battles. The controls, as far as the chi-techniques, sometimes got a little annoying. Remembering what does what got a little frustrating during big battles. It may have been my KB (getting worn out), but there was a sense of input lag even while switching weapons and interacting with objects. The story (like I said, I didn't pay much mind) was a little underwhelming, but who cares? I have a 4 barreled shotgun. GG.

Well this definitely is a strange one.
To those that message me every time I write a recommendation saying “you write long recommendations” … THIS is going to be a long one.
I have a thing for first person puzzle games at the moment, and I was rather intrigued by this games trailer and description. I think what interested me most, was the sense of ‘mystery’ that I got from the trailer. It doesn’t tell you what it is about, or why you are there or what’s going on… and to be honest this game has a real mysterious feel to it throughout the whole thing, you’re asking yourself questions on the who, what and whys but in fairness they aren’t answered all that clearly.
And that isn’t necessarily a bad thing.
I think games that are open to interpretation are great in their own way. The whole mystery and wonder to this game is great and all, but the structure and direction can sometimes make you just feel lost. At least for me anyways, that’s just my opinion of course, but there was a few times during the play through that I just asked, what the hell am I supposed to be doing here…
The puzzles themselves are very interesting, they are creative, they really make you think and make you put things together in ways that I’m not really used to. They are unique kinds of puzzles and there is a lot of symbols and shapes and colours that you have to try and think about what they might mean and what the logic behind the puzzle might be.
The music in the game is very moody, it really brings out that feel of the game. Which for me was quite cold, and dull. There isn’t really a whole lot of “bright” warm colours in the game, there is still colour, but it feels dulled down. There’s also a lot of white in the game, which some people may think ‘pfft well that’s “bright”’ but to me it’s an empty kind of white. The whole game is set in ancient looking dull buildings with strange structures and dull empty colours. You’re on your own with no one around and no one to comfort you but these strange surroundings and sounds and noises that give it a little bit of a creepy twitch to it.
Personally, I liked this game. With the high amount of positive reviews, I wanted to point out some of the flaws of this game that made it hard for me to truly enjoy it. It is not bad, and the pixelated graphics give nice retro feel to the whole experience, while telling a futuristic cyberpunk story. Some of the characters were nice to follow. Some puzzles could be solved in a few ways, unlocking different achievements. Overall I kept playing this game, which is enough of a reason to say it can be enjoyable.
There always will be a 'but' at some point that changes the whole statement, right?
Well, as I said, some characters are interesting to follow. However, the story switches between three main ones, with short flashbacks where we follow side ones. The voiceover on some of them is bad, and one of the main characters sounds so awfully unnatural I was at some point considering quitting the otherwise interesting plot.
The switching between MCs points of view is probably intended to show variety of classic cyberpunk landscapes. Expensive apartments, rundown basements, abandoned factories, sprinkly-clean laboratories, neon skyscrapers etc etc., all the while mentioning stuff that cyberpunk is most known for. Global corporations, cloning, gen. engineering, all-powerful AI, androids, cyborgs, virtual reality, loss of identity, background brutal warfare etc. Nothing of that sounds particularly new. There are some new, sometimes amusing ideas, but they are wasted with overwhelming majority of the usual.
The animation. oh boy. Pixelated graphics have their appeal, which i personally enjoy, yet they are so badly animated for some characters, you'd think this game is not really retro, but 20 years old. Maybe that's the idea. I wouldn't mind, but while all character's close-up portraits are nice, as are most sceneries and animations, some fail horribly. Two of the MCs look like they were made with MS Paint. Graphics range from eye-catching to blocky gibberish pixelgore.
Okay, I am proud of you if you managed to read it up to this point. So I'll just make my opinion short: don't buy this game for full price, it's not worth if you're into indie retro ones. But if your friend shares it to you, or you buy it in a bundle, play it, it's actually enjoyable, even if a bit too plain.

I picked this up on the Humble Gems Bundle, and it indeed a hidden gem that I am glad to have picked up.
I haven't played a point-and-click adventure game in quite a while, but this was a good foray back into that territory.  The setting and writing was very enjoyable, the art excellent, and the music immersive.  But the main point of this kind of adventure is exploring the story, which requires a good story to be a good game.  Technobabylon doesn't disappoint me here.
As someone interested in the virtual, metaverses, etc, I was on board immediately with the concept that the Trance provided, and other sci-fi concepts (such as gengineering) had enough grounding in modern science to give a bit of a "This could be the future" edge.  But it's not all dark, gritty, and brooding.  There is a LOT of dialog to explore, and there were quite a few moments I laughed out loud, mostly due to AI personalities (Turret + Cheffie = absolutely hilarious)
The puzzles were largely simple for me to figure out, and the only places I got stuck and had to look online for help were when I was missing something entirely -- it's not so bad you could call it pixel-hunting, but you still need to be thorough if you find yourself getting stuck.  Death is handled in a forgiving manner, simply rewinding back to a state just before you died if you did something foolish.
I ended up playing through this twice -- the second time with commentary and to pick up 100% achievements -- and I bought a copy for my sister and recommended it to a friend.  I'd recommend it for anyone who enjoys point-and-click adventure types, cyberpunk settings, and have a taste for automeals served by an AI so cheerful it should be criminal.
Overall play time for both runs was ~20 hours for me. Given my second run was much faster, I'd say you're probably looking at a 10 to 15 hour experience. That may not seem like much, but it was a very enjoyable time, and I've put more hours into games and got less out of them in the past, so I'd say it was worth it.
Also, I want that "nom nom nom" sound, and I don't know why.

Everyone else has said most of how I feel about this game so I'll try to keep mine short and sweet. Heroes of the Storm was the first moba I liked enough to get past the learning curve. I've played WoW, specifically PvP, since WotLK.
Battlerite takes the adrenaline from the best arenas or teamfights I've been in, and cuts out all of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t meant to waste your time. I can get on Battlerite and play like 3 games in 15 minutes, or I can play countless games for hours, and every game is intense and gets your blood pumping.
Possible the only BIG FLAW is the matchmaking, which is understandable. Due to the learning curve online play is intimidating at first, but I think many will find if they start with a few A.I. matches, then jump into multiplayer, yes you will still most likely be rekt for a few games...but eventually you get your feet under you. It's like a trial by fire. Either get better at the champion, or die and lose. When you make a critical mistake, the game tells you so via the other playing killing you. That mistake becomes much more apparent when the consequences are so final and blatant like losing.
It is frustrating at first, but given a few matches, it begins to flow much easier. I have found if I set a goal to play a champion to level 6, by the time I get to about 5, I'm performing exponentially better than I was at levels 1 or 2. This, amongst other games like this, is a SKILL BASED combat game. It's meant to be fun and simple, but not simple enough to not pose a challenge to get better.

I've played for a "few" hours.  I've been a player, faction leader, and now I help run a server called Light vs Dark.
Briefly:  The part about this game that I think separates it from similar games is that EVERYTHING is built block by block.  There is no "turret" block.  YOU build the turret.  Ever been playing MineCraft and wish you could build a spaceship and have massive battles in space?  Or maybe have a better build mode?  Well, StarMade might be for you then.  You can easily build massive structures and designs.  Battling can be fun, if you don't take it personally, and ALWAYS save a blueprint backup!
Pros:  Building your own ships is fun.  If you like building aesthetically, you can.  Or if you want to roleplay, you can.  Combat with smaller ships can be a lot of fun with friends (and enemies).  If you want, build an empire and subjucate the universe to your power.  There are also *some* tools to do modding, like server wrappers, custom decorative blocks, and changing recipes.  AND best of all, you can try the full game for free and play for as long as you'd like.  Just download the demo or go to
and download it and create a free account.  If you want to support the game, definitely go buy it.  I got my money's worth for sure with thousands of hours played.
Cons:  The playerbase has been going down lately, and a big part of what makes this game fun is playing with other people.   I run a server that used to have 30 people on it at a time, but now it's been quiet.  This is sad to see.  There are also bugs, since it's a rather small development team, but they do move at a surprising pace (if you compare it to how quickly MineCraft used to release updates).  Also, I should mention that this game isn't for everybody.  Many people will try it, die and fail, and quit.  Also, some players will create really intensely laggy ships and crash their games, so my suggestion is to build realistically sized ships or join a server with active admins who will help keep things running smoothly.
When you play tips:  My suggestion to anybody is to team up with other new players when you try the game out.  Fly with friends and you'll have a much better time.  And do not take on powerful factions unless you want to get creamed.  But don't let the rating on steam discourage you from trying the game.  We could use the new players, and some of you will be like me, and enjoy the game for thousands of hours.  :)

I was really excited when this came out, and still am in some way. Finally a game where you can control your own designed ship from inside, walking through them, "living" in them like you would in a static base in other survivals.
In theory there is nothing stopping you from building huge ships with fully decorated interiors, there simply is no point to it from a gameplay perspective. In fact, there is no gameplay really.
Update after update they add things like prettier lighting, new logic blocks, new functionality blocks but they still to this day didnt bother about fundamental things that actually make the game a game.
Ship interiors are pretty much useless since you can control all systems from the "core" block. Placement of thrusters or even weapons can be pretty much random since own projectiles can pass through your ship so you can effectively place them inside. Center of mass and center of thrust can be disregarded alltogether. In the end you see a lot of cubes flying around that consist of randomly mashed together system blocks since there seems to be no real benefit from carefully planning a nice looking ship design. Sound, as you may think of as a given, does not really work. Homebases and everything docked to them are invulnerable and since there is not much need for more than your homebase, you cant even raid other people. Basically all the game offers right now is mining blocks to build a bigger miner to then mine more blocks.
It may be early access and the devs surely were not sleeping but I have to say they are investing their time and effort into the wrong direction. Until that changes we are stuck with a voxel ship designer tool ( thats right, not a game ). The fact that most MP servers are empty - if you can find a populated one with good ping in the first place that is - suggests that I am not the only one who finds the current state of the game disappointing.
I really want to like it and wish them well but right now, nuh uh. Cant recommend it.

Final Fantasy Type-0 HD is a game with a contrived plot and awful counterintuitive gameplay that hardly lives up to its Final Fantasy name even as a spinoff.
From a gameplay perspective, FF Type-0 HD's combat is extremely simple. The game is balanced around the idea that you have around 16 total characters to play each mission; it pits you up against enemies stronger than yourself with the idea that you'll die and carry on the fight with another character, so throughout a mission you might have several party members die before you finish. This makes gameplay very unsatisfying, and to make matters worse, the actual controls and options you have in combat are very limited. With such a large cast, no one character is all that satisfying to play. You cannot jump (generally speaking) so there is no aerial combat beyond specific skills that have that effect. Each character has a total of four skills that they can use, so any one character you play will be very limiting. On the other side of things, summons/Eidolons are extremely unbalanced and OP, made to where you can oneshot most enemies without issue and even give bosses a hard time with them. But even killing enemies isn't very satisfying, since in order to reap the benefits of killing an enemy, you must wait a few seconds for the game to register that they're dead and you're locked onto them so that you can suck up their Phantoma. You know how in other FF games, after winning a battle, depending on the game you could just go walk up to an enemy and pick up their loot or just automatically get it? That system made it effortless, but here you actually have to sit and wait a moment, stopping in battle just to collect your rewards. Its clunky and takes you out of the action. Finally, like FFXV, you can just hold attack buttons to do the attack combos rather than needing to continually press the attack button, meaning you as a player don't even need to do that much actual "controlling". Despite this, enemies can be a pain in the butt to fight and the camera makes it even worse since some attack combos force you to face away from enemies due to the way characters jump around and the way the camera abruptly shifts to adjust with that. And when you combine all this, with all these balance and gameplay issues the gameplay just isn't satisfying.
Unfortunately even the problems don't even stop at the gameplay. The story is contrived; the plot revolves around the fact that characters can't remember the details surrounding a friend's death and uses this to create drama, but the reason for the amnesia is that soldiers have their memories wiped so as to not be weighed down by such tragedy. That might make some degree of sense but the story has one particular character told what happened surrounding this dead character, so you just get this really stupid angry drama created over a problem that can't be helped because the government thinks mind wiping is a good idea. This sort of drama can only occur because of this. Combined with the fact that the military that Class Zero works for actively works against itself due to being full of leaders that act like teenagers mad when they can't get their way, and the whole game just feels contrived and unrealistic. These characters don't feel human. And when these characters are inhuman and unbearable and placed in boring cutscenes where the characters just stand still with the camera going back and forth with them just talking, its tremendously boring and hard to bare.
Finally, while not very important, let me just say that this remaster is awful. The new models don't blend in well with the rest of the PSP environments and bizarrely the FMVs, which are supposed to be higher than game quality, still retain the same sort of details and textures present from the original PSP models, making the FMV characters and in-game characters look bizarrely different. The PSP models had textures on their clothing that made them look like actual fabric, but now they look smooth and almost plastic-y. This might be okay if there was some consistency, but there isn't. This lack of consistency doesn't even stay only between the FMVs and character models; most of the game is full of new models and textures being placed right next to old ones, making the game artistically clash. There's also nearly blinding bloom and lighting and for some reason reflections on things that shouldn't be reflecting anything (seeing light reflect off grass, for example). The game is just a mess graphically and I really think they would've done better had they just left all the textures and models alone without any sort of updating.
That's not to say the game doesn't have its high points; the music is fantastic. The hard rock during boss fights, the dramatic Latin singing during certain tracks, and just strong use of the orchestral music in general made cutscenes and gameplay exciting at times. In addition, the boss fights can be fairly well designed and decently challenging without feeling like you're being overwhelemed. They have learnable and exploitable attack patterns, and the mecha fights can be interesting, such as fighting a multi-legged mecha enemy that can climb up walls. The port is also decent, although I warn anyone playing to avoid setting the max AA setting unless they have a super powerful computer due to its usage of downsampling as a form of AA (something the game neglects to tell you, hence some people's issues with the game having framerate drops I imagine).
But despite this, the game just isn't very fun and not worth it in my opinion. Pass on this one. Maybe if they make a sequel they'll fix some of the problems present.

As a fan of both Japanese RPGs and parodies, I am surprised how badly this game fails at both. I'm not sure if it's appropriate to criticize level design or battle system (not to mention the story) - you don't expect "You Only Live Once" to be a good platformer, right? But it also lacks humour. I am about half through the game, ad so far, there's been not a single decent joke. Mark Leung's ROTB was way better in this (playing it was still a pain, though). What this game does, however, is repeats most common flaws of JRPGs. One can think it IS the promised parody at work, but it's done in such unentertaining way, that any good JRPG of old (not to mention modern indies) with their inner jokes and self-parodies easily beats it.
The JRPG tropes are widely presented - with equal parts love and criticism - in popular culture nowadays - from Eat Lead to Abenobashi to Sophie Houlden's "The Linear RPG" to Robot Chicken. To make an entertaining game, it's not enough to put in a vampire wannabe and a world map that looks like Dragon Quest's. Not anymore.

I went in thinking "This is exactly what I was looking for in a stealth game, even though I never did thought about that". A Rogue-like stealth game, it just makes so much sense and it's great!... on paper.
The problem is, this game falls short. A great idea that is, in my opinion, just not polished enough.
You start with a throwing knife and a gun loaded with 5 bullets. The aiming and hit-scan is wonky, sometime I aim properly and miss my target where sometimes I just run and gun to get headshot after headshot. And the throwing knife... the problem with it is that it's a THROWING knife. I have a hard time thinking that a stealthy person on a mission would throw away its only knife and then be weaponless.
Also the guards will sometime see you from afar and yet, sometime you could be near enough to whisper insults in their ears and be unseen. Oh, and when they see you, they will shoot. Either you get the 1 shot-kill treatment or the "80's movie vilain" treatment; 6 shoots and still be alive.
The 2 powers that you have, see thru wall and slow time, are nice but the X-ray vision is hard to get used to. There is no cooldown on the screen to tell you when to use it again and it shows you a cone to display the enemy sighting range... or so I think? Sometime the cone go thru the wall and it gets confusing fast.
And this is just a pet peeve of mine but the menus and options are not easy to navigate. Pressing ESC to quit is not enabled, the screen resolution options makes the UI moves left or right if you transition it. I'm fetching far, I know, but everything adds up in the end.
Dev, you have an excellent premise for the game, just need a bit more polishing

[This gets more comprehensive as I go, I swear.]
Shadow Warrior places you in the size 5's of Lil Wang, an aspiring tattoo artist, working as an intern for a vaguely communist law firm. Your boss sends you out on a coffee run and to see if the Soul Edge is still on sale at the local Trader Joes, only to find that the manager stole it, and a 55in plasma when they canned him for taking panty shots of ladies in the restroom. After a brief and harrowing stay in the stores dog kennel, you find the guy dead, a victim of his own clumsy handling of a Baby's First Meth Lab, and blows himself up to death, and dies. But, also being messed up from falling through the roof, his demon bro, Hojo, decides to aid you on your coffee run. And also something about his world being on fire 24/7. Hojo lives in east LA. So you, Wang, make a deal to save the planet California, in exchange for Hojo not letting you burn up in the exploded guest house behind Trader Joes. You agree, and then the rest of the game is you skull-murder-f**king 2 dimensions into oblivion. I didn't pay much attention to the story, to be honest.
The murder everything mechanics are meaty, and the sword feels like you're actually ace at it, even when you're just blind-fire swinging at a crowd. The enemy types, while not many, are diverse and require you to adapt to defeat them. They come in Chump, Flying Chump, Suicide Bomber, Giant Elfromancer, other guy, and Shadow of Colossus. Frankly, there wasn't any one point where I was bored. Even though I beat it on filthy casual setting there were spots that got a bit intense. The level design is pretty darn good, with secrets and hidden homages to the classic 1967 version (called 'retro zones') that feature pixelated lewdness. Which is comical. Humor goes a long way with me. The dialogue and voice acting is [mostly] great, and the banter between Wang and Hoji cant get to be a riot. I like that the satire was constant, being self-aware without breaking the '4th wall'. Audibly, the music and effects are great and mix well with the environment and situation (e.g. battle music / idle music) Visually, it's pretty impressive and runs like silk on my mediocre-a$$ hardware, so fps drops weren't an issue during big, gory battles. The controls, as far as the chi-techniques, sometimes got a little annoying. Remembering what does what got a little frustrating during big battles. It may have been my KB (getting worn out), but there was a sense of input lag even while switching weapons and interacting with objects. The story (like I said, I didn't pay much mind) was a little underwhelming, but who cares? I have a 4 barreled shotgun. GG.

This is an excellent card game in the vein of Magic the Gathering. For something so new the amount of cards in it are staggering. With so many different choices in card selection it gives you a real feeling of options in strategy which is sometimes lacking in newer card games which have a smaller stable of options to choose from. I especially like the way in which you build decks which narrows your options of how many cards of which class/type you can have by a selection of three different commander cards and these cards are always "in play" when the match starts with that deck offering you even more strategic choices by knowing that those cards can always be made available as soon as the match starts without an element of chance attached to it, leaving you feeling less at the mercy of chance than you sometimes feel in a card game that relies solely on the first hand being completely random.
The build and barrier to entry is really smooth to me. You gain levels and money by playing matches against the computer at first in challenges or a campaign, while it's not really a straight forward story campaign and more of a series of ai matches with specific decks it still feels good to proceed through it because you gain cards of each type by completing the campaign of that type and you also gain cards by gaining a level, completing a match for the day, or specific challenges in the game. This creates a feeling of gaining a lot of different cards throughout play and that collection and expansion of your options continues easily without paying anything, at least in as far as I've played. Though from what I see in the shop you're not gaining items that are inherently better than what you gain through unlocking booster packs by gaining levels so paying doesn't seem like it creates that much of a power difference unless you're paying a ton. And buying booster packs or decks in the game through the in-game earned currency seems to cost a huge amount so the slow grind to be able to do that versus straight up buying may also contribute to a game where the top players are that much better because of the money spent but it's almost as if it's unavoidable in a game like this and losing doesn't bother me that much. You are, sometimes, at the mercy of random cards landing and I have beat people who have played a lot longer with the first deck I made so even buying your way to victory (in as much as having played the game much longer represents this similarly to buying your way to a better deck) isn't a clear path to an easy victory.
Matchmaking is a little iffy in that you seem to just get matched against whoever is trying to play at the time. My comparative lower level and playtime makes me unsure of whether or not I'm just bad at the game or if I'm always being matched against people who know the game better or have better decks. But there are so many ai options in the game I never feel too discouraged from playing the game at all by being consistantly outmatched in player vs player because that's not the only way to earn currency or experience.
If you like collectible card games at all give it a shot. It's free and I've had more fun with it that way than the previous Magic computer games I've played.

I feel like this game is a love it or hate it kind of game. I always see such high praise about it but I myself feel no love for 95% of the game. I'll explain why with some minor spoilers ahead.
So I've played all the past AC games and enjoy the gameplay. The first time I can remember experiencing something in an AC game I didn't particularly enjoy was the ship tutorial in AC3. I hated that segment and was very glad it was optional to use the ship throughout the game. Unfortunately I went into AC4 thinking that the ship would be optional. It most definitely wasn't.
I knew the game dealt with piracy but for some reason didn't look up just how much of the gameplay was based on the ship. But because it's such a big part of the game it made me dislike the game. If I'm on land for a huge portion of time then yay, fun times. When I have to board the Jackdaw and I don't have fast travel unlocked for wherever I have to go, groooooooan. So needless to say I did as little ship play as possible and avoided upgrading it as much as possible. Also your crew sings sea shanties. Not necessarily a bad thing until you've a) heard that one particular song too many times or b) been stuck on this one part for too long and that one jerk starting up a shanty nearly every time you return to checkpoint is pushing you over the edge. Luckily you can tell them to shut up, which I didn't realize until late in my playthrough.
I dislike the main mechanic but aside from that, I wasn't too fond of the story. You play as Edward Kenway who is a pirate  who wants to be rich.  He's obsessed with scoring a big stash of gold to support his girl back home who didn't want him to leave in the first place. That's really all there is to this character. To me he wasn't likeable, and the story all revolved around him needing money so much. Even the more interesting characters in the game are sidelined while he goes hunting some big score. For a series that delves into history so much and introduces you to so many intersting characters, I feel they fell kind of short here. But that (much like my strong hatred of the ship battles) is obviously just my opinion.
Otherwise the game is what you'd expect from AC. There's hunting back again from AC3, combat is similar to previous games, weapons from previous games, etc. If you've played AC you know what you're getting into and there's nothing really stand out here.
So if you're looking for a pirate game where you can sail around and have giant ship battles and plundering booty, this is a good game for you. If you want to play AC but also want to be a pirate, you're in luck. If you're like me and you hated the ship gameplay in three, I'd avoid this one (and AC Rogue).

The Swindle is a long-form stealth action platformer hybrid and one of the best games I've played in recent history. That said I can definitely relate with the complaints that are being made in the majority of the negative reviews. Those are:
-Wonky controls
-Impossible levels
-Inconsistent glitches
From what I can tell, The Swindle was built with the same controls design as Gun Monkeys... and quite frankly that was my biggest gripe with Size Five's previous title. These are definitely not your typical controls and it'll take you some time to get the hang of them and understand them. My biggest frustration was figuring out that when you stand close to an edge and turn around you end up sliding down the wall, resulting in many unfortunate alarms being set off without knowing why until you figure out this mechanic. Second biggest was learning the rules of mounting a wall from below. For some reason just colliding with the bottom corner is not enough to hang on but jumping directly underneath it while facing it is. It's inconsistent but it works. And that's the thing, while not intuitive it was built by design and it is a clever way of mounting a wall (although I'd prefer to push down to slide down it like every other game)... it's just you have to figure it out by yourself that that was built into the code and I can see why that would put off a lot of newcomers. As for me, it didn't take long to get the feel for things and I was able to feel in control in no time. I would suggest that there be some kind of tutorial that forces you to learn these things so that you don't go in blind not knowing the controls of the game. There are plenty of puzzles a game should present, what your controls are should not be one of them.
Being procedurally generated instantly brings on more scrutiny about fairness and with this game it's definitely easy to pass it off as short-sighted in design when in the first level you can sometimes only get 1 lousy percent of the loot because you don't have any of the upgrades needed to do certain puzzles yet. With the time restraint of 100 days, each day you lose to a lousy RNG dice roll seems like quite the unfair price to pay. I couldn't say whether or not it actually is always possible to beat the whole game despite the seed you have as that would take a lot more meticulous research of the game's underlying code to determine that but I can say that more often than not the levels are fairly generated and it's just you not doing well that's the real issue. Again, for someone new to the game, this will probably push you the wrong way and might make you feel like it's not worth the time but for me, I like a game that spits in my face and calls me mean names and waves in my face my flaws and that I could and should do better. I like to be pushed and be given levels that rub in my face that my upgrade path I've chosen was the wrong one. It's brutal and not very nice but in the end I play games for the challenge of figuring out how to beat it and The Swindle by design is a puzzle to figure out in every inch of it.
Now there are against-the-grain design choices, and then there are is just plain broken. Climbing a wall and having an enemy's sightline clip through and set off all the alarms is just not fun. Being clearly behind an enemy that doesn't spontaneously turn around suddenly turn around without cause... is not fun. But these bugs are few and far between and I imagine they'll get cleaned up.
The game is playable by all my standards and the bugs aren't bad enough that I shy away from itching for more. Losing your cover in a heist is not the worst thing to happen, the game let's slip ups and bad level generations happen and you can still pull of the final swindle with time to spare. It is brutal in the sense that you can lose 10-15 minutes of your time if you screw up at the end of a lucrative heist but you don't lose the game, something that Spelunky tended to relish in doing.
That's what I love about The Swindle though, it makes each successful heist count big time and each one that you do in succession count even higher. The game expects you to die and so when you don't you feel like a god and the game let's you relish in it. By design, this game was meant to be for those who wanted to dive deep into it and learn it's nitty gritties and tell you to go grow up if you don't. It's a bold move for sure but I love it.
So should you buy it? Depends on if you are going to take the time and have the patience to get to know it. This is not a game for those that are easily put off by failure. You'll be frustrated with it and want to kick it across the room plenty of times but as a result when you do pull off that final swindle the reward is much more grand and delicious.

Like Medal of Honor, but called Call of Duty.
One of the best WWII shooters I've played that has aged decently well. Works best when it makes you feel more like just another soldier instead of the missions where you feel like James Bond, but either way the game is gorgeous and really just a lot of fun. Veteran may feel a bit cheap at first but keep playing and you'll get the hang of it and realize that for the most part it's pretty fair.
++Fantastic sound design
++Gorgeous, colourful graphics that still look really nice today
++Game runs like a dream on modern hardware and operating systems
+Brilliant first-person animations
+Back when Call of Duty could be lighthearted and not dead serious the whole game. A welcome change for what most people would expect in the series in that regard. Can bring the seriousness of the war when required.
+Shows three different sides of the war, all handled decently well. Pretty unique concept for WWII shooters.
+The only CoD where you can quick-save
+Set-pieces are handled well
+Weapon variety is decent
+Voice-acting is of high quality
+-Run of the mill multiplayer, but it's still enjoyable
-+Veteran is strange in that health
+-I don't miss health regeneration when there's no health kits on Veteran and there's waves and waves of enemies, but it's not too much of a big deal. I also imagine it wouldn't be too annoying on easier difficulties either.
-+Characters can be humourous and are likeable, but only appear very, very shortly
-Animations were always pretty dated
-Singleplayer is far too short. Lasts only about 5 hours on Veteran.
-I've always found weapons to not feel impactful enough in the CoD games. This is no exception.
-Campaign pacing is poor
-Not a lot of weaponry and you'll be using the same ones constantly across all factions since the best ones are so rare
--Game gets repetitive and tiring quickly
--Ridiculously linear to the point where it's just stupid. Even moreso than the rest of the games. You cannot fall off ledges, you cannot mantle waist high walls and there is one direct path and that's it throughout the entire game.
Sound: 10/10
Graphics: 9/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Content/Replayability: 3/10
Overall: 8/10
Very worth playing, although in all honestly, you wouldn't be missing much by just playing Call of Duty 2 instead. But if you like that and want more then this should easily fill your needs. A really great WWII FPS.

OK, first a disclaimer, this is the first review I have written.  Not first video game review first review EVER.  So I haven't reviewed a fridge, a bacon sandwich or a book on the Easter bunny.
To begin, some things I like about this game
The tutorial.  Not only is any kind of tutorial great, especially for games like this.  But an actual good one? Priceless.  The tutorial in this game got me up to speed on how to play this game and introduced new mechanics well.
Sound/Music.  Now I must confess I am a GW fan boy but in my opinion they got the sound effects in this just right.  The music is great to boot.
Art direction.  Again I believe they have nailed it, Gothic Sci-fi, will skulls all-over.
Things I'm not so keen on
The graphics.  This is a small issue but I just wish they were a bit more polished.  They are nice, just not amazing.
The meat of it....BBQ Chicken, tastes great but can be messy.
This is a turn based strategy game. In which you carefully move and manage a team of the finest Blood Angel Terminators, to circumvent and vanquish terrible Genestealers, and accomplish various objectives.
It is set in the famous 40K setting from GW.  This is a grim future where humanity's once advanced technology is in decline, beset by foes on all sides, no hope, no final victory only a slow and painful decline.
The section of the universe this game focuses on is groups of highly advance indomitable Space Marine Terminators undertaking boarding actions on vast Space hulks.  Fending off the lightning fast Genstealer menace (think xenomorph).
Its very much an elite group of butt kicking stone blocks, versus overwhelming deadly, agile, supreme killers.
Now as I have mentioned I am a huge fan of this Universe so I would whole heartedly recommend this game!
Now from a point of view of someone who knows nothing about this 40k nonsense and doesn't know his Bolter from his Las pistol, this game is still worth a look in.  Some of may go over your head or seem a bit grim and weird, but I think a good time can still be had with this and you never know it might get you into the geeky miniature painting gaming stuff :)
Buy this if you are a fan, give this a chance if your not and it happens to be on sale.

This is sadly unplayable until they fix AI ship spawning (oh god especially the trader ships). I WOULD recommend this game, as I’ve been playing it since it first came out (before steam), but the frustration of constantly being rammed into by trader ships, which spontaneously acquire some sad case of severely impulsive autism when flying towards a shop, followed by the insane lag caused when they kamikaze into the trader posts (which probably contributes to their lack of any brain cells) makes this game heartbreakingly difficult to play. Not to mention, when they start overheating from the damage, the player can easily just strip parts from the unconscious ship, leaving an infinite supply of free stuff. But that aside, it's unbelievably frustrating to build a starter ship because in order to build anything without getting caught in the trader ships’ suicide missions, I have to entirely leave the shop sector. And if I run out of supplies, I have to fly all the way back to the shop, which is quite risky considering the obvious. But wait, there’s more! I don’t NEED to buy anything because I can probably just steal what I need from those mangled trader ships! See the problem? I realize that I can simply turn off collision damage, but that won’t stop the knockback effect. So if I’m out of my ship and it gets hit, it’s GOING to disappear forever. I also realize that I could turn inertia back on, but that would make flying long distances very frustrating because I would either have to 1, hold down the forward button for at least half an hour, or 2, sit here charging warp drives until I’m 99 and hooked up to an IV. I would much prefer to set the engines to max and let inertia take care of the rest while I leave to go get some work done for a couple hours.
It seems to me that they rushed this update out the door way to quickly. If you're going to release a major update, at least take the time to stabilize it first. Making a game unplayable, even if only for a short while, is only going to deter incoming customers and upset those that already own the game. Rushing things out the door is literally what EA does.
But other than that, excellent game! I will change my vote once this problem has been dealt with.
Oh and also, I’m autistic myself. So don't think I'm attacking the disabled, 'cause I'm not. :P

I'll start off by saying that despite me personally not liking this game, it is for sure NOT a pay to win game.  People that complain about it being one either didn't play enough or are just salty about not being good with the mechanics of this game.  I would actually argue that it is a bit too easy to obtain cards in this game without really paying anything.
The draft mode makes it incredibly easy to obtain cards and it's not difficult at all to at least break even, given that you are at least somewhat decent at the game.  This makes me wonder how Lightmare plans on staying in business when they give away cards so freely through the various rewards.
With that said, this tcg does have a very different spin from the other more classic card games and is not quite to my liking.  The simultaneous turn is interesting but the mindgame it provides causes some imbalance between the factions and may cause some frustrating gameplay experiences.
The community for this game feels like it's full of elitist card gamers that are too cool for other more mainstream games.  Overall my experiences with my opponents have been mostly negative due to bad manners.  Regardless, I am fairly impressed with the community manager's passion for this game and I would recommend this game eventually when and if it does become more balanced.  For now the small elitist community itself and the somewhat mediocre balancing is keeping me away from this game.

Final Fantasy Type-0 is a very different game in term of story and gameplay from other FF titles. Many aspect of this game, including story an d gameplay is centered arounf death and dying. This game is a remastered version of the original PSP one and here's some difference from the original game.
1. Immensely improved graphic esp. for the main cast.
2. Magic is less powerful than in the PSP version
3. Eidolens are balanced so they feel strong even when underleveled.
4. Running speed has increased
5. Improved camera angle.
6. You can speed up the game
7. New difficulty mode
8. Multiplayer is deleted
9. One extra costume
Story: 7/10
Final Fantasy Type-0's story is WWII set in a fantasy land. This land is dominated by 4 countries and are empowered by their respective crystals. You follow Class Zero, a mysterious groups of elite student, as they defend their country from a militarist country who seeks to unify the world through collecting crystals.
The overall tone of the game is rather dark compared to other FF games as it features a lot of war theme like child soldiers, deaths, militarism. The key concept in the story is that the memories of the dead is removed by the crystal to make characters feel numb about losing their loved ones. This emphasizes the fragility of life, a theme that occurs throughout the story and gameplay system. Being part of the Fabula Nova Crystallis: Final Fantasy series, free will is the main theme, which will come in part much later in the story.
Overall, the story is satisfying. While the game has some light moment like every JRPG ever, it still succeeds in bring a distinct atmosphere and explores the themes mentioned above, making it one of my favorite plot in FF series. However, some events or concept are not explained thoroughly during the gameplay and requires digging through the lore.
There are 14 main casts and many don't enjoy a lot exposure. Most don't have a deep back story and character develpment as the spotlight is focused mainly on Ace, Machina and Rem. The chi-chat between mission with your fellow classmates become the only means you get to know them more.
+Interesting story and theme
-Lacks in-depth development on many playable characters
Gameplay: 8/10
You get to choose to play as 14 characters. In the mission preparation screen, you need to choose 3 as your active team. When 1 of the team members die, you can replace them with another members in reserve or survive him with pheonix down if you are quick enough. The game ended when all members are dead. The 14 characters offer very unique play style. From close-ranged to ranged user, from melee to magic oriented user. Each character has very distinct set of move and thus require different technique to master. Jack is a katana user. He moves extremely slow, yet hit quickly and heavily. The time-lapse between each hit is very long as he focuses on killing enemies with 1 hit. Cater is a magic gunman. Her normal attack ignores defense and the gun charges up itself when idling, allowing a stronger shot. Deuce is a bard and her normal attack summon a spirit to evolve around her and damage any enemies near. She can also enhance or sabotage others. Leveling characters gains AP, which can be used to unlock new abilities and has even more variety. A downside is that the game doesn't allow you to ignore certain characters as there may come a time where you need them.
The game also introduces the Killsight system, which allows characters to deal heavy damage on enemies weak spot. The killsight may appear when the enemy performs a certain action, for instance, reloading guns. And the killsight won't appear if you try to button-mash so it takes a bit technique to play the game.
Eidolen appears in this games. They are extremely powerful summon creatures on your side. To summon them, you need to sacrifice the caster's life but they can help if the situation is too overwhelming. If you are not a friend of sacrificing lives, you can unleash powerful attack by team attacks or team magic but these requires a team of 3 to cast.
Like Persona series, FF involves sidequesting, exploration and spending time with friends between main quests. You are provided a limited free time in between story quests and doing the above mentioned things will cost time. You can train in the courtyard to level up. You can talk with your friends or NPCs. You can take on side quests that gives useful rewards. You can explore the world map. When the time count to 0, you will have to advance the story.
There are 3 types of quests. The first is advancing dungeons like in the story missions. The second is more tactical as you order troops across a map to gain control on the land. The third is trivial quests that can be done during free time. In the first and the second type, there are SO requests that requires you to complete tasks like "Not dying", "Kill enemies", "Find something" with a time limit. Completing these tasks will give you rewards but failing them will result in death.
If you feel that you characters are too weak but don't want to grind, the game also provide an option for characters to train themselves. You simply have to enter "Secret Trainig". The selected character will gain exp when the game is off and the longer it is, the more exp he gets.
The game has high replay value. The first playthrough only show 50-60% of the game. The second playthrough will unlock more in-depth story quests and to fully explore the whole game, you need the third playthrough.
One down thing is that the AI of your allies is pretty crappy. Sometimes they don't attack unless you are using a certain character's ability to force them attack. Apparently it is intended but rather unnecessary.
Another downside exclusively for keyboard user is that you cannot customize the mapping and the mapping is very weird and uncomfortable. Like console, you have to hold down a button to lock on the enemies. On keyboard, it makes it hard to press other buttons while holding one of your finger on the lock-on button. So using a controller is advised.
+Variety of character mechanisms
+High replay value
+Smooth combat
+Unique and interesting boss fight
+Lots of sidequests and places to explore and do
-Crappy ally AI
-Bad keyboard mapping
-Takes too long to unlock everything (3 gameplays)
-Forces you to use every characters
Music: 9/10
Like other FF titles, Type-0's music is not disappointing. Composed by Takeharu Ishimoto, the composer for The World Ends With You, FF7 Crisis Core), it hassome memorable battle theme and event theme. The audio quality is enhanced from the PSP one.
Graphic: 7/10
There are a significant change in lighting and main charcaters texture. It's definitely an upgrade from PSP. However, many NPC still looks bland and despite the graphic update, several locations design are still basic. The levels look like rectangle boxes, which is understandable as it is only a remaster.
Verdict: 8/10
Despite being only a port from PSP, it is one of the better FF title in recent years with memorable story and unique and varying gameplay.

While I’m no self proclaimed fan of pixel graphics in modern video games, there was something that drew me towards Technobablylon. Perhaps it was the fusion between cyberpunk and neo-noir genres and the similarities I could observe between this game and one of my favorite movies of all time, Blade Runner. Technobabylon has an intriguing plot of its own, which I won’t spoil but I can assure it that it is quite original and this time, you’re actually getting your money’s worth. There were a few instances which required that you return to a previously “swept” area and use the newly acquired itmes in your inventory. I’m not a fan of backtracking in general but at least there weren’t many such situations. The point & click interface runs smoothly but it took some tinkering with the game’s graphical settings before I was satisfied with the result and the dialogue font is a bit pixeated for my taste but it wasn’t that much of a strain. On the other hand, the  soundtrack truly stands out and the many commentaries (on each scene and on some interactions) from the developer and publisher, reveled just how important this project has been to them. I respect that. All in all, you’re in for a decently lengthy adventure, should you choose to give Technobabylon a try. It really has few flaws and I hope we may see a sequel to it one day.
+ Excellent storyline.
+ Beautiful art style and tech-noir setting.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
+ In-game commentaries from the dev team.
- Some puzzles involve backtracking to a previous scene.

I'm not much for point and clicks-- I only got this off a humble bundle. But I stuck through to the end and finished it it  two sessions. It turns out I really liked it.
The main pros:
• The story is great. An immense amount of thought went into background details about the universe. I feel like I know things about the place that these characters live.
• The voice acting is well done.
• The characters are likeable, but flawed. They're human-like.
• Most of the puzzles are intuitive and well-considered. They often offer multiple approaches.
• The sci-fi science is believable-- and chilling.
The main cons:
• The game often tries to put the characters in urgent situations that would demand immediate action, then asks you to solve a multi-room puzzle that involves backtracking across the map. Pacing is entierly thrown out the window.
• The art style of the characters is dramatically different from the enviornments. And a lot rougher. The result is a disconnect between the actors and the scene.
• A fair few of the puzzles rely on obscure 'find the hidden object' solutions. Not all of them-- but more than enough to distinctly annoy you.

They say "Crime doesn't pay." Well, in The Swindle it does but its DAMN hard to pull off! In The Swindle you have one simple task, steal as much you can and get away with it. Between you and your shiny cash is a arsenal of defense bots and cameras, mines, etc. The problem? You don't start out with much at all. Armed with a trusty club, you must claw your way up slowly and arm yourself by spending the hard earned cash you stole. On top of all that you only have 100 days(100 lives/heists) to beat the game. All the elements of The Swindle work well, the graphics, the overall theme, the abilities, the music. The problem lies in the one core mechanic of this game. The Roguelike nature of this game is extremely unforgiving and downright unfair at times, placing defenses and traps in areas that simply cannot be overcome, Either due to lack of ability or placement. The early game is perpetuated with this type of problem and it isn't exactly gently explained through tutorials, because there really isn't any. The game gets better after you have collected quite a few of your gizmos/abilities but you always feel like your in a race to keep up with timer/enemy. Which once those 100 days are up, its back to the beginning. Nonetheless The Swindle is a brilliantly fun game that just needs a little balancing and tweaking.

I could swear I already wrote my review for this game. It must have un-reviewed it when I refunded it.
The game claims to be a very difficult roguelike stealth game. What it turned out to be for me was a poorly designed action platformer with unresponsive controls and little to no room for creative problem solving or advancement through mastery.
The levels are procedural, but rarely-if ever- will you see something that you didn't see your first time through a given map type. While the levels do branch, they branch like the roots of a tree: splintering off into an eventual dead-end, offering you the chance to backtrack -a lot- instead of providing alternate routes through a level.
Progression through these levels is so harshly gated by ability unlocks that it feels like a metroidvania more than a roguelike. Your abilities don't HELP you solve difficult problems, they simply decide if you can solve the problem or not. You see that branch of the level with LITERALLY NO ENTRANCES beneath you? Better already have teleport or explosives at your disposal, because there’s -no- other way to get to that  room (and the loot therein) on foot and no coming back to specific levels after you leave. This might be less frustrating if abilities unlocks were somehow tied to player skill, instead of simply purchased with the currency that you grind/collect at a infuriatingly slow pace on each level.
About the currency collection: It’s incredibly frustrating. Money is easy to get and hard to keep, as any loot a character has when they die evaporates with the character. An understandable mechanic, weighing the risk of death against the allure of additional treasure, but that relationship falls the pieces when the character is killed so often, and so quickly, by things they can't control:
-Jump button doesn't jump and land in spikes.
-Attack fails to register and the guard turns around and kills you.
-Wall jump is misaligned by a few pixels and you jump out a window.
-Get stuck in a portion of the level that is INESCAPABLE.
The game is rife with bugs and design flaws large enough that paired with the level of punishment for each player death it turns money collection into a slog.
I guess my statement about skill in regard to skill usage carried a sentiment that can be applied to gameplay as a whole. It would be far more tolerable if skill played a larger role in it. The only skill (other than winning arguments with the awkward and unresponsive controls) that I found useful was patience. Not once did I run into a situation who's solution wasn't immediately apparent, instead the majority of situations I encountered were instead challenging because their solution was (while obvious) tedious to solve, and the same as the 14 before it.
When compared to other any other modern game in either genre that the Swindle claims to be part of, stealth games, or roguelikes/roguelike platformers, The Swindle's lack of refined design, nuanced gameplay, and functional controls stand out like sore thumbs.
Also there's no room for any stealth in the game by the way. No sound or light mechanics, enemy guard have a sight line of only a few units, and there is liitle to no way to "sneak" past guards. You just wait for them to turn around and hit them with your hitting stick.
I will say the game looks and sounds very nice, which it should considering how resource heavy it is.
Wait for an 80% off sale and decide for yourselves, but I wouldn't give this game away. It sullies the roguelike and stealth genres in my opinion.

I'm not going to lie about this game: I'm terrible at it. If I was placed in a tournament against a potato with random electrical currents running out to control the game, I would probably still only have a 50% chance of winning.
However, that's not going to stop me from trying to make a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥review so that I can get the last achievement I need for the Steam awards. If you like this review, please click the helpful button (I dare not ask for the funny button for reasons that should be clear to you right now) because that would be tight as fu-
Character Types
Unlike the typical moba fare of ADC, Jungle, whining for roles, ETC. you pick the character you play outside the match lobby and the toxic players will berate you for not picking a character that corresponds to the random chance that you were put on a team with them instead of not picking a character and team comp that revolves around them whilst in a lobby. This is what experts in the modern gaming world call "non-toxic" nowadays.
There's three archetypes: melee, support, and ranged. Once you find a class you like, you then pick a character, each of which is extremely different. For every 30 players that picks their character main based on some semblance of skill, there's a player like me who picks who they think looks coolest or is the most fun. The former is to be referred to as a "player" and the latter as a "casual babby no status nooby wiener". Since I'm too lazy and stuffed from Thanksgiving earlier tonight to care, here's the rundowns on each.
Support characters aren't so much support as they are characters more reliant on stuns, slows, poisins and heals. Melees are the ones you think are great until you realize they can't attack more than one character at a time, essentially like having a projectile but being way too close. Rangers are the best class, because my main Ezmo is one.
Customize
This is what you'll try to use to prove you aren't lame. Every time you open a chest, it will be filled with bounds of disappointment because outfit and weapon skins are ridiculously rare and usually aren't a character you play. Also, if you have even the slightest bit of OCD anywhere in your mind, you will never be happy to use a character skin since their weapon doesn't match, or vice-versa.
Modes
There's only one mode per se, (Professionally referred to as the "ARE YOU NOT ENTERTAINED" mode) but many different players and numbers you can play it with. Custom is what you'll use and never be happy with to play with the 2 or so people who also play this game and are your friends. Standard 2v2 is what you'll use to have fun. Standard 3v3 is what you'll use to have lag since apparently adding two more people to the arena is all it takes to implode the game's servers. Co-op vs AI is what you'll use to finish off daily quests. Ranked is where you go to get absolutely destroyed, and then subsequently verbally pounded into the dirt.
Summary
This game is amazing, and although your view of it is probably permanently scarred by my bad jokes and terrible review, it's definitely worth buying. It features fast-paced gameplay, extreme fun, and... and... I don't know, I forgot half the relevant material I was supposed to cover anyways. Buy it.

This game has been a favorite of mine for a while. If you like tower defense then this game is for you. It also has an RPG leveling system and 4 classes to choose from (More with dlc) which are all very different from one another. You have the freedom to adjust your play style in many different ways. The loot system s really fun. It can be frustrating sometimes to spend all of your money upgrading a weapon then finding a better one shortly afterwards. The game has really weak system requirements so if you're like me and can't afford a gaming PC then you'll be happy to know this is easy to run. The DLC is actually really good for the price. It offers a ton of extra content. Steam workshop helps with this as well.
I wouldn't pick this game up if you don't have a team of friends to play it with in mind though because by yourself its not even close to the fun you'll have with friends. Also there have been a ton of mods floating around. Really overpowered weapons and armor aren't rare in online games, however this is adressed by separating the game into two playlists. One with steam workshop support and one without. You might think "Oh well if I see something modded then ill just throw it out" now, but the allure of better weapons and more money is really hard to fight.
Overall this is and awesome game if you have people to play it with. I'd stick to the more legit game types though unless you want something in particular from the steam workshop applied.
Note: I have a bug that prevents me from starting online games. Which is a major issue and I can't get it to fix.
