I really liked this game a lot, but then I've always loved the drawings of MC Escher. A deep, considered, puzzle game. Not good if you're looking for quick action, not a great deal of story or character development (though there is some), but the puzzles really require some consideration, a bit of trial and error, and later on particularly a deep understanding of the mechanics that are progressively introduced. It's the kind of puzzle game that would drive a lot of people to looking up instructions for solutions I think, or others still to try 100 times then sleep on it and suddenly have the answer.
A lot of people have drawn comparisons with Braid, which I haven't played, but I really felt this was more inspired by Escher's original drawings than any other game and similarities in mechanics were not intentional.
Others still have stated the controls are clunky or slow, which I also disagreed with. I played on PC, with keyboard only (no controller). The pace of the game is slow, but this fits well with the style and atmosphere and the nature of the puzzles. The character moves slowly, but this gives you quite fine control over where he's standing and how he's sliding around when you shift gravity, which becomes critical to solving many of the later puzzles.

I really, really enjoyed this game. I'm not generally the biggest fan of RPGs - I tend to favor point 'n click adventures and visual novels. This game is like a hybrid RPG and VN. Plus, I liked the art style and the story intrigued me, so I purchased it.
First, let's talk about the gameplay. I saw other reviews mention that it gets grindy, and I would agree with that. Especially towards the end when the only person who will engage in discourse with you is Judge Boasting. (This is where "tones" get very important.) But that's my only complaint. Otherwise, it was really fun. I think the combat style is very unique and would absolutely play another game like this, with or without the same characters. The hardest element to master was tones, but once I really understood how that worked it was less frustrating and more of a fun challenge.
Then there's the art. Obviously, this game was made with RPG maker. So when I talk about art, I actually mean the character sprites. And they're really lovely. Between the fictional European (vaguely British) setting and the way the characters were dressed, I was reminded of the Professor Layton series. To me, that was a very good thing. It's one of my favorite game series.
And the story! So wonderful. There's a lot of dialogue, but it's very well written. You get a strong sense of who the characters are without being told explicitly what their personalities are like. And the world-building is excellent. Througout the game, you learn bits and pieces about St. Lauden. It starts to feel like a real place. Well, perhaps a real place in another universe.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. And I especially recommend playing through the game multiple times to pick up on all the little secrets. (Also, there are essentially two endings. You'll definitely want to see them both.) Even if you're like me and don't particularly care for RPGs, give this one a chance! I can't wait to see what this game developer does next.

Ok, so admittedly the story has some confusing parts to it especially near the end when 'everything changes' (you'll probably have to watch all the extra cutscenes it puts in the 'history' to actually realize what's happening), but I really like the mature nature of the game, and the very adult themes it presents.
The story doesn't focus on any one character, rather treating 'class-0' as a single unit, but each one of the 14 playable characters is unique in both personality and play style.  I occasionally hear some complaints about the game's difficulty, but I never felt frustrated by it's difficulty, and the game does allow you to adjust difficulty up or down at save points so I feel this is an unjustified complaint.  I never had issues with the game's camera, but it does move quickly, and the game is very fast paced.
There is a LOT of extra content that you probably won't be able to do without at least a little bit of grinding, but unless you are trying to 100% the game, most of that falls into more 'bonus dungeon' type content.  The game does feature a new game+ feature, so if you miss something on a play through don't worry about it, and since the game has adjustable difficulty even early 'easy' missions can be made into something appropriately challenging for your higher level characters.
I feel the sound track is excellent and fit's the game's themes very well.
TL;DR if you enjoy the Final Fantasy series and want to see a FF game with more mature themes, this game is solid.

I picked up this game during the summer sale because it was cheap, had a cool name, and looked like something that would let an aging gamer have fun without having to train up on fast muscle twich response. It's been all that and more.
Space Hulk is a strategy and tactical game that emphasizes the strategy and tactics without adding lots of gimmicks or complicated options. Random dice rolls keep things a little unpredictable and can make a level easier or harder depending on which way they land. It's similar to other random + skill games like backgammon, cribbage, or other tabletop RPGs. I also liken it to Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea, Valkyria Chronicles, and Archon, as far as the importance of unit movement and positioning goes. The downside to its simplicity is that it can be a bit repetitive at times. To help with that, it offers the ability to speed up some of the animation, and later introduces units with different capabilities. The combination of units on any given level are predetermined, which creates different challenges like a limited number of ranged weapons compared to melee or finite ammunition weapons.
I've seen several reviews and comments about the game being too hard and melee combat being nigh impossible (which it kind of is). Many of those players however, seemed to miss key elements of the game, or were trying to play it the wrong way. Much like how open combat must be avoided in the Metal Gear games, melee combat should be avoided in Space Hulk. But that's part of the strategy and tactics. There are several other aspects that a good RTFM takes care of, such as the rules for Genestealer movement, weapon ranges, and automatic weapon unjamming. It's definitely worth a read-through to avoid some frustrations while playing. It can be fun to figure out all the details of the rules through gameplay, but chances are that if you're the strategy/tactical gaming type, you'll eventually want to know all the quirks and check to see what you might have missed.
For me, each level takes about 30 to 60 minutes to play through; YMMV. Once you get the basics down, the relearning curve after putting down the game and coming back to it after a couple days or weeks is minimal. That makes it a great game for a somewhat casual gamer, but I've also given it multi-hour spans and gone through several levels at a time. I frequently forget that you can save the game in the middle of a level, but it just feels wrong to leave one in the middle uncompleted, especially given that 30 to 60 minute timeframe.
Maybe it's just the way I set up my strategies, but most of my play throughs seem to be either dismal failures with perfect storms of consecutive horrible dice rolls against a single point of failure, or 100% clean-sheet victories with multiple redundant safeguards to ensure success. There are a handful of levels where I encountered the middle ground of escaping with half my space marines alive, and those levels are just begging for a replay.
Aside from random elements such as Genestealer spawning and dice rolls, some of the choices that can affect the outcome of a level are: What order should I deploy my units? Should I make a run for it or stand my ground? Will my melee unit be able to hold out long enough to protect my flank in this corridor? Do I have enough command points if my bolter jams and the number of enemies around the corner is 5 and not 3? Should I destroy that door for a longer line of sight, or leave it closed to delay my pursuers? If I turn this corner, will I have enough range to defeat the next wave, and what is the likelihood they will  be able to close to melee range and if so what are my chances of survival? If I lose my flank, will I still be able to clear the level?
You can look to other reviews to cover things like music and graphics and animation; I've no complaints with any of it. If you're looking for a fast-twitch gaming experience or a game where you can just hit "attack, attack, attack, defend, magic, attack" over and over, this isn't the game you're looking for. If you like puzzles, puzzle games, strategy and tactics games that require making correct choices in advance of where they become critical, planning, or tabletop games, then Space Hulk is worth purchasing. I don't remember what I paid for it duing the sale. $5? Definintely. $10? Sure. $20? Maybe if you're a Warhammer 40k fan or tabletop player.
And a final note: A well executed Space Hulk level where your Terminators have their backs covered, plenty of command points on reserve, and clear lines of sight to mow down legions of Genestealers is incredibly satisfying. Hearing, "Bolter jammed" followed by, "Weapon functional. Flank secure" in that calm Terminator voice over a floor littered with the bodies of expired Genestealers and their blood, will be music to your ears.

The Good: Seems like a very faithful recreation of the board game, which I have always wanted to play and never had the opportunity. So you get the board game without a lot of the niggly details that come from setting up a board game, making sure you understand the rules, and finding another player to play against (though you still need to do this if you choose to play multiplayer). If you like strategy board games with dice rolls, this is definitely worthwhile to check out. The graphics are nice. Sound f/x and voice acting, all top notch.
SIDENOTE: I see some of the reviews and it seems like they want so much more than what this ever tried to be, which is an adaptation of the board game. That's why I bought this. If they had made a bunch of needless changes, it becomes less and less what it should be. If you want some other game, say, XCom, there's nothing wrong with that, but if you want XCom, go buy XCom.
The Bad: It will never fully replicate the feeling of rolling dice yourself, but that's a small loss. What bugs me about this game is that you are paying for about half of the game. And then you have to pay for the rest of the missions and you can't even access different 'chapters', yet the option is so clearly staring you in the face on the main menu locked. As much as I enjoy this game and the Warhammer 40k universe (and especially the Dawn of War series, which doesn't do this), this just rubs me the wrong way. At least have an alternate chapter you can access and then have additional chapters to purchase, if you will, so it doesn't quite seem like you are selling me an incomplete game.
Same with the additional campaigns that are there, staring you in the face with a lock symbol. At least don't put them there until after you buy them as DLC. Maybe include a DLC section, like many games, so that they remain separate and apart.
I know the DLC culture that game companies have embraced is the thing now, but I rather loathe it. I tend to wait until much later, so I can buy the most complete version of the game right off the bat (often the 'game of the year' edition).
LAST WORD: If you like Warhammer 40k and/or if you like board games, check this one out. My complaints really don't win out over what I enjoy about this game.

I will try to not spoil anything from the story but the game tries to be at least somewhat similar to the classic it was named after so anyone can guess that the story is not all that important - though I really enjoyed it, mostly because I'm a sucker for japanese stuff and the story's locations ooze Japan.
Progression:
You can progress in the game, unlike in the original, this one has an upgrade system. For money you can upgrade your weapons (except sword, those upgrades are unlocked through the story), karma points that you get from certain items and visceral fights for special moves and KI crystals for abilities. While this system is more than welcome in my eyes and provides a way to play as you wish (and as such provides a possible reason to replay the game) it's flawed in that it's too powerful. You get healing on the first map basically and on lower difficulty that means you can only die if you want to. Hell, I only died when I fooled around (the character cannot swim... which is sad).
Combat:
As mentioned it tries to be samewhat similar to the original shadow warrior and while the combat does feel a tad oldschool in a good way it's obviously not 100% like that was which is neither good or bad, it's just different. I'm enjoying myself big time with this baby, the fighting itself is nicely done, the spec moves spice it up well and what I really liked is that most of the game can be played with just a sword. Hell, I think everything can be murdered with just the sword if you buy proper abilities to compliment your style.
The sole thing I didn't like about combat was how "encounter-based" it was. Basically after every fight, you get karma points depending on how visceral it was (accumulate enough and you can spend it on upgrades). While this is neat, the result is that enemies 90% of time only attack you at certain locations, in groups, instead of being all over the map like in the original title. Make no mistake, these locations are tightly packed but sporadic fights are rare and it's easy to notice the holes in between that can be felt as a downtime of sorts. You can look for secrets and pickups in those areas too but it's just not fighting all along the way. This is not particularly good or bad, it's just that it's different from the original and as such, from my expectations a bit.
Visuals:
Okay, I'm playing the game in 2015 (heck, it's dec. 30. so nearly '16) so obviously not the best visuals one can see out there but it does the job. The whole game looks/feels a bit cartoony (not cellshaded) so there is no problem with it and the map designs were spot on for me. I like everything japanese (maybe not the earthquakes and such) and this game has it all. Japanese themed enemies, people, iconical things like bamboo forests, temples, spooky graveyards and even smalltime neighbourhoods that are usually ignored when it comes to mystical fights in a japanese themed game.
Overall:
Maybe 4 out of 5. The game has it's pros and cons certainly (I managed to get out of the map during my hunts for secrets multiple times..., and even got an error message when I tried to use shurikens on first boss though it did not affect gameplay much). If you want to have some lighthearted fun you won't care about that anyways and this game is all about that. It's modern enough to not scare those that don't like oldschool away in the first second but oldschool and simple enough to just sit down and relax while murdering the cr*p out of everything. Secrets are all over the place so if you are a collector, you will have quite the stuff to find - especially if you don't like cheating as in checking forums or vids on how to find them :3

Oh starmade... This game is quite addicting.
So looking at this you might think, hmm a minecraft clone, but in space... But that's not fair to Starmade. About the only similarities with Minecraft are that it is block based, Java and is focused on building.
Starmade is all about building. Building factory setups, building ships, making stuff bigger and better. It has a lot of tools to help you do this with symmetry planes, a slider to select a number of blocks to place at once, advanced filtered block removal/replacing and so on.
A big part of Starmade is putting systems together. Whether the be their excellent logic system, the power system, or weapon systems. They are all quite interesting and give a lot of different interactions.
My only real complaint with the game is that it is rough around the edges. There is a lot of depth of building and blocks and system interactions, but the NPC system is practically non-existent. There is little reason to explore and the Pirate ships are incredibly outdated with many models that simply don't work.
However, these are EA complaints. I expect it to be a bit rough. They've made great strides in the last year and I'm hoping this next development leg starts to fill out the content gap.

Good points

Bad Points

Last Word is an interesting concept for a game, where the order of power in society revolves around a person’s ability to have the last word in a conversation. Whoever has the last say holds power over the other person in the conversation, requiring that person to follow their commands after the conversation is finished. This idea is the backbone of the game, as the player works to themselves have the last word in conversations against the various opponents in the game.
This leads to an interesting battle system, which while following a sort of JRPG style attacking system, has the twist of the player using words rather than weapons for attacking. This system is also surprisingly complex, where there are different attack style options, different strengths for attacks, and strength counters for each attacks strength, all resulting in a confusing experience when first learning the system – Something the game does little to rectify through the tutorial.
The game features good background story/lore, where the characters all have depth to them, leading to an enjoyable experience learning about them. This is perhaps one of the game’s best features, allowing the player to talk with each guest every chapter to reveal this information a bit more each time.
Overall, I would easily recommend this game at a low price, though at full price I’m not as sure. I was able to finish my first play through of the game in 4 hours, and my second (to 100% it) in an extra 3, so the playtime offered is in my opinion too little for a full price purchase, and I would wait for it to go on sale.

I cannot think about anything in Technobabylon I particularly did not like.
From the awesome score, to the witty dialogue, creative and complex puzzles and engaging cyber dystopian atmosphere, Technobabylon opened on a high note, and up until the credits, damn well held out on a strong stellar beat.
It's the type of game that if you're not a long term follower of Wadjet Eye Games (like me), you'd be like "how did I not know of this?" and then seek them out for more.
But on Technobablyon, lets discuss the pros.
On gameplay, the simple style of "one room but a hell of a lot to do" is fun, yet brain taxing. It must be me and my diet of modern hold-your-hand grade 5 logic puzzles, and shoot-pointblank-don't-think FPS's, but it took me a while to figure out a few of the challenges. That's not really a bad thing, as the puzzles are (mostly fun) and very creative in thought and execution (the CI program on the synths ensures hilarity), and overall, it's a refreshing experience for cerebral activity in their gaming. Just be prepared to use the noggin! ;)
Characters are mostly cliche-free ridden, with talented but vulnerable Latha, transgender protagonist Max (a minor but still notable detail), and "old-man" technophobe Charlie, a Texan who finds himself caught in a situation he doesn't want involving his deceased Sri-Lankan wife. In fact, very noticeable are the diverse and different ethnicities and characters; again it's something new and different in media. (Heck, the setting of fiction Newton city is India, not "New York," or even LA!!)
The music sets the world mood excellently. From the calming sooth and placid feel of escapist Trance lobbys, to dour, gritty feel of investigate megacity murder, the audio matches the setting, tone, and pace mirroring the on screen action.
The writing is wry and writty; sardonic Max makes one sarcastic quip after the next, and Charlie has his own way of handling things, as does Latha, but really, so do all characters, major and minor alike, with a writing humorous style in  constant flow. On note of the characters, the voice acting is quite impressive, with characters carrying the wit and humor far, and giving some mostly convincing dramatics. The narrative engages, and the plot catches, though listen and pay careful attention to the narrative earlier than later, otherwise you'll miss a few things, as well as some "oh wow!" story revelations.
I can tell that it was a small studio (probably very small actually) that made TB, but there was a lot of love and care put into it and it shows. The game is very charming, and in the days of 4K res, 60fps, blah, blah, it at least gathers an unhealthy, grimy ambience to the entire cyberpunk setting. One other thing to appreciate, despite the small studio size, Technobabylon retains from feeling like a tiny indie game with peesy commercial value. Give or take a few noticable modern things, if this was back in the day and you'd said a big studio made it, I'd have swallowed it in one go.
Some minor gripes: one puzzle involving a crime scene you stumble into is particularly hard to solve because of a particular items lack of visibility. I quite stumbled onto it by accident, but this could have been spelt out a little better. Another thing, at times the narrative and plot convolutions are hard to follow. Truthfully though, since when was cyberpunk known for ease of rite, accessibility, clarity and understanding? TB's narrative clunks are all intentional right? XD
So where does that leave us?
If you're a cyberpunk aficionado, love classic pointers, and like engaging logic puzzles (relative to the brain drizzle on today's market), you'd be a nob to ignore Technobablyon.
This was my first Wadjet Eye Games game, and I'm definitely checking out the rest of their catalogue.
Final verdict? For general gamers, 9/10, but for point click adventurers/cyberpunk fans, a definite 10/10.
Buy this game, and enjoy!!

Technobabylon is yet another terrific title on the books of WadgetEye Games that offers a deeply engrossing story combined with challenging gameplay set on a stunningly atmospheric, retro and futuristic 2D backdrop. It is one of the most complex and captivating games I've played in a long time and if you're a fan of point and click games or just love the Cyberpunk genre; it's an absolute essential purchase.
The game takes place in 2087 in the City of Newton -  an AI run City where genetic engineering dominates humanity and an online Trance craze has taken over society where human interaction plays secondary to online communication. The City is also ran by CEL - the Police, who see and control everything. The conspiracy-driven narrative follows the story of three playable characters;- Charlie Regis a CEL agent and his case officer partner Max Lao along with Latha Sesame; a jobless Trance addict who spends her time fixed in a fantasy online world as opposed to the heavily controlled Newton. After a spate of bombings in the city and a criminal on the run who steals people's memories - the 'Mindjacker'; the game flourishes into a sublime and depth-ridden tale of corruption and intrigue. Elaborating any further would be a huge spoiler but it is simply an incredibly well crafted narrative that is extremely thought-provoking and powerful.
The general gameplay is similar to that of classics in the genre and modern titles alike such as Blade Runner and Gemini Rue. It's a puzzle-oriented point and click adventure with some very difficult and well-designed puzzles. Some have been very smartly implemented and can often leave you feeling confused and hapless. The satisfaction when you solve a problem and progress a wonderful feeling though as well as earning achievements. Voice acting is also present and is supported by some very appropriate music that adds to the amazing atmosphere. The writing is also very impressive with many clever fictional futuristic aspects being added that brings intrigue and understanding what happened in the past. Some of the script terminologies are very complex though and users sometimes have to decipher and guess what the game is talking about as some things aren't explained clearly. You will gradually understand everything as your progress though, as the narrative begins to fall into place and terms are elaborated in greater detail.
Overall; Technobabylon is one of the best games I've played this year and another massive success for WadgetEye Games and Steam debut developer Technocrat. The game is complex, challenging, engaging and a remarkable experience throughout. It will take 12-15 hours to finish and with plenty of achievements on offer; there is certainly replay value here also. A must buy!

You know it's going to look good from the video & screens above & so you know it's going to need some relatively decent hardware to make it look like that so ignore the idiots who have a $500 PC & who are complaining it won't run well at max settings....

- Virtually no graphics, even matches themselves are simulated with sports commentary -style text notes.

Final Fantasy Type-0 HD has both impact and a complete lack of impact. It's got some of the most graphic scenes in a Final Fantasy game since the final scene of Crisis Core and it's rather gritty representation of war as you watch soldiers and children alike get blown up, set ablaze and just battered and beaten in just the opening scene. The war story of the game is great as it's just dark and repeatedly hits you with shock moments from weapons of mass destruction and a variety of magic that decimate humanity.
None of this is down to any of the characters though, every character is about as flat as its non-HD characters. The 14 playable characters you're given at the start of the game have little to no depth to them, which seems apt as they're in Class Zero, zero character that is. This isn't helped by the game's attempts to not actually focus on any character interaction until the final third of the game where at that point you've just stopped caring.
It suffers in the final moments where it brings up the Fabula Nova Crystalis meta-lore (the stuff that started in FFXIII) out of nowhere and it leads to the final sections making no sense, but instead of a focus or explanation on the story, the game focuses on the characters and it makes no freaking sense. The closing scene could have been AMAZING, it was good and impactful, but I don't care for these kids, they're a collection of tropes.
The combat is alright in that sort of action style, the camera is a large issue as when things start moving fast you can barely keep track of where you are let alone what you're looking at. There are bizzare RTS sections that don't really work and while there are sections of the game that look SO pretty, SO attractive, at the same time only the playable characters got a nice HD treatment, so everyone else has about three polygons for a finger and large pixels of a texture, it was a PSP game afterall.
Overall, it's alright, two halves of different games and apparently there's a whole load more story on the second playthrough, but I'm not invested enough to really bother.

I will try to not spoil anything from the story but the game tries to be at least somewhat similar to the classic it was named after so anyone can guess that the story is not all that important - though I really enjoyed it, mostly because I'm a sucker for japanese stuff and the story's locations ooze Japan.
Progression:
You can progress in the game, unlike in the original, this one has an upgrade system. For money you can upgrade your weapons (except sword, those upgrades are unlocked through the story), karma points that you get from certain items and visceral fights for special moves and KI crystals for abilities. While this system is more than welcome in my eyes and provides a way to play as you wish (and as such provides a possible reason to replay the game) it's flawed in that it's too powerful. You get healing on the first map basically and on lower difficulty that means you can only die if you want to. Hell, I only died when I fooled around (the character cannot swim... which is sad).
Combat:
As mentioned it tries to be samewhat similar to the original shadow warrior and while the combat does feel a tad oldschool in a good way it's obviously not 100% like that was which is neither good or bad, it's just different. I'm enjoying myself big time with this baby, the fighting itself is nicely done, the spec moves spice it up well and what I really liked is that most of the game can be played with just a sword. Hell, I think everything can be murdered with just the sword if you buy proper abilities to compliment your style.
The sole thing I didn't like about combat was how "encounter-based" it was. Basically after every fight, you get karma points depending on how visceral it was (accumulate enough and you can spend it on upgrades). While this is neat, the result is that enemies 90% of time only attack you at certain locations, in groups, instead of being all over the map like in the original title. Make no mistake, these locations are tightly packed but sporadic fights are rare and it's easy to notice the holes in between that can be felt as a downtime of sorts. You can look for secrets and pickups in those areas too but it's just not fighting all along the way. This is not particularly good or bad, it's just that it's different from the original and as such, from my expectations a bit.
Visuals:
Okay, I'm playing the game in 2015 (heck, it's dec. 30. so nearly '16) so obviously not the best visuals one can see out there but it does the job. The whole game looks/feels a bit cartoony (not cellshaded) so there is no problem with it and the map designs were spot on for me. I like everything japanese (maybe not the earthquakes and such) and this game has it all. Japanese themed enemies, people, iconical things like bamboo forests, temples, spooky graveyards and even smalltime neighbourhoods that are usually ignored when it comes to mystical fights in a japanese themed game.
Overall:
Maybe 4 out of 5. The game has it's pros and cons certainly (I managed to get out of the map during my hunts for secrets multiple times..., and even got an error message when I tried to use shurikens on first boss though it did not affect gameplay much). If you want to have some lighthearted fun you won't care about that anyways and this game is all about that. It's modern enough to not scare those that don't like oldschool away in the first second but oldschool and simple enough to just sit down and relax while murdering the cr*p out of everything. Secrets are all over the place so if you are a collector, you will have quite the stuff to find - especially if you don't like cheating as in checking forums or vids on how to find them :3

I don't think I've ever played a metroidvania, or platformer for that matter, as long as Hollow Knight. And to my suprise, despite it's long 30+ hour length,  I was never bored. Its huge world is full of interesting secrets and meaningful encounters with the many bugs that inhibit it. It's also filled with boss fights and other challenges, many of them hidden and not even mandatory. Hollow Knight is chock full of content and the easy to learn, but hard to master and punishing gameplay keeps it fun all the way through.
It does suffer from a couple problems. My PC had some problems running the game (especially with a lot of enemies on screen) and although glitches were rare, they were definitely annoying. There is also a problem that all players will encounter: the difficulty curve. Like many metroidvanias (like the also excellent Ori and the Blind Forest), the journey gets easier at the end. This is because your character gets many power-ups along the way which makes him more powerful. With the exception of the final boss and the colloseum, I had little problems during the latter half, while the first hours could often be crushingly difficult.
I have some other issues with the game design. When you die, you leave all your money behind at the place where you die (in the form of a ghost version of yourself). This means that if you want your money back you have to go in that direction next time, because if you die a second time without retrieving it you lose it for good. This discourages exploration even though the game's world is very open-ended. There is a way to circumvent this, but once you find out that you can do that, the damage is already done.
Aside from that, I was often frustrated at sections with surfaces such as spikes of thorny vines. When you hit these, you lose some of your health and respawn at an earlier point. The respawn points can either be very forgiving, or feel awfully unfair. Especially during a latter chainsaw-filled platforming portion of the game (an enormous difficulty spike), this became increasingly apparent.
A small nitpick that I nevertheless wanted to mention is the placement of the warp points. Especially if you want to go to the Ancient Basin, which you have to do multiple times, you have to traverse one of two suprsingly long paths. It was not a big issue, since the game is a pleasure to play and the promise of a new item or new lore was enough to make the journey worth it for me, but a quicker way would have been nice.
I have spent most of this review summing up problems, but it's only because everything else is incredible. Every time I went back to Hallownest, something new and exciting would be awaiting me and if I would start gushing about everything I like, I would be at this much longer than I already am. Frankly, all I can say is this.
Buy Hollow Knight. Now.

I wanted to wait until I had a good few PvP matches under my belt to give this game a review and I have to say, this is one of the most fun card games to come out in a while. While it does fall under the Free to Play card game model of buying boosters to get cards, what this game does that many others don't is that it gives you plenty of cards to play with even if you don't purchase them. This is done by playing through the in-game campaign that unlocks a starter deck for each faction AND while you level up from playing, you get booster packs with each level (this is true up to my current level of 7, a booster at each level)
The free boosters are offset with the stipulation that the cards unlocked through free boosters and starter packs cannot be traded for other cards. This means to trade cards you must purchase them either through real cash or the in game currency LP (Light Points). As of now, I have bought 2 packs with real money and last night was able to buy my first pack through LP. I have to say that it feels satisfying, knowing that people do not get penalized for not spending cash on this game. People who do won't necessarily have an edge over other's, they just have more odds of getting Rare, Epic and Legendary cards through means of buying more packs.
As for gameplay, I really like the feel of the game. There's 2 ways to win; Destroy their base or get their Morale to 0. Destroying their base is typical: assault them hard enough to break through their defenses. Morale gives a different spin on things where with each loss of a unit, they lose a certain amount of Morale. If Morale hits 0, they also lose. I found this to be particularly interesting when I won a game through this way without actually trying. I had a decently strong offensive built and the only way my opponent could survive was through mass small units of defense that were just there to block my attacks, they also respawned each round. They held off my offense for quite a long time but with each unit that died, they lost Morale. Ultimately, they saved their Fortress but lost so many units in the process, their Morale hit 0 and I won. I thought that was pretty neat.
PvP seems to be a good mish-mash of different decks and styles of play. Some seem to counter others better. I'm no pro at games like these but I enjoy them and I'm hesitant to play PvP since I, like most people, don't like to be dominated in any game. In my experience thus far I've won more games than I've lost and what's better is you learn certain tactics by seeing how others play this game.
As with many card based games, there's a lot of rules you have to digest, but if you stick with it, go through the Campaign and Academy modes, you will learn a lot and have a hell of a lot of fun playing this game. I can't recommend this game high enough.

The game have nice look to it. I can’t say much about the sound since I mostly played it muted. The story is a very small portion of the game and was for me uninteresting, even though I liked how they moved it forward through small portions of a journal. For more important things like the gameplay and puzzles I have more to say. The puzzles are good and the level of challenge increase mostly in a constant direction upwards. You spin the level (change the direction of the gravitational pull) to move you or obstacles. At some levels you can even change how the pull is for individual objects. This is cool and different. You can also change your character to a inverted version which has the opposite gravity pull the the normal. I do have some bones to pick with this game however.
- A lot of the puzzles are more about timing rather than figure the puzzle out.
- The do not use the visual illusions of the artworks close to enough. Mostly it’s just in the back/foreground rather than a part of the gameplay.
- Half of the game is the same levels repeated but in a “hard-mode” called “mirrored world”. The levels here are harder and plays slightly different, but why not different level design with new artwork? They also tease you twice with having colour to the game. This should definitely be done for the whole mirrored world if you ask me.
- The simplicity of the game makes most levels beatable just by spinning back and forth a bit to see what happens. This is not a big downside at all but it did take away some brainwork.
- Even though I did get stuck sometimes (but only when I played it late at night balls deep in wishes for sleep) the game never made me feel smart for beating it.
I do believe that if they gave you more freedom like letting you change to your inverted self whenever wherever, instead at specific spots on specific levels, it would be harder to know when and where to use it. However, a lot of levels wouldn’t work if that was the case.
For words to end this miserable excuse of a review I would like to recommend it to puzzle fans. This is a different puzzler than most and worth the playthrough for the genres fans. If you’re not that kind of fan I would direct you to start with a more humorous puzzler like “day of the tentacle”.

I am unimpressed.  Yes, this is a faithful adaptation of the 1989 board game, right down to telling you exactly what the Space Marines and Genestealers rolled on their six-sided dice each turn.  And that's a problem.
Movement grids, turns and six-sider-based combat mechanics are all  useful approaches to creating a game that can be run on the limited processing power available in a group of human players.  On a computer that could do so much more, it just seems rather pitiful.  The grid based movement and action point system make your tactical options very limited while the randomness of the six-sider engine ensures that even an optimal strategy can be overwhelmed in one or two turns of bad (simulated) rolls.  (And, conversely, sloppy strategy can still triumph, if the dice favour you.)
In the original game, seeing your squad crushed without recourse because the dice simply turned against you was an accepted part of play.  Playing with a group, seeing a friend suddenly get demolished by a run of bad luck could be a source of hilarity.  But playing solo, in a computer game that didn't need to rely on something as crude as a handful of d6s, allowing victory or defeat to lie in the hands of virtualized plastic cubes seems inexcusably lazy.
The setting is cool.  The graphics and sound are adequate.  But the mechanics of the board game needed a major overhaul to make the transition to a digital environment, and they didn't get it.

R3E was absolutely terrible not so long ago. The interface was a nightmare and the racing odd with the huge coloured markers etc. If you judge it on that, let me tell you that it's now a completely different game.
The interface now makes sense, and is one of the best you'll find out there. The game is F2P with purchases for content (but the ability to enter certain events without purchasing the content and the option to try before you buy). There are frequent sales so you don't have to spend a fortune.
Cars are very impressive with the physics being better than iRacing, Project Cars and Assetto Corsa but not quite as good as RFactor 2. Tracks, while not laser scanned, are not too far off the quality of RF2's non-laser-scanned tracks. The geometry is generally accurate, but of course you don't get the exact bumps, but laser scans quickly become out of date so this isn't as big an issue as one might expect. Sounds are the best you'll find anywhere, really expressing the clunky rattling shaking madness of a real race car.
Netcode needs a bit of work [cars behave strangely with high pings and disconnects happen], but multiplayer is in alpha I believe, so hopefully that'll improve in time. The usual issues of only 30% finishing and loads of wrecks apply in public servers but plenty of leagues exist to cater to the more serious racer. Single-player features the most enjoyable AI I've raced against.
In short, R3E is VASTLY better than it was, and now deserves a place among the elite of sim-racing.

Last Word is smart. Not just fun, but smart.
I haven't played many games in the last few years, and definitely not one like this. That's where I'm coming from. But it was good. It has a lot of tiny details, which is why I spent so many hours playing. A thing here, a thing there.
ATMOSPHERE
The game has a spirit, or mood, with the way the characters are named and the music/sounds keeps you enlivened and motivated. There's only one real area, but it's dense with activity.
The game looks good in general. Clear. Expressive. The cat is so cute!
The music was also very good.
"BATTLE" SYSTEM
It was extremely fun, and I didn't find it hard or complicated, but I was still figuring things out in the middle of the game. There are no penalties for losing, so my advice is that if you don't understand the system, fight Seymour Saymore a lot in the beginning to try and learn.
ENDING
There are several endings. One is your basic fare, which is good. But then there's the unexpected ending, which is nice. It brings more of the mystery elements.
The bad/good thing of the game is that it's too short. I wish it were longer, which is bad. But I want more, which is good.

Some years ago I was playing League of Legends a lot and I was quite good at it, yet I'm absolutely regretting 95% of the time I've spent playing it. LoL was the MOBA that focused a lot on competitiveness and fast, dynamic gameplay, yet it was full of awfully boring content like leveling up, farming and gold to buy items that make your gameplay greater, walking across the big map for hours and hours to get to the teamfight, boring "laning phases" etc... The format of 5v5 also forced you to be in a team that easily could get easily immoralized by someone killing himself on purpose to annoy his teammates, which resulted in a bad gameplay experience for all 10 players. You still had to play the game until the bitter, hopeless end, unless you surrender after at least 20 minutes of suffering. You also had to play the game a lot or spend quite some money to unlock characters and crucial "runes", that make your character stronger. Worst idea ever.
LoL aimed to hook new players with some pretty, flashy gameplay (all the boring MOBA stuff aside) and make them earn the full experience, which I think is an unacceptable misuse of conditioning human psychology (see addicting games like Cookie Clicker). This is why the fanbase turned to be so big, combined with silly "eSports"-ideology and making the game look like very serious business. (It's just a game ffs)
Enough with this rant for now. Let's talk about Battlerite.
After years of playing difficult, fast-paced video games, like Super Smash Bros. Melee and LoL, I got to find Battlerite and it's absolutely amazing. My friends gifted me the game and I immediately got to play it while skyping with them and the hype was unreal. We didn't hesitate to tell all our friends about it and now we're about eight people, slowly growing in numbers. Why I talked about LoL in the beginnning so much, is because Battlerite reminds of ALL the good aspects of the game, which are improved even further when it comes to the variety of skills and mechanics and other stuff. It's not just the core gameplay being so brilliant, but I'm also impressed how I don't have the slightest déjà-vu concerning bad aspects of LoL's gameplay. NO SALT, NO UNLOCKING SH*T, NO FARMING AND WALKING AROUND FOR AGES, NO HOUR-LONG MATCHES...
JUST
FULL PVP-ACTION WITH SKILLSHOTS ONLY AND NOTHING ELSE.
There's really nothing unnecessary about the gameplay, which is why I want to proudly congratulate Stunlock Studios for this glorious project!
Also there's other nice stuff like the gameplay recording thing and a built-in platform for sharing plays. Stunlock Studios are still working very eagerly on the game, even having released a balancing patch with other non-gameplay finesse based on community feedback. The community's great as well.

Here's my verdict on FF Type 0: Fun to play, horrible story execution.  Also the characters show no personality because the story takes no time to focus on any of them.  When I unlocked the "what if" scenario at the end and it showed them as normal students I actually found myself liking them as opposed to the blank slates they are generally presented as throughout the game.  At first I thought having each character from the get-go was a welcome change of pace for JRPGs but I quickly discovered that part of the character building in JRPGs comes from having them gradually join you in addition to having interactions with the rest of the characters.  So although I enjoyed the gameplay, I cannot recommend this game from a story perspective.  I find the best games balance the two out but it comes down to personal preference.  Is gameplay more important to you or is it story?

IMPORTANT NOTE: This is a coop-only game. You
need a coop buddy to play with. Voice-chat is highly recommended. It is best played via Local-Coop, but Online-Coop is playable too if you can get the network working.
this is a top-down puzzle game that emphasizes on solving puzzles in coop. It has about 30 different levels, starting from easy levels that introduce game mechanics, to the harder ones that you really need to have some time trying and thinking. You can complete the game in 2-3 hours.
The puzzles themselves are not hard, and most of them rely on solving in coop. For example, in one of the early stages, player one can see landmines, player two can shoot enemies. Both players have to traverse together to avoid stepping on landmines while shooting the enemies to keep both players safe.
The graphics and musics are simple and cute, it suits the game pretty well. As a simple indie game, you don't need to have a high-spec rig to play this game. But you might want to tone down the in-game volume so you can use voice-chat.
The hardest stage is very frustrating though. It is hard in a very frustrating way, and to win that stage you will need to be extremely lucky.
I play Online-Coop with my friend, and we encountered quite a lot of connection issues. For one, it has some random lags while playing (even though we are very sure our network is working very fine). Glitches occurs occasionally after the lag is recovered. Since this game is not that popular, there are very few network-issue solutions online.
We have to keep doing trial-and-error to find an optimal network solution when playing this, sometimes we need to switch host, sometimes it is better when we both use VPN etc. It is very inconsistent.
And because of the network issues, we struggled in a lot of harder stages, since some of them rely on coop timing. That is why, playing in Local-Coop is highly recommended.
One tip for improving the network lag while playing Online-Coop: make sure both players are using the same graphics settings (especially the screen resolution). It helps in my case.
Most of the achievements are easily doable. However the hardest stage is extremely luck-based and very very frustrating to clear, making one of the achievement hard to get.
Some of the achievements cannot be unlocked by the host player, therefore you will need to play in Online-Coop and take turns hosting for both players to unlock those. Not sure if this is a glitch or dev-intended.

TSW in its current state gets a 6/10. The simulation and mechanics of the trains can't be faulted and I do like how it concentrates on the finer details of running a large diesel engined train. I like how you can walk around the trains and decouple carriages etc. The graphics and sound effects are gorgeous.
It seems like a lot is missing though to take advantage of the new detail levels of the trains in this simulation.
Some big negatives unless I am missing something do the devs really expect me to get out of the train and try and work out the correct signals to change when switching tracks? Where is the map overview? Or why do you have missions where I have to walk over a 1000 metres of the entire train length just to move to the next stage? Grognards might love this but if you want to appeal to a larger audience the majority of people will see this as a tedious exercise in frustration and stop playing the sim.
IMO it would have scraped in with a thumbs up but but I find it puzzling and disappointing Dovetail is already selling an addon for a game that seems barely out of the alpha stage. That smacks of greed especially considering the core game is US$40 and only contains one track!
I can see a good future for this title but I must give it a thumbs down as I do not believe it represents good value in its current state. My advice to any buyers considering this is to wait until more content is added - preferrably without being a paid addon.
EDIT: I am more than willing to change this to a thumbs up if and when Dovetail adds some more meat to the sim and maybe re-lists it as an early access product. The core of the game is solid but it needs more.

I would define Shadowgrounds Survivor as "Weekend light fun".
It's almost the same as the original, just a bit deeper: Different characters blasting their whay through alien hordes using different weapons and skills, going from point A to point B grabbing supplies, shooting everything and discovering secrets.
As simple as that, the game is short and limited: Three characters, each one with two different weapons and a tipe of grenade, not a big amount of enemies to shoot at, some levels with the smallest variation (There's some defense zones, and in the end you get a mecha) and.. nothing else.
The campaign lasts over 3.6 hours (Or that's what Steam says). After beating it, two new difficulty levels are unlocked, several survival maps and extra options (If you found enough secrets) to help you or make things silly in the second playthrough (If you want to do it).
Also it has a map editor and coop, although I don't think that it has a very active communitty.
In short, is a REALLY short game that does not a lot of things, but it does them right. Its not a great game but it is also not a bad game. If its on sale and you want to spend some time killing aliens, this is a good choice (Even better if it comes with the original), if you are looking for something more than a short distraction, look elsewhere.

Excellent in the beginning and middle, but falls off a bit towards the end.
The gameplay is top notch, and it's genuine fun to chop things, explode things, shotgun things to bits, and mix and match.
There are a few nitpicks however:
*There's a very annoying weapon switch delay that tends to kill the pace of a fight. Not sure why it exists.
*Enemies can get quite damage spongey towards the end of the game. Maybe it's because I played on hard, but those big guys took 9 rockets to kill and they're very common towards the end of the game.
*The amount and type of enemies you encounter towards the end of the game gets quite frustrating. You get very few "fodder" foes to give you some easy kills to relax a bit, it's all elite enemies that take a ton of hits to kill. Great enemies to fight every once in a while, but not all the time, and not multiple at once.
*Fall damage seems to grow insanely fast. I thought I could afford to fall one floor since the player character is a ninja, but that just makes his knees explode.
*Hit detection is a bit wonky. Sometimes an enemy will swing or strike a good bit distance from you, but you'll still take hits. Sometimes you can go nuts slashing on something point blank, but never actually hit it. This is rare, though.
*Some of the most god awful boss fights I've ever seen in any game. The same gimmick, repeated five times!
Despite the nitpicks, it's so cheap I have to recommend it. There's a very nice point in the middle of the game where difficulty feels perfect, and when this game works, it's a joy to play.

I don't think I've ever played a metroidvania, or platformer for that matter, as long as Hollow Knight. And to my suprise, despite it's long 30+ hour length,  I was never bored. Its huge world is full of interesting secrets and meaningful encounters with the many bugs that inhibit it. It's also filled with boss fights and other challenges, many of them hidden and not even mandatory. Hollow Knight is chock full of content and the easy to learn, but hard to master and punishing gameplay keeps it fun all the way through.
It does suffer from a couple problems. My PC had some problems running the game (especially with a lot of enemies on screen) and although glitches were rare, they were definitely annoying. There is also a problem that all players will encounter: the difficulty curve. Like many metroidvanias (like the also excellent Ori and the Blind Forest), the journey gets easier at the end. This is because your character gets many power-ups along the way which makes him more powerful. With the exception of the final boss and the colloseum, I had little problems during the latter half, while the first hours could often be crushingly difficult.
I have some other issues with the game design. When you die, you leave all your money behind at the place where you die (in the form of a ghost version of yourself). This means that if you want your money back you have to go in that direction next time, because if you die a second time without retrieving it you lose it for good. This discourages exploration even though the game's world is very open-ended. There is a way to circumvent this, but once you find out that you can do that, the damage is already done.
Aside from that, I was often frustrated at sections with surfaces such as spikes of thorny vines. When you hit these, you lose some of your health and respawn at an earlier point. The respawn points can either be very forgiving, or feel awfully unfair. Especially during a latter chainsaw-filled platforming portion of the game (an enormous difficulty spike), this became increasingly apparent.
A small nitpick that I nevertheless wanted to mention is the placement of the warp points. Especially if you want to go to the Ancient Basin, which you have to do multiple times, you have to traverse one of two suprsingly long paths. It was not a big issue, since the game is a pleasure to play and the promise of a new item or new lore was enough to make the journey worth it for me, but a quicker way would have been nice.
I have spent most of this review summing up problems, but it's only because everything else is incredible. Every time I went back to Hallownest, something new and exciting would be awaiting me and if I would start gushing about everything I like, I would be at this much longer than I already am. Frankly, all I can say is this.
Buy Hollow Knight. Now.

So, this game is EXTREMELY fun to play with a couple friends.
As a terrible designer and builder I can safely say that my role in StarMade is to steal unclaimed ships.
So, my first experience was rather interesting.
I went mining with my friends and we gathered some ores over the course of an hour and made millions off of it, which was an amazing start. We started to build a ship of our own, but we decided others' ships were much better and we'd work much better stealing and running. So we did just that at the spawn.
Over the next week, the Spaghetti faction got a reputation for stealing ships on SystemHack. So that was fun. It got to the point where our mothership was tiny compared to our biggest ship, but we still called it Spaghettimother since our big miner was NOT a residential ship.
However we lost interest after people learned to claim their ships, and with our owned ships we got bored of fighting pirates and exploring the same small pentagon-faced planets.
All in all, this game is fun for progressing and quick empire-building. But once you've done the main stuff, there's no fun in just flying around the same few planets. Of course, professional builders would say otherwise. I've seen some amazing builds, ranging from tiny X-Wings and TIE Fighters to giant flying buses, huge warp rings and cresent-shaped fighters that could house a large village of people inside it.
For a player who wants to just have fun exploring and fighting, this game gets boring quite quickly with the fact I have to rebuild and repair my ship block by block after every fight if my shields go down. I'm sure others think differently, but I think more exploration methods would really make StarMade better.
Oh, also, travelling is a bloody awful burden. Took me an hour to get to the edge of the galaxy. Went and had a good meal while I was waiting. Warping doesn't help much either.

I'm a huge fan of tabletop games, although never got into Warhammer 40k in particular (I was more into Legions of Steel, which has much in common with the Space Hulk board game as it turns out).  I first played the PC version of Space Hulk back in the mid-90s, and it immediately addicted me with its puzzle-like levels and brutal, unforgiving gameplay.  I originally grabbed this title purely due to my desire for an update.  It was a bit buggy at release; however, it's been cleaned up dramatically and is now quite solid IMO.
It does take a while to get used to the way you have to deploy and move your squad.  Some complaints you'll see about randomness is likely the result of someone not getting this completely under their belt.  I can also see people's point about wanting some kind of development over time for your squad members, but I'll admit I prefer the more puzzle-like format of the missions keeping you focused on your objective, and sometimes Terminators will fall in pursuit of it.  If there was xp-based leveing up of your squad, many people will just save-scum to ensure progression rather than focus on the puzzle at hand.
If you're a fan of turn-based squad combat or table-top wargames, and crave some challenge, I would imagine Space Hulk would fit the bill for you nicely.

Infinity Wars chose a desperate time to release. With the recent release of the Hearthstone open beta, many people will be swarming to that and overlooking this TCG. Unfortunatly for them, they'll be missing out on an amazing game. Firstly, over Hearthstone, it actually has a comprehensive single player. It also has numerous factions, all of which have definitive styles of play. Most of the cards are well balanced (With a few exceptions, Verore Death Worshipper anyone?), and it's possible to get cards quite quickly. Additionaly, it has mechanics that shake up the usual set-up that was introduced by Magic:The Gathering, and they work wonderfully. Microtransactions might be a slight problem for some, as not all of the shop items can be bought with in-game currency, but it doesn't stick out too much. There's also a slight problem with the tutorials, as they require you to beat minor puzzles to get through them, and some people might not have the time for that. The biggest problems I've had with the game are glitches. It is an early access game, yes, but it constantly worries me. Firstly by appearantly losing my level 2 reward, then by temporarily getting rid of my progress, it can get pretty annoying. Overall though, Infinity Wars wins my vote over with it's varied card types, interesting mechanics, and beautiful animation.

First of all, it cannot be overstated that beta is beta. There are missing sounds and animations, placeholder art, the interface needs reworking, and some things are just generally really rough around the edges. I'm going to assume that these things will be worked on and improved before the game is officially released. I have concerns about this, but more on that later.
Infinity Wars is, in all aspects that are not likely to change during the beta, an excellent trading card game. The cards look great,  the gameplay mechanics are really innovative and fun, and there's plenty of modes for experienced players and free to play people alike.
Speaking of free to play, Infinity Wars makes Hearthstone look like it's made by EA. I got a 15 card booster today just by logging in. The draft mode - directly copied from HS - has an entry fee of around 0,30€ (1,73€ in HS) if you convert the premium currency to real money, or 1000 IP, which you gain from playing. Going straight 0-3 gives you over a third of the IP back, and over five wins pays the whole thing back already. You also get free cards and boosters from simple daily quests, doing the campaign missions and leveling up, which is fairly rapid.
While I'm going to recommend the game, I'd still suggest that you don't get into it just yet. My internal alarm bells are going off at the Infestation set preorder boosters. Why are they adding new cards when the already existing ones aren't finished yet? There are much more pressing issues than adding more content right now, and I can't be sure that the game gets to the level of polish I'm expecting it to.
It's probably going to the best f2p card game on the PC regardless of how much or little it improves from this point, though.

I had no end of problems with the Steam version of Starmade which required removing it from my library and then deleting it via steam entirely. Reinstalled in the C directory and now it runs.
Having said that...
Starmade, the not-minecraft-in-space-which-looks-alot-like-minecraft-in-a-way.
If you don't have trouble with Java, if you are one of the lucky ones who doesn't have constant issues with stability and if you're right handed, you'll probably develop a love/hate relationship with the game.
Fully keymapping isn't implemented so any left handers like me trying to use the numberpad for your controls find out that the devs don't recommend using it cos it's still being used for dev work.
The build mode is fiddly at times, graphics are okay if rudimentary, planets eat your fps and as ever, getting resources is a grind. The problem with the build mode is trying to create ships one block at a time - yes, the advanced build mode allows placing of multiple blocks, but it's ghastly to use and unnecessarily annoying. You can't manipulate shapes, you can only place blocks which can dry up the creative juices rather quickly.
On the other hand, if you like building spacecraft, this is currently the leader in the woefully under-represented spacecraft building genre. There are a few other similar-ish games (for the building part at least) snapping at it's heals though, such as Interstellar Rift, Avorion (currently on greenlight & demo available), Empyrion and Starship Corporation to name a few. If you want an alternative ship builder, go with Interstellar Rift, if you want survival, try Empyrion.
TL;DR
If you're patient, overflowing with creativity and have luck with java, you'll be okay for the most part, otherwise research alternatives.
I still give it a thumbs up though as it has a lot of potential.

The Bridge is an interesting and unique indie puzzle game with a number of flaws.
The game is heavily inspired by Braid, but both the puzzle design and the art style are quite different. This time around you can adjust the direction of gravity and this is indeed your main tool in solving the levels. The game introduces a few new mechanics along the way and once you are finished with the main levels more challenging mirror versions are unlocked.
The M.C. Escher inspired art style is probably the best part of the game. The hand-drawn black and white artwork is gorgeous and the visual design leads to some very interesting (and physically impossible) levels and mind bending puzzles.
Unfortunately the puzzle design is not particularly consistent. Some puzzles have clever and satisfying solutions whereas others simply rely on very precise movements and rotations. Overall I was still enjoying the puzzles, but quite frankly some of the levels could have used a redesign.
The controls could have used some work too. Movement is quite floaty and everything feels a little bit sluggish. This is certainly not a deal breaker in a puzzle game, but it's still mildly annoying.
Despite its flaws I enjoyed The Bridge and would recommend it to fans of puzzle games. However, the mirrored levels in particular are fairly challenging, so if you are not very good at this type of puzzle solving the game can get very frustrating.
I played through both the normal and mirror levels and found the overall difficulty level pretty good. I did get stuck on a few levels for a while, but eventually I managed to solve those too.
I received the game for free from a giveaway, but this didn't affect my review.
The good:
- Great hand-drawn art
- Unique core concept
- Mind bending physics and puzzles
- Good level of challenge
The bad:
- Floaty and sluggish controls (I was using a gamepad)
- Some poorly designed levels
- Audio is very basic
- Obnoxious marketing of the developer's new game (which looks lot less interesting anyway than this game)

A great game for the right kind of person, but I just personally wasn't feeling it. The game sorta pitches itself as having dialogue-based "combat", but I don't really feel that's the case. You speak to NPCs as you would in any other RPG in the non-combat phases, but when you enter the "combat" phase, it's more of a rock-paper-scissors game where "rock" and "paper" have been renamed abstract concepts like "power" and "aggression". No actual dialogue happens during "combat" at all. It's all abstract.
There is more to the combat to make it more complicated (and arguably more convoluted) where there is a sort of tug of war game you're trying to win, and in order to use certain tact-based types of attack options, you first have to build up a requisite stat by using power-building attack options first so that you can sacrifice power to gain tact. It's a weird system with a lot of different types of points and meters, where you sacrifice your A points to build up your B points so that you can sacrifice your B points to use a C attack, but your enemy uses a D attack which lowers your E points, etc etc. The game does a very poor job of explaining how all of this works, so you just have to keep talking to your one practice NPC over and over again until you start to make sense of it.
At the end of the day, the game feels to me like rock-paper-scissors needlessly complicated with ten different types of points/meters to watch.
"Dialogue fights" is a cute idea in theory, but that's not really what ends up happening in practice, and what does end up happening in practice I just didn't take much of a fancy to.

There is something to be said about Breath of Death VII, although I'm not sure what it is. On the surface, Breath is nothing more than a mediocre parody game, offering little in humor and even less in story. The characters are just barely charming enough to carry the player through, and while the settings can be interesting enough, only the main character serves to be anything more than 1-dimensional. The story doesn't do the genre justice, and leaves a lot to be desired in writing. Story is often the sole reason one plays a typical RPG, and its always dissapointing when that falls through.
Whatever you do, don't buy this game expecting a wry and witty parody to challenge your beliefs of modern gaming. Buy it because it's a wonderful game.
I can't begin to state how much I love the battle system in this game. Taking cues from Earthbound and Dragon Quest, Breath of Death implements a 1st person turnbased combat system that looks wildly archaic, but fits with the time its emulating. Like the games that inspired it, the enemy sprites are sparsely detailed, and there isn't even a backgroud to speak of. Attacks are picked from a sad little wall of text from the right, and give the damage and whatever status effects it might cause. No attacks are animated, save for the enemies flickering when being attacked. I wish I could make this sound more appealing, but the retro flavor fits the battles perfectly, allowing the player to focus on the numbers. If the thought of number watching turns you off, please, feel free to avoid at all costs, but I personally loved it.
Calculating attacks and knowing when to heal your characters is crucial. There is a sacrifice for every choice you make, and the game implements an engaging combo system that can make or break the tougher battles in the game. Believe it or not, combat is extremely fast paced for an RPG, as with every turn, the enemy's attacks become stronger. This is a non-issue with the earlier battles, but becomes a deciding factor in mid to late-tier encounters, especially bosses. If your usual plans involve delicately whittling down health while keeping yours up, prepare to have your butt handed to you. Your offense is the best defense, and the streamlined item selection saves you any micromanaging you'd usually worry about in other games.
After every battle, your health is completely recovered at no cost, and depending on how quickly you dispatched the opponent, a small amount of mana will be restored. In battle, mana is essential for getting out of a tight spot, but there is only so much, so use it wisely. Like mana, potions can be found throughout the game, and serve as an instant heal in battle, but are worth stocking up for the later battles. And as a rule with any classic RPG, save often, as you can save anywhere, so be warned; you will die in this game. Just when you think you've leveled well past the normal encounters, the difficulty spikes, so don't be afraid to grind.
In fact, the game rewards grinding, as each area offers only a finite number of encounters.  As an added bonus, you can initiate an encounter at any time on the menu, so you could get all the fights out of the way and then explore the new enviornment at your leisure. Of course, you could go the classic way and enjoy the occasional random encounter, but I found the freedom to choose a very considerate nod to the player.
Grinding also opens the lovely door of the level-up, which is handled ingeniously throughout. A tiered system takes place, with every level gained offering a choice. Sometimes its statistical, choosing health over magic, for example, but on occassion, moves can be chosen. This is where the game shines in replay value, as there are numerous branching paths that expand organically as you evolve your characters throughout. Some moves only offer minor decisions, such as faster combo boosts over more power, but whenever I was challenged with taking a strong area attack over a single devastating blow, I would struggle. The amount of options are staggering and can lead character development in wild directions, but even then, I never felt the game become unbalanced.
Replay value can also be found within this game, as there are multiple hidden dungeons and secret bosses that offer weapons and armor you can't find anywhere else in the game. That on top of the multiple difficulties and character customization, Breath of Death more than exceeds the measely 3$ dollar price tag. The game its bundled with is also considered rather good although I have yet to play it, so its hard for anyone to come away unsatisfied.
All in all, Breath of Death VII is worth your time no matter what you're looking for, as it welcomes both newcomers and veterans alike. Whether you're looking for a corny in-joke or an engaging combat system, this game is definitely worth giving a shot.

Short Version:
FF type-0 is what I've come to expect from a FF entry, great gameplay, so-so soundtrack, terrible story. Forget the FF title as much as you can, lower your expectations, and you might find yourself having a good time.
Long Version:
Gameplay - Taking aside the port side of things (rigid controller settings, next to no support for anything outside xbox, yadda yadda) this game plays very nice, the combat is interesting and can be approached in a variety of gameplay styles, there are a lot of different missions/objectives and the newgame+ mechanic feels well integrated with new stuff to do each spin of the cycle.
Story - Loosely based on the same universe as the XIII's entries, the story tries to take a more mature approach with a constant war setting and lots of convictions/lives and blood/deaths on the table. The plot is extremely convoluted and can only be understood after replaying the game 2/3 times while actively seeking side content and reading material in-game, most characters are underdeveloped and/or overlooked. All this makes for a very poor excuse of story that ends in only a semi-pleasent note.
Sound - The main theme is pretty powerful and the composer seems to know since it is used throughout too much of the soundtrack. There are some very decent tracks and most of them fit the setting but the overuse of the main melody prevents me from enjoying the soundtrack as much as I could. The japanese VA is, of course, extremely welcome as it fits like a glove.
Graphics - The movie like scenes look very good and are a pleasure to watch. On other hand, the in-game cutscenes look terrible, with worse than soap opera "you talk, I talk" conversations and only a few select body movements for each character. As for the game itself, it looks decent, but there aren't a ton of different areas/dungeos/settings.

A very amusing game, with charming and stylish art, story, and sound design.
It looks like your typical turn based rpg, that's set inside a single mansion, but it's not quite what you expect.
Basically there's two parts of the gameplay. The first part is investigating topics by talking to other guests that's locked in the mansion with you. You investigate and gather informations about key topics and you use it to move the story forward.
The second part, that is the meat of the game, is the discourse, the battle system. In this game, conversation is serious business, and having the last word can give you literal domination toward your discourse partner.
It's basically one-on-one turn-based rpg battle. But you don't take turn stabbing each others with swords of course. You take turn in abstract discussions, and try to gain the last word.
You have choices on what to do. You throw disruptive remark to mostly gain power. You can throw submissive remark to trade your power with tact, and finally you can throw agressive remark to actually move the conversation toward your end. Other than that there are things you must consider, like your and your opponent's composure, which is basically your defenses, the tone of conversation (tones have paper-rock-scissors relationship, and they have different effects or can destroy your opponent's composure), and of course various personal skills everyone have.
Basically, a pretty charming and stylistic twist on typical turn-based rpg.

CONS:

-"Lag spikes" did occur on 2 occasions but seem to be pretty rare or atleast on my PC.
-Not a whole lot to this game other than a few missions/scenarios. Supposedly more coming?

Final Verdict:
Firstly, this game ran fine on my "mid-range" computer with nothing special on it. 60 FPS on Ultra settings was pretty consistant throughout the playing session which lasted about an hour. Game play was fine and entertaining but I can see where a player could get bored quickly due to lack of gameplay. I suggest anyone who is looking at purchasing this game to please do your homework and make sure your computer can handle the work load this game brings with it. As stated above, the game will eat up your virtual memory so make sure your graphics card has the required specs to run this game and be sure to play the game on the settings YOUR computer can handle.
