This is a puzzle game along the lines of Braid. Rather than using Braid's time mechanics, it plays on the mechanics of gravity. The majority of puzzles in the non-mirror world (2 parts to the game, mirror and non-mirror) can generally be solved by turning the screen or walking in one direction or the other. This meant that I was initially disappointed with the difficulty of the game, although there were a few puzzles that took me a few minutes of head scratching to work out.
I found the best part of the game came with the mirror world that increased the difficulty and provided the puzzles with more action-based solutions that involve you moving your character around and so he becomes part of the puzzle rather than an object you slide into the exit.
The art work is great as is the sound. Most people will probably find the pace of the character's walking speed too slow but you'll rarely need to move him that much once you learn about twisting gravity. It also has quite an 'artsy' story and atmosphere to it. Personally, I ignored it but the depth of it may appeal to many people.
Like most puzzle games, you'll either love it because the puzzles appeal to you or they will twist your brain and frustrate you to quit. I'm a logical, visual thinker so most of these puzzles played into my strengths and I enjoyed even the hardest ones. If I can offer one bit of advice, it's that some puzzles are easier if you think about the end position and move back in steps from there.

I played the original board game of this once or twice back in the day, but I'll be honest with you...it was one of those games I found to be SO heavy in rules and the many little exceptions thereof, that I never really got my head around it enough to enjoy it.
Fortunately, with the advent of these nifty new thangs they have these days called "video games" - that is, ones more complicated than Space Invaders or whatever was around when the Space Hulk board game first reared its ugly mug - you only have to remember about HALF the rules, and the computer remembers the other half for you.
It even helpfully points out all the options you have for your next move, as opposed to "tough♥♥♥♥♥♥for not remembering rule number 357 in the manual, that may just have saved your life back there". God bless video games for allowing people like me to unapologetically live out the rest of our days as the unrepentent dumb-arses we truly are.
So what of the merits of said video game, then?  Well, they say there's no accounting for taste, and the rather poor metascore of this amazingly well-designed turn-based strategy game would seem to lend some credence to that assertion. Heck, I don't even LIKE turn-based strategy games that much, not least of all 'cause I'm such a tactless buffoon, and yet this one has proven thus far to be just challenging enough for me, while still eminently completable. Thus far.
Admittedly I'm only about seven or eight missions in, and more than one of them has required multiple attempts to conquer. But if you're willing to gradually learn from your errors and accept that sheer dumb luck plays something of a part (though not TOO huge a part...careful forethought and planning will still mostly see you through), then you just may find this as addictive as I've found it so far.
It's very "more-ish" actually. The only reason I'm not gonna play another mission right now is that it's 5am in the morning and seeing since the last couple of missions took me an hour or so to complete, I should probably just finish this review and go to bed before the sun rises, like "normal" people supposedly aspire to doing. Good thing I don't currently have one of those evil "job" things to stop me from being so gosh-darned productive with my life...yes indeedy, GOD BLESS VIDEO GAMES.
And God bless Steam for giving me thousands of the cursed things to play before I finally lay down in a pauper's grave with "Did Nothing, Achieved Nothing" as my epitaph. But they'll be wrong, oh so wrong. 'Cause I've been a SPACE MARINE, ♥♥♥♥ you all. A Space Marine who has led squads in successful missions against the wretched Genestealers. Saint Pete'd better be takin' THAT♥♥♥♥♥♥into account when I'm linin' up for my place in Paradise, I tell ya...
Verdict: 9.5/10.
(Oh, and in the interests of a more "balanced" review, just a couple of quick criticisms...namely the almost complete absence of in-game music, and the somewhat overly expensive price tag, given "what it is". But that's why Steam have about a dozen-plus sales a year...for cheap-arses like us, right? I'll say it again...GOD BLESS STEAM. Can I have some free stuff now, please?)

Okay, so there are a couple things missing that would have made it an instant buy. 1. It's missing character customization, which while not necessary, would have been a big draw. 2. It's missing a good narative. They could have made the campaign feel more continuous by having some cutscenes or something, but instead the game feels very 'instanced', and you kinda have to figure out the story through the mission briefings/missions themselves.
Now, aside from those things I think this is a good, smart game. It feels like the movie Aliens meets WH40K- you root for some of the biggest badasses in the universe to mulch some xeno filth and get out alive, but of course the aliens are smart, agile, and extremely deadly if they get close to the humies. So, the game retains the feeling of dread at finding out exactly how many genestealers are around the corner, and how likely you are to be pressed for AP/CP (the action points you use to command your units to do anything). The game is difficult, but never seems outright unfair. The Terminators and Genestealers feel suprisingly balanced considering one's ranged profficiency, and one's melee profficiency. Providing the map isn't nothing but corridors, the genestealers have plenty of chances to get the drop on you and eliminate your troops one by one. Genestealers actually have some interesting abilities. While their units don't have special attacks, or really any variation (except for the broodlords), they can choose to either be stealthy, or to play the waiting game and build up forces, or to just rush the Terminators every turn so they can't continue through the mission, and pray units get through to cut them in half. This is because the Genestealer player (or AI) can choose to put units at any number of spawn points, can choose whether or not to reveal units at certain times, and can make big moves each turn due to having more AP.
Overall, I feel like the game is a good buy. The Terminators are weighty and have heavy firepower, which looks and sounds great. The Genestealers are appropriately creepy, but could probably have benefitted from some better move animations and dodge animations, but otherwise look like a fearsome foe. The game knows it's theme and keeps to it. Even though the game deals with a lot of hallways which could have been a lot more boring, they find ways to keep them interesting (flickering lights, gore, weird tech, ominous mists and steams, all the usual wrought metal and skulls you love from the Imperium, etc.). The gameplay is fun, with different objectives on each map for the Terminators (rescue, destruction, retrieval, escape, etc.) and so it stays fresh through the campaign.
Finally, the shoulder cam is awesome, the emperor protects, and I rate this game an 7/10.
DLC 1: Sword of Halcyon: Ok so for some reason I can't figure out how to write a separate review for the DLC packs, so I'll post them at the bottom of this review. The first DLC pack I played through was the Sword of Halcyon campaign. I played through singleplayer as the Blood Angels. In total the 5 missions took me about 5 hours to play through on Normal difficulty. The campaign has it's pros and cons. Essentially, the gist is that you are on the ship Sword of Halcyon which has just crashed into a space hulk in the warp, and you are responding to the influx of genestealers within the first hours after collision. What I find cool about this is that the main game took place 600 years after the space hulk Sin of Damnation was infested, and the terminators are slowly and methodically manuevering through that space hulk to their objectives. In this campaign, time is no luxury. Genestealers are quickly moving through the ship and your terminators are tasked with securing vital areas of the ship like the armories, bridge, and the inner sanctum of the ship full of holy relics, all in order to attempt a defense. It feels climatic because the briefings and missions run into each other in a logical, continuous way. In addition, the missions challenge the player by forcing them to keep pressing forward, with two missions actually tasking you with destroying or sealing off genestealer spawns, forcing you to run straight at the genestealers which can be nerve-wracking and potentially disasterous. This could be a really fun campaign to play in co-op or versus I think.
Now, that's all well and good, but the campaign also has some weaknesses. Though each mission mixes up the squads, it only does so aesthetically with name and model changes. Aside from the first mission, each scenario has two squads of 5 terminators; 1 seargeant, 1 heavy flamer troop, and 3 regular storm bolter troops. This is a sore point for me because I kept waiting to see an assualt cannon troop or a Librarian, and it never happened. You'll get familiar with using those units, and that's not really a good thing. I would have rather had changing squads making me have to adjust and adapt more through the campaign. The two other main beefs I have involve the lack of broodlords and the usage of bulkhead doors. I really thought I should have fought a broodlord or two on the final mission; it just would have felt right and ramped up the challenge of the last mission. Bulkhead doors are only in one level, and the store page makes it sound like they'll be a key feature of the campaign, but they aren't. Bulkheads are a great concept hardly touched.
Altogether, I grant the Sword of Halcyon DLC campaign a 6.5/10. Dissapointing, but still somewhat enjoyable, and not a waste of $5, especially if you have someone for MP.

I'll readily admit, when I first saw the game in the Free to Play lists, I thought it was going to be a remade version of my favorite 3D card game, Duelists of the Roses.
What I got was something probably as good.
The card system in this game is easy to understand, but a challenge to master, the mark of a well designed, well thought out game.  You could probably spend hours if not days just planning out an ideal deck for whatever adversary pokes it's nose around the corner.  Even if you don't, there's plenty of starter decks, booster packs, and individual cards you'll earn over the course of your Infinity Wars career that will keep you coming back for more.  I like the unique card system, and the way you've built it the system would probably work for nothing else but this game.
Graphics are rather intriguing too, with only a handful of effects but hundreds of animated pictures for your cards, not including all the flavor text.  Everything is designed well, looks great, and best of all, makes you wonder what sort of crazy new animation lies on the next new card.  However, some of the animations I must say seem a bit...short...or bland, to the point they almost don't need to be animated in the first place.  And adding in a few alternative effects would help, like different ways for the fortress to be destroyed depending on the severity of your win, how you won,  and so on.
I'll score this game out of 20 for graphics and out of 30 for gameplay for a total of out of 50.
Graphics get 16 out of 20 for the aforementioned cards that really don't seem animated.  Try working on those and the score will definitely improve.
Gameplay will get the following scores:
Controls: 10 of 10.  Really well designed card control system, which allows you to choose to either play the card immediately or look at its information before playing.  In addition to this, allowing you to see the new cards played is always welcome to help you strategize better, and keeping both people blind until they hit the End Turn button is a very good decision, very sensible.  The commander concept also adds in a rather clever twist.
Competition: 8 of 10.  I cannot rate multiplayer simply because there is no way to account for every player in the game.  I can however account for the Campaign mode.  Which is very good.  Campaigns slowly progress in difficulty, actually a little too slowly for my tastes.  I'd like a little more challenge before I hit mission 20 or so please.  Other than that keep it up here.
Consequence: 10 of 10.  I cannot praise the card system enough in this game.  You will definitely be rewarded for returning and grasping a further understanding of your cards and how they work in conjunction with each other.  Learning which commanders you need for your deck and getting cards every time you get victories, level up, or do something noteworthy is a definite plus, which will keep you coming.  There aren't any real punishment as far as I've seen, which to me is good for a card game like this, since it's not meant to be a hardcore experience.  Outstanding.
All in all this game gets 44 of 50.  And that's a score I'll raise a glass to.  Glory for the Flame Dawn!

First off, no, there aren't six other games that came before this one. Second, I wish there were as many that came after, because this one is amazing.
It's built like an old Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest title: four-directional movement on a tiled plane, hub towns that are roughly the same size as your sprite on the overworld map, turn-based combat (which has a design that actually reminds me more of Mother or EarthBound than FF), retro synth music, pixel art graphics, and lots of recolored enemies.
However, while it's definitely meant to evoke the old era of JRPGs in technical design and some of its aesthetics, it's not a copy/paste replica by any means. Combat is surprisingly difficult. Even just outside the tutorial dungeon, random encounters can easily spell your death until you get a second party member; speaking of which, there's a fixed limit to random encounters for each area, meaning they'll stop after a while. You can force an encounter at any time by opening the menu and choosing “FIGHT,” even after the random encounters have stopped. It doesn't necessarily force you to backtrack for healing, either — after winning a fight, your HP is restored fully, and you regain a bit of MP, assuming you spent any.
Which you will, more likely than not, since most characters' standard attacks are woefully inadequate for survival.
It doesn't take itself seriously at all, and though I personally found its brand of fourth wall-breaking comments and sarcastic acknowledgement of (J)RPG clichés and mainstays to be a bit overdone, it's also still endearing in its delivery.
All in all, I would definitely recommend it.

TLDR; Game rates an 8 out of 10 as a fun, story-driven romp with clever mechanics.
This, is a dramatically clever take on rpgs, crossed with tug-of-war. And it works absurdly well! The idea to use conversation as a combat mechanic is quite well done, and the skills and abilities, while powerful, never feel so overwhelming that the game becomes unbalanced - in much the way that old rpgs expected a player to grind up to max level to survive the final boss, a player needs to reach almost the pinnacle of conversational acumen to stand against the verbal hail of the last boss (and the secret boss). Further, this rarely, if ever, hits the point of formula - you cannot rinse and repeat every opponent, and more than a little thought is required to reach victory every time. More importantly, this game is fairly short - hitting the pinnacle takes only a few hours, tops - the grind is barely noticable. I finished my first run in ~8 hours, and that was because I was trying to get 100% completion.
The writing is the gem in this piece, and it comes through very well. In originality, if nothing else, the script nails its goals precisely, and with a lot of panache. It's like the most civil attempt to slaughter a dinner party by cutting wit alone. The sound effects are also pretty good, and there is some minor voice acting (You too will want to slug Seymour by the end!) which adds to the experience. Replay value is a little limited - there are some clear points where you will know you missed something, and the game is short enough that such hints will tempt you into a replay, but I only see someone going after 2 or 3 rounds of it initially. The mechanics and skill to win may see you firing up the game again every once in a while (the end boss fights are really quite amusing), so save just before the end, but otherwise? meh.
The visuals are quite simple (but pretty stylish, all the same), and the exploration, while extensive (there are almost no details that won't matter at some point), is by no means large (effectively, the game takes place in 4 rooms, with exploration being limited to using various topics to unlock different reactions).
The music is pretty good, if not spectacular.
TLDR; Game rates an 8 out of 10 as a fun, story driven romp with clever mechanics.

Heh. This is a lemmings-like game that seemed to have some cool ideas.
But it's all over the place, in mechanics, level-design, and difficulty. These are related, but I have specific problems with each overall area.
The problem in the mechanics is that only some are physics driven. This makes puzzles very messy, at times. Instead of being certain of an elegant solution, you may get stuck in a dead end, because the current setup is almost a solution, and you're lost in many slight variations, hoping chaos will solve the situation.
The problem in level design is, in part, derived from those very mechanics. The levels seem all over the place. Some have very specific, discrete ways of placing the items, thus becomes an exercise in logic. Others, however, use the physics in a chaotic way that's difficult to predict - a replicate, when timing is involved.
A new items is also introduced every 3 or 6 levels. So things move very fast, and no idea has any time to setup interesting problems. Some of the levels are too easy because they're just introducing an item, and once those are gone, you have a new item in front of you.
Finally, also related to the previous, is difficulty.
There are 4 sets of basic levels, plus a 5th that you slowly unlock as you beat the other levels.
The 4th set is supposedly the last "canonic" one. It's also, by far, the easiest.
The first level of the 5th set is also the hardest one in the game (judging from my experience and also forum posts). This isn't quite true - however, it relies on a very specific placement of an item. I actually tried that (before looking up the solution), but it apparent was very slightly off place (it wasn't clear at all, visually), and the game didn't recognize it.
This is a big problem.
I think this game was made mostly
the workshop. The levels never settle into a specific line of thinking, there are too many items, etc.
It would make sense for all of this to be explored in user-made levels, but the designed set of levels isn't very good at all, in my opinion.
One achievement is very cool. Because it forces you to setup a level (with the level editor) in a certain way. I'm not sure if this was just to suggest people to try the workshop levels. But there could be an interesting metagame here if there were more achievements of this type.
Given Klei's track record, this game is rather unexpected. Even the artstyle seems very generic (contrast it with the more unique Eets game, which, I think, was this game's predecessor).
So yeah, I wouldn't suggest this one. Maybe the workshop levels could be good.

Woah, what a game, 100% within 36 hours. I barely have anything that I disliked about this game, it's almost perfect. I will just list a few things that bugged me a little bit
1. There are 3 ways to move from place to place without having to actually move, 2 tram ways and 1 stag way, while this makes you reach most places, things like the Forgotten Basin still can only be accessed by going to the King Station and then running there which is quite the problem since there are so many objectives in that area (A hidden grub, 2 new items for moving around, a hidden charm, the key to the good ending of the whole game, one of the spell upgrades, it's a lot basically) It was pretty annoying getting to that area over and over again, is what I am saying basically. (EDIT-FIXED)
2. Limited viability of charms: You have quick slash which is one of the most op charms in the game and only takes 2 charm notches but then you have countless of other spells which give you more SOUL, charge SOUL faster or do things to your spell, most of them either so limited usage that you basically never use them at all. Let's say you have a boss where you cannot heal, this is where having honey blood and jonis blessing at the same time is awesome but if you can heal properly at a boss, you will use anything but some quicker soul charge or useless stuff like that.
3. The Quick Slash in general: Once you obtain that charm, you basically won the entire game, you can overwhelm almost all future bosses mandatory for the normal story with you DPS, you don't even have to dodge anymore which is definitely a huge problem since that lame strategy even makes the last boss a piece of cake.
4. More uses for Geo (The currency of the game) I have bought everything before even having finished the last colloseum trial, the game needs something expensive, even if it's something little.
Other than that the game is honestly perfect, the art, the whole combat system, it's just beautiful. I don't really understand the people comparing this to Dark Souls, I mean yeah it's challenging but not only are the real challenging things just optional bosses but also, I don't see why a game is "like Dark Souls" just because it's challenging when legitemately everything else is completely different than Dark Souls, like seriously, stop it. I also saw someone complaining about the difficulty and saying only/mostly people that have played Dark Souls can enjoy Hollow Knight but that is honestly just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t again. This game is a challenging sidescrolling RPG, it's not meant to be a game that you can relax with while sitting on a couch, although I was still able to do that because I knew exactly how to play since I have played Dark Souls previously, that honestly just got me into the game faster than others, sort of a small head start. The game requires you to learn from your mistakes and fix those within the next time you fight a boss, if you are too stupid to learn from your mistakes and rage instead, then this game obviously is nothing for you but nontheless, I suggest you to work on that problem of yours instead of calling this a bad a game because it's everything but that. The game is challenging but not unfair. I haven't even mentioned the art and soundtrack yet, I am usually someone that only plays games for the gameplay aspect of it yet it emediately caught my eye, the transition from area to area is straight up the smoothest it could be, the world couldn't be more detailed, you have a few suddle character side quests which gives you more insights into the lore of the game yet you are not required to do specific tasks, you just listen to honest, straight, short dialogue if you want to and get more of it by looking into bugs' minds, this makes the story telling very suddle as well, as mentioned I am the kind of guy that only plays for gameplay which is why I like this kind of story telling. The lore is indepth yet simple and it doesn't force its lore towards you unlike a game like Witcher 3 which literally just feels like playing a book. These are the best parts of the game that caught my attention as well as the issues I wanted to adress while playing the game, I don't want to go more indepth on things, neither do I really want to analyze everything bit by bit so I'll stop right here, buy the game during a sale if you have the chance, absolutely recommendable !

Update 07/21 - As I predicted. Just look what they are planning to release for the price of another WHOLE GAME. Stray away from this game people, as I pointed out it is nothing but a DLC launch pad. I am just surprised at the price of the DLC I mean Jesus Christ.
If you don't have a high end pc capable of running the newest of hardware-intensive games, dont even think about buying this game.
I was so excited about this game I actually bought a brand new desktop with AMD FX-6300 processor pushing 3.5ghz and 4.0 when boosted. Nvidia GTX 1050 w/ 2gb of onboard ram. 16gb cooled ddr4 RAM. Windows 10 Pro 64bit.
This game still occasionally hiccups on my BRAND NEW system. Which was terribly dissapointing since I did basically this new desktop namely to run games like this. Which it does with flying colors on any modern optimized game. Ill go into more detail a little later about this.
I played this game during Alpha, and the developers did listen to the community and released quite a few community-oriented updates. Then all of the sudden after the 4th major update DTG decided it was good enough to release and get out of alpha. A totally premature calculation. This game is still not graphically optimized, its lacking a SUPER amount of gameplay and content, and for the 35$ price tag you are getting what feels like a demo [in my opinion]. This feels like a training simulator for these 3 very specific, albeit almost identical, locos. And when you are done with the tutorial there are very limited scenarios for you to play. Also, there is NO WORKSHOP content. And no Route editor to speak of. Sooo just like previous DTG releases it feels like this one is probably a DLC platform ENGINE more than anything.
On the plus side this games first person mode and the free roam abilites are a FRESH idea in the world of simulators. It adds to what is a pretty immersive experience but it doesn't solve or subtract from the lack of content this game offers right out. The graphics [when running at steady fps] which isn't often, is very beautiful and awe-striking. But in the same breath you better not accidentally try crossing a platform on the train a certain way or your av will get lodged into the service somewhere most likely underneath the track. I've experienced this problem mostly with the SD loco when trying to travel between lead locos and cut outs.
This game does have, however, that little spirit that all games I have ever loved has. A certain chromosome, if you will, that attracts you back to it. I can't explain it but any true gamer can relate to what I am talking about. I first experienced this trait with Star Wars Galaxies which was an old school MMO and i've more recently experienced it with games like Call of Heroes and Skyrim.  Let me make a point here real quick before you carry this overboard. I am in no way relating this game at ALL to ANY of those previously stated games, it is not debateable that those games have this one beaten in every sense. With that being said this game does have it but i'm afraid its hard to get to because of all the technical shortfalls in what I feel is a "deadline date" game. You might ask what that is, I came up with the phrase awhile ago when Mass Effect 3 came out, the developers were forced to put out an unfinished product because of publisher and sponsors DEMANDING the game be released by a certain time. This is a perfect example because later on 2 or 3 months after the premature release EA was subpeona'd to court and they had to pay substantially for their malphiseance. And subsequently released gobs of free DLC to try to right the wrong.
In closing, if this game were left in alpha indefinetlely and buyers were promised more than 3 locos when the game was READY and approaching release I would have more hope for this game. But as I see it TSW is nothing but a inevitable DLC engine for 3rd party devs to pump their Pay 2 Enjoy 3d renderings into. I wish I wasn't so cynical but history does, after all, repeat itself.

This game has some pretty good ideas and some parts of it are fun, but unfortunately the implementation is very poor.  The main thing that makes a lot of it not fun to play is the repetitiveness.  Many of the levels have the same pattern: a super easy part in the beginning of the level (to get you used to the mechanics?) and then a harder part you need trial-
and-error/good RNG to solve.  So then you end up repeating the easy part over and over while trying to figure out the hard part once.
The repetition wouldn't be so bad if your character wasn't so slow.  It's like your character is walking in molassas.  The default walking speed should be at least twice as fast as it is now, with a toggle key to make your character slower if it's needed for precise movement.
The other big annoying issue is that the hard levels are hard for the wrong reason.  The puzzles themselves are actually a bit too easy.  What makes some of them hard are unexplained mechanics due to the level order being randomized, the floaty controls, and the fact that enemies can spawn right on you.  That said, most of the levels aren't really that hard, even the ones that are called "Hard".  The one actual difficult level (and again, it's difficult for un-fun reasons) is about 10 times harder than the next hardest level for some reason.
Positive things I can say about it: the graphics and music are charming in an unpolished way, and we didn't have problems connecting to servers (not too much lag either).  The levels that weren't badly designed were actually pretty fun and creative.   But overall, I'd say you should only get this game if it's on sale or free.

COD is a somewhat good game with issues.  Sort of like having a bipolar girlfriend.
So, I have mixed feelings on this.  On one hand I'd like to recommend the game, but on the other, I wouldn't.
I like the WW11 setting.  I get a feel for the atmosphere.  But the gameplay is extremely irritating.  Enemies are bullet sponges.  You can't mow them down with a machine gun or at close range with your primary weapon.  Most times, after 3 or 4 shots, they fall to the ground only to get back up, brush themselves off and continue fighting you.  A couple times I found myself reloading after what I thought was a kill (close range 3 rounds into the enemy) and during my reload animation the a$$ hat got back up and killed me.  WTF???  Anyways, now I know better.  I make sure they're dead before reloading.
I found hit detection to be a problem, as well.  I've shot numerous rounds at enemies that were directly in my sight and found myself having to compensate to make hits.
The most annoying part is your team/allies.  They get in your way and can get you killed.  There's nothing like walking through a corridor or staircase with a member of your squad directly following behind you.  As you turn a corner you find yourself in conflict and want to retreat back around the corner.  But you can't because your a$$ hat teammate is humping your leg and won't back off.  *Dead*  So I always let that f****r go first if possible.  When you need a quick escape, you can bet there will be someone, somewhere, that will get in your way.
For a war game, first of it's kind or not, I am struck with awe that there is no way to sprint.  I am talking about the original COD here and how it was originally designed.  I served in the Army, and one of the first things they teach you in basic training is the 3-5 second rush.  So, needless to say I was very irritated trying to advance from point to point  without being able to rush for cover.  This may be a minor gripe, but I feel it's important to have something like that in a war game.  I can't understand why it wasn't there.  Oh well, let me walk to this cover point while I get shot up.  Need a health pack?  Let me walk over to the health and hope I don't die in route.  Sometimes you'll grab a health pack only to get shot the f**k up in the second it took you to turn around to take cover.
I somewhat like the game, and like I said, only playing it to play through the franchise.  I had high hopes for it since it was given a lot of praise.  But I wouldn't recommend it unless you want to do what I'm doing or are a fan of COD and haven't played it yet.

Last word is a neat little idea that presents polite dialogue as an abstracted battle of wits wherein the loser finds themselves compelled to do as the one who gets the 'last word' says.  The game focuses on on a rather peculiar such happening in high society of St. Laud where a mystery is afoot. Suspect in the happenings of the evening are the various movers and shakers of the government, military and other important individuals, but among them all stands a strange outlier, yourself.  In the role of Whitty Gawship the peculiarities of the evening are secondary to just why you've been invited to these proceedings while having no such lofty status.
The cast is literally colorful, being color-coded to their affiliations.  That they're all interesting with their own experiences and perspectives on the higher functions of St. Laud will be quickly apparent.  Through the combined information one discerns from the lips that sink ships lie the answers to all the questions you will wade through as the evening progresses, the ominous proceedings and circumstances ever on the forefront of the minds of the guests. Getting the last word can seem daunting at first, but thankfully there are many ways for you to improve your gift of gab and show the shakers and snobs that you are not a woman with whom is to be messed.
The visuals and music set the tone of the game effectively, with classically inspired pieces befitting a higher function ranging from relaxing to more pressing matters as the hours pass and the wine runs empty. Connoisseurs of the sparkling finest and the flow of conversation both will at the same time become more tense and verbose. Among all of the discussion, gossip, chatter, intrigue and investigation only one thing is for certain.
One photographer would like to have a word.

Buy? Maybe. Requres 360 Controller/Emu. Early SNES-style RPG clearly influenced by Dragon Warrior and references Earthbound with comedy 4th wall stylings. Fights in Dungeon/Overworld require the player managing their MP, which is restored slightly by their battle speed and inns/save spots. Players can manually invoke random battles by choosing fight from the menu to level grind or abuse random fight limits, which will stop giving random battles once you complete X amount of batles in a dungeon (overworld as well, but a high number). You can paint yourself into a corner of unescapable death and game over if you manual save in a spot where you can't get enough MP, or if you don't choose the most optimal level up rewards. Fantastic soundtrack (Battle is an all time favorite) and apparently pretty short. Battle graphic fidelity is argurably weaker than NES Dragon RPGs. It's basically a love letter to old school RPGs, and I may possibly finish it.

I'm not a huge 40K fan, although I do enjoy the universe they've created.  I've tried Space Marine, which had some really good qualities, but ultimately was a fairly large failure of a game.  I've tried Dawn of War II, and enjoyed it, but it doesn't feel that much like a Warhammer game - it's more of a strategy game with warhammer skinning.  Not that that's a bad thing - it's a very good strategy game (at least, in my opinion), but it doesn't really capture the flavor of 40K.
Space Hulk, on the other hand, manages to take a lot of what makes 40K special - the bleakness, the fight against overwhelming odds - and capture that essence pretty damn well.  This comes in part due to the fact that it's pretty much a straight reimaging of the board game of the same name, but that doesn't make it any less fun.  In fact, one of the reasons I'm enjoying it so much is that the Board Game takes while to set up, and requires 2 people to play.  It can be great fun, but despite owning the board game for a few years now, I don't think I've played it more than twice.  Maybe three times.  This game, however, has already gotten me more play time, and I've been able to see more missions than I ever have on the board game.  And the board game cost $100 - AND you're lucky to find it these days - it was a limited run printing.
This game pits you as the commander of a squad of space marines against a hoarde of aliens - sound familiar?  In fact, the original game was inspired by the movie Alien & Aliens.  Anyway, you command your squad to objectives - enter a room, kill everything, retrieve some artifact - and then see how well you pit your skills against the oncoming alien horde.  And horde is correct - unless there's a specific "kill X genestealers (the aliens) to win" objective, there are unlimited enemies.  That's right, they just keep coming.  And, to make it worse, the odds are never in your favor.  The best you can hope for is to keep them at range and kill them before they get to you, because if they do?  It's over.  Oh, sure, you have a chance - but not much of one.  So you have to plan, and plan well, and even when you plan the best f***ing plan the imperium has ever seen?  Yeah, you still need a bit of luck on your side.
This does make it frustrating - but far from impossible.  And even those times you lose, you'll learn, and you'll know that it was the luck of the dice, and next time, maybe things will go better.  It gives you the freedom to try out different strategies, and take some risks - after all, if you need luck on your side anyway, why not try that risky gamble, in hopes that it'll pay off?
The levels aren't very long - no more than 30 minutes that I've seen, per attempt.  Quicker, obivously, if things go really bad really fast.  And prepare to lose some guys as well - it'll happen.  But that doesn't mean the game is over - your remaining troops can still win the day.  And losses aren't permanent - so if a guy dies in one level, he'll be back in the next.  Which also gives you some freedom to take risks and not worry - your marines are there to complete the mission, and if that means dying for the cause?  Well, that's they're job, and they'll do it.
So yeah, I highly recommend this game.  When it first came out, apparently it had a lot of issues, but as of this writing (v1.5) it seems fairly well polished, with the only major complaint is that the animations can be kind of slow.  But that's intentional - these are guys in 2 ton armor suits - they're not going to be quick.  Again, adds to the flavor.
So yeah, if you get a chance, and like strategy games - I highly recommend you check this one out.  But feel free to wait for a sale - I got a copy for $2 in the Summer 2014 sale, and it's likely you'll be able to get a copy for about that cheap again in the next few months, if not during the Winter  2014 sale.

The combat was... Interesting, it was third person Hack and Slash, but it felt wrong.  It definitely feels like a bad (cheap) port to PC, as far as I played there was a mash attack, a button that depending on the length of time held would cast a different spell, and a wall (protect) spell and that was it, that's the extent of the combat for what I played.  You fight soldiers, mechs and some bosses with unique gimmicks.
The story itself felt good, it made me interested.  Watching the intro cutscene and the start to the game felt great, I even shed a tear during the introductory cutscene to the world (not even kidding).  I was so excited to start playing and get a feel for this gritty, dark, bloody world...  And then I got throwing cards and minor spells.  And then during the cutscenes I got black screen cut away's for every scene transition AND camera change.  Why does it need to cut to black to go from different peoples face shots.
I cannot recommend purchasing and playing this game, I'm sorry but I just can't.  Get any of the other Final Fantasy games, or almost any other game in general.

Space Hulk is an odd gaming experience. It's pretty much a pure port of the board game, which is probably the main issue I have with the PC game.
I played the board game about 10 years ago and really enjoyed it, and this is a nice way to play the game if you don't have any humans nearby to play with. But, like chess or monopoly, the human interaction is part of the fun; playing against a computer is...well...souless.
In my opinion, what this game needed was some RPG elements, like gaining experience points to upgrade your squad, or a more engaging storyline. Something to elevate it beyond the boardgame in a way that compensates for that lack of human interaction.
As it is currently, there is no sense of attachment or engagement, which makes the level by level progression of the game feel a little unfulfilling.
The game also feels a bit too unfair - the terminators cannot move very much in a turn, their bolters jam at every oportunity, you have a 1 in 4 chance of winning/surviving close combat, the bolter has a 35% chance of killing in the first shot, and the more reliable weapons have very limited ammo. As far as I can see, your only option is to constantly play defensively: placing your men in key positions and setting them to "overwatch" or "guard"; which is difficult when playing an offensive mission.
The odds are against you, you will lose often (even in the early missions) and it will start to become boring after a while since it is a machine beating you, and not your buddy who you can laugh with afterwards. You also can't switch and play as the Genestealers in the campaign, so you are stuck as the lumbering terminators with unreliable weapons.
In short - if you want to play the Space Hulk board game alone, this is a good option. If you want a fulfilling gaming experience, move along. The regular price is a bit too much for what the game is. If you want to check it out, wait for a sale.

EPIC DARK SONG ABOUT WAR AND FRIENDSHIP!
Story: Best FF story I have been playing so far (IV, V, VII, VIII, IX, XIII). Why? You ask? Dark and twisted plot ever!  It's not about love anymore, it's about war and relationship amongs comrades! There is some romance indeed, but the whole game is soaked in sacrifice and heart-broken feelings. You should try to exploit all available endings.
Characters: There are 14 characters you can play, yet SE did a good job to distinguish personalities and characteristics between every single one of them. They are both at high school age but already strong in mind and body. You cannot forget one even you didn't tag along with him/her well in the game. Furthermore, with side quests and communication with NPCs throughout the game, you could find out more about their habbits, hobbies and more. This is a gold mine for mangaka or novelist!
Gameplay: the triple chars combat control it's not really impressive and new, yet they still bring entertainment throughout the game. Of course with total of 14 playable chars, you will have a hard time to choose which one is the best and try a lot of combination. Once you get familiar with the game, you will find it's not too hard and you will only play with favorite chars. Howerver, SE knew this and they require you take a good care of all of them, or at least 6 members to do some rotation in later part of the game. If you have played The Last Remnant, another good game of SE, you should be fine with all char development.
Time is essential and it is a very important element in Type 0 HD. You have a very litmited time to do quests and travel around. Communicating with other NPCs and chars could gain some extra hours but it is not much. So choose wisely! (you will have chance to accomplish all once you finish and play New game +, do not worry much!)
Besides RPG, the game includes RTS elements as well. You will command army and squad and do some strategic move to decide outcome of battles. Quite interesting!
Sad news for explorers: Type 0 HD's world  is not as big as other FF games. But it still contains some amusing hidden areas with treasures and surprises. And you still need chocobos to travel around!
Ah chocobos! Type 0 HD has a good chocobos breeding system that you can experience and produce some rare chocobos to support you in travelling and combating! And that's all! Not much but enough for this game.
The camera is sometime annoying with bad view angle and motion, but when you get to the speed and control, everything should be fine. I suggest you play with a controller, Xbox one should be good.
Graphics: it's a HD version of PSP version years ago, not quite beautiful and stunning for current trends but it's overally good. Characters and weapons are well done with high texture details. Environment isn't as good as characters but you still WOW when first visit the Academy.  Skill effects and summoning cutscene are still SE style: awesome and epic.
Sound: not really a strong point of game, sometimes it is repeatitive and annoying.
Music: Epic theme and music that suitable for war backgroud of the game. And remember to stay tune until last second of credit after you finish the game, one of the best song of FF is there, with heart broken scene too T_T
Pros:
- Dark and twisted story
- Various playable characters with interesting characteristics
- Trio character combat control brings some entertaining and strategic choice
Cons:
- Combat is repeatitive
- Trio character combat with NPCs is bad with poor AI and power.
- Small world to explore

First and foremost, this is the very first time that i absolutely despised the music in a Final Fantasy game.
Tracks that would otherwise be pleasant are constantly repeated until they become absolutely unbearable.
Remember the classic Final Fantasy theme? A pretty chill rendition of it is what plays over the whole campus (which is where you will spend most of your playtime) and it never stops regardless of what's happening.
With that out of the way, as a videogame FFT-0 tries to strike a balance between fast action and RPG, failing miserably.
I will admit i have not played for too long, but in the 5 hours i played the only choices i could make were about who to take on my main party and which accessories to equip.
Character progression is linear, equipment choice besides the aforementioned accessories is linear, gameplay as a result is linear.
Level design is also a bunch of hallways in which you kill from 3 to 10 enemies and then proceed. Or just proceed by running.
I feel like the biggest failure in design comes with a mechanic that i can only describe as "Critical Cheese":
To put it simply, before and after an attack your lock-on icon will become either Red or Yellow and if you hit the enemy in that window of time you will do a stupid amount of damage to it, which almost always ends up one-shotting mobs and bosses.
I understand what the idea was, but the numbers are absolutely stupid.
The controls are also extremely weird and floaty.
Story-wise it wasn't very interesting for me. Feels like i heard the warrying kingdoms and the "Empire" trying to conquer the world too many times, maybe it will be better for people who are not jaded by this kind of story.
Overall not very interesting, i never felt like i wanted to know what would happen next.
However, there is one thing that really rustled my jimmies:
Right at the beginning of the game, in the intro cinematic, the first thing that happens is a kid and a chocobo get killed off, which is a scene supposed to show how horrific actual war is, however the way they handled it felt like a very cheap "Let's kill off the chocobo"-tear card.
It's like if a pokemon game made by a completely separate studio started off with a Pikachu slowly dying and agonizing for 10 minutes.
It was just cheap and annoying.
However here are some pros:
-Quinn
-Sice
Btw nice character names.

I'm actually rather stunned, this game is pretty good. If you liked games like Ori and Dust: An Elysian Tail... then you'll probably like this one, but it's way less forgiving. For $15 the value is unbelievable though. I wish all indie games had easily $1-2 an hour or more for worthwhile gameplay.

For the price, if you're a fan of games like Dragon Quest or Final Fantasy from the NES-era, then you should undoubtedly find this a great throwback to the past. You play as Dem, in a world where the only thing left on the world is death and monsters. You'll meet an array of strange characters, but understand the game is far from difficult. The game is beatable in about 2-4 hours for even a casual player, and as you'd imagine, lacks a lot of depth story-wise. The level up mechanic is neat, wich a simple multiple choice system allowing for different builds and experiences with each playthru. The characters are one dimensional and a romance between Dem and amother character comes out of nowhere. However, the game makes sure you understand that is somewhat the point. Not just a traditional JRPG experience, but a meta experience of classical RPG and video game tropes. If you don't mind a game that lacks some depth to it, but has a quirky sense of humor, you'll love Breath of Death VII - The Beginning.

This game is far more that "Minecraft in Space." You can build a home among the stars, design ships which you can share with other players to buld and make their own (both in-game through the store stations or dropping a blueprint/schematic for another player, or by downloading a design from a player). Ship design dores require some thought about where your ship systems will be placed and how big they need to be to achive the goal you seek.
There are roaming space priates, so watch out! You can use radar jammers to prevent detection by them, or, if you want an up-close look, you can go into the brave world of cloaked ship design and get up close and personal to a pirate station without ever being detected.
You can create your own AI fleets to do your bidding and defend your stations, or even mine for you, and claim systems as your won, either for yourself, or for members of your faction. You can also choose to travel to another galaxy and make it your new home, and create warp gates networks to hurl you across the universe.
The game is still very much in development, so expect changes to be made that will render your old ship designs obsolete from time to time. As of this writing, the power systems are undergoing a major overhaul which actually will simplify reactor design significantly.
You will need to sign up for an account to play on public servers. This is done to protect your login name. You can play without signing up, however, and can run your own local game if you like.
I recommend revewing and editing the key configuration before playing the game too much (esp. make the movement controls consisten when in astronaut mode vs ship flying mode, othewise you'll be confused why E/Q behave differently all of a sudden)
For Linux players, I recommend lauching the game outside of steam with a script:
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="~/.steam/steam/SteamApps/common/StarMade/StarMade/native/linux:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH"
cd ~/.steam/steam/SteamApps/common/StarMade
./starmade-launcher
Also, be sure your steam controller is powered off... it will work with a regualr  USB joystick/flight yolk however.

Okay, first off, this game has a really original premise. Lots of games are set in the post-apocalypse, but I'm pretty sure this is the only one where it's after the end of the world and every character is undead.
This game is a nostalgic RPG-lover's dream, with the feel of an old, SNES-era RPG with most of the problems of RPGs of that time removed. The encounter rate is low, you regain all your HP after battle, and battle and leveling mechanics are simple enough for anyone to grasp, yet add enough complexity to make things interesting and encourage the player to plan ahead.
This game may have had me frustrated a few times, but its clever writing, kick♥♥♥♥♥music, unique story and user-friendly battle system ultimately won me over.
Recommended to RPG fans, both old and new alike. Or even anyone who wants a story they (probably) haven't heard before. Just remember to save often, as some battles may have your undead party end up... er, un-undead.

I will review all my humble bundle games and see which is worth playing and which is not! Like a lot of people i buy H.B. games as a pack because i want some of the games, but not all. I will play for 5 minutes (or a litlle bit more) and give you my opinion on it. Sometimes the game will surprise me, sometimes it will be a total dissapointment. Just keep in mind this is my opinion only and is not an objective view of the game. You might actually like it!
The review will be constructed into 5 parts:
1. Game description (from what i've seen in the time i've played).
2. Did i finish the game (YES/NO/Maybe in the future) and why.
3. Pros/Cons.
4. Final thoughts.
5. Rating
So let's beggin...
1. Game description:
Puzzle game with an interesting twist. You control the world around you and the character. Your goal is to enter a door. Sounds like the most simple thing ever right? You are wrong. So wrong. The game ramps up the difficulty quite fast and it varies so much from level to level. I find that some puzzles take 1-2 minutes while on others I spent 10 times as much. The only problem is the difficulty in some levels  is not from the puzzle part of the level but from the hazards that kill you. You have to act fast to avoid them. Visually it’s nothing much. I would have liked a few more colors but I guess that was the idea, to look like a sketch. There is a small story and it is a little philosophical. I kinda enjoyed it.
2. Did i finish the game? In the process
I still have the game installed and I will finish it one day. The fact that sometimes I have to replay the level several times due to me being killed by the hazards is annoying. However I never felt like I was cheated by the game. I actually deserved that death because I didn’t  go the way the puzzle wanted me to
3. Pros/Cons.
PROS:
- Interesting mechanic
- Nicely designed levels
- Interesting story
CONS:
- Bland visuals
- Annoying traps
4. Final thoughts:
I like this game despite the downsides mentioned earlier. If you like puzzle games get it. It’s nothing that will blow you away but it’s a nice game to sit back and relax playing a few levels between bigger games.
5. Rating
7/10

Well, this was a very nice surprise from the people who buggered up Watch_Dogs. Assassin's Creed IV - Black Flag can be seen as a new high point for the franchise and with the ability to traverse the world in a boat Wind Waker style, the hours of playtime don't take long to pile up.
This time the setting is the 18th century and the player is in control of swarve pirate captain Edward Kenway (the father of the very "British" Hatham Kenway and the grandfather of the very angry Conner Kenway). Throughout the game, Edward will sail the high seas in search of a great treasure and like him you will lose yourself in a lust for gold. Then you'll remember that you're playing an Assassin's Creed game and you'll have to spend a decent amount of time tailing someone before you get to feel the sea breeze in your beard again. But fear not, your missions on land can lead to great rewards and eventually you'll earn enough money to fully upgrade your ship, giving it enough firepower to blast the entire Caribbean to hell and back.
Although this game does have a few issues, mainly the fact that its optimisation is all over the place (a deal breaker for some of you out there), I can recommend this game simply based on the hours of fun that I got out of it. With a large map, that's mostly made of seawater, and the songs of sailors filling the air, you'll have a decent amount of fun sailing your ship into the horizon.

Let me start off by saying this is an incredible game. There's lots of content and the game is growing bigger step by step. I'm going to dive into some subjects a lot of negative reviews talk about and try and explain my viewpoint on them.
The multiplayer is currently still developping. There are dedicated servers, and you can create your own lobbies. Multiplayer at the moment isn't very crowded, however you can have some good and fun races.
Contrary to the Free to Play tag this game isn't free to play. A better tag would be Free Demo, but it seems this can't be helped. I'm going to compare the game with league of legends, because it's a well known free to play game. In league of legends you earn in game currency for playing, and that currency can be used to buy things. Next to the ingame currency there is a currency buyable with irl money. In RaceRoom, there is no ingame currency, just vRP, which can be bought for irl money. That's also why I don't think the Free to Play tag applies.
Now on to the paymeny model. Paying 50€ upfront for a game and unlocking all the content is very nice, but there will most likely be content you don't like or feel like playing. In RaceRoom, tracks, cars, trackpacks and carpacks can be bought seperately. Say you don't like DTM, but do like GT2, then you can just buy the GT2 cars. One thing to note is that if you want all the items, you'll be looking at a price quite a bit higher than 50€. But to put his into perspective, in league of legends you pay +- 10€ for a champion, in RaceRoom you pay +- 2.5 euro for a car.
I should also note that content can be tested for free, so you have an idea whether or not you like it.
The interface has been upadtes, is new easy to navigate and comprehend, but you still need a mouse to be able to quickly navigate menu's
I do believe you need a wheel to play this game. You can you a gamepad, but then you're just not getting the complete experience.
The sounds in the game are incredible, especially with the new transmission sound update.
Graphics are great and the game runs on older hardware however there is only Dx9 support if I'm not mistaken.
As an ending I'd say, try the game out, test drive some cars, and if you like it buy some cars you enjoy driving.

The trailer for
proclaims that it features "pixel perfect physics," a feature that should leave you wary. Without a cyborg brain it is pretty much impossible to use pixel-perfect physics to your advantage, so instead you will suffer at its whims. Be prepared for projectiles and jumps to go awry based on pixel-perfect technicalities invisible to the human eye.
This might seem a small complaint since the odds of getting stymied microscopically over and over are pretty small, but it plays into another of my complaints: knowing whether I'm on the right track. In developing a solution to one of the puzzles in
I might think, "Oh, I will use this springboard to launch an item to that upper platform." But the item bumps into something else. Well, maybe I need to position the item differently. Or maybe I need to time the launch a little better. Or maybe I'm totally on the wrong track, a fact I will discover after a dozen different permutations that reveal that yes, I am on the wrong track and yes, my implementation is physically impossible. I feel less like I am solving puzzles and more like I am bumbling around with the game's systems.
All that aside, I think the sound design is polished. The game does fun little orchestral cues, e.g. a nervous warbling of strings when the creature teeters at the edge of a cliff. Think Looney Tunes. In fact, it would seem Looney Tunes is a large influence on the design in general, including the visuals, although I would say it's more "new" Looney Tunes in that regard, if that makes sense.

Before I start complaining, I'm going to get something straight: This is an amazing game and probably the best train simulator I've ever played. I love the series and, bugs aside, this is a great simulator. That being said, let's get into the actual review. The game has been out for a few months now, and I just bought it a couple days ago. I'd heard lots of complaints about the game having performance issues, but I figured that by now they'd be fixed. I was wrong. As most of the community is saying, this game has some MASSIVE frame rate problems. I'm not sure if it's trying to load the entire map at once instead of what's in the immediate area around the player, or the whole mechanical physics thing is screwing it up, but this is pretty bad. When I'm working in the yard I get an average of 15-20 fps. When I'm running trains on the mainline it averages around 20-25 fps. What?? Huh?? That makes no sense whatsoever. I'm able to run Battlefield 1 maxed out on ultra settings and I get a smooth 60 fps, and a simulator can't even get 60 fps on the LOWEST settings? That's pretty bad, especially considering that this game has been out for a couple months and they STILL haven't fixed this issue. I tried all of the graphics settings, and nothing changed. If you're someone that only plays simulators and runs games on a lower end pc, you might not find this as a huge issue. But for someone who plays most of today's high end games maxed out with no issues, this is pretty sad. Before you decide not to buy the game, I will say this: it IS playable, but at a really poor quality. But for someone who plays constant-intense FPS games, Train Simulator was the game I'd sit down and play for a relaxing and SMOOTH experience. And while this game is addicting, amazing, and fun, it's really depressing to have to play it with such low fps. I really hope the devs get their act together and fix this issue, because if nothing changes this will be the last game I purchase from DVT.

The game has definitely some potential. You can see it there. Quite nice and smooth graphics (little bit old but for mid-to-high spec PCs it's fair enough to race online maxed out without major stuttering, try it, it's free :P), interesting choices of licenses (WTCC and DTM are some of my favourites). Decent FFB though i have to admit I didn't take the time to set it up as maniacally as I did in Assetto Corsa or other titles (and I have no RL track racing experience, judging it only on the amount of info to help you get the most out of the car). Good sounds and effects even if sometimes quite "artificial".
I'm not a big fan of the payment model (Want everything? You have to pay TOO much. And I don't like overlapping content that you have to buy more than once if you want it available for single/multy, even if at a very high discount rate if already owned in a form or another). Prices for individual pieces of content are reasonable though, if you consider it's a sim. Can pay for a track/car pack and race in a series or just cherry pick what is of your interest and run it (with a good saving early on, but less content in the long run).
Big problem: very few people playing it online (monitored different times during the free weekend and had an average of 200-250 players online at the same time scattered on different servers/series/tracks, only a handful of fields worth a try, less if you own only partial content or like only some series).
To conclude, as a general rule of thumb, take care when you choose to buy experiences (complete series packs) if you want to race online. Almost desert servers in 2 out of 3 that I own and tried. They're good only for discounts on multiplayer content of same class/series if you're into buying much stuff of that pack (mainly tracks if you stick to a single car of that category). They're still nice and fun for single player against AI if you like complete series/championships with accurate liveries and so on (did I mention the discount on multiplayer part?) but didn't investigate this possibility too much. If some of you has any further insight on this I will update the review.
Definitely worth installing and trying out some of the non-free content to feel the experience. Hope in the future they manage to get more people into it and have some good online race battles. The potential is there, let's see if it can be developed into something...

The Stanley Parable is a very interesting specimen of the modern gaming scene. Utilizing Valve's own Source engine, this game features a variety of new and interesting mechanics to both mess with the minds of the players, as well as to create a fun filled, decision based adventure based on the various choices engendered by the participant. You, the player, play as Stanley himself as he attempts to solve the mystery of his mysteriously missing co-workers in a seemingly quiet and uninteresting workplace, until his world is completely turned on end by the revealations he discovers. This, in turn, forces the player into choosing his or her own narrative based on his or her own decisions. I had heard of this game several years ago, but had never gotten the time to actually play it myself, but I sure am glad that I did. The Stanley Parable should be considered less of a game and more of an experience, because of the various features it has implemented causing for the creation of a personal chronicle or story, along with the different gameplay aspects and choices in narrative that it offers the player. It makes the player resort to using their own prefrences to effect the eventual outcome of the game, causing for some downright hilarious and uttely incomprehensible results. With a boring yet realistic asthetic to perfectly complement the gameplay, as well as an unpredictable and unscrupulously cynical narrator, this game is a must play for any Steamer ready to have a fun time. I give this game a five star rating for its sheer ingenuity, unmatched hilarity, and seemingly endless amounts of gameplay.

I have to say, given the amount of time this has been out, and it's only taken 12 years for me to 'give in' and give CoD a shot, because I've always seen the game-series itself 'tarnished' by it's more modern work, especially all this guff being created with advanced-advanced-advanced warfare.
The series itself of CoD, is more robust, proper and rooted properly with their earlier work. Subsequently- this makes the mark, and makes it an honour to play such a game.

It's a great game, runs smoothly, does its job, offers challenging and exciting missions. As well as being historically rigourous when it comes to uniforms and the storyline itself- to an extent. You do get the off bluff of 'destroying hundreds upon hundreds of soldiers in one small area' sort of guff.
Other than that. It's amazing. Wonderful. Brilliant. I thouroughly recommend it!

This game has a really nice balance and a lot of depth to the strategy. I used to play Magic a few years back (it got too expensive to keep up) and while this has some similarities, I think I might actualyl prefer the style of Infinty Wars. I've seem some complaints that this is "pay to win", but have not found that to be the case. After going through just 2 of the single-player campaigns (there's one for each faction) and about half of the academy tutorials, I've accumulated enough booster packs to build some fairly formidable decks. Deck building definitely gets addictive and there's great nuances to balancing your card selections, especially when you start mixing more than one faction into a single deck. I'm not usually too big on multiplayer games, but really enjoy the PvP in this. Matchmaking is quick and the games have a great pace. Overall a great game, my only gripe so far is that the in-game currency is slow to accumulate versus the real Lightmare currency that costs actual dollars. I've logged about 10 hours of game time and amy barely even halfway towards being able to buy a booster pack with in-game currency. However, I've mostly been playing Academy and Campaign single-player matches, and it looks like the standard PvP gives you about double the currency of the single-player matches, so that's a plus. Anyway, its free to play, so try it already!

Pretty fun little RPG-with-a-twist.
Combat is replaced by 'discourse' so you win by getting the upper hand in a battle of wits and words. It's worth pointing out though that you're trading verbal blows in a sort of abstract fashion - you don't use actual dialogue in battle.
The game is relatively short for an RPG (ignore my playtime, I left it running for overnight and longer so I could get all the steam cards!) and set in a mansion over the course of one evening. Apart from the discourse, you'll be talking to the same few characters repeatedly about different subjects, allowing you to unlock new topics based on what you find out. There's a few basic puzzles and some stuff to collect as the plot unfolds.
+ Innovative and fun concept which feels cohesive - the entire game is themed on words, right down to the character names.
+ Decent enough story, though the one-setting-one-evening nature of the game is pretty limiting
+ The verbal combat is fun once you know what you're doing
+ Art style is simple but engaging
+ Music is good - reminded me a little of To the Moon in places
- Really needs some options - pretty much the only options you get are how often the characters make little introductory sounds, and what music plays. No resolution options, for example, or volume bars. (That I could find, anyway!) Mouse support would be nice as well!
- Some of the in game descriptions of how things like the tone wheel work are a little ambiguous, in my opinion. Once you 'get it' though you should be fine in nearly every combat, particularly if you don't mind doing a bit of grinding early on. I have to admit the first couple of battles were a little bit 'what on earth?!!'
- Not exactly a con, but explore *everything* before you talk to anyone with a lock above their heads (which moves the story on). I didn't realise and missed a couple of things that then became inaccessible, so it's no longer possible for me to 100% the game unless I replay everything (which I'm not really inclined to do). My fault for not realising until I'd already saved over my progress really...!
- My main issue with this game is the lack of content and variety in settings and characters. There are very few people to battle with and you only have a few rooms to explore in the house. Talking to the same characters over and over gets a little repetitive.
All in all it was an enjoyable experience and for the price I can forgive the limited content. It would be great to see a sequel that's more fleshed out with more people and places as I think there's a lot more that can be done with the idea. I'd recommend giving this one a go though for an evening's worth of intelluctually-themed intrigue.

[Spoiler-Free Review]
A quick-paced, deliberate, self-aware and irreverent RPG even Generation Y can play - if they can get over the visuals!
Breath of Death VII introduces us to Dem and his band of minions as they take RPG tropes from yesteryear (i.e. top-down presentation, menu based combat, magic and dungeon exploring) and reimagine them to fit within a world of immediate gratification and life-on-a-schedule.
The story is sharp and witty, the characters are interesting and unique (as much as a skeleton can be anyway) and the combat  is almost slideshow-like as battles can take little more than 10 seconds at times - this usually just consists of you mashing furiously on the action button. Your characters even automatically heal after every battle - less time flipping through menu after menu with upkeep.
In this way, it's a bit of a "My First RPG". it's the most approachable RPG I've ever played and brings enough "new" to the genre to recommend.  A dirt cheap stroll down RPG memory lane.

+ Good physics. A little more forgiving than perhaps it should be, but they do use race driver feedback, and it makes it more accessible.
+ Awesome content. Unless you like open-wheelers, then the content is stunning, from DTM to Group 5, from WTCC to GT Masters.
+ You can try out any car before buying it, which is an awesome feature.
- The pay model has its benefits and it's disadvantages. Firstly, you only have to buy what you want, which means you can in theory pay less than a normal 'all-up front' game, in which I often find I don't use all the content anyway. The disadvantage is that it is on the expensive side for sure, though much cheaper than iRacing and there is no monthly subscription. You also only need one car from any group of cars to be able to compete with the others, like iRacing.
- The servers are still not stable, but is something they are working on, and is improving at a decent rate.
- Would be better if the circuits were laser-scanned, though the upcoming Nordschleife will be.

Woah, what a game, 100% within 36 hours. I barely have anything that I disliked about this game, it's almost perfect. I will just list a few things that bugged me a little bit
1. There are 3 ways to move from place to place without having to actually move, 2 tram ways and 1 stag way, while this makes you reach most places, things like the Forgotten Basin still can only be accessed by going to the King Station and then running there which is quite the problem since there are so many objectives in that area (A hidden grub, 2 new items for moving around, a hidden charm, the key to the good ending of the whole game, one of the spell upgrades, it's a lot basically) It was pretty annoying getting to that area over and over again, is what I am saying basically. (EDIT-FIXED)
2. Limited viability of charms: You have quick slash which is one of the most op charms in the game and only takes 2 charm notches but then you have countless of other spells which give you more SOUL, charge SOUL faster or do things to your spell, most of them either so limited usage that you basically never use them at all. Let's say you have a boss where you cannot heal, this is where having honey blood and jonis blessing at the same time is awesome but if you can heal properly at a boss, you will use anything but some quicker soul charge or useless stuff like that.
3. The Quick Slash in general: Once you obtain that charm, you basically won the entire game, you can overwhelm almost all future bosses mandatory for the normal story with you DPS, you don't even have to dodge anymore which is definitely a huge problem since that lame strategy even makes the last boss a piece of cake.
4. More uses for Geo (The currency of the game) I have bought everything before even having finished the last colloseum trial, the game needs something expensive, even if it's something little.
Other than that the game is honestly perfect, the art, the whole combat system, it's just beautiful. I don't really understand the people comparing this to Dark Souls, I mean yeah it's challenging but not only are the real challenging things just optional bosses but also, I don't see why a game is "like Dark Souls" just because it's challenging when legitemately everything else is completely different than Dark Souls, like seriously, stop it. I also saw someone complaining about the difficulty and saying only/mostly people that have played Dark Souls can enjoy Hollow Knight but that is honestly just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t again. This game is a challenging sidescrolling RPG, it's not meant to be a game that you can relax with while sitting on a couch, although I was still able to do that because I knew exactly how to play since I have played Dark Souls previously, that honestly just got me into the game faster than others, sort of a small head start. The game requires you to learn from your mistakes and fix those within the next time you fight a boss, if you are too stupid to learn from your mistakes and rage instead, then this game obviously is nothing for you but nontheless, I suggest you to work on that problem of yours instead of calling this a bad a game because it's everything but that. The game is challenging but not unfair. I haven't even mentioned the art and soundtrack yet, I am usually someone that only plays games for the gameplay aspect of it yet it emediately caught my eye, the transition from area to area is straight up the smoothest it could be, the world couldn't be more detailed, you have a few suddle character side quests which gives you more insights into the lore of the game yet you are not required to do specific tasks, you just listen to honest, straight, short dialogue if you want to and get more of it by looking into bugs' minds, this makes the story telling very suddle as well, as mentioned I am the kind of guy that only plays for gameplay which is why I like this kind of story telling. The lore is indepth yet simple and it doesn't force its lore towards you unlike a game like Witcher 3 which literally just feels like playing a book. These are the best parts of the game that caught my attention as well as the issues I wanted to adress while playing the game, I don't want to go more indepth on things, neither do I really want to analyze everything bit by bit so I'll stop right here, buy the game during a sale if you have the chance, absolutely recommendable !
