I've now spent about 50 hours playing CSX: Heavy Haul, and I'd say far more effort went into making it look good than making it a better simulator than TS2017.  Secondly, in that many hours I've done about all the things I can do it in.
Some impressions:
1. Buggy - This really had way too many bugs to be released. I'm a software developer, but I felt more like I was at my second job on their test team.  This release feels like marketing needed to hit a date and get revenue, and customer experience was removed from consideration.  Some of the big and small frustrations I experienced:

* On a downhill slope of 1.5%, notching the throttle down slows a 50-70 car loaded train.  How could that possibly have gone unnoticed in something designed to be a SIMULATOR?  You'd know more about physics if your only experience was watching the Roadrunner cartoon.
* Signals never change, preventing you from completing scenarios
* Basic math like the number of yards in a mile appears to be out of reach. 1 mile = 5280 feet / 3 feet/yard = 1760 yards.  I wish we used metric in the U.S., but if you're going to measure in miles and yards, how hard can it be to do that math?
* Snow disappears in ice & snow scenario, and it's one of only a handful of scenarios.  Really?  So few and still untested?
Yes, there are big challenges moving to a new graphics engine, but it may have been too much too soon.  While the modeling of swinging airlines is a nice realistic touch, that clearly could have been put on the "later" list so they could focus on the core reliability and performance of the simulator. To their credit, things are improving noticeably as V4 is now out.
2. Boring Scenarios - I much prefer the puzzles and challenges of switching over long-haul runs.  I was very surprised how few scenarios were included, and how little switching is involved considering this simulator is focused exclusively on freight.  Taking a train from one place to another on the mainline can have its challenges (assuming the throttle and braking are somewhat realistic), but ultimately freight is about getting stuff from supplier to consumer.  Lots of room to take this realistic world and build trains from sidings, take them somewhere, then delivery the goods.  The Empire Builder board game has more interesting railroading.
3.  Closed World - During the years of development of CSX, you'd think they must have built some tools similar to the World Editor of TS2017 for use internally that could have  been released to users.  At least a consist and scenario builder if not the whole World Editor.
Portal 2 still has new scenarios being built by users more than six years after it was released because it has a decent built-in editor, not to mention the wide-open possibilities when using their stand-alone editor.  Imagine what CSX and the Unreal Engine could be with the same tools.

Although the trailers had been very promising, Stanley looked to the customer review section seeking further advise. Some reviews seemed rather strange to him, but nearly all of them were enthusiastically positive about the game. Realising that additional research would also hold the risc of heavy spoilers for the experience, Stanley decided that the information he had gathered so far would have to suffice. He hesitated for a mere moment before he eventually purchased the game.
While playing it, he found that none of the comments in the review section had been able to convey how much one could enjoy 'The Stanley Parable'. He wanted to help the others in search of guidance. He wanted them to understand that this game holds something profoundly beautiful, that its philosophical potential was not to be underestimated, that it could be an invaluable source of entertainment, so he decided to add his comment to the store page.
Stanley felt that he should point out the availability of a free demo as well, since it could be of assistance in the decision of a potential customer.
Of course, the game had influenced him by now and he considered it terribly amusing to write a comment that matched its tone, even though it was unlikely that this effort would be acclaimed by those whom he sought to help. And yet, he couldn't help but to feel oddly satisfied when it was done.

Holy ♥♥♥♥, what a game. Hollow Knight gets so many things right. There is a serene beauty to the profoundly dismal atmosphere, and all of the hand drawn artwork and animation is top notch. Visuals aside, this is some of the best 2D combat and platforming to come out of the indie scene. Your character moves with such fluidity and precision, perfect for having your reflexes and constantly tested. And the map is such a joy to explore, in a world fully realized and fleshed out, where most every corner will reward your sense of exploration. Even if the story is quite minimal, there is enough lovingly-crafted world-building, lore, and endearing characters to keep you engaged.
I will say, though, that the acquisition of certain items is sometimes accompanied by a dip in the challenge, and the difficulty curve may take a bit to catch up. It certainly does grant a sense of progression though, as you will eventually find yourself barely trying against certain areas and enemies.
Overall, Hollow Knight is without a doubt worth your time, should you find time to invest in it.

A great game with some glaring flaws. First, you need to get over the overload of proper nouns that are completely new and don't make sense to you. Then you need to get past that the characters are more or less tropey caricatures that aren't by any means deep or too real.
But underneath all that is a good plot that takes the realities of war on frankly, themes of death and the importance of rememberance, epic music, an actiony and competent battle system with 14 (fourteen!!) playable characters and plenty of side stuff to explore and flesh out the world. This is the first Final Fantasy game in years that I've been excited to play again and again to see more of the story and characters...as well as one of the only ones to leave me with an ending that made me FEEL things. You're going to be confused, but if you're able to feel out a plot more than needing to understand every bit of it, this could be a game for you.

There are times wherein it feels the check point saves are incredibly far apart and other times where you feel like you just saved, so there will be a couple points where you need to do long stretches of the same mission again if you die.
Level design isn't anything stellar by modern standards however if you can appreciate this game for when it came out, it becomes more interesting.
If you can pick it up in a bundle on sale, go for it.

Final Fantasy Type-0 is pretty cool, I guess.
Originally a PSP game exclusive to a mysterious island nation no one is actually sure exists, Type-0 is a spin off game part of a long lived video game franchise mainstream journalists pretend isn't as good as it actually is. Type-0 is part of the Fabula Nova Crystallis series of Final Fantasy games which includes Final Fantasy XIII and other games nobody actually cares for.
Luckily, outside of a few shared concepts, Type-0 lacks anything to do with the XIII trilogy so don't expect Toriyama's waifu to show up anytime soon.
You play as everybody. I mean Class-0, an organization of highly gifted individuals who work as special operatives for both the school they attend and their nations government. As a departure from other Final Fantasy games, Type-0 is told as a gritty war drama rather than a grand adventure across a continent.
The Militesi Empire, one of the four crystal states and named after their obvious love for humanitarian affairs, invades their neighboring Dominion of Rubrum while also dispatching a special unit directly to Akademia, the magic academy and capitol Rubrum. With the use of a special type of magitek armor that allowed them to jam the Vermilion bird Crystal and, in turn, block the use of magic to the academy cadets and legionaries on the ground. Without their big crutch or the use of Eidolins, this games summons, the Legionaries and Cadets are quickly overwhelmed and pushed to the verge of defeat.
That is until Class-0 arrives, who seem to be unaffected by the magitek's crystal jammer. With the use of magic, the Class-0 cadets push through the Militesi lines and make several surgical strikes on enemy positions which not only disrupted Militesi air superiority, but also destroyed the crystal jammer and allowed the Rubrum defenders to push back the enemy attack.
That's some WW2♥♥♥♥♥♥right there.
The setting is probably Type-0's strongest aspect, while the Final Fantasy series is no stranger to war, it was never actually represented as the focal point of a game outside of maybe Final Fantasy Tictacs. I do love me some final fantasy Tictacs.
Every theme from the series itself is reiterated to do with military or war. Ultima becomes a weapon of mass destruction rather than just a spell, summons are used as wrecking balls on battlefields, there are plans that do fire magic bombing runs, and even with all that they managed to fit in things like human super weapons and giant robots.
Combat strays away from the usual FF formula, while random encounters are still a thing, every battle plays out in real time, and managing your parties health and mana works in conjunction with active dodging and finding openings for attacks. Timing your attacks at just the right time also counts towards a counter attack which lets you punch one clean chunk out of your enemies stomach. I mean, I'm no doctor or anything, but that doesn't seem possible, what with the bones, and cartilage, and organs.
Oh yeah, the characters.
Class-0 consists of fourteen characters, and while Ace seems to be the series representative of the party, each member seems to be as important as the other. Every character has their own skills and specialties, some are better at magic while others are better at getting in close, and others still work at dwindling down enemy HP from afar. Every character has a unique play style, and while some are obviously superior to others, it's still a neat way to add variety to your game. Or you could always just stand back with Trey and fire a charged bow at your enemies like a total coward.
By the way, they're all named after trumps. The cards, not the president candidate guy with the goofy hair.
I do have some gripes with the game, though. It was originally a PSP exclusive and it clearly shows, even with the updated HD graphics. And although 30 fps isn't a killer for me, I should probably point out that the game does not run at 60 fps and will sometimes dip with certain graphical settings on lower end hardware, it was no ways an actual deal breaker for me.
There's also a bit of a grind at certain points of the game, which makes sense considering what the original game was. And sometimes quest drops take so long to find you may as well just order them from Amazon.Rubrum and wait for them arrive a few weeks later. Some characters are also definitely more fleshed out and balanced than others on the battlefield, but the ones that aren't as good are still viable to use.
But should you play, Last Story: I can't actually make this joke because Last Story is an actual game now?
Yeh, I would say so, the game is constantly on sale if the full price isn't to your liking. There are also multiple endings for people who want to go back and give the game a few more runs, but in my opinion, the first ending is perfect for how the game is presented. Still, I have 30 some hours into the game and I'm probably going to go back to Orience sometime in the future.

The devs should definetly rewatch '80-'90 flicks to refresh and improve that in the next game.

This game came just before a slew of others of the same idea did---a builder game with space ships/stations.  I'd bought this with another one that's since died, called "Blockade Runner".  Thing is, Space Engineers came along, then a couple years after Empyrion.
Yes, this is comparable to those two---which have the same idea behind them but better execution.  This feels like a messy cluster of the same idea that's harder to do stuff in, and less pretty.
Edit: Seems my review is being voted down as "Not being helpful", fair enough.  There's a lot of people that like this game---but simply put?  I don't.  And I think there is better.
Also after playing for some time, I can state---my opinion of the game has not changed.  The tutorial was an absolute mess---it doesn't explain well some of the mechanics of the game like how to roll your ship so it's level.  Speaking of that, having to constantly align yourself to everything to even get your bearings is a frustrating mess.
The bulding in itself is simplistic---that's nice enough, however it gets frustrating when you realize everything kind of has a bland block look to it.  Everything.  From the weapons, to the mechanical blocks.
There's also a distinct lack of sound in regards to doing things---it becomes very noticeable as you go on.
The upside is that there -is- things to do in this game.  It seems large, and I'm sure if you're able to get past the clunky mechanics, the bland textures, and the lack-luster physics (I'm looking at you, wonky ships and the "Aligning" mechanic), that there's fun to be had...
However I couldn't get past it.

I've done my fair share of roller coasters and fair rides without problem so I considered myself intolerant to such matters, but It may have been becuase I was dehydrated, hungry, tired, or any other external causation that makes you sensitive to disorientation, but I quickly decided that whatever the reason, it wasn't worth the trouble. What happens when you add dice to a game? You randomly win or lose through no skill or fault of your own.
Now the art of playing these tabletop games is to tip the odds in your favor. Except in Space Hulk, you regularly can't. You have your Space Marine standing in a 1 square wide corridor you have to pass through. None of his battle brothers can fire past him. Attacking allows you to kill 1 or 2 enemies in front of you (if the dice like you) - any more and you're dead. Too bad, then, that they spawn in groups of 3.
Overwatch to the rescue! Setting your Space Marines to overwatch, they can shoot any number of enemies (3, 6, 9 - don't care) during the enemy turn. So you spend your 4 AP moving 2 squares and going into Overwatch. Bam! Enemy group killed. Next turn. Bam! Enemy group killed. Next turn. "My weapon has jammed" - oops, bad dice roll, your Space Marine is dead.
Maybe experienced DnD players can enjoy this kind of gameplay. I can't.

This game was a big surprise for me.
I would recommend this game to anyone bored and looking for a few hours of an actual challenge.
Most games that iv played relied upon fast reflex and button mashing, whereas this game truly makes you take your time and plan 4+ steps ahead to gain the upper edge and beat your opponent.
But anyhow back to the actual review.
In this game you are suspected to be just a regular woman, invited by chance to a get together of strangers. the world is consistent of a single house that you must fully explore to learn the lore of it and the people gathered inside. The game is built around the idea that words are power, and the better you are at getting your point across the more powerful you are.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pros:
-Difficulty
Learning the mechanics of the game was a bit of a hassle for me. At first I was losing every single argument left and right because the instructions were to be honest a bit frustrating. Though after your 5th match you start to understand the concept. And by the end of the game you will without a doubt fully grasp how conflict works in this universe.
-Story Ritch
I would have never thought I could learn so much lore in a story just by repeatedly talking to the same people over and over but truth be told. There is a very big story in the game that goes outside of the initial story that the player can ever touch. Just pay attention and read everything that people have to say, it's well worth your time.
-Graphics
The graphics in this game are very unique. My honest opinion wavers greatly on this subject because for a game like this, I don’t think graphics was one of their main concerns, but! i will say that they did put a lot of well-done detail into the games environment, and the use of colors for the characters makes a lot more sense once you’ve ventured further into the game.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cons:
-Repetitive
I suppose any kind of mind game would be repetitive if you had to do it over and over and over and over again. For a con part of a review, this argument is actually very weak, but the repetitive factor is still there so I think I should at least state that it can occur. But honestly it’s like playing checkers, playing 700 matches of checkers non-stop can be repetitive for anyone as well. The game did do a good job however about giving each player their own play style so no 2 matches are alike, That being said, if you’ve played against a single character enough times you learn their strategies and you can play around it flawlessly!
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Shadowgrounds Survivor is the unmistakable sequel to previous years top down horde mode shooter Shadowgrounds. Unmistakable because if you didn't see the title you'd be hard pressed to tell them apart.
That's not to say Survivor doesn't introduce a few new features, multiple playable characters and a more detailed level progression makes the game a good deal more engaging as you go along. The storyline is as was in the original utterly forgettable and can be easily ignored.
The greatest strength of Shadowgrounds Survivor is once again it's use of atmospheric lightning which does a good job at turning otherwise bland encounters with the alien horde into something a little more suspenseful, lending somewhat from the horror genre.
The problem is also, once again, that this is a genre that has done it all before, the top down shooter horde mode gives you nothing new, nothing you haven't seen a hundred times before. You go from room to room in a linear progression stopping only to pick up the occasional ammo pack in between scripted attacks by the same massive blob of aliens you've already killed in the last ten rooms. Even the boss battles mostly boils down to the same run and gun tactics as the rest of the game making playing the game feel like a grind the more you progress.
All in all as with the original the problem is that Shadowgrounds does nothing to innovate. It adds nothing that you didn't see in the last five games you played int this genre and that makes it a tiresome experience for anyone but the most hardcore fans.

9.1/10 Outstanding game.
Normally I would have a more strung-out intro than that, but as a digest, I stand by it. This was my first encounter of Assassin's Creed as I wasn't overly impressed with the series so far, it didn’t seem something I would like so I didn’t bother. However …pirates. Yeah, pirates. In a nostalgic haze reminiscing of the title Galleon, I jumped at the chance to buy this when it came on sale.
Now, I dabbled with the 1st Assassin’s Creed with the whole Italy rooftop malarkey and it wasn’t (for me) exciting or compelling at all. There is still the rooftop shenanigans and walking around all stealthy aspect, but it balances that out by giving the player an open-sea adventure too. The transition from land to sea is flawless, and it provides an alternate game style to delve into. Its GTA meets Pirates of the Caribbean.
There is so much to do in terms of side-quests that you could spend weeks alone collecting the collectables, pillaging the loot boxes and digging (sort of) for buried treasure. Yet the main story is also immersive and long enough to invest in, without getting too strung out.
My only qualm if any is the 1st person breakaway sections that occur at certain points that take you out of the body of the main protagonist and plop you into the office. I felt this section was somewhat lacking and completely dis-associates you from the pirate world when you don’t want to be. I get it though, it’s a story telling device used to understand and progress the AC world rather than the Black Flag world.
I picked up a couple of other AC titles to try since finishing Black Flag and I’m not exactly liking the experience, so perhaps if you are like me then you are not in eager anticipation of AC Syndicate. Having said that, this title is a promising advance on the series and I hope the future iterations provide this much depth and experience in a fantastic location and period of time.

This is the story of a steam user. They enjoyed browsing reviews of popular interactive video simulations on thier moniter.  Before purchasing said simulations, they would often read online reviews.  This gave them an idea of the meaning of subject matter, and what they would experience. Other might consider this a meaningless pursuit, somewhat pathetic endeavor, reading what others had experienced instead of experiencing it themselves. Sometimes they started for days without purchasing a game. And the steam user was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change the steam user; something they would never quite forget. They had been reading various reviews of a game, The Stanley Parable. They sat there wondering if they should experience the simulation for themselves. They thought to themselves, "Should I read the rest of this review, or should I download this game?"

The steam user continued to read the review, wondering how it would end? What clever wordsmithing would this strange  user type? Why were they reading this voice in a distinctly British voice, comparable to actor Kevan Brighting? Did everyone else read the text that fell before their eyes read it in this voice? Perhaps, the steam user read it was meant to sound like a poor Argentinian beggar? But then the user realized that the narration of The Stanley Parable was only suitable for a proper voice, one you'd hear on the BBC telling you about other people's experiences.
The Steam user paused for a moment to wonder why the reviewer was switching narrative styles, and why it was reading for themselves. Yes! The person exclaimed, understanding the meaning. Or not, because they needed to be quiet for some reason. This was indeed an exciting and strange review, one they would tell all their friends about when they were finished with The Stanley Parable Review. They couldn't turn thier eyes away from the blocks of charactars, arranged  words that were arrange in sentances that in a way that were facinating to the eye. This was a great experiance.

I have to start this recommendation with a caveat… Make sure you get this cheap or bundled, because it is really short. The various endings, dialogue paths, and hidden specials give it some replayability and you should at least be able to milk a few hours out of it, but not nearly enough for the current $15 price tag.
That being said, time spent in the game in quite entertaining. Few games have made me laugh and question my actions quite like The Stanley Parable.
Not at all my type of game, yet it sucked me in right away. The narrator is outstanding, at times I couldn’t quit laughing, at other times I had to question his motives. The narrative itself is very interesting and the various paths give you plenty to question about the game and possibly life itself. For what little interaction there is the controls are smooth, and the graphics are fine for the genre. Get it, but make sure you get it on the cheap!
I went into this game very hesitantly. After playing the similar (and decently well received) Gone Home and being utterly unimpressed I wasn’t sure that The Stanley Parable would bring anything to the genre to get my attention… I was wrong!
Very quickly I ran into a couple of issues with the narrator, and couldn’t progress because I was laughing too hard. Not long after that I hit another section and the laughter stopped, now I was questioning my choices and the narrators motives. I’d got wrapped up in the lighthearted comedy that I’d forgotten there were darker overtones and the narrator brought me back down in a glorious way, so now I had to do another play through and get more info. Then another, and another. After 3-4 hours I’d explored a good number of the secrets and endings. I looked at guides trying to find more, but realized I’d got most of what I’d be willing to get (sorry, I’m not playing a 4 hour minigame to get an ending), and that’s where my only real knock against this game comes in. For all of the great details, it just doesn’t feel like there is quite enough. I really want there to be another dozen endings and secrets… It’s like a good date that ended just a little too early. I had a really good time, but I’m not sure whether or not we’ll see each other again.
On top of the obvious gameplay narrative there are plenty of funny details scattered about the game (take a minute to read the white boards, and check out some of the scattered documents!). Where in Gone Home I just breezed through and skipped any non-essential details, here I found myself looking for the little details, even waiting for all of the projector slides in the conference room to play through.
The only UI to speak of is the menus and they’re fine, there’s not much there because there doesn’t need to be, and yet they provide more Video controls than some AAA titles. It’s nice and clean and get’s the job done.
They’re fine for what they are. You’re not going to be blown away unless Duke Nukem 3D was the last 3D game you played, but they’re crisp and I never saw any unintentional anomalies.
Really the only sound is the Narrator’s voice and occasional environmental noises. The only complaint is that everything you interact with sounds like a keyboard click which isn’t bad, but a little odd at times. If you judge the sound purely off of the Narrator then this game might be in the top 10 for best sound design ever. As noted in the Overall, the Narrator is simultaneously hilarious, insightful, and even a little creepy at times.
I’d have this as a must own. The only serious complaints I have are that it’s a tad too short, and the current asking price is too high. If you can get it on sale or in a bundle it’s 100% worth it. Very few games I’ve ever played have run me through the emotional gauntlet that The Stanley Parable did in such a short amount of time. If you don’t like stories that are open to interpretation you’ll probably leave unsatisfied, but if you think interpretation is part of the fun, you have to check this out! Even as a must own I’ll give it a 7/10 because it is so short and your actual options are pretty limited. If it were 10 hours of unique content or so, and had more secrets and endings it would easily be a 9/10.

Update.  Seeing the news on the 1.4 release of June 1st, my on the fence, thumbs down review, is now no longer an on the fence thumbs down.  It is 100 percent thumbs down, as DTG has proven, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that they are going to treat this sim, EXACTLY the same as TS20xx.  They honestly and sincerely do not care about realistic physics, and instead prove that they are the kings virtual train arcading eye candy.  As long as the majority of end users, don't have a clue about real train physics, nor the concept of Newton's laws of physics, they will never attempt to make a more realistic "simulator".   If you look back throught old TS20xx physics complaints, you will see they match the complaints of TSW and it's physics.  Which now proves, their lack of care.  Now they are moving on to their next TSW money maker, and just wait till you see what I will say is a safe bet at a rediculously priced set of editors for TSW.   And if they release another route, before releasing editors, I can't use the words in my mind on this forum.  Folks, do your homework. Look long and hard into the forums for both TSW and TS20xx, and when you see alot of the same complaints showing up in TSW, beware of spending money on this.  DTG advertised TSW to be the most realistic "simulator" ever released.  EPIC FAIL.  They advertised, and hyped Simugraph to be the cutting edge programming that would deliver the most realistic physics ever seen to this date, in the history of virtual railroading.  EPIC FAIL.  Let's just say that Open Rails as well as Run 8, far exceed DTG, and TSW in realistic physics.  And if you still want to purchase this, wait for the Christmas Sale and 80 percent off,  or find a sharply discounted key elsewhere.
ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW
To start, I did the "beta", and decided to give it a shot when the true and current beta began.  I initially was curious to see if there were any improvements from the "beta", and there were absolutely none.  I initially started off with a second gen i5, installed a gtx 1070 in that, and was lucky to see mid 20s for fps.
This week I built a new computer.  i7-7700, asus maximus ix hero, ssd m2 and regular ssd, 16gb ddr4 3200 ram, and the gtx 1070strix i previously purchased.  In the settings menu, most settings are on ultra, or high, with shadows down to medium, because really, I don't need shadow perfection.  Also have the fps target set for 62.
I can run consistently at 62 fps, but one part that still needs improvement is when an ai train loads, it pauses even this game for a few moments, then starts up at 10fps and a sudden return to 62 fps.  With another train in view, it holds at 56 fps.
I would really appreciate it if DTG could release a new scenario, maybe over a 10 mile section of track that uses one of the yards, heading into the hills, with a very heavy dose of train traffic and populated yards and sidings, just to see how that would effect this machine.
Sounds are below average.  I don't know if these brits that designed this have stood trackside here in the USA or not.  But the sounds are too quiet.  The rolling stock sounds are turned way down, and are diminished.  Stand trackside in the usa, and even new wheels on good welded rail is loud.  And then throw in the pinging of the wheels, the squeaking and groaning of the truck springs and the flange squeal, our trains here in the USA are LOUD!  Not so in TSW.  The SD40 and GP38 sounds are ok, but again, they miss the signatures within their sounds that make them both unique.  The AC4400 sounds.  Lets just say, those are an absolute travesty, and an insult to the advertised realism, not to mention my ears.  General Electric, meet the Hoover Vacuum Cleaner Company.  These sounds, in no way whatsoever, even begin to come close to capturing the essense of the GE FDL 16 engine.  And all three locos, utilize the same horn.  Again, that is an insult to the advertised reality that was promoted during the development of this game.  I don't know at what point, the people at DTG listened to these sound packages, and proclaimed, "ya baby, we nailed those sounds!", But they missed, and missed big.
Physics, without going into detail.  They leave a lot to be desired.  The mark was greatly missed here too.
Sandpatch?  After all the enclosed activities and tutorials are done, it does get boring.  There just isn't any action here. And it doesn't help that the only people who can create ANYTHING at all for TSW in regards to scenarios, are all at DTG.  And IMO, dating back to MSTS, Sandpatch is over represented in the community with even the releases of it over the years, all have been boring after a while.
I would have to say, that this is about the equivalent of the intiial 1st gen release of railworks.  EXCEPT for one area.  The graphics are very good.  Even on the slow computer, with all settings on low or off, it still looked good.  And with a top end machine, they look even better.
I am now at the point where I am supposed to choose a thumbs up or down.  I wish steam would implement an icon that goes in the middle, with a fence logo on it, to represent being on the fence about a release.   I am giving it a thumbs down at this time, because I don't believe DTG delivered what they advertised they were going to deliver.  I see on many various game reviews, that releasing absolute buggy train wrecks of computer software, is the norm these days. No pun intended there.  But I am old school, and believe that if you are gonna advertise and claim your product will be of a certain quailty and deliver certain things, but fall miserably short on release, I cannot give DTG a pass on that.
Do I recommend this game?  If you have an absolute top end 7th gen i7, or a 7600 i5, or equivalent AMD processors, with either a GTX 1070 or 1080, and a good gaming motherboard, then yes I absolutely recommend this.  That's if you can live with the misses in the physics and sound dept.  But if you have a machine slower than that, I would only purchase if you can find a discounted steam code for it.
If DTG can fix various things within the sim, I would be happy to change this to a thumbs up, but remember, it's an on the fence thumbs down at this time.

I've been playing this game since fairy early in the closed beta, and even then it continued to challenge and entertain as a superb strategy tcg.  A few points (some large, some small) that seperate Infinity Wars from other major TCGs such as Magic and Hearthstone:
1) Both players take their turns simultainiously, once both players have locked in their actions for the turn (you cannot see what your opponent decides to do until the turn happens) everything unfolds at the same time, making for fun and balanced (no 1st or 2nd turn advantage to exploit) game pacing.
2) The 3 combat zones, and command zone (4 zones total) in which cards can be moved around make for great strategy.  You must utilize the zones to your advantage, as well as bluff and use mind games to keep your opponents on their toes.  Your opponent might be pulling their hair out because of your use in manuevering your troops between the support and attack zones, leaving them unable to be dealt with.
3) All the artwork on the cards is animated!  This might seem like a superficial point, and well it is, but it's something that Magic is unable to do, and Hearthstone only does on their 'golden' cards.  In Infinity Wars all cards have artwork that has some level of animation to it, giving them a little more personality and depth.
4) It's still in beta!  There's still so much more in the works that it's amazing.  Even as is the game is a blast to play, yet in the future the game will only bloom and become even more robust and smooth in both gameplay and functionality of the UI.
5) It's FREE!  Much like Hearthstone, this game can be played with zero dollars of investment.  Through minimal daily effort it's possible to ammass a collection capable of building a fairly competitive deck, or at least enough points to start doing drafts (Rift Runs) on a regular basis.

Okay, I love this game.
Review - Honestly the gameplay is secondary to the story. It's a perfect fit for it, but the story is definitely where your attention will be.
Basically this is rock-paper-scissors with strategy, levels, and special skills. If that does not appeal to you then you need to play it anyway so you can be proven wrong.
You spend turns choosing from 9 options depending on two resources, 2 of which are gained from 3 each of 6 total of the 9 options, the last 3 being "attacks." Each set of three has three types, with one option to each type per set of three options. Type 1 beats 2, 2 beats 3, 3 beats 1. Matching these favorably gives you a bonus to your attack, and your resources if you have certain skills equipped.
There are levels involved, but it's quite easy to level up. You just need to spar, you'll level up even from failing.
That's pretty much it, actually. Granted, it's very likely I'm missing things as I just played through from start to finish and it's currently 3 A.M. as I write this, so please forgive any errors or general stupidity on my part.
Commentary - This was fantastic. It's a brilliant idea, a wonderful execution, and lovable if not memorable characters. (Well over 90% of which is due to the shortness of the game rather than lack of good writing. I'd go so far as to say 98-99% even.)
My only complaint (if it can be called that) is that the "true ending" was really easy to figure out, and the final post-credits scene difference was obvious to predict. (This is assuming there aren't multiple endings based on who you pick after the final code. I'm sure I'll be finding out some other time.)
Everything below this I'll classify as "spoilers," though I'll attempt to avoid them:
- I love the option to discourse Mew. The first time I could talk to her I was ecstatic at the thought, and the later ability to do so is fantastic. (Especially since she's the strongest character.)
- Entirely irrelevant, but the scene involving copying the "word" gave me major deja vu, which I consider a good thing.
- Seymour seemed to be unaffected by the Last Word at one or more points, I've already forgotten the specific instances.
- While the ending was nice, it was greatly annoying to not know that the final code was impossible to get. I swear I counted every tile it seemed in an effort to figure it out.
- Similarly, I find it fitting that the final line gives the last word to Boasting, even though the line that followed from the beginning was used. I realize I worded that horribly, but even that seems fitting to me personally. :P
- Definitely worth the 10 dollars. Every cent, for the story at least, if not for the gameplay.

So far only 7 hours in, but given the "Mixed" review on the Steam Store, I was reluctant to pick this up on sale for $10.
I'm very happy with it at this point. I played the first 2 hours and despite loving the initial cut scenes (setting the dark tone), wasn't truly hooked until the battle sytem and customization opened up a bit. Now I can't get enough.
The aesthetic is a lot like FF8 in the sense that it's a modern vibe that maintains the typical FF-anime feel. It's set in the same universe as FF13, which was never my favorite, but does a better job providing resources for you to catch up on the lore, should you want to.
You're essentially playing an action RPG with 14 playable characters (not incuding the eidolons that are super fun) that all use different weapons and balances of magic and skills to contribute to the fight. I can't imagine getting bored of the combat, as each of those 14 characters adds skills and spells (or even entire mechanics) to their repitoire every time they level, which is quite frequent. Combine all that with the fact that you're using 3 people at once, and we have a game where no two fights are the same. There are a number of design choices in the game that keep things fresh.
I'll update as I play a bit more, and fully expect this to be another Final Fantasy adventure that I log 50+ hours with.

This game was a pretty good time-killer. It was quirky, entretaining, and different. It is roughly divided into two phases, an investigation phase which is more passive, and a battle phase where you are more actively engaged.
The investigation phase doesn't have anything very special, you basically chat with people and gossip about different topics, leveling up your knowledge on these topics and getting to know more about the cast. While its nothing special, it's not unrewarding as most of the times you will get experience by discovering all sorts of events. The conversations can be pretty entretaining, and there are a few secrets here and there,
The "battles" are kind of weird, and the tutorial is not the best (long text  thrown at you explaining things, instead of showing it to you). Therefore, you learn mostly through trial and error. The first battle, usually used as a tutorial, is 'wasted' as you are forced to lose on the first turn (granted, it's meant to show how bad you are at first, but still, it doesn't feel fair to be thrown into a battle that you will lose for certain, without even knowing what is even going on).
Instead, you get the second battle to be the tutorial. As i've stated, you are told in text all in one go how battles work, and you have to remember how it all works from the start.
Maybe if in the first battle you could have two turns or more to try things out before you are inevitably beaten, or maybe if you got the tutorial commands one turn at a time, it would be less confusing.
While the presentation of the battles might not have been ideal, they are very engaging, especially compared to other turn based RPGs. In the "investigation" phase you are more passive and allowed to rest for a bit. In the "battle" phase, you will find yourself thinking ahead all the time, and being extra attentive to every aspect of it. A mistake might cost you the match, and it makes it a very engaging kind of fight. The battles are like playing a two games of Rock-Paper-Scissors, in which you have to choose between three types of moves (increase power-increase tact-attack), between three types of each move (low,medium,strong) and betweeen a sort of elements which affect how much damage the enemy/you take (circle-square-star).
While the game does become kind of repetitive after a while, the fact that it is fairly short, and that you get several skills to make battles different, makes up for it. The main problem will arise if you are trying to reach max level for some reason.
The last gripe, would be that there are two things that if you miss (checking a wine bottle before a certain development, and sitting on a chair in every chapter) you won't be able to get 100%, which is kind of annoying without a "new game+" or a "start certain chapter" feature.
I had a pretty good time, it still has room for improvement but it is a very solid game.

Have you ever wanted to be a silent skeleton knight, adventuring across the post-apocalyptic landscape with a perky ghost, nerdy vampire and suave zombie trying to determine what disaster left the world populated solely by the undead?
No? What's wrong with you?

Pros
-You're a pirate.
-Booty, plunder, treasure.
-The Sea Shanties, probably the best part of the game.
-Graphics.  Beautiful and very well designed for the period.
-Sailing, it's smooth, immersive, and tons of fun.
Cons
-Directional controls.  Want to jump in a paticular direction? Too bad Kenway wants to jump off a cliff.  Want to run through a tavern? Kenway wants to jump on every piece of furniture and ledge in the building, then you have to press a different button to get him to come down.  The number of buttons involed just in basic free-running is 3, 4 if changing direction!  This really breaks the flow and leads to considerable amounts of frustration.  Contrasting terrestrial controls with sailing really brings the game down.
-Combat. This is just terrible.  Basic melee combat is clunky, response is minimal, damage is arbitrary, and switching gadgets is cumbersome and their impact is negligible.  Even assassinations are nothing new from the previous games and since stealth is still a guesswork of trial and error you will end up in melee more often than not.
-Story.  Ubisoft is still clinging to the time-travelling gene machine at the heart of an 80,000 year old sci-fi battle between authoritarianism and liberalism.  Kenway starts out as a narcissist advocating anarchism but through the power of friendship realises the value of liberalism and his purpose in life.  Through it all you are dragged into terribly designed missions, running over the same maps that you played hours ago, with characters that you don't care about, and listening to a protagonist that you hate.  And you HAVE to do the main story because it's the only way to get upgrades.  And finally, just like all the other AC games you get pulled away from the game to faff about in the not-so-real-world-in-present day because Ubisoft wants to make sure you're not having too much fun and they think it's great to break up the immersion.  Seriously, WTF?
-Uplay.  This will make you want to give up before you even start the game.
-Killing animals.  The game encourages you to slaughter endangered wild life, in fact you will be required to kill several in order to craft upgrades but if you kill a cow you get a passive aggressive scolding saying your ancestor did not kill domestic animals.  If you kill a herd of cows then the game reloads for you...WTH is wrong with your Ubisoft?

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #55 - Eets Munchies
Eets Munchies is a puzzle game that took me back to my days playing Lemmings.  You play as Eets and his single-minded quest to get cake.  But Eets is not terribly smart.  In fact he'll happily hop of a ledge into oblivion if you let him.
To avoid that, the trick is to strategically place items that will help Eets get to his goal of eating his cake.   You place these items prior to starting the level.  Some items are simple like planks that you can place for Eets to walkover.  But other items that you place you click to interact with, and these items will interact with the environment.  Take for example the "Inhale Whale" which you click on and it will inhale Eets and then exhale him to move him up at an angle.
I also was reminded of Angry Birds as I continued to progress through levels and the game would introduce new kinds of items to use that work in different ways.  Another reminder is the way each level has the basic goal of getting to the cake, but also a secondary goal of getting up to 3 additional treats.  It's pretty easy to make it to the cake and progress to the next level, but the game awards you for getting each of the 3 treats as well, which is where the game can get tricky.
I adored the art style.  It has a zany cartoon feel, like something I'd see in Ren & Stimpy.  And the sound effects are matched perfectly with the art.  I thought they did some nice work here.  My only complaint is the music starts feeling repetitive after awhile, but as far as complaints go that's pretty minor.
One other thing that sets this game apart is the level editor.  I thought this was a really cool touch to add.  The level editor is pretty easy to use, it's basically just drag and drop.  You can build the levels and populate it with the items that you've unlocked from regular play.
I definitely appreciated the inclusion of the level editor as I think that helps add replay value.  I remember playing Angry Birds, and never found myself really replaying levels once I beat them.  I definitely would have felt the same about this game, so it's nice to have the level editor to make your own levels, or get your own from Steam Workshop.
You might be a little turned off by the price, as there are definitely cheaper puzzle games to be had (particularly on mobile).  But the game is undeniably fun, and given the high potential for replayability, I still think it's a fine value.

Update :- I have found a way to fix the main problem that I have with this game and that is to change traction control preset 0 from 0 to 100 in the car setup in the garage before a race (i.e. in practice or qualifying). I think what I was experiencing is called power on oversteer. Though I still cant believe that it should be anything like that bad in a real car :(
Note this wont help you brake or go around a corner, it just means you wont spin off the track into the corner when you gently accelerate !
I cant believe the developers have made this game so inaccessable when all they need to do is change 1 variable and it would be 30000 percent more playable to people who try the game !
Btw I come at tihis as someone who generaly prefers more sim like games like gt legends, grid, dirt, test drive unlimited 2, nfs shift 2, race injection etc. But even with hundreds of experience on probably 20 different racing games I couldnt make it around a lap without it crashing from oversteer !
I still hesitiate to recommend this game because of the sheer anount of frustration this issue caused me
Here is my original review :-
Raceroom experience is a very frustrating experience!
This is mainly down to what I consider a fault in the physics model !
The frustrations are :-
1 (and this is the big 1) ) When accelerating out of a bend the car oversteers and crashes back into the bend it has come out of ! This is most noteable on raceroom raceway, on the corner at the start of the start finish straight.
The track goes around a corner and up a hill, yet the car just uncontrolably spins with oversteer back towards the corner if power is applied.
No amount of opposite lock corrects it, and it doesnt feel like the back end is trying to overtake the front end due to too much power. It feels like its turning in a circle for no good reason. Grrr !
Though I have a feeling this is a common fault with a lot of so called sims. How many cars in the real world do you see spinning into the corner they have come out of ?
This issue is probably more of a problem on raceroom raceway than most tracks. But that track in the standard yellow car (Canhard R52, sillhoutte series ?) sure does highlight it!
Btw I have a g25 wheel and pedals and a fast pc (gtx970 etc). So I dont think my problems are down to my setup.
Also I have witnessed many many drivers having the same problems on that track, so its not just me. Though the experienced drivers do work around the problem.
2) If you do crash off, then the game takes 20 seconds to get going again. Either the car wont move at all or it just spins you into the opposite direction or you end up doing doughnuts. It will not spin and point in the right direction ! It doesnt matter if you are really subtle and gentle on the power or really heavy the result is the same ! Grrrr!
I think other than this the physics are very good, the sound is very good, the graphics are a slight improvement over race 07, but not as good as say need for speed or project cars.
Oh and I think the actual online multiplayer mechanics are good, which probably makes it one of the best online racing games, sim or otherwise on the pc (if and for me this might be too much of an if :- If you can adapt your driving style to ignore what I consider to be faulty physics).
I like the way you can test drive the cars before buying, though generally the content is too expensive. Particularly buying multiple items doesnt give enough of a discount.
Anyway, it would be a very good game, if it wasnt for what I consider to be a fault in one aspect of its physics model that makes it soooo frustrating :(

Don't let the looks fool you, there is nothing silly about this game!
You basically need to guide Eets (the white bunny...thingy...) towards the cake. Eets can only walk straight and is dumb enough to jump into pits of certain death. Your task is to basically "guide him" to the cake, optionally feeding him other candies, puddings and whatnot on your path. Eath puzzle gives you 3 candies and 1 cake. Whereas you cannot directly interact with Eets, you can change his path by laying down items on the ground (which may modify the scenario or Eets' behaviour). There are 5 "Worlds", each with 12 puzzles, the last of which is an extra "Mystery World" which does not contain any candies - just the cake.
I like to brag that I like puzzle games (and that is true). I got this game (like most) in a bundle and didn't expect much. The cartoon-ish graphics, the silly music and the very concept made this title sound like a child game, but you will quickly be surprised. After the first world you will actually have think quite hard to grab all the candies. As a puzzle game lover, I found every single puzzle fair and reasonable, no "dirty tricks" needed.
Sadly the replayability value is low.
The achievements are well designed and flow naturally with the game, but sadly they don't add any extra challenge that the game does not already naturally offer.
The Linux port is flawless.
Go and get it if you like puzzles.

They tried but Valhalla Hills just falls flat. From the makers of Settlers the influence here is obvious, each round plays like a game of settlers, just simplified. Therein lies the problem however. What made settlers great, the long games with sweeping empires sprawling across the map and hours spent meticulously placing buildings only to have them burned by rival factions is all missing here.
Valhalla Hills is played map by map, each one randomly generated but basically the same. The gameplay consists of building a town and the ultimate goal has you taking warriors up a hill and fighting a handful of static 'ghost' enemies, that's it. They're so short and simple I'm calling them rounds here because each one can take you from at least 15 minutes to get the minimum to win up to maybe an hour before you fill the whole map and you have to end it anyway. Each time you start all over on another map, build, get to the top of the mountain, rinse and repeat.
There's also a metagame where you're supposed to be earning 'honor' for your vikings which does carry over round to round. It's a cute mechanic and you can name your vikings, give them hats etc. but ultimately a trite one that artifically pads the metagame.
So this is all well and fun your first 5... 10.... 15.... 20 times playing? After that you've seen all the game has to offer, there's no challenge or depth to what you're doing it comes down to repetition for the meta.
Additionally there's multiple isues with the AI and UI, you can easily find yourself food/housing/tool blocked and not even know it until you're practically stuck and sometimes need to start over. Many times your vikings will stand around having a party when a building is near completion or they'll wander around looking for apple trees. One more thing to mention is there's exactly two songs to the game's music, one for battle and one for everything else. They're both well done but get SO tired after hours listening you'll just want to turn the music off. Sound is practically nonexistent besides that with everything being extremely muted or simple, nothing stands out in the sound department.
Might be a good buy for someone looking for something bite size they can sit and relax with but if you're looking for a new settlers game, keep looking.

Although the trailers had been very promising, Stanley looked to the customer review section seeking further advise. Some reviews seemed rather strange to him, but nearly all of them were enthusiastically positive about the game. Realising that additional research would also hold the risc of heavy spoilers for the experience, Stanley decided that the information he had gathered so far would have to suffice. He hesitated for a mere moment before he eventually purchased the game.
While playing it, he found that none of the comments in the review section had been able to convey how much one could enjoy 'The Stanley Parable'. He wanted to help the others in search of guidance. He wanted them to understand that this game holds something profoundly beautiful, that its philosophical potential was not to be underestimated, that it could be an invaluable source of entertainment, so he decided to add his comment to the store page.
Stanley felt that he should point out the availability of a free demo as well, since it could be of assistance in the decision of a potential customer.
Of course, the game had influenced him by now and he considered it terribly amusing to write a comment that matched its tone, even though it was unlikely that this effort would be acclaimed by those whom he sought to help. And yet, he couldn't help but to feel oddly satisfied when it was done.

This is the story of a steam user. They enjoyed browsing reviews of popular interactive video simulations on thier moniter.  Before purchasing said simulations, they would often read online reviews.  This gave them an idea of the meaning of subject matter, and what they would experience. Other might consider this a meaningless pursuit, somewhat pathetic endeavor, reading what others had experienced instead of experiencing it themselves. Sometimes they started for days without purchasing a game. And the steam user was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change the steam user; something they would never quite forget. They had been reading various reviews of a game, The Stanley Parable. They sat there wondering if they should experience the simulation for themselves. They thought to themselves, "Should I read the rest of this review, or should I download this game?"

The steam user continued to read the review, wondering how it would end? What clever wordsmithing would this strange  user type? Why were they reading this voice in a distinctly British voice, comparable to actor Kevan Brighting? Did everyone else read the text that fell before their eyes read it in this voice? Perhaps, the steam user read it was meant to sound like a poor Argentinian beggar? But then the user realized that the narration of The Stanley Parable was only suitable for a proper voice, one you'd hear on the BBC telling you about other people's experiences.
The Steam user paused for a moment to wonder why the reviewer was switching narrative styles, and why it was reading for themselves. Yes! The person exclaimed, understanding the meaning. Or not, because they needed to be quiet for some reason. This was indeed an exciting and strange review, one they would tell all their friends about when they were finished with The Stanley Parable Review. They couldn't turn thier eyes away from the blocks of charactars, arranged  words that were arrange in sentances that in a way that were facinating to the eye. This was a great experiance.
What about the game though? Was The Stanley Parable a game? Was it any more of a game than the review than the of game that that they were reading? Time passed in both, both involved some type of interaction with a computational device. The same could be said of taking a maths test, and from their experiences they had heard that it was a horrible game, very non-linear that most people pressed X to continue on and scrambled to finish the game correctly, and despite the graphics being amazing, the plot bored most users. This review was written on the 21st of March 2016. Some things may have been patched by the time you play this.
PLEASE READ: I have collected every collectible and 100%ed the game save one possible health container. This review recommends FreezeME with some caveats, however. There will be very minor spoilers in this review (I will try to be vague). If you don't wish to read them you can skip to the last paragraph.
FreezeME is a 3D Platformer Collectathon in the same vein as Super Mario 64. I grew up on games like Super Mario 64 and Banjo-Kazooie and I've been looking for a Collectathon that would scratch that itch.
In FreezeME you play as R, a girl with a camera that when aimed at certain enemies and certain parts of the environment you can take a picture of them and freeze them in their place for a limited amount of time. The time varies with each enemy. The game features 4 worlds, a hub world, and a few challenge levels that are accessible through the hub world.
-Story-
Fat the Cat kidnaps R's dog and R has to get him back. It's a simple story but I don't think anyone will be playing this for the story.
-Character Design-
The characters, except for a few, are all rather plain and dull. Most of them are cartoony pigs with a shperical body and lacking back legs so that they presumably bounce to get around but that is almost all of the NPCs. The enemy designs change every level, though they are really just reskins.
The main character, R, probably has the most interesting design in the entire game.
-Collectibles-
The game throws you in and only tells you how to jump (which we should really all know how to do). The things it doesn't tell you about are the unique parts of the game such as the collectibles and their purposes.
-Controls and Camera-
The running and jumping is obviously inspired by Super Mario 64. This is not a bad thing. Everything feels fairly good. It feels like it would be at home on the Nintendo 64 which isn't entirely a compliment. One thing that the N64 platformers all failed at was having a good camera. FreezeME fits in with them perfectly in that regard. The camera is awful. While walls will make the camera zoom in (which is how it should work) once you move away from the wall the camera doesn't zoom out to its previous position which can become very annoying if you are in one of the few places in the game with lots of walls. In some parts of the game there are alternate gravity sections not unlike Super Mario Galaxy. Due to the stubbornness of the camera I am of the opinion that the game would have been better without them. You can't have these gravity sections with an un cooperative camera.
I must also mention swimming. There aren't many opportunities in the game to swim which I see as a good thing because it isn't very fun due to how inactive it is. You hold the B button and that's it. And aiming underwater is made more needlessly difficult due to the camera.
-Sound-
The music is nice enough, though I don't think I would listen to it outside of the game. None of it is very catchy or inspired but it's fine as it is. There are green statues which exchange Cubes (think Jiggy or Power Star) for 10 Green Pig Coins. When you walk up to them they emit a very loud and irritating laser sound. If the volume was lower it would be bearable. I would like to believe that the devs left it at that volume on accident but it's so loud I find it difficult to believe that.
-Level Design (SPOILERS)-
The world are all very nice and colorful and easily distinguishable from one another.
The first and second are fine as they are. There are no major problems with either of these two worlds.
The third is where some problems begin to seep in. It has both ice and quicksand. The ice wasn't that bad. Mostly annoying. I know it's supposed to be hard to pick up momentum on ice at first but this made it hard to get off the ice if you were on the edge between ice and ground but the ground was higher than the ice. You would try to jump on the ground but without momentum you wouldn't move forward and would just land where you originally jumped from.
The next problem was quicksand mostly for the same reasons. You would try to jump out of it and sometimes you could but sometimes you would be stuck and then you would get sucked beneath and die.
The last world looks nice but I think the implementation and design completely lacked forethought. The world suffers from a stupid difficulty spike and if you fall in the lava down below you're as good as dead. Each time you touch the lava you take damage. There are no invincibility frames so you have a chance to survive. All of a sudden you have to make these incredibly precise jumps, thankfully there are plenty of teleporters so you don't have to do it all at once (I forgot to mention teleporters, didn't I?).
Teleporters make traversing each world a lot more convenient. The only real problem is that you have to wait for each teleporter to cycle through the list of teleporters.
We can't forget the Challenge Levels, can we? They are difficult but fun levels (one even gives a not-so-subtle but funny nod to Super Mario 64). The biggest problem is that you can't just automatically restart and you have to wait to die in some cases. Depending on the height you're at this can take up to 10 seconds and because of the difficulty you're going to die quite a few times. A quick restart option would alleviate some of the aggravation.
-Boss Design (SPOILERS)-
The bosses are rather boring. If they all had more character to them I think I might have a different opinion. The first one is simple enough once you get a feel for the game and is fine for a first boss.
The second is where it gets frustrating. Not because it's difficult but because of the diversion the boss tells you in the beginning that he 'just mopped the floor' and if you look you can see the refection of everything in the floor. You, him, and the precariously swaying chandelier. This was a failure to implement the famous "Chekhov's gun" principle in the game. You think that you're supposed to pay attention to the floor. You think that the reflection matters in some way. You think that maybe you have to make the chandelier fall on him. Nope. You hit him. 3 times. And then 3 more times. That's all.
The third boss is where I started to have trouble with them. Not because it was particularly difficult but because the boss has no 'tell' as to when it is vulnerable. And then when you do hit it sometimes it takes damage and sometimes it doesn't even when you did the exact same thing.
The fourth boss is the same way. Sometimes he takes damage and sometimes he doesn't. Another thing is that he runs around and is much larger than R. This means that sometimes you will get caught in front of him and can't escape and that's it. You take damage like every half second. You're dead.
The fifth boss suffers from basically the same problem as the fourth but the main problem isn't the boss but the gauntlet you have to pass before the boss. This could also be included under level design. Most of it is fine and after a few tries I had no problem getting to the last part but on the last part it locks your camera so that it would play more as a sidescroller which would have been fine it also made it so that you could only move on one axis. This results in you accidentally tilting up or down (and you don't know because of the camera's distance and your lack of control of the camera) and you end up walking off the edge and into the lava below. And you have to start all over.
-Conclusion
If you absolutely love the classic 3D Mario games then you're sure to find plenty to like in FreezeME. If that's not your style then I'm not sure I can recommend it for you in particular.
With all this said, I can safely say that I am looking forward to FreezeME 2, presuming it is better than the first.

Great concept. Played enough to see 3 full levels and 4 single-action levels. Great level design, it could be a really fun game. Unfortunately, that "COULD" is based on two very simple things that have gone wrong.
1. Controls, particularly with a gamepad: The keyboard mappings are fine and make plenty of sense; however: any wall-interaction movement is appaling. Try to walk near a wall and you'll end up grabbing it for no reason, and when you want to grab it you'll keep running past the wall. Getting a wall-jump to register correctly is a test in patience (provided there's a floor for you to start again) and many platform jumps which look like a sure-footed landing may turn into a ledge-grab, or you just may fall off and have to backtrack a significant amount. Small movements to rotate in place to set up for a series of jumps don't seem to exist. In 2D sections (particularly single-action levels) 3D controls still rule; you can miss a wall jump very easily because the game things you're slightly moving in/out of the plane of movement. Which for purposes of a 2D level is impossible. I could go on
2. Camera. Requires a lot of manual moving as you play. Navigating small spaces, and the camera doesn't show you any hazards, falls, or anything around you; just a lot of environment that obstructs you.
Gosh. It could be a lot of fun. I really want it to be. But until the controls get cleaned up, the game feels like more of a chore.

Call of Duty is an interesting subject to discuss. The longevity and multiple entries into the series are a continual cause of debate, argument and even insult. And it all started here in 2003 with the very first entry.
I'll keep it relatively brief here since I go into a lot more detail in my episode on Call of Duty for my web series Knee-Deep in the Dead (found
).
CoD sets you up in three different campaigns, American, Russian and British and was one of the first FPSes to really work towards a larger, battlefield experience. Two levels that showcase this goal the best are the invasion and defense of Sainte-Mère-Église in the American Campaign, and the Battle of Stalingrad in the Russian campaign.
The sound design and environments are one of the best stand outs of Call of Duty. The guns are all loud and reflect their real-world counterparts. Some negatives would largely be the very baseline AI, lack of enemy variety and the fact that, even when you have allies around you, enemies more often than not target you.
Call of Duty is a fascinating object of study when it comes to evaluation of the evolution of a game series. In playing the first entry, you can see all of the budding elements that would eventually become core "staples" of the campaign: scripting, having to wait for sergeant to boot down the door, press "F" to do thing, simple AI and stories seemingly assembled solely for the set pieces. Also, a side note is that it seems a /bit/ overpriced on Steam...$20 for a 12-year old game is kind of silly. You'd likely be better off getting the War chest, since it has the expansion pack to CoD and Call of Duty 2. Which has one of my favorite CoD levels ever, the Battle of Pointe du Hoc.
Nevertheless, the first Call of Duty is an important entry in the series to play, though it's much easier without nostaliga goggles and truly seeing it for what it was: an immersive, action shooter that helped ensure the FPS genre kept fighting WWII for 6-7 years afterwards.

Here's my review after over 140 hours of play.
First I need to qualify myself, as this is my first review. I'm a sim gamer, pure and simple. My most played games are Arma3 (1000+ hrs), Cliffs of Dover (500+ hrs) and DCS (600+ hrs).
A (fair) bit further down the list are Train sims (TS2017), ETS2, and motor racing titles.
Let me address the biggest gripe of CSX Heavy Haul. Frame rates.
It's a fact of life. Cliffs Of Dover is an old game (2011), but get on a server and an AI spawn in will kill the frame rates for a second or two. So will Arma3, so will DCS. Hell, I even get it in TS2017 on my aging PC.
It can be annoying, but it doesn't promp me to demand my money back or stop playing the game. I guess I'm easily satisfied.
Next, I don't drive the trains simulated in the game for a living. I don't know (or really care - to a certain extent) how accurate they are.
So, I've stopped playing TS 2017 as the graphics in CSX are far, far better. I like the idea of being able to get in and out of trains, operate turntables and re-fueling. I approach the services menu much as I would do a delivery in European Truck Simulater 2. It simulates what I imagine an engineers job driving on the Sand Patch Route would entail.
Now to the content. They're are 46 scenarios (service + object based). There is a limited sand-box mode. It is possible to create your own scenarios (I have two currently listed in the Guides section) and a list of achievements to attempt.
All in all, I compare this favourably with ETS2 where I'm looking for a relaxed session of gaming and won't get a scenario closed out early because I failed the mission parrameters. Sure, it has inperfections, but I rate it the best Train Sim currently available. Hopefully the future will improve this title.
Do I recommend this game? Hard to say.
I'd recommend this game to simulator enthusiats who are slighly boring, ex-train spotting, over middle-aged and have plenty of time on their hands while waiting for the next instalment of Star Citizen.
And we all know how much we've spent on that incomplete game, don't we?

all in all i can say i don't like it at all. but if you are new to the genre then i would say go for it, a card game like that no matter how lacking is still better than most anything else. and you can use it as a stepping stone to something better. and frankly when i say something better there are not many products online that are better than this unless you want to go the underground route with things like lackey and octgn.

When initially launched, I thought this might finally be 'the' ultimate train simulator. Unfortunately, DTG managed to botch their opportunity with the release of Train Sim World. I'm not even going to mention the FPS problems because they have already been hammered to death and there are many other problems detrimental to the game overall.
Firstly, the physics frankly suck. The brake system is beyond wonky and the throttle system in the game is puzzling at best. As it stands, each notch only generates amps up until a certain speed. For example, if you put a locomotive in notch one, your amps would drop to 0 once you reached 10 mph. This is not how it works at all in real life and is a huge fail on DTG's part. The couplers, air brake and MU connections are also very dumbed down. MU connections hook up automatically along with air hoses, and angle♥♥♥♥♥ are not simulated on the rolling stock.
Secondly, the sounds are atrocious. The GP38-2's 16-645E recording is probably the best of the three locomotives but they are still weak and the recording is poor overall. The SD40-2 sounds are a bit bizarre. They sound more like a rendition of a 710 prime mover rather than the 16-645E3 it should have. To top it all off, the AC4400CW sounds are the worst representation of any locomotive prime mover in the history of train simulators. Do you think the Kuju GEVO sounds from Railworks are bad? Well wait until you listen to TSW's AC4400CW. My vacuum cleaner sounds more accurate.
Finally, the overall game play is just lacking. In all honesty, this game (I can't call it a simulator) is very incomplete. There is no editor, so you can't create scenarios or set up custom consists. This restricts you to the handful of scenarios included with the game. The scenarios are very poorly put together and do not really represent real world operations. Apparently you can receive track warrants in CTC territory now? Just goes to show that DTG still has no clue when it comes to U.S railroading operations. The service mode is kind of neat but also has its flaws. The trains are all restricted to their 'timetable' which really limits any sort of freedom in this mode. The walking, while kind of fun, gets old after a while and becomes annoying.
In conclusion, this is just another big disappointment from DTG. In its current state, it is merely a rushed beta being offered for $40. If DTG actually improves this disaster in the future, then I would be happy to write a new review. However, I doubt they will and I do not recommend Train Sim World in its current state.

Let's start with the
~_~
-> heavy reading - if you want to learn about the game world and lore you will need to read a lot

^_^

Dovetail has been a big stinker in the simulator world for the past few years. FSX: SE was a flop (IMHO) and their own "Train Simulator" series were renowned for their expensive DLC. But this is a new engine, and as a big flight sim guy, I believe the name-sake to this "Flight Sim World" will probably utilize the same engine. Graphics are tremendous. Pure 64-bit processes, and the level to detail is great. Almost ALL the switched, circuit breakers, fuses, A/C controls, all work. What's great is you can actuall move around the train as a person, get out, switch tracks, get back in, etc. I was pleasantly surprised at how much there is to do, and you do stay busy. Its a real learning environment where you WILL need to read the manual on how to pressurize the brake system after an emergency engagement, etc, etc.
As for the bad: The current graphics engine needs MAJOR improvement. I've got a 8GB 1070 and i7 processor, and while I get 60FPS easy when standing still, as soon as you move the mouse, you get major stutters. The saving grace for me was the fact I know Dovetail has recently been working overtime, and their almost-daily release notes gives me hope this is a short-term bug.
Also a minor inconvienience, I have 3x 27" monitors set up to 5760x1080, which works amazing for Flight Sim, BF1, etc etc. But in this, when I set the resolution, is zooms in so its unplayable. I have to reset my res to 1920x1080 and play off a single, center monitor until they can get their aspect ratios down.
I do hope they plan to implement mulitplayer, more locomotives, and more routes shortly. As it stands, you get 3 locos, and one "map". But there is plenty to see and do. I give this game a moderately high replay value (if you are into trains and simlator software).
Overall, this is a fun game (I put 6 hours into it on its first sitting), and I think future development is only going to get better. I highly recommend this.
