In a nutshell, this game combines the best features of other sims and puts them together in one fantastic package.  I'd like my review to start on 1 aspect that has taken a lot of criticism, and that is price.
Here is my experience:
I bought £25 worth of vRP's (the ingame currency) and with it purchased the following:
90% of the tracks, DTM '13 pack, and a car from most of the other classes.
I have yet to see a multiplayer game i can't join with the content I own and I have countless hours of entertainment ahead of me with the custom championships I can make with all the different classes.
All of this with £25 which compares very favourably with other sims out there.  So I absolutely disagree with criticism that it is too expensive, you just need to be smart with how you buy.  (A quick note with how to get discounts, is you must always buy 1 pack at a time, to see the discount for duplicate content reflected in the next pack you buy).
On the subject of gameplay, as i say it's amazing, the FFB is powerful and very informative, at the same level (or better) than RF2's FFB which is regarded as the holy grail of FFB).  Physics feel very realistic the cars feel controllable, you don't feel like you're gonna die on every corner which some sims do.  The tires have a grippiness that is lacking in other sims and when you push them over the limit, you can feel (and hear) them fighting for grip whilst still being controllable in a drift.  Drifting the 4wd cars is an absolute blast!  The sounds are absolutely industry leading and the sense of immersion is just incredible.  Put it this way, once you play RRE, you realise there is more to sim racing audio than just engine noise and tire squeal. (and some don't even do those very well)
Multiplayer is a big positive too, you can always find a game running and i really like how it is implemented. Players may only join in practise and quali sessions which means you don't have randoms coming in the middle of a race and wrecking you intentionally or not because they don't really care about the current session.  Anyone in a  race has skin in the game and I've yet to see anyone driving in a careless or trolling manner.  Another great thing is the netcode is really good as well as the fact that contacts are handled well. In Assetto corsa for example, if you scrape some paint off someones car, the car will behave like it's been blown up by hand grenade!  Not here, contacts are handled in a  realistic and believable manner and makes close racing much more enjoyable and competitive.
So go ahead and try the free content, I have no doubt once you do, you will be heading straight to the store page for your first pack!

As someone who has missed the bygone era of 3D platformers, I decided to give FreezeME a whirl and fortunately, I wasn't disappointed.
FreezeME pays homage to Rare's classic platformer Banjo Kazooie and Nintendo's Super Mario 64 and Super Mario Galaxy so people familiar with those series will feel at home with FreezeME. The worlds are big, bright and colorful with puzzles/tasks spread across each of them. People who have played Super Mario 64 will be familiar with completing individual tasks and being rewarded with a star for their troubles; it's the same premise with FreezeME but instead of stars, you're rewarded with golden cubes. The scope of the worlds is impressive with individual planets (al a Super Mario Galaxy style) reached by launching R from a cannon.
I was at first hesitant to make my purchase after reading other reviews and thoughts about the control system and mechanics. Controlling R certainly feels "heavy" and not as fluid as controlling Mario in Super Mario 64. Jumping and landing can be sporadic in places but controls, at least in my case, have began to grow on me and fortunately, it hasn't deterred my enjoyment from the game. The camera work is also not as refined though still adaptable with free reign to adjust camera options and predictability in the settings. I personally use an Xbox 360 controller's right stick to control the camera and hitting the "Y" button to center the camera behind R when needed.
The soundtrack is very bright and colorful; I'm fondly reminded of Grant Kirkhope's Banjo Kazooie effort and Koji Kondo's Super Mario 64 score. In no way does it grate on you and it's pleasant to listen to.
To conclude, FreezeMe is a good effort from an indie developer and while it certainly lacks the polish and fluid controls I had come to expect from Nintendo and Rareware platformers, you can't go far wrong with FreezeME for its price-point.

Back in the good, old days, we had classic after classc like Super Mario 64, Banjo Kazooie, Crash Bandicoot and Beyond Good & Evil. Then... nothing. Super Mario Galaxy was great, but it was also the last, awesome 3D platformer. We could debate whether SMG2 was better, but personally, I felt it was more a SMG 1.5, or expansion to Galaxy 1. It wasn't exactly as new and refreshing as SM64, SM Sunshine and SM Galaxy were. But nevermind that. Way off topic, sorry.
Ever since Super Mario Galaxy, I've wanted a new 3D Platformer, but no one has delivered. Mario was scrapped, returning to his 2D roots and the semi-2D Super Mario 3D World. Banjo was abandoned. Crash, uh, crashed. But just when all hope seemed lost, we got a game called FreezeME. True, the title is a bit generic and off-putting, and yes, it's an indie game from people you have probably never heard of. The main character doesn't even have a name, and the story is something generic like a dog being kidnapped. Something tells me it might be in another castle... hehehe.
But get past all that and take the game for what it really is, and you'll be well rewarded. We're talking a 3D platformer in the style of Super Mario and all those, and it's pretty darn good. It might no be the *best* game out there, and it's not the longest game out there. But what it is, is a very old-school, excellent 3d platformer with a whole lot of style, and, even more important, a whole lot of love put into it. This isn't a quick cash grab from greedy publishers who don't know what makes these games popular. This is a game by gamers, for gamers. A game that really shines with love. These guys aren't just games like you and me. These guys really love their games, and most of the time, it feels like this is a game by them, for themselves. A love letter to themselves, in a way. We are just fortunate enough to get to take part in this and enjoy the game for ourselves.

There are things to enjoy in The Bridge.  The art style, particularly in the animations and how they are drawn, are wonderful.  The music isn't intrusive.  Good things.  It's once we move past that things get less pleasant.
Lets be up front: The Bridge is a physics-based puzzle game.  You can infer this between some of the store quote and the theme of the game, but nowhere on the face does it say this, and I really wish it did.  If you enjoy physics-based puzzle games, there's likely something to latch onto here.  If you do not, which means you are rather like me, then this game is just ... rough.  Seeing a solution and having to battle the execution is the worst kind of feeling when you're problem solving.  Add on top of this the controls are rather sluggish (Not unresponsive, but it simply takes a while to do anything, and if you have to undo a large portion of movement it just too long) and it really is off-putting.
Compounding the rather bitter feelings I was left with are the Developer's absurdly intrusive push to sell you on their new game Tumblestone.  It's just that extra bit of unpleasantness that really makes the whole thing sour.  Literally the first time I boot up your game and I'm asked to check out your other one before I've seen a title screen.  Then when I've finished, decidedly haven't enjoyed myself and wish to move on, there is ltierally a Steam install window for Tumblestone.  Truly a wonderful way to ensure I won't be looking at any of your work in the near future.
I haven't - and won't - finish this game, so I can't comment on the length, but the price is really a matter of how much you enjoy the genre.  If you like this kind of thing, developers need support.  As you might expect from the above, they won't be getting mine, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't get yours.

It’s impossible to say what makes some games so bad they’re good, but I believe being earnest is a large part of it. A game that doesn’t have the best writing or systems can still get by on leaning into what it does have as hard as it can, without a hint of shame at its shortcomings. I think that’s why I ended up liking Chronicles of cyberpunk as much as I did, despite some very strong early misgivings. I’m not going to sit here and tell you it’s something amazing, but it’s certainly worth your time if you want something rough and weird and different.
You are a citizen of a dystopian cyberpunk hellhole, an almost alien city that feels like a cross between Transmetropolitan and early 90s CGI. The angular mannequin people here are a mix of humans and cyborgs, living in strained harmony under the watchful eye of Big Brother. Yes, he’s literally called Big Brother in the game world and you are one of his top agents, charged with undertaking different tasks for him every day. However, on this one particular day you receive a letter that sets you on a very different path, one that promises to reveal the darkest secrets of this bizarre world.
This is primarily an adventure game, told in first-person as you scoot around the city and talk to people. You won’t have any inventory to worry about and only a handful of action sequences where you need to run from something or shoot something. That places it more on the walking sim side of the genre, and indeed you’ll spend most of the game running from place to place, automatically completing tasks for folks by your very presence. While you’re out and about you’re free to explore and see what the citizenry has to say for itself, as well as marvel at the absolutely insane architecture adorning the district.
Don’t get too excited about all of this, because the core gameplay elements are only passable at best. For starters the story is bad, and is told in one of the worst ways possible. It’s a complex plot with plenty of twists and turns through the tropes of cyberpunk but you get everything fed to you through dialog boxes, including dramatic reveals and startling deaths. The world has the static feel of something like old Morrowind, where you have a fully realized and populated world of people who do absolutely nothing except when you’re not looking and then tell you about it later. There’s also no advantage to exploring aside from turning up additional weirdness because there are no branches to the plot.
Beyond the story, Chronicles of cyberpunk is a chore to play. Your objective is always posted in the top-right and features such scintillating tasks as “Get food in DINER” and “Say hi to drone”. It’s the lowest-effort way to keep the player on track and is a noticeable drag on the fun. Despite the simple polygonal graphics it runs really choppy, with constant animation hiccups. Before you start the game, the full range of Unity engine settings from Fastest to Fantastic is available to you and none of them change a thing. There also aren’t any in-game options for basic elements like controls or volume, leaving you stuck with default keys and other important settings.
I was tempted to punch out of this one based on the technical limitations alone, but I stuck around to have breakfast with my giant monitor-brick drone roommate and collect my mail from the flying postman outside my window. On the way to DINER I stopped to watch the flying cyborg cats drift by and speak to a head in a jar. I became engrossed in the world and its profound weirdness just to see what else was hiding around the next corner. The maps tend towards flat, empty stretches to hike across but they’re filled with nonsensical architecture, pulsating devices, and hilarious citizens who sound like they’re debating metaphysics in Google Translated tweets. It’s shoddy in places and well-constructed in others, a mad crush of design that builds with the story enough to get me invested in the plot by the end despite how badly it’s paced and expressed.
Chronicles of cyberpunk isn’t a good game. There are too many problems with the narrative, the quests, the translations, and even the game engine itself. But I enjoyed the 80 minutes it took to finish and I’m glad I did it, not because it was good but because it was so very, very different. A lot of games try to capture that untouchable magic of the strange and this is one of the rare ones that does it, just in a rickety, confusing package. It plays like Jazzpunk with E.Y.E. Divine Cybermancy’s text, two inscrutable games on their own that this crossing tops in how unapproachable it is. But approach it you should, even for a moment, to glimpse the mad and broken wonders within.

Being a long time Stronghold Crusader player, I had the expectation for this game to deliver the original Crusader experience, and I must say, Stronghold Crusader 2 doesn't fail in it.
- The gameplay and the units are still the same: build your castle, your army and defeat the enemy lords with your superior economy and military. It really feels good to command endless units in desert warfare, while fighting with the constant need for gold, popularity and supplies. SHC2 gameplay is a bit more stale in the economic side, but more mobile in the military side and the new units+buildings fit very much into it.
- The Skirmish mode is what carries the game on its back: largely customizable games against and with the AI and human players provide virtually endless possibilities. You can even work on the same castle with your friend, and the AI can be quite challenging even for veteran players with its offensive attitude. Creating and shaping castles on your own style is the true beauty of this game and succeeding in defending it gives a rare feeling of accomplishment, even from game to game.
- Player customization feels alright. You can choose your own crest, your own name and building style, and there is no more need for some casual play. However, there is no option to differentiate yourself more with i.e. some lifetime stats or ranks. There are achievements, sure, but they don't feel as much yours as some custom accomplishments, as everyone can earn them.
- In story and character detail, Crusader 2 is sort of a setback compared to Stronghold or Stronghold Crusader's skirmish trails. There is virtually no story in any point of the game, and AI characters have descriptions no longer than a few lines. While the game partially succeeds in hiding the importance of a story for playing skirmishes all the time, the skirmish trails still feel bland for not having at least an average storyline.
All in all, while Stronghold Crusader 2 may not appear strong story-wise, it delivers excellent gameplay and a great feeling for it. 8/10

This is the most realistic railroad equipment simulation to date, (especially more so after the update(s)).
TSW is a winner in 3 main "Fidelity Experience" categories:
1.Graphics (visual)
2.Aural experience (audio or sound)
3.Physics (feel or perception)
Based on personal experience with Train Sim World (TSW), I will review each of these categories below:
Graphics are Impeccable in this (I run on Ultra settings)! It breaks all the barriers in any simulation game in this department! I have not experienced anything as photorealistic as TSW in a simulation game. (not touching AAA games)
Aural experience is much better after the recent Test Beta 3.5, and so far and overall yields some of the best and authentically correct audio experiece ever. The main advancement I believe is the fact that now the sound samples are very high quality too (both in size, length and fidelity), not restricted in audio quality like in all other railroad simulators (TSxxxx, Run8, Trainzxxxx)  Although, there is room for updates in this area, particularly and primarily the diesel locomotive engine sounds are still not perfected (albeit still being higher quality recordings), leaves room for more to be desired, but still being so far ahead of any other title.
Physics - (I have NOT tried the initial Beta in Dec.2016) - with all the updates rolling out, TSW just promises to be better than anything in my experience with any (rail) simulator. I strongly say I am definitely more satisfied with the perception of physics in TSW than anything I've spent time with in the past.
However, there are complaints from users, but how credible and what nature is their complaints leaves only to wonder...However, I have made some substantial investments to my comp "machine", and cannot say enough for people to do same: Get some decent hardware tech on your rig first!
Verdict: I STRONGLY recommend Train Sim World (TSW) to anyone who loves railroading, because TSW can be enjoyed as not only a train engineer, but also from a railfanning perspective aka trainspotting. You can physically climb out of the locomotive and walk the land, check your consist in First Person View and even more locomotive operation related jobs/tasks/chores.... I simply love it!

The game is a parody of older RPG's, but it's not particularly clever or funny about it aside from a few one-liners.  It mostly just uses that label as an excuse to put little effort into the plot, which is a real disappointment given how many RPG parodies manage to actually be entertaining while mocking the genre's cliches.
The game's real strong suits are its combat and levelling system.  On each level up, you either pick between two or four stats to increase or two versions of an ability, allowing you to specialize each character.  The combat is suitably tactical on hard, though the random encounters will become incredibly grating and tedious and you'll rarely reach the encounter cap.  Whether you win or lose has more to do with whether enemies manage to hit the same character or use hit-all attacks than your own foresight.
If the selling points appeal to you, then go play any of the countless games made in RPG Maker that do them better for free.

Since I have spend over 30 hours on this game, I decided to give a little review:
Hollow Knight is a 2D metroidvania action adventure in which you delve into the depths of Hallownest. The art style is great: every npc, enemy and you yourself are bugs and the handdrawn graphics add to that. Each region has a distinctive setting and enemy types creating obstacles in your way. The game itself is challenging in its paltforming, but tends to focus more on exploration and combat. If you like games that do not take you by your hand and explain everything, but give you the freedom to explore the world and learn its secrets in your own pace, mixed with a beautiful artstyle and great soundtrack, then this is just the game for you.
And 15$ is more than justified for "Hollow Knight"; the devs keep improving the game and add FREE DLC!
So if you are thinking about getting this game, then just do it; you most likely won't regret it.

A nice lampoon of Breath of Fire and Final Fantasy. This is basically Breath of Fire that makes fun of the genre. If you don't know what that means, read on.
This is a classic "RPG," a la Final Fantasy. You run around on a big map to get places, then you run around on a smaller map once you get there. All the while, you get in random battles and gain experience (and of course loot) to level up.
From what I can tell so far, the story basically drives you to never need to visit the same town (or really any location) twice, which is a nice change from other games in this genre, which tend to have you based in one location for a while, completing quests nearby, then moving on to the next "base."
While this game may be meant as a joke, it's actually fun to play. If you ever loved Dragon Warrior, Ultima, Final Fantasy, Breath of Fire or Fire Emblem (or even Rogue, for that matter), check out Breath of Death VII.

This game has come leaps and bounds beyond where it used to be. As it stands now, RaceRoom Racing Experience (R3E) is a fantastic sim that is easy to get into and fun while still being realistic and tricky.
The biggest thing you'll notice immediately compared to other racing titles is the sound. Oh lawdy the sound. No game comes even close to the quality of R3E sounds in every area and best of all they are still regularly updated and improved!
Physics in R3E is where a lot of the 'purists' will decry it for not being harsh enough, not being mean enough, not punishing you hard enough for mistakes, but I find all of that as a positive not a negative. The physics feel just as tight and clean as the other major racing sim titles without being as punishing as some of the more 'popular' options.
Force Feedback (FFB) has always felt decent in R3E but used to be more of a mixed back for many wheel users. The most recent update addressed this by adjusting the defaults for many common wheels (I use a G27 and it now feels great right away) based on feedback from the community. The results are great and the FFB now needs much less fiddling for the finicky users and feels better than ever on default settings.
Content pricing is usually a big issue for most people, but considering the high quality of the cars and tracks the price they ask is very reasonable. Not to mention the price is lower than some other games with similar pricing models.
All in all there's no real downside to at least downloading it and trying it as there are free tracks and free cars avaialble for anyone to use along with time trial competitions that run for 1-2 months at a time. You just have to try it! =D

R3E is really a terrific racing sim! It was perhaps launched too early with many features lacking or functioning badly, but recently, though still in beta, it has really delivered in my opinion.
I also have the "other two" contemporary racing games, AC and pC and I must say that I find R3E most fun of these three. For example, I think BMW M1 Procar is even more fun to drive in R3E than it is in pC which I find a blast in pC also. R3E is not perfect, at least yet, but it surely has its strengths. Sounds are just awesome and with the recent 9GB "patch" they got even better. FFB is also best of the three games and it deliveres the road feel really well and doesn't even require hours of tinkering with settings to get it right. AI is also the most competent of the three by a big margin, so R3E is perhaps the best choice for the single players at least until AC and pC improve their AI algorithms. Graphics are also quite good, although not on par with pCars, but on the other hand, R3E runs also very well on my three monitor setup.
But hey, physics are the most important thing, no? Here R3E fares also well. Physics aren't perhaps the most accurate on the planet, but still very believable and with awesome FFB I like the driving feel a lot. I say it again, I think R3E delivers the most fun experience of the three. Still, R3E is by no means arcade racer and leans heavily towards simming side of the genre.
As said and at the time of writing, R3E is still in beta and a work in progress. It is still quite polished and offers pretty much full experience already. It has no weather or full night, but it is otherwise pretty much a full deal IMO. Things I dislike the most are annoying load times, which surely improved with the latest patch, but are still on the annoying side especially on the menus. Micropayment system is completely a matter of opionion and it really doesn't bother me. You can have just one experience set and that gives you several tracks and a class of cars and that's basically all you need. If you wan't more, different packs give good value for money and you get discounts for the packs of the items you already may own.
If you like sim-like racing games don't hesitate to try the R3E.  You can do it for free, but of course with very limited options for driving.

Eets Munchies is a fun puzzle game i've gotten to try during the free weekend. It reminds me of the many types of puzzle games you find on mobile devises where you have to lead something to its objective with items placed in the world. in this case that you'd be the creature Eets to the cake in each level. There are a handful of placeable items I have seen so far, some that change the state of the world like bombs, some that change the state of Eets like buffs to jumping or removing the ability to jump entirely.  There are also items that you interact with in real time like cannons or whales that act as jump pads.
Eets Munchies comes with a puzzle maker and has Steam workshop support so you can make puzzles to share with friends and strangers alike. Overall i've got to say that Eets is a stand up puzzle game, it may be small but I have not seen any negative quality's so far, its got neat art and a decent soundtrack that fits the style. I would recommend Eets munchies to fans of small puzzle games or mobile games. Eets is not that hard either, so it really could be fun for the family.

Shadowgrounds Survivor (SS) is an above-view shooter which sees an array of characters stranded at various points upon the surface of the moon Ganymede. The not-so-original plot of mass alien invasion is at the core of the game and in turn, provides whichever character you currently control - plenty of enemies to shoot and kill.
Along the way, you control the typical grunt, armed with a pistol, pulse rifle and rocket launcher. There's also the female sniper who also has a pistol, railgun and plasma rifle. The last of the controllable characters has a flamethrower, shotgun and minigun at his disposal. None of the stages are particularly hard on standard difficulty and SS itself is not a particularly long game either. I completed it in under 4 hours, with the final 'stage' of the game actually being easier than earlier parts of the game.
However, you can play the game in co-op and this makes it much more enjoyable as a result. A worthy purchase, I'd give it 7.5

This game wants to be a spiritual successor of the classic Settler-series, but the old games offer more control for many different things. During my playtime I often experienced design decisions that the ~15 year old games solved way better.
Here are some examples:
- No possibility to prioritze the building order (e.g. Bakery finished before the Mill)
- No option to restrict certain goods from being stored at the warehouse (e.g. The Toolworker has his own storage space, yet his produced tools get stored in the warehouse)
- Said Toolworker keeps on piling up ressources in his storage, although he has no order to forge tools. Those ressources are leeched from other buildings.
- Storing food in a normal warehouse, while a food storage with more than enough space is nearby
- When vikings (with a profession) are tired, they sleep in a nearby house. If no home is available, they sleep under a tree. The assigned carriers who assist the production however have to always sleep by the trees, even though there is enough space in the dwellings. I assume that this is because being a carrier is not a real profession.
Overall, this is not a bad game. But all those little things add up to making Valhalla Hills being inferior to the old Settler-games.

FreezeME is a fun 3D platformer with a charming world.
If you've played many games of the same genre, you'll most likely enjoy this game.
You've got the basic and easy to understand double jump, wall jump, wall shimmy, slide and more abilities that have popped up in tons of other platformer games. However, the game has a cool little feature that allows you to take a photo of moving objects using your camera, which will freeze them on the spot. Gravity doesn't affect them, and you can use them as platforms. It's interesting, and doesn't feel like a cheap gimmick.
You can access multiple different worlds through the hub world. As you progress by grabbing collectibles, you get access to new areas. Worlds are quite large, and allow you the freedom of choosing where you want to go, and what collectible you want to try get. The entire thing really reminded me of Super Mario 64. There's a good variety when it comes to getting collectibles. There are different types of things to collect, as well as multiple ways of actually getting said collectibles. You might be required to kill a boss, complete a platforming challenge or race someone.
The graphics and worlds look vibrant and cute. At times I felt like maybe some of the objects placed were a bit too random, but most of the times it wasn't a problem. The music feels very authentic, and does a very good job at sounding like the soundtracks of games you played in the good ol' days.
Overall, it's a real joy to play. I never really encountered anything that was really problematic, and the dev seems to be constantly improving the game, which is good. Solid gameplay, colourful worlds, and awesome soundtrack that do a great job at capturing the atmosphere the game was looking to replicate. Check it out!

Interesting puzzle game that revolves around MC Escher concepts and artwork.

The difficulty seemed to ramp up dramatically towards the end of the main storyline, and it was a bit of a chore to try to complete that. The first mirror level looks to be about the same, so I ran out of motivation to continue. The mirror levels look to be the same as the first 24, only with different twists on each, so they seem a bit repetitive.
That aside, very clever and unique. It's probably best if not played in one sitting so as to give your brain a break.
One thing that is slightly frustrating is that the puzzles require both an element of discovery and have a reliance on physics, so even if you know instinctively what you need to do, you may be futzing around a bit trying to get the timing right. That was my least favorite aspect, for sure.
I'd give this a solid 3.5 out of 5. Clever, if somewhat frustrating and repetitive.

I wish there were more of these games on Steam.  FreezeME is a full Super Mario fix and plays well on the Steam Controller.  Would I say it's perfect?  No, but there's a lot it does right:
Pros:
-Surprising amount of professional polish to: area designs, menus, animations, etc.
-Great game layout as far as traditional Super Mario like game goals go.  With bonus/challenge areas, revisiting same locations to get more challenging gold cubes, etc.
-Captures that Super Mario platformer "themepark" feel pretty much spot on.  Where you can see all the challenges around you that makes you want to keep exploring more.
-Lastly, GREAT VIEW CAMERA.  It doesn't try and get too smart and most importantly, it lets you flip the axis to what you like.
Cons:
-Freeze Camera aiming is a little weird/takes some getting used to.  A more intuitive control scheme where the view stays in 3rd person, but auto locks onto the freeze camera target and back again might work better.  Or t least make it a check box, so you can have either/or, depending on what works for the player.  To me, it's weird moving a little tracer line around from whatever side angle your view happens to be at when you bring the camera out.  Also, the aiming is a little dicey, it needs an acceleration curve or some kind of smoothing.
-Wish there was a sprint feature where you would start to run a little faster outside, like the LEGO games do in open world exploration areas.
-I wish the main character had a little more personality, the black haired glasses thing is fine, just a little too "Plain Jane" to stick in your mind and remember.
Overall though, I'm very happy with this game as a pretty good Super Mario fix, of which there are not many this true to form on Steam.  I paid full asking price and would do it again.

Pros

-Really short (but worth it).
This short little game is impressive and I feel like it did everything right. I'm more of ahardcore gamer myself, I love things like Dwarf Fortress, FTL, or anything that'll give me a bit of a challenge. I'm also a sucker for a good story though, and I like anything that'll make me start wrapping my brain around it. This game is heavily story driven with a mixture of clue and RPGness. And everything works together towards the goal of not only telling the story, but creating a believable setting.
While others have stated that the game doesn't properly explain the 'Whys' of the setting (why getting the last word has power in this world), the game does take the time to nod at this and pretty much say that the residents of this world don't know, and in turn, we the audience won't know (though maybe it is discoverable in an alternate ending)? Whatever the case may be the developers are excellent writers. We have a variety of characters, some are complicated and will be developed over the course of the game (IE, the servant and Seymore) while others are simple and 'translucent.' What you see is what you get, but they also have their own sort of depth (their dreams, their hopes, etc). Even the most unlikable characters will have redeemable qualities and will make some common cause with the protagonist. In the end, not all characters need to be deep complicated messes, and not all mysteries will necessarily be 'solved.'
And the combat mechanics plus unlockable abilities meant that as soon as you started to get into the swing of things you would start delving deeper into this elegantly simple but complicated system. The AI has trouble properly exploiting this, but it 'knows' enough to provide a challenge over the course of the game. By the end I was consistently winning and I would have been bored if it dragged on much longer. As it is, just enough challenge was coded in to last me until I reached the first ending.
Which was fine because in a way this is a game about discovery and exploration, most of which is buried in dialogue. If you do get this game I recommend you save between chapters (right before the next chapter) in different slots. This way you can return to an old chapter to review certain conversations, which might advance some story elements towards the end of the game.
Again, if you like to read AND play video games, this game is likely for you. Hopefully you'll enjoy it as much as I did.

Before I begin: I'm not talking about plot at all as it's a quirky, weird experience with a pretty interesting story.
The easiest way I can describe this game is 'Clue meets Professor Layton'. Everything about this title is charming - the dialogue is humorous and moves the storylines along, the puzzles require a bit of dumb luck but once you dig through the game and find them all the setting feels pretty robust.
The gameplay is split into two components: 'Investigation' and Conversing. Through investigating the setting and speaking to characters who inhabit the space with you, you gain mastery and experience on a handful of intersecting plotlines. The conversing 'mini-game' is almost like playing three games of Rock-Paper-Scissors at once. Each step you take towards defeating your opponent results in a different 'stat' losing some of it's power. These different tiers are set atop an actual game of R-P-S... so starting out it seems more complicated than it is.
The only negative comment I'd say regarding this fun game is because of how the gameplay is configured there is quite a bit of repetition both in investigating, purchasing items, and winning conversations. This is relatively minor due to the short length of the title (and I was playing to 100%, which I hit around 10 hours).
It's pretty remarkable for how polished this game is in it's current state given the small staff. I hope we see more in this Tale of Last Words!

One of the funniest games I have ever played. It is extremely clever and I don't believe I have seen a game with a battle system/basis this unique. These battles are actually called "Discourse" in the game. See, in this world, people can temporarily command and gain power over others by winning arguments or conversations. It is hilarious to watch it all unfold. You can purchase skills like "firm handshake" and "elegant smirk" which give you bonuses to tact and verbal power. Equipment consists of bow ties, and the more bow ties you have the more skills you can equip. Once you win a discourse you get people to perform actions you need to advance the story, such as giving you the password to a safe or opening a door. Also, by gossiping and/or chattering with other characters you unlock new information about characters, events, and/or objects. Chatter is more for progressing the story and is a bit more character specific. Last thing I will mention on actual gameplay; you can also buy information on topics.  (The exp points you gain from finding information and winning a discourse are dollars which you spend on the afformentioned topics and/or skills). I spent $20 on wine information and was able to spot new items I previously saw as ????. With those items, I unlocked more gossip and chatter with different characters, and thus I was able to advance the plot. This was a relatively short, but memorable game. Along with the wonderful battle structure and skill progressions mentioned above, the game has beautiful water-color like 2D graphics. It reminded me of older titles like Suikoden 2 (with bolder colors) or more recently, LISA. The soundtrack and sound effects in this game also contributed greatly to the unique charm the game has. You could wait for a sale but it is easily worth its normal price of $10.

Nostalgia... Anyone who played Vengence Of The Blood Angels on the Amiga/3D0/Sega Saturn will look at this with a sense of nostalgia, but ultimately thats the whole problem with Space Hulk.

If anything, this is an incredibly faithful conversion of the old board game, of which I am a fan (40k and all its incarnations od spin offs are, in general, brilliant as a social past-time) but it shows not only its age, but the age of the actual board game with the limited rule system and the fact that its just not fair.  The AI is meant to throw everything at you.  No learning where they attack from, no, random encounters, multiple deaths and much swearing will ensue....
You would think someone (Games Workshop?) would come up with rules for development of a bolter that doesnt jam, or at least a method of investing points into keeping your equipment working.  Simple touches like that would expand the playability of this.  as faithful as it is, its showing its age.   A much needed revamp by GW is needed before anyone considers trying to put it on a computer or console.  I love space hulk for its atmosphere, and its nice to see some investment after the horrible THQ situation, but we want multiplayer FPS based missions with the ability to develop a character in the 40K universe, and this is just a nod to nostalgia.

If you liked the old-school RPGs (Mother, Dragon Warrior, early Final Fantasy) as a kid, then this is a no-brainer purchase. It's insanely cheap, and the maker of it obviously has a lot of love for old-school RPG mechanics.
There are some interesting improvements on the old school formuia, too. Random battles are there, but only a limited number in each area. Once you run that number down to 0, no more random battles. You can still select "Fight!" from the menu at any time, though. That not only eliminates the endless random battles old RPGs had, but also allows you to go almost immediately from battle to battle if you're grinding.
I also liked the branching level-up system. You get to decide how you want your characters to specialize. As a hint, ALWAYS pick the +1 attack when it's there!! It literally means +1 attack, not +1 TO attack.
The game is a decent length (I think 10ish hours?), filled with satirical humor, solid gameplay, and a ridiculously cheap price. BUY IT.

First off - the game ran pretty smoothly at the normal settings with my PC setup.  If I turned up the settings on it, the game started getting framey, so it doesn't appear to be very well optimized.  However, the game looked fine on the normal settings and was pretty smooth throughout.
PROs
+ Very fun combat.  It is an action RPG, with some timing involved where you can do large amounts of damage to enemies if hit at the right time.  This system was well implemented and was fun to play.
+ Engaging story.  I liked the storyline in this game.  There were plenty of epic set pieces in the cutscenes and there was weight to what you were doing.
+ Bad-a characters.  All playable characters kick some serious butt and are all fun to play (even the flute had its moments)
+ Music was real good, especially a call back to one particular song :)
CONs
- Mission flow.  Each mission had these period of time in between where you roam around and do stuff, which got pretty annoying when I was just trying to finish the story.
- Too many seemingly unwinnable battles.  Now this could be just me, but there were a lot of battles in this game where it felt like I was getting cheaply killed.  And most of the time, losing this battle had no impact on the mission, as I completed the mission after dieing anyways.  And this happened numerous times... I am not a big fan of the unwinnable fight mechanic.
- The game was basically shoving new game + down my throat the entire time.  All of the trials, and a bunch of the tasks, were all way out of my level range.  So there were a lot of times when I would just skip to the mission day with several days left on the time remaining because I couldn't really do anything more.
Overall this was a fun game to play through, although I don't see myself playing through it a second time even though the game gated like half the content to that.  I would say it is worth the playthrough though.

Hollow Knight is a three-way lovechild between the games Super Metroid, Dark Souls and Rogue Legacy.
From Super Metroid you have the defining characteristics of a Metroidvania: exploration, unlockable movement techniques and power-ups. Hollow Knight has an atmosphere similar to Dark Souls, where both story and lore are revealed through dialogue and exploring your environment. From Rogue Legacy you have the melee combat, with sword slashes in four cardinal directions as well as dashing, knockback and downslash-jumping on enemies.
Hollow Knight excels at what it does, and I recommend it with one caveat:
When comparing the difficulty to Dark Souls, Hollow Knight is quite easy early on in the game. But later on the difficulty ramps up quite a bit, and a few of the boss fights can be compared to Dark Souls at its hardest. If you don't mind a real challenge, then I think you'll appreciate Hollow Knight like I do.

Personally I like what they have done with TSW, and it feels that they are heading in the right direction.
It is indeed a new engine to work with, and for the moment it may require powerful hardware, but think that in 1-2 years, the PC specs will not be the same as they are today. I own an AMD FX8350 processor and GeForce 1070 GTX, but even with the framerate that I have I am satisfied (locked at 30). They really made big improvements since the beta, I used to get only 15-20 FPS, now I'm constanly at 30 and I'm sure that they will keep up the good work with this title.
The graphics in my oppinion are eye-candy, a huge leap from the previous TS games, well done with that, Dovetail. The only issue I found that is that if you enter a tunnel, the cab is still lit as if it's daylight outside. Maybe they'll fix this soon. Otherwise, really detailed locomotives and cars - you'll even see the brakes working.
The audio is good, but still there were better (see Armstrong Powerhouse). I wish there would be more 3D audio support - going around the locomotive and hearing different sounds like the generator or the diesel engine - as right now they're kind of constant in-cab or ouside of the cab. I also wish there were track joint sounds, especially on junctions, right now it  kind of lacks them.
As for the gameplay, I just love the new walkaround mode. Going around the engine, uncoupling and coupling, changing switches, starting the engine as it should be started, these are things that I always wished there were in Train Simulator. I also wish the game had 2-way radio support with dispatcher (sort of like FSX), but maybe i'm just thinking too far ahead.
I like the new mode - services.. I think that even TS20xx should have had that as well.
The lack of a scoring system however like in TS20xx is a bit disappointing, but I'm counting on future updates to solve that.
Overall, the game is packed with detail, and it can be played as simple or complex as you want. There are online manuals  (even an actual CSX operations manual) to help everyone have a deep understanding of rail operations and signalling. There is still room for improvement, but seeing what they've done with this product until now, you have thumbs up from me.

Short list of things that bother me about this release:
1. Crappy graphics: I have games for half the price with much better scenery.  The trees, bushes, buildings, etc all look like 10 year old graphics technology.
2. Horrible frame rate: Seems to be CPU bound.  I have a not-so-hot CPU but a decent graphics card and get 50-60fps in other more graphically appealing games, but rarely get over 20fps in this game.  Did they outsource development to people with no regard or knowledge of optimization?
3. No free roam:  You're limited to scripted content (scnenarios, tutorials, services).
4. Bugs (obvious ones that should have been caught and corrected before release) - a couple of examples: Can't finish some scenarios if you do something out of order of what the scripting is expecting. UI indicates a certain track speed limit ahead, but when you reach the marker, the actual track speed limit does not match.  Distance markers on the HUD seem to be straight line distance rather than track distance.
5. Poor audio.
6. Long loading time (which might be okay if the other problems didn't exist).

This game has its drawbacks, but it is the most rewarding and immersive of all the modern racing titles currently on the market. It has clearly been tainted by early reviewers, because it was launched in such an incomplete state that it´s difficult to comprehend why they did it. As a result of this, combined with a terrible pricing model, the game has received a bad stigma, but one which is entirely undeserved at this point in time.
So, if you have heard bad things about FFB, lack of content, poor framerates or anything else, rest assured that these issues have been fixed, often to the point of excelling in each area. The development team are one of the most forthcoming, open and honest  in the business, admitting mistakes where they have been made and explaining any decisions they make.
But we live in a world where racing sims are on the up. So how does it compare?
Where Project CARS lacks complete series, immersive sounds and consistent AI, Raceroom excels in each of these areas.
Where rFactor2 lacks in updated graphic shaders, performance and complete series, Raceroom is more than adequate in each.
Where Assetto Corsa lacks good enough AI for an offline experience, Raceroom blows all competition out of the water.
In summary, this game has fantastic content (albeit with the modular pricing structure - but see below), competitive AI, great netcode, superb physics and THE MOST AMAZING SOUNDS EVER HEARD IN A RACING SIM.
Don`t buy content on Steam - go to their shop where you can bulk-buy VRP, spend an average game`s value and build your own game to your liking.
